case_summary.text: GST/Cenvat Credit: Where during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax, if appellant engaged in activities of trading and commission agency did not maintain separate accounts regarding taxable and non-taxable services, it would not be entitled to credit of service tax

ST : CENVAT - Trading activity was not an exempt service under rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit rules, 2004 prior to 1-4-2011; therefore, prima facie, there was no requirement to maintain separate accounts or payment under rule 6 on that activity by manufacturing units
Cenvat - Pre-2011 amendment, separate account was not required for trading activity as it wasn’t an exempt service earlier

Cenvat Credit : Credit of commission paid to sub-agents cannot be denied, merely because there was no methodology to determine commission, so long as commission paid is not disputed and details are verifiable from bank certificates.

ST : Assessee not paying Service Tax on trading activity could take credit of tax paid on services vis-a-vis input services only on pro rata basis as per formula stipulated in rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004

Cenvat : Where assessee, a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods, did not maintain separate accounts for commonly used inputs/input services and chose second option available in rule 6(3)(ii) and reversed proportionate credit, merely because assessee failed to intimate department regarding option exercised under rule 6(3)(ii), it could not be said that rule 6(3)(i) would automatically apply to instant case
Benefit of Rule 6DD(k) not available if no amount was debited in P&L a/c reflecting commission payment to agent

INCOME TAX : Benefit of Rule 6DD(k) is not available if assessee claimed to have sold goods with help of commission agent but there was no amount debited in his profit and loss account reflecting commission payment

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a licensed chillies commission agent, acted only as an agent and not as a principal, its turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of its principal, and thus it was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q
Cenvat Credit : An assessee is not entitled to input service credit of services of commission agent; view in assessee's favour taken in CBEC Circular is not binding on Department

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a licensed chillies commission agent, acted only as an agent and not as a principal, his turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of his principals and thus, he was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q

Service Tax : For period prior to introduction of Service Tax Valuation Rules, 2006 with effect from 19-4-2006, in case of a Clearing and Forwarding Agent, only remuneration and commission paid to C&F Agent by principal is chargeable to Service Tax and not expenses reimbursed by service recipient

GST/Service Tax : Where assessee was engaged in procurement of purchase orders for its principal 'R' on commission basis, which included to inform 'R', to dispatch goods to customers, pursuing customers to make payment directly to 'R' and raising debit notes to 'R' for making payment of commission, service provided by assessee not covered under 'clearing and forwarding agent service'

Service Tax : If a receipt is for reimbursing expenditure incurred for purpose of providing services, such 'reimbursement' cannot be regarded as having character of 'remuneration or commission' received by clearing and forwarding agent and, therefore, same is not includible in value in erstwhile Rule 6(8) of Service Tax Rules

Cenvat Credit : 'Customs House Agent Service' and 'Shipping Agents and Container Services' for purposes of export are eligible for input service credit; but, services of overseas commission agent are not so eligible.
Cenvat Credit : Services of commission agents (whether foreign agents or domestic agents) are ineligible for input service credit

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was acting as an agent for a foreign shipping company and it raised invoices on importers/exporters/ freight forwarders certain charges and a part of amount received from importer/exporter/ freight forwarder was retained by assessee and balance part was transferred to account of its principal and concerned importer/exporter/ freight forwarder had deducted tax at source on entire amount of invoice raised by assessee on them, since assessee was unable to divulge to
Commission agent eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q: ITAT
Commission agent eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q: ITAT

Cenvat Credit : Exempted goods have to be excisable goods; hence, imported goods, which are traded, cannot be considered as exempted goods and rule 6 of CENVAT Credit rules, 2004 would not apply thereto

IT : Where assessee could not adduce any evidence that C & F agent deducted tax at source while making payment to carrier so as to prove that amount which was paid by assessee to C & F agent represented reimbursement of freight paid by C & F agent on behalf of assessee to airlines, provisions of section 194C were applicable

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a licensed chillies commission agent, claimed TDS credit of certain amount under section 194Q, since assessee acted only as an agent and not as a principal, thus, its turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of their principals, he was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a licensed chillies commission agent, claimed TDS credit of certain amount under section 194Q, since assessee acted only as an agent and not as a principal, thus, its turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of their principals, he was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q
Cenvat Credit : Service tax paid on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products, is not eligible for input service credit

Service Tax : Where assessee exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it and availed credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, it was not eligible to avail cenvat of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services for trading of imported goods

Cenvat Credit : Credit of service tax paid on GTA Services under reverse charge can be taken based on TR-6 challans even for period prior to 16-6-2005 when reference to said challan was added in rule 9(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules; rule 9 is procedural aspect and cannot be used to deny otherwise eligible credit
Cenvat credit Rule 6 doesn't apply to transactions not amounting to service
Cenvat Credit : Service tax paid on commission in respect of trading goods is not eligible for credit because same is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was carrying on business as a commission agent by selling chillies on behalf of farmers to registered dealers, assessee was to be granted credit of entire amount of TDS deducted on sale of chillies
Commission agent entitled to full TDS credit u/s 194Q even if income doesn’t match sales value on which TDS was deducted
No TDS liability on reimbursement of exp. incurred by C&F agent if separate bill was raised by him

Service Tax : Where service tax demanded under reverse charge on foreign commission agent's services would be available as Cenvat credit to assessee, such demand was revenue neutral and, therefore requirement of pre-deposit was to be dispensed with

IT : Where agent of foreign shipping lines collected amount from customers on behalf of shipping lines, on termination of agency agreement, what was left with assessee after payment to Principals would constitute commission/trading receipts of agent

Cenvat Credit : For period upto 15-6-2005, when rules did not prescribe any document for taking credit of GTA services, TR-6 challan has to be considered as a proper document evidencing payment of tax; hence, credit taken on basis of TR-6 challan was valid.

Cenvat Credit : Commission paid to foreign agents for 'sales promotion' is different from 'selling commission'; sales promotion commission is eligible for input service credit, while 'selling commission' is not so eligible

Service Tax : Where assessee collected amounts from its clients towards various fees paid to DGFT authorities (application fees, licence fees, etc.) on actual basis, then, such collections made in capacity as 'pure agent' were not includible in value as per rule 5(2) of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006

GST : Where applicant entered into agreement with Overseas Commission Agent located outside India to arrange supply of applicant's goods outside India, transaction being out of ambit of import of services applicant is not required to pay GST on reverse charge basis under section 5(3) on commission paid to Overseas Commission Agent
IT/ILT: Where sales and purchase are recorded in books of account on principal to principal basis, then activity could not be held to be activity with commission agent or broker

Service Tax : Where assessee was receiving goods from their principal and also delivering goods so received to serve interest of principal itself, he was acting as 'consignment agent' and commission so received was liable to tax under Clearing and Forwarding Services; not as 'Commission Agent' (Business Auxiliary Services)

Service Tax : Commission paid to foreign based agent for promotion of export of pharmaceutical products cannot be charged to service tax on reverse charge basis prior to introduction of section 66A from 18-4-2006
Reimbursement of exp. to C&F agent won’t invite sec. 194C TDS if claims were made on actual basis
Sec. 194C TDS is required on 'any sum’ paid to C&F agent including reimbursement of expenditure: HC

Excise & Customs : Where, in respect of exempted goods/services, assessee has paid 6% amount under rule 6(3) of CENVAT Credit Rules and recovered same from buyers, since said amounts stand already paid to revenue, same cannot be demanded again under section 11D of Excise Act or section 73A of Finance Act
Cenvat Credit : Where C&F agent services availed fall within definition of input service, credit thereof is available even if value of said services do not form part of value of final product

Cenvat Credit : Rule 3 does not stipulate maintaining separate account as a manufacturer and as a service provider; hence, credit availed as a service provider can be used to pay excise duty payable as manufacturer and vice versa
IT : No TDS liability on reimbursement of exp. incurred by C&F agent if separate bill was raised by him

Cenvat Credit : If an assessee has taken input service credit of common services used for both taxable and non-taxable services, his entire credit cannot be denied; department may only seek compliance with rule 6(3) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004

INCOME TAX : Where assessee paid commission of certain amount, since assessee had submitted tax invoice and TDS certificate as proof of transaction and no objection was raised against same by revenue, and further, payments were made through bank account, impugned addition made on account of said commission paid under section 69C was to be deleted

Cenvat Credit : In case of assessee engaged in manufacture of goods as well as provision of services, Goods Transport Agency's Services received by him under reverse charge are 'output service' for period prior to 19-4-2006 and service tax can be paid thereon utilizing Cenvat Credit

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-company entered into Consigning and Forwarding Agreement with various persons across country for providing last-mile storage/warehousing and dispatching/forwarding services and it deducted tax at source under section 194C at rate of 2 per cent on payment of commission to CFAs, since services provided by CFA were in course of carrying out work as per direction of assessee, TDS was to be deducted under section 194C and not under section 194H

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 16 of the Central Goods And Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit - Period April 2006 to 2008 - Whether it could not be contended that since definition of Rule 2(e) underwent amendment with effect from 1-4-2011, whereby, it was indicated that trading activity would fall in category of services, therefore rule 6(3)(c) could apply to trading activity only after 1.4.2011 - Held, yes - During relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax - Appellant company acted as a commission agent was also engaged in trading activities - Whether since appellant was not paying service tax on trading activity, credit of tax paid on services vis-a-vis input services could only be taken on a pro-rata basis as per formula stipulated in Rule 6(3)(c) - Held, yes - Whether however, since no separate accounts were maintained by appellant with regard to taxable and non-taxable services, apportionment as provided in Rule 6(3)(c) would triggered - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in denying credit of service tax - Held, yes [Para 12][In favour of revenue]GST/Cenvat Credit: Where during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax, if appellant engaged in activities of trading and commission agency did not maintain separate accounts regarding taxable and non-taxable services, it would not be entitled to credit of service tax

FACT: The appellant was engaged in trading activities as well as in commission business. The appellant obtained centralized registration with the service tax department under the category "Business Ancillary Services".

Evidently, the appellant's records were examined by the internal audit party of the department. The audit carried out revealed that the appellant had been claiming credit of service tax on various common input services which were used both for its trading activity and its business of commission agent.

As far as the commission agency business was concerned, service tax was paid by the appellant, while no service tax was paid for trading activity. Thus, the audit party came to the conclusion that excess credit of service tax had been claimed by the assessee.

The stand taken by the appellant was that during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax. It was alleged that due to an incorrect audit objection to the alleged utilization of cenvat credit qua the exempted services, the appellant had paid up the purportedly excess amount, which was, otherwise not payable.

The Adjudicating Authority, however, was not impressed with the stand taken by the appellant and, therefore, proceeded to reject its claim for refund.

The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order passed by Adjudicating Authority.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: Clearly, during the period in issue, i.e., 2006-07 and 2007-08, trading activity, which was one of the businesses, carried out by the appellant was not amenable to service tax. The amendment to rule 2(e), stated that there was no liability to pay service tax of trading activity, during the relevant period. [Para 9]

In this context, it may also be relevant to note, how exempted services was defined in rule 2(e) of the 2004 rules till 31-3-2011 and thereafter.

Both before and after amendment, 'exempted services' meant those taxable services, which were exempt from whole of service tax and, included those services on which service tax was not leviable, under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.2]

Therefore, given the rule position, what would govern the matter would be the determination of the issue as to whether or not, a particular service is amenable to service tax under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.3]

Since, the trading activity was not amenable service tax at the relevant period, surely, the apportionment as provided in rule 6(3)(c) would get triggered. [Para 10.4]

Having regard to the rule position and given the admitted fact that no separate accounts were maintained by the appellant, with regard to the taxable and non-taxable services, clause (c) of sub-rule 3 of rule 6 of 2004 rules would apply. [Para 11]

For the foregoing reasons, there was interference is called for with the order of the Tribunal. Accordingly, the questions of law framed are answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 12]

; therefore, allegation of suppression was invalid.

Revenue argued that activity of trading could be considered as services and since during material time, it was not a taxable service, it should be construed as 'exempted service'. Since assessee has not maintained any separate account in respect of the dutiable/taxable goods/services and exempted goods/services, payment at 10 per cent/ 5 per cent of the value of the exempted services was to be made under rule 6(3). Assessee argued that trading was deemed as exempted service only from 1-4-2011; hence, demand for period prior thereto cannot be made on that count.

HELD: The goods which the assessee had traded are imported goods. As per the definition of exempted goods under rule 2(d) of CCR exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-C.E., dated 1-3-2011 is availed.

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum at the rate of 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. [Para 5.2]

Secondly, as per rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the assessee has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply.

Even assuming but not admitting that the assessee has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, rule 6(3A) which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the assessee has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the assessee has not been disputed by the revenue and the revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the assessee in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the assessee has taken ineligible credit, the question of assessee violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all. [Para 5.3]

If the assessee reversed input service tax credit attributable to trading activities according to standard accounting principles, the same would suffice for satisfying the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6. [Para 5.4]

As regards the wrong availment of credit during the period 2005-08, another show-cause notice has already been issued to the assessee which has been adjudicated and pending before Tribunal. Thus, the department was fully aware of the practices followed by the assessee and has also approved of the same. In view of the above, invocation of the extended period of time to demand service tax is also not sustainable in law. [Para 5.5]

service only from 1-4-2011

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force with effect from 16-08-2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit up to 9-09-2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10-09-2004. [Para 5] Under the Credit Rules, 2002 input service is defined in rule 2(c) as any taxable service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service. Rule 3(1) provided that an output service provider shall be allowed to take credit (service tax credit) of the service tax paid on input service, in the enumerated manner. Sub-clause (a) of this Rule provides that where an input service falls in the same category of taxable service as the output service, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 16-08-2002; sub-clause (b) stipulates that in any other case, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 14-05-2003. Sub rule (2) of Rule 3 provides that for the purpose of these rules, two services shall be deemed to be falling in the same category of taxable service, if the input service or output service fall in the same sub-clause of clause (105) of Section 65 of the Act.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 3 states that where a service provider avails credit on any input service and renders output services which are chargeable to service tax as well as exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be, he shall maintain separate accounts for receipt and consumption of input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of taxable output services and input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be. Sub-rule (5) of rule 3 enacts that where a service provider opts not to maintain separate accounts, as stipulated in sub-rule (4), he shall be allowed to utilize service tax credit for payment of service tax on any output service only to an extent of an amount not exceeding 35 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on such output services. [Para 6]

On a true and fair construction of the relevant provisions of the Credit Rules, 2002, it is apparent that credit could be taken on an input service falling in the same category of taxable service as the output service in respect of which the service tax liability arises and discharged from the available credit. It is axiomatic that trading in goods is neither a taxable service and could not, in the absence of a legislative/statutory fiction provided, capable of being construed as an exempted service. [Para 7]

Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, 2004 sets out the obligations of a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) provides that no cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) enjoins maintenance of separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input or input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service; and the quantity of input spent for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and authorizes taking of cenvat credit only on that quantity of input or input services which are intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing taxable output services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 carves out specified exclusions to the requirements set out in sub-rule (2). Sub-clause (c) of rule 6(3) stipulates that the provider of an output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

If the assessee claims that the amount paid to the C&F agent by the assessee represents reimbursement, the onus is on the assessee to prove that it represents the reimbursement of the claim. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle was cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case was gone. From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l), the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided that it is made taxable. Therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. It may also be said that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air travellers. If in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-travellers. On the other hand, it may be said that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited. The tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the petitioners that because of section 67(k), the nature of the tax itself changes was incorrect. Section 67(k), which provides the ‘measure of the tax’, is not unconnected with the main levy of the tax. The provision of section 67(k ) does not in any manner alter the nature of tax and does not shift it from the service rendered to the customer to the service rendered to the airlines. The contention, therefore, was clearly incorrect on facts.

The further argument that the notification dated 26-6-1997 restricts the tax to the commission alone and is repugnant to the scheme of the tax was obviously incorrect. The basis of the argument that the commission received from the airlines by the air travel agent is taken a measure for imposing a levy on a different service rendered to the customer by the agent, was itself incorrect. Therefore, the argument that the impugned provision of section 67(k) is repugnant to the general scheme of the Act was to be rejected.

As far as the second contention of the petitioner with regard to rule 6(7) was concerned, the language of rule 6(7) itself suggests that it is an optional matter. Therefore, the members of the petitioner-association, who had not exercised the option would had no concern with the validity of that rule while those who had opted for it, and majority of them having done so, could also not challenge the said validity.

In fact, it was not necessary for the High Court to take stock of the petitioners’ contention regarding the unconstitutionality of the rules but, even otherwise, there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found with that rule much less in the light of the submission made by the petitioners. The High Court was in complete agreement with the department that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration section 93 and section 94(2)(a) jointly. Indeed, there is a specific power under section 93 to grant exemption in any manner. Section 94(2)(a) speaks of the rule-making power on the subject of collection and recovery of service tax under section 66 and section 68. What is suggested by rule 6(7) is nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations. It was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule- making power. It does not amount to an independent levy again. Therefore, it was to be held that there was nothing wrong with the rule in question. This rule provides for an independent measure as the basic airfare. For this reason, no merit was found in the writ which was liable to be dismissed.

The expression ‘commission agent’ has been explained by the Notification dated 20-6-2003, reported in 155 ELT, N-171 [No.13/2003-S.T.]; vide Paragraph 2.1.3 it has been clarified that C & F agents working on commission basis do not fall under the definition of ‘Business auxiliary service’, inasmuch as they are substantially covered within the definition of C & F services. It has, further, been clarified that under section 65A of the Finance Act, 1994, it has also been provided that in case of overlap, a service would be classified under the head, (a ) which provides most specific description, (b) in case of a composite service, having combination of different taxable services, the service which give them their essential character and (c ) in case the test of (a) and (b ) does not resolve it, the service which comes earlier in the clauses of section 65, i.e., the service that was subjected to service tax earlier. Since insurance services and C & F services are more specific in description and were also subjected to service tax prior to imposition of tax on business auxiliary service, the insurance agents, C & F agents working on commission basis would fall under those respective categories. From this, it follows that a particular service can be taxed only under one head of service. [Para 6]

There was no merit in the appeal and the same was to be rejected. [Para 7]

1 and rule 8 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether cess on green leaves is a part of expenditure incurred in business of growing and manufacture of tea and it is allowable as a business expenditure - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, while computing composite income derived from sale of tea grown and manufactured by assessee entire cess would be claimed against taxable income - Held, yes [In favour of assessee] FACT: The assessee filed a return of income of Rs. 661.15 crores and claimed a deduction in the amount of Rs. 11.41 crores under section 80-I, Rs. 218.62 crores under section 80-IA and Rs. 20.20 crores under section 80-HH. The Assessing Officer assessed the income under section 143(3) at Rs. 814.66 crores and restricted the deduction claimed under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH to Rs. 11.06 crores, Rs. 201.08 crores and Rs. 18.57 crores respectively. The Commissioner issued a notice under section 263 stating that on verification of the records, it was revealed that the following expenditure, though having a bearing on the profits of the units, had not been considered for allocation, i.e., (i) Research and Development (R & D) revenue expenditure - Rs. 33,95,42,336; (ii) R & D Capital expenditure - Rs. 12,39,73,377; (iii) Interest paid - Rs. 32,16,45,000; (iv) Agency commission - Rs. 35,59,51,682 (including Miscellaneous expenditure). The Commissioner stated that as this expenditure had a bearing on the profits of the units, it should have been allocated proportionately. An excess allowance, the notice stated, had resulted in an under-assessment of Rs. 9.87 crores. The Commissioner by his order, came to the conclusion that the research expenditure incurred by the assessee is inextricably linked with the business of the assessee, including business in those products which are manufactured in the units entitled to a deduction under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH. The expenditure as noted by the Commissioner, had been allowed in computing the income under the head 'profits and gains from business or profession' for the whole of the business of the assessee, including of those units which were entitled to the aforesaid deductions. The logical corollary was held to be that in computing the profits derived from an eligible unit for the purpose of the aforesaid deductions, an appropriate part of the expenditure would have to be allocated to the units. As regards agency commission, the assessee had stated that an amount of Rs. 35.59 crores had already been allocated in arriving at the profit derived from the eligible units that was included under the head of advertisement. The assessee stated that there was no omission on its part and the amount should not once again be allocated in arriving at the profits of the units in respect of which a deduction was sought under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH. The Commissioner held that the interest and agency commission which relate to the whole of the business would have to be allocated to the eligible units. During the course of the hearing before the Commissioner, pursuant to the notice under section 263, a query was raised to the effect that cess which had been imposed on green leaf tea was required to be claimed entirely against the agricultural income in view of the decision of the Gauhati High Court in Jorehaut Group Ltd. v. Agrl. ITO [1997] 226 ITR 622. The assessee relied upon the provisions of rule 8 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and submitted that in the case of an assessee, who is engaged in growing and manufacturing tea, the composite income calculated in accordance with the provisions of the Act, is required to be apportioned between the income on the manufacture of tea and income from agriculture in the ratio of 40 : 60. According to the assessee, cess on green leaves is a part of the expenditure incurred in the business of growing and manufacture of tea. The Commissioner in his order under section 263 relied upon the judgment of the Gauhati High Court while coming to the conclusion that cess on green leaves was liable to be claimed entirely against agricultural income. On further appeal, Tribunal set aside order of Commissioner. It held that that the jurisdiction under section 263 had not been invoked properly and the entire cess could be claimed against taxable income.

No. 26AS then only CPC may deny the credit of TDS for relevant nature of receipt. Since the receipts of interest and commission on which TDS has been claimed under sections 194A and 194H are fully declared in ITR, the entire TDS claimed under sections 194A and 194H needs to be fully allowed. Hence the proportionate TDS disallowed is absolutely unjustified and, therefore, deserves to be allowed. [Para 2.6]

■ As regards the disallowance of TDS credit under section 194Q is concerned, the Bench found that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia. Therefore, the turnover on which tax is deducted under section 194Q is not the turnover of the assessee. Hence has rightly not been shown as such by the assessee. Moreover a Kachha Arhatia acts only as an agent for his constituent and never acts as principal. Therefore, the remuneration of Kachha Arhatia consists solely of commission and he has no control on the profit and losses made by his constituents.

■

The assessee has drawn attention of the Bench to sample invoices on which TDS was deducted under section 194Q by the principal buyer and the corresponding vikray parchi issued by the Mandi to the respective farmers. These documents clearly show that the amount invoiced by the assessee to the principal buyer and the value of goods transferred by assessee to the farmer is exactly the same. Therefore, turnover of the Kachha Arhatia is merely the commission paid by principal buyer on which the principal buyer deducts TDS under section 194H and which has been duly shown as income in the ITR by the assessee. Therefore, the TDS deducted by such principle buyers by virtue of provisions of section 194Q is eligible to be claimed by the Kachha Arhatia in his ITR on the grounds that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia and is duly registered as such with the Mandi. Perusal of the vikray parchi issued at the Mandi to the farmers and the corresponding invoice raised by the assessee to the principal buyer undoubtedly establishes the fact that the assessee has no control or margin in the sale facilitated by him and earns merely commission from such transactions.

■

The assessee has no domain over the goods sold to the principle buyers. As clarified by Central Board of Direct Taxes in its Circular No. 452 of 1986), so far as Kachha Arhatias are concerned the turnover does not include the sales effected on behalf of principals and only commission (gross) has to be considered for the purpose of income tax. Therefore, TDS deducted under section 194Q by the principle buyers cannot be refused by invoking rule 37BA read with section 199.

■

As the sale facilitated by the assessee for the farmers is not the turnover of the assessee and the income from such transaction (commission) being duly offered for tax by the assessee in his ITR, the TDS deducted both under sections 194H and 194Q deserves to be fully allowed. Further the Form No. 26AS also depicts that the invoices on which TDS has been deducted under section 194Q also has TDS deducted under section 194H. Thus the contention of the assessee that he is merely a Kachha Arhatia is potrayed beyond all doubts and needs to be accepted.

■

Therefore, the Assessing Officer is to be directed to allow TDS claimed under section 194Q by the assessee. [Para 2.7]

HEADNOTE: Section  199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with rule  37BA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 -  Deduction of tax at source -  Credit for tax deducted (Commission agent) - Assessment year  2022-23 - Assessee was carrying on business as a commission agent by selling chillies on behalf of farmers to registered dealers - In return of income, assessee claimed TDS credit of certain amount - However, Assessing Officer allowed reduced amount of TDS credit - Whether following principle of consistency and in view of CBDT Circular No. 452, dated 17-3-1986, since assessee was only a commission agent, he would be eligible to get credit of entire amount of TDS - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned order was to be set aside and Assessing Officer was to be directed to grant credit of entire amount of TDS to assessee - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 8] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was an individual and carrying business as a commission agent by selling chillies on behalf of farmers to registered dealers (GST Dealers). The assessee filed the return of income for the assessment year 2022-23 admitting a total income of Rs. 10.51 lakhs.

■

The CPC processed the return of income under section 143(1) wherein it was observed that the CPC had allowed the tax credit amounting to Rs. 10,271 as against Rs. 48,593 claimed by the assessee in the return of income.

■

The assessee also filed a petition under section 154 seeking re-processing of the return by allowing the correct TDS credit claimed by the assessee, wherein the CPC had rejected the petition filed under section 154.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The CBDT Circular No. 452, dated 17-3-1986 relied on by the assessee and the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Thota Venkateswarlu v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 290 (Viz) of 2024, dated 27-8-2024] wherein the Tribunal has relied on the decision of this Bench in the case of Yegneswari General Traders v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 39(Viz) of 2024, dated 18-3-2024] have been gone through. From the above it is clear that Kaccha Arahtias turnover includes only the gross commission and not the sales effected on behalf of their principals. In the present case, it is a fact that the assessee is only a licensed commission agent in Agricultural Market Committee Yard, Guntur. Therefore, the Circular issued by the CBDT (supra) squarely applies to the assessee and hence the assessee is acted only as an agent (kaccha arahtia) and therefore it is eligible to get credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source and there is no short fall of TDS as concluded by the revenue authorities. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to grant credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source in the case of the assessee. [Para 7]

■

Considering the identical facts and circumstances of the assessee's case with that of the appeal decided by the Tribunal in the case of Yegneswari General Traders (supra) wherein the Tribunal has relied on the decision of this Bench in the case of Thota Venkateswarlu (supra) and Subba Reddy Mareddy v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 96(VIZ) of 2024, dated 25-11-2024], following the principle of consistency, there is no hesitation to set-aside the orders of the revenue authorities and direct the Assessing Officer - CPC to grant credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source in the case of the assessee. Thus, the grounds raised by the assessee are allowed. [Para 8]

■

In the result, appeal of the assessee is allowed.[Para 9]

Consequently whether the demands are sustainable and whether penalties are imposable. [Para 8] It is true that the services which the assessee rendered with respect to handling of cargo and processing, etc. are classifiable as cargo handling services if it had rendered them in isolation. However, custom house agent himself also renders these services in addition to the services under CHA Regulations, 1984. It has been recognised by the CBEC that all these activities are part of the custom house agent activities. If these activities are considered as part of custom house agent services, then the amount charged by the assessee should form part of the assessable value for the custom house agent services. However, in the instant case, the assessee claims that it has rendered the services through other agencies and it has only collected the amounts from its clients to the extent the service providers charged from it. In other words, it has not charged anything extra for these services over and above what the service providers have charged from it. As per rule 5 of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, any expenditure or costs incurred by the service provider should be treated as consideration. However, this rule has been run down by the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Intercontinental Consultants & Technocrats (P.) Ltd. [2018] 91 taxmann.com 67/66 GST 450. Therefore reimbursable expenses cannot be included in the value of the taxable services rendered by the assessee. However, it needs to be ascertained whether the amounts it has collected from its clients are the same as they were charged by the service providers. Otherwise the remaining amount becomes the consideration for their services as Custom House Agency and needs to be included in the value of taxable services and service tax to be recomputed. [Para 9]

In view of the aforesaid, the services rendered by the assessee during the course of custom house agency services in the form of handling of cargo, etc. do not form a separate taxable service falling under 'cargo handling services' or 'port services'. It is a composite service rendered by the custom house agent. The amounts charged by the assessee from its clients do not get included in the value of taxable services rendered to the extent that they are reimbursable expenses. This is a fact to be verified from the invoices and accounts. Therefore, the matter required to be remanded back to the Original Authority for the sole purpose of computing the duty liability after deducting the value of reimbursable expenses from the invoices. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section  199  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with rule  37BA  of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Credit for tax deducted  (Illustrations) - Assessment year  2023-24  - Assessee was acting as an agent for a foreign shipping company - It raised invoices on importers/exporters/ freight forwarders for ocean freight, terminal handling charges, documentation charges, etc. - A part of amount received from importer/exporter/ freight forwarder was retained by assessee and balance part was transferred to account of its principal - However, assessee could not have divulged this information with importers/exporters/ freight forwarders as otherwise, customers would push it for a better deal - In such circumstances, concerned importer/exporter/ freight forwarder had deducted tax at source on entire amount of invoice raised by assessee on them - In turn, foreign shipping line deposited due taxes - Assessee had been filing its return of income, declaring such gross receipts as its income which it was entitled to receive - Assessing Officer allowed TDS credit proportionately - Whether since on account of business expediency, assessee could not have divulged this information with importers/exporters/ freight forwarders but information relating to deduction of tax was furnished by deductor to Income-tax authority and same was contained in Form 26AS of assessee, assessee should be allowed credit in respect of entire amount of TDS as reflected in such Form - Held, yes [Paras 9, 10 and 13] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was acting as an agent for a foreign company who was a resident of Hong Kong. It raised invoices on importers/exporters/freight forwarders for ocean freight, terminal handling charges, documentation charges, etc. A part of this amount received from the importer/exporter/freight forwarder was retained by the assessee and the balance part was transferred to the account of its principal.

■

The assessee filed its return of income and claimed credit for TDS as per Form 26AS. However, the Assessing Officer allowed TDS credit to the extent of receipts offered to tax by the assessee in its return of income and disallowed the balance TDS credit.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal of the assessee by relying upon section 199 read with rule 37BA(2).

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

Section 199(3) enables the CBDT to make such rules for the purposes of giving such credit including the rules for grant of such credit to a person other than that referred to in sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) thereof. Pursuant thereto, rule 37BA has been notified by the CBDT. [Para 8]

■

According to sub-rule (1) of rule 37BA, such credit for TDS has to be allowed to the person to whom payment has been made or credit has been given on the basis of information relating to deduction of tax furnished by the deductor to the Income-tax authority. As in the instant case, such information is contained in Form 26AS which is also according to the said rule, thus the assessee should be allowed credit in respect of the entire amount of TDS as reflected in such Form. [Para 9]

■

Although sub-rule (2) of rule 37BA enables the recipient of income to file a declaration with the deductor to the effect that such TDS may be reflected in the name of the other person. But this enabling provision is not mandatory. However, if the necessary requirement in the rule is fulfilled, then, the deductor has to reflect the TDS in the name of the other person in which event the said person would get credit in respect of such TDS. Otherwise, TDS credit has to be allowed to the person from whose payment such TDS has been deducted. As in the instant case on account of business expediency, the assessee could not have divulged this information with the importers/exporters/freight forwarders. [Para 10]

■

The assessee has also ensured that the foreign shipping line has deposited due taxes on the payment made by it to the non-resident shipping line. It also understands that, the said non-resident shipping line is complying with the obligations under the Act including filing of its return of income in India. Moreover it is not the case of the revenue that the assessee has not offered the correct income to tax as well as there is no qualification by its Auditor in the audit report. [Para 12]

■

Therefore considering the totality of the facts and circumstances, the balance tax credit in respect to TDS is to be allowed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 65, read with section 76, of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Period 16-7-1997 to 31-10-1998 and 1-11-1998 to 31-8-1999 - Whether for a service provided by clearing and forwarding agent to be taxable, such service has to be relatable to clearing and forwarding operations and can be in any manner and it is not necessary that said agent must deal with goods directly - Held, yes - RZC were procuring orders for various tobacco products manufactured by appellant-company from dealers and passing on same to appellants, from whom they were receiving commission in lieu of service so provided - Whether said services were definitely connected with clearing and forwarding of various tobacco products being manufactured by appellants - Held, yes - Whether RZC were a ‘clearing and forwarding agent’ of appellants and service provided by them were liable to tax - Held, yes - Whether since appellants had already been penalised, there was no justification for imposition of separate penalty upon their director - Held, yes [Para 9] Notifications and Circulars - Trade Notice No. 59 of 1999, dated 4-10-1999 issued by Mumbai Commissionerate-I

FACT: The appellants were engaged in the manufacture of tobacco products. They entered into an agreement with RZC, appointing the latter as their agent for the purpose of marketing their product, booking orders, managing, supervising and developing of the market. In consideration of the services rendered by the said agent, the appellants were to pay commission at the rates mentioned in the schedule to the contract on the net sale proceeds of the orders received through the agent. The appellants were issued show-cause notice, alleging that as they were availing services of RZC, who were working as ‘clearing and forwarding Agent’ on commission basis, they were liable to pay service-tax. The appellants took a stand before the adjudicating authority that the service rendered by RZC did not come under the purview of clearing and forwarding agent and the same was entirely different. As such, the question of payment of service tax did not arise. During the course of personal hearing, they contended that after the amendments in the Service Tax Rules through the Finance Bill, they should have been issued a fresh show-cause notice. The Commissioner confirmed the service tax of certain amount, not paid by the appellants. In addition, he also imposed penalty on the appellants and their director.

On appeal :

HELD: In the Trade Notice No. 59 of 1999, dated 4-10-1999, issued by the Mumbai Commissionerate-I, the clearing and forwarding agent has been defined as ‘any person who is engaged in providing any service, either directly or indirectly, connected with clearing and forwarding operations in any manner to any other person and includes a consigning agent’. The details of the activities given in the said Trade Notice are only few of the activities undertaken by clearing and forwarding agent, as is apparent by the use of the expression ‘normally’. As such, it is clear that the activities given in the said Trade Notice are not exhaustive but are inclusive in nature and describes the jobs to be normally undertaken by the clearing and forwarding agent. As per the definition of clearing and forwarding agent, he is a person who is engaged in providing ‘any’ service, either directly or ‘indirectly’ connected with clearing and forwarding operations, in ‘any’ manner to any other person. The use of expression ‘any’ and ‘indirectly’ in the said definition of clearing and forwarding agent, is indicative of the fact, that the scope of the services to be provided by clearing and forwarding agent is quite wide. He is not only the person who is actually dealing with the goods who has to be termed as clearing and forwarding agent. Even if the services are indirect, but the same are connected with the clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner, of the other persons, he would be covered by the definition of clearing and forwarding agent. In the instant case, admittedly, RZC was procuring orders from the dealer and passing on the same to the appellant, from whom they were receiving the commission, in lieu of services so provided. The said services were definitely connected with the clearing and forwarding operations of the various tobacco products being manufactured by the appellant. It is further seen that the taxable service has been defined as any service provided by clearing and forwarding agent ‘in relation’ to clearing and forwarding operations in ‘any manner’. From the above, it is clear that the service has to be relatable to the clearing and forwarding operations and can be in any manner and it is not necessary that the said agent must deal with the goods directly. As such, the lower authority had rightly concluded that RZC was a clearing and forwarding agent and services provided by them were liable to tax. [Para 9]

Commission paid to the various agents cannot be stated to be a service used directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products or clearance of final products from the place of removal. In the absence of any material on record, as noted above to indicate that such commission agents were involved in the activity of sales promotion as explained earlier, the commission agent is directly concerned with the sales rather than sales promotion and as such the services provided by such commission agent would not fall within the purview of the main or inclusive part of the definition of input service as laid down in rule 2(l) of the rules. [Para 5.2(viii)]

Commission agent's services were also not 'activities relating to business' :

The includes part of the definition of 'input service' includes "activities relating to the business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security". The words "activities relating to business" are followed by the words "such as". Therefore, the words "such as" must be given some meaning.

The words "such as" indicate that what are mentioned thereafter are only illustrative and not exhaustive. Thus, the activities that follow the words "such as" are illustrative of the activities relating to business which are included in the definition of input service and are not exhaustive. Therefore, activities relating to business could also be other than the activities mentioned in the sub-rule.

However, that does not mean that every activity related to the business of the assessee would fall within the inclusive part of the definition. For an activity related to the business, it has to be an activity which is analogous to the activities mentioned after the words "such as". What follows the words "such as" is "accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security".

The activity of commission agent, therefore, should bear some similarity to the illustrative activities. None of the illustrative activities, viz., "accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security" is in any manner similar to the services rendered by commission agents nor are the same in any manner related to such services. Under the circumstances, though the business activities mentioned in the definition are not exhaustive, the service rendered by the commission agents not being analogous to the activities mentioned in the definition, would not fall within the ambit of the expression "activities relating to business".

Consequently, CENVAT credit would not be admissible in respect of the commission paid to foreign agents. [Para 5.2(ix)]

On the issue of allocation of cess on green leaves, it seems that rule 8 stipulates that income derived from the sale of tea grown and manufactured by the seller in India shall be computed as if it were income derived from business, and forty per cent of such income shall be deemed to be income liable to tax. Rule 8 provides for a legal fiction for determining what part of the income of an assessee, who is engaged in the growing of tea leaves and the manufacture of tea, would be regarded as being attributable to income from the manufacturing operations and liable to tax. As a result of the fiction brought in by Rule 8, the entire income which is derived from the sale of tea grown and manufactured by the seller is required to be computed, in the first instance, as if it is an income derived from business. 40 per cent of the income which is so derived, is then deemed to be income which is liable to tax. The expenditure which was incurred by the assessee on the payment of cess on green leaves, is expenditure which is liable to be taken into account in computing the income of the assessee from the business. As a matter of fact, this view has been taken by the Calcutta High Court in the case of the assessee itself, i.e., Hindustan Lever Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 11 taxmann.com 64 (Cal.). The Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court relied upon the decision in CIT v. AFT Industries Ltd. [2004] 270 ITR 167 / 141 Taxman 433 and held that the amount of cess so payable was deductible. In view of the fact that the decision of the Calcutta High Court holds the field now insofar as the assessee is concerned, there was no merit in the challenge which has been advanced on behalf of the revenue to that aspect of the order passed by the Tribunal. The Tribunal rightly held that the entire cess can be claimed against taxable income. [Para 19]

HELD: The adjudicating authority of the impugned order had observed that there exists no specific condition in rule 6(2) for keeping the separate stock/storage of common inputs to be used for manufacture of exempted goods and dutiable goods, but keeping of separate accounts is necessary. HELD: According to sub-section 6(6) of section 194C it is observed that TDS is not required to be made in the case of engaging the vehicles in business of plying, hiring or leasing goods carriages, with a condition that contractor should own 10 or less than 10 goods carriages at any time during the previous year and furnish a declaration to that effect along with Permanent Account Number. It is apparent from the above, that the vehicles should be used by the assessee in the business of plying, hiring or leasing goods carriages and contractor should own 10 or less than 10 goods carriages and furnish the declaration to that effect and also furnish a Permanent Account Number. order, the assessee had entered into agreement with various companies for providing C&F agent service. The facts brought out by the Commissioner (Appeals) further clarifies that as per agreement between the assessee and companies the assessee is providing various services which include distribution of goods for which the assessee has charged commission and other income, etc. The agreement between the parties further specifies various expenses to be incurred by the assessee on behalf of the clients and reimbursement of such expenses by the clients. It is admitted fact that in line of C&F business the C&F agents will incur various expenses while rendering services to their clients and the same will be reimbursed by the clients against invoices/debit notes. In the instant case also the assessee has incurred various expenses on behalf of clients and while billing to the clients for services rendered a separate bill/debit note has been issued to recover various expenses incurred on behalf of the clients. The assessee in the books of account has accounted services charges/commission received from the clients for rendering C&F agent service as its income but reimbursement of expenses has been squared off in the parties account. On the other hand, the clients have deducted TDS on total payments made to the assessee including reimbursement of expenses. Thus obviously there will be a difference between total payments made by the clients and TDS deducted thereon as per Form no. 26AS and gross receipt booked by the assessee in its books of account. The Assessing Officer has noted difference in gross receipt as per books of account of the assessee and gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS. The assessee has explained difference between gross receipt and claimed that said difference is on account of reimbursement of expenses. The assessee had filed reconciliation explaining difference with party wise service charges received and reimbursement of amount received towards reimbursement of expenses. The Assessing Officer never disputed these facts. However, he rejected reconciliation filed by the assessee only for the reason that the assessee could not prove with sufficient documents that reimbursement of expenses was accounted in the books of clients. [Para 7]

The reason given by the Assessing Officer to make addition towards difference in gross receipt appears to be baseless and incorrect because the assessee can file whatever evidence the Assessing Officer wants to prove its financial transactions with its clients but it is incorrect on the part of the Assessing Officer to expect the assessee to produce books of account of its clients. The only reason for the Assessing Officer to make addition towards difference in gross receipt is doubt and suspicion on expenses booked by the clients in their books of account. The Assessing Officer is miserably failed to understand the concept of accounting because deduction of TDS on total payments including reimbursement of expenses itself is a sufficient proof that the clients have accounted expenses incurrred by the assessee on behalf of the clients. The clients have deducted TDS on total payments including reimbursement of expenses because of this there is difference between gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS reported by the clients while deducting TDS under sections 194J and 194C, when compared to gross receipt reported in the books of account of the assessee. The assessee is following the method of accounting as per which it was accounting service charges received from the clients towards rendering various services as its income and reimbursement of expenses is squared off in the parties account. The assessee has filed a party wise reconciliation along with ledger account explaining the difference. As per chart filed by the assessee the gross receipt towards C&F service charges and other income exactly matches with gross receipt booked by the assessee in its books of account. The assessee had also reconciled difference between reimbursement of expenses and as per bills filed by the assessee amount received from clients towards reimbursement of expenses is more than the amount of difference noticed by the Assessing Officer from Form No. 26AS. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making addition towards difference in gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS and as per books of account of the assessee.

The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts and also by considering reconciliation filed by the assessee has rightly deleted addition made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 8]

The appeal filed by the revenue deserved to be dismissed. [Para 9]

In the instant case it was recorded that the respondent was already paying service tax on commission received from airlines/shipping lines under business auxiliary service since 10-9-2004. The original authority recorded that the show-cause notice did not specify as to who is the client to whom the respondent is providing service. Original authority considered both the scenario, airline/shipping lines as a client or exporter/shipper as a client. In case the respondent is acting on behalf of airlines/shipping lines as client, it was held that they are covered by tax liability under BAS. Further, examining the issue the original authority viewed that commission amount is necessarily to be obtained out of transaction which is to be provided by the respondent on behalf of the client, that is, the exporters. The facts of the case indicated that the mark-up value collected by the respondent from the exporter is an element of profit in the transaction. The respondent when acting as agent on behalf of airlines/shiplines was discharging service tax with effect from 10-9-2004. However, with reference to amount collected from exporters/shippers the original authority clearly recorded that it is not the case that this amount is a commission earned by the respondent while acting on behalf of the exporter and said mark-up value is of freight charges and are not to be considered as commission. Based on these findings the demand was dropped. No impropriety is found in the said finding. The grounds of appeal did not bring any contrary evidence to change such findings. Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (81) ELT 3. [Para 5] In this case, Court’s attention was drawn to the departmental circular according to which in a case where the manufacturer produces dutiable final products and also final goods which are exempt from duty, it is not reasonably possible to segregate inputs utilised in manufacture of the dutiable final products from the final products which are exempt from duty. Based on this, the Court held that the manufacturer may take credit of duty paid on all the inputs used in the manufacture of final products, on which duty will have to be paid and in view of this clarification by the Departmental circular, the Court saw no reason as to why the assessee should not make a debit entry in the credit account before removal of the exempted final product; and, hence, it cannot be said that the assessee had taken credit for the duty paid on the inputs utilised in the manufacture of the final exempted product under rule 57A. The Court, therefore, took the view that the claim for exemption of duty on the disputed goods cannot be denied on the plea that the assessee had taken the credit of the duty paid on the inputs used in manufacture of these goods. The ratio laid down in this decision was squarely applicable to the facts of the instant case and maintenance of separate books of account at the initial stage cannot be considered to be a condition precedent for the purpose of claiming the benefit of exemption to the respondent-assessee. [Para 6]

Even rule 6(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 says that notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rules (1) and (2), the manufacturer or the provider of output service, opting not to maintain separate accounts, shall follow either of the following conditions, as applicable to him. Even otherwise rule 3 says that the manufacturer or producer of the final product or provider of output services shall be allowed to take credit on various items enumerated therein. This issue had come up for consideration before the Allahabad High Court in the case of Hello Minerals Water (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India 2004 (174) ELT 422, wherein it is held that reversal of Modvat credit amounts to non-taking of credit on the inputs. Hence, the benefit of the notification granting exemption/rate of duty has to be given on the final products since the reversal of credit on the input was done. Accordingly, the Tribunal’s order in the instant case was justified. [Para 7]

HELD: In the case of Raja Rajeshwari Intl. Polymers (P.) Ltd. v. other amount of similar nature. The credits also include loans and trade credits and also other receipts, be that of cash or kind. These may be in the name of the assessee, i.e., capital account or in the name of a third party. In the instant case, the impugned credits appeared in the books of account of the assessee. Therefore, same were liable to be considered in the hands of the assessee as per provisions of section 68. [Para 7] In the instant case, the assessee was Katcha Arhatia. The role of Katcha Arhatia is to provide a platform to the sellers to sell their produce in the market. The transactions of purchase and sale made at the business premises of the Katcha Arhatia do not represent his own purchases and sales. He only acts as a commission agent on behalf of the seller and the buyer. The documentary evidence, in the instant case, established beyond doubt that agricultural produce in the form of kapas and narma, equal to the quantity shown, was indeed purchased/sold on the respective dates. [Para 7.1]

However, what the assessee had not been able to establish but the revenue had been able to establish, was that the produce in the form of kapas and narma was indeed purchased from 51 parties mentioned in the assessment order, for which addition was made by the Assessing Officer. That finding was supported by the enquiries made by the Assessing Officer during the course of the assessment proceedings, i.e., the non-service of enquiry letters by postal authorities on 12 persons, the statements of the two persons and the village sarpanches, recorded by the inspectors during the conduct of enquiries and inability of the assessee to produce any of the 51 parties before the Assessing Officer. Moreover, it was not a case where the identity of only a few persons was not established, the number was 51 out of 52, which was too large. Identity of only one person was established. Besides, the assessee had not been able to produce any documentary evidence in the form of stamped receipts/simple receipts as to when amounts covered by the purchase of agricultural produce were paid to the parties in the subsequent assessment year. The payments for purchases had not been made by cheques through banking channels. Besides, the assessee had not produced any evidence, nor placed any material to show that those parties/farmers existed in the respective villages. [Para 7.2]

Two sister concerns of the assessee had purchased the agricultural produce in auction through the assessee. The purchases made by them in the presence of the officials, supported by documentary evidence were genuine. It was a fact that the amounts due from the two sister concerns had been shown outstanding and the nature of such credits was purchases of cotton and narma from the assessee and such entries appeared in their books of account. The assessee, in his books, had shown the amounts due from his sister concerns as sundry debtors and the corresponding credit entries in their books of account justified such action. Therefore, no fault could be found with the entries made in the books of account of the sister concerns, because their balance sheets depicted correct position about their assets and liabilities. But if the credits appearing in the balance sheet remained unexplained, the same would warrant addition in the instant case, because the credits appeared in the balance sheet of the assessee. If those credits were not genuine, the balance sheet would show the difference on asset side, higher than the total of liabilities. Therefore, the addition under section 68 would be called for in the instant case, and not in the cases of sister concerns. [Paras 7.3]

In the instant case, the assessee had not carried on any trading on its own. He had earned income by way of Dami on the transactions effected through him as a commission agent. Income received by way of Dami was fully supported by documentary evidence. Therefore, the question of rejection of book results did not arise in the instant case. Moreover, there is nothing in section 68 that the books of account must be rejected before making an addition under this section.This is an independent and deeming provision and will apply if the assessee fails to offer an explanation of the source of particular receipt/credit appearing in the books of account or if the explanation given by the assessee is found to be not satisfactory by the Assessing Officer. [Para 7.4]

It is not correct to say that the inspector cannot record the statement of any person. The Assessing Officer made enquiries through his inspectors in exercise of the powers conferred under the Act. Moreover, such enquiries only confirmed the fact that the persons had not been found existing at the given villages and obviously they had not sold the cotton and narma through the assessee. No material had been placed by the assessee to controvert such findings. In fact, when the assessee was confronted with the results of such enquiries and given copies of statements recorded by the inspector, no request was made to the Assessing Officer for allowing an opportunity of cross-examination. Thus, the objection raised in that regard was untenable. [Para 7.5]

The assessee was required to establish the factum of existence and identity of the parties and the fact that those persons had actually sold the produce to the assessee. [Para 7.7]

HELD (PER TECHNICAL MEMBER)

It is seen that rule 6(1) specifically prohibits Cenvat credit being allowed on such quantity of inputs as used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Therefore, there is no authority in law for availing Cenvat credit on the quantity of inputs intended or used for the manufacture of exempted goods except in terms of rule 6(2), which allows the manufacturer to avail the Cenvat credit only in respect of that particular quantity of inputs, which is intended to be used in the manufacture of dutiable goods subject to their maintaining separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of final products. But if separate accounts are not maintained, though Cenvat credit is availed, then sub-rule 3 of rule 6 provides for payment of amount equal to Cenvat credit on dutiable inputs for cases covered under sub-rule (3)(a ) and in respect of all other inputs, sub-rule (3)(b) of rule 6 provides for payment of an amount of 8 per cent or 10 per cent of total price (excluding sales tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods), of the exempted final products charged by the manufacturer for the sale of such goods at the time of their clearance from the factory. Thus, reversal of the credit taken or availed under rule 6 is not contemplated by the rules. [Para 15]

If the interpretation put by the majority order is held to be correct, it will render the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) ibid providing for payment of an amount equal to 8 per cent or 10 per cent rather otiose. This militates against an interpretation, which renders it superfluous and is of no significance. [Para 16]

It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacturer of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts had to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It cannot be given, as the amount of reversal of credit has to be worked out in a manner prescribed in the Rules. There was no such prescription prior to the amendment. This decision of the majority will make the amendment superfluous. Such interpretation has to be avoided. [Para 23]

In the light of the aforesaid discussions, it was held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. [Para 26]

FACT: The assessees, namely, FA and FW, were sourcing agents of two foreign companies, ‘DSI’ and ‘B’ which were importers of readymade garments. The assessees identified vendors (garment manufacturers) in India for procurement and supply of garments to said companies. They also provided operational assistance to vendors to ensure supply of goods to foreign companies as per terms and conditions of purchase orders and ensured payment by foreign companies to them. Besides that the assessees also engaged services of foreign commission agents for identifying customers and rendering marketing services on their behalf. For the above activities, namely, (i) service provided to foreign companies, (ii) operational assistance provided to Indian vendors and (iii) services received from foreign commission agents, the Commissioner confirmed demand of service tax under the category of ‘Business auxiliary service’ and also imposed penalties.

On appeal :

HELD: The assessees rendered services of the same description to the vendors. The assessee-FA rendered services to DSI by identifying the vendors in India for procurement and supply of garments. They co-ordinated with vendors for production, logistics and shipment of goods ordered, to DSI. FA rendered services to vendors by attending to the processing of purchase orders placed by DSI, by giving necessary operational assistance in the execution and ensuring the receipt of sale proceeds. These services were rendered without a contract with the vendors and were incidental to services rendered to DSI. Similarly the assessee-FW had rendered services to the foreign company-B by monitoring production and export of garments by the vendors as per B’s orders. ‘B’ was the recipient of the service. FW had Research & Development facilities and assisted ‘B’ to decide the designs of the garments. The services rendered to ‘B’ and ‘DSI’ were correctly treated by the Commissioner as not exempt as exports during the material period. Only on 1-3-2007, such services when delivered and used outside India by a recipient located outside India, were extended the exemption. [Para 4]
