In that sense, rule 6, if invoked, can deal with only prospective credits availed after output activity becoming exempt and not credits availed before the output activity become exempt. [Para 21] As submitted by the assessee, even CERA authorities, while raising objection and making the assessee reverse cenvat credit availed during 2010 till obtaining of Completion Certificate, adopted the same basis of square feet area which attracted service tax as compared to square feet area which was converted into immovable property after receipt of Completion Certificate. This basis is, therefore, acceptable to revenue authorities. It was such basis which was adopted by the assessee in availing only proportionate credit after receipt of Completion Certificate. [Para 22]

Since the assessee is not required to reverse any credit availed by it on valid input services availed during the period 2010 till obtaining of completion certificate, the said amount reversed by it under protest cannot be retained by the revenue authorities and has to be returned to the assessee. [Para 23]

In view of the aforesaid, the assessee is not liable to pay 8%/10% amount of value of service became exempted after receipt of Completion Certificate under rule 6.

The cenvat credit on input services received after obtaining Completion Certificate cannot be wholly allowed to the assessee. Since it had availed only proportionate credit by maintaining separate accounts, the same is sufficient compliance of the legal obligation cast upon it.

The assessee can be said to have 'maintained proper separate accounts' as required under rule 6 having availed credit only to the extent input services in taxable activity, on the scientific basis after obtaining Completion Certificate.

The assessee is not required to reverse cenvat credit availed during the period when output service was wholly taxable before receipt of Completion Certificate, in accordance with law.

The assessee is eligible to seek refund of the amount paid under protest towards credit availed from 2010 till receipt of completion certificate. [Para 24]

In this regard, it may be noted that in the course of assessment proceedings, the assessee had prepared its country accounts for India, allocating total revenues and expenses of the assessee to India activity and filed the same before the Assessing Officer. This fact has been recorded by the Tribunal in its order in the assessment year 2000-01. In the light of this observation, Circular No.742 is not applicable in the instant appeal. [Para 16]

HEADNOTE: Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) noted that assessee had submitted evidences with respect to ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of assessee showing payment made to parties - Assessee had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases and sales - Department however argued that one-to-one mapping shown by assessee was not correct for reason that in purchase bills of these parties there was no narration with respect to quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as colour etc. - Whether in case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be sufficient compliance and therefore, assessee could not be further burdened to show colour and number of diamonds - Held, yes - Whether therefore, it could not be said that in purchase bills assessee should have mentioned this details as that was not trade practice - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts, Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly considered that purchases from these parties was genuine when part of purchases from same parties was not disputed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 23 and 24] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating purchases of diamonds in question as bogus  INCOME TAX : Where assessee had paid commission to four entities on export of diamond and had furnished all relevant details in respect of said commission alongwith details of service tax collected thereon, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure as non-genuine and bogus

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Commission) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer received information from investigation wing that assessee had debited expenses in form of commission from four different parties - Enquiries were conducted and found that all 4 companies had same address and they were not available on addresses mentioned in income tax return and no business activity was being carried out from those premises - Based on said information, Assessing Officer disallowed commission expenses claimed by assessee - It was noted that all four entities were assessed by same Assessing Officer and commission income shown by them was accepted - It was further, noted that commission had been paid on export of diamond stating details of exports made by assessee, respective commission and details of service tax collected thereon and assessee had also produced details of other commission expenditure incurred by assessee which were also identical - Whether in view of above facts, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure in question as non-genuine and bogus - Held, yes [Para 26] [In favour of assessee]

assessee which binds assessee as principal. In fact the assessee is the person responsible for deducting tax at source within provisions of Chapter XVII-B with respect to such payments made by the C & F agent as intermediary. The contracts in the instant case entered into by C & F agents with service providers have been entered into in the normal course of agency and it cannot be said C & F agent exceeded his authority or has committed any fraud or wrong against a third person by entering these contracts. Thus, the assessee was in fact liable to deduct tax at source for payments made through C & F agents for the expenses incurred through C & F agents as the said C & F agent are merely acting as an agents being intermediary between the assessee and third party service provider and it is in fact the assessee who was claiming these expenses in its profit and loss. No doubt these C & F Agents are independent contractors but once they deal with third party service providers such as customs authorities, port authorities, warehousing authorities, transporters and other service providers for clearance of import shipments, they only act as an agent on behalf of their principals, i.e., the assessee and their action with third party service providers bounds the assessee done in the normal course of agency. Hence, this matter needs to be set aside and restored to the file of the Assessing Officer to identify the disallowance under section 40(a)(ia) which requires analysis of nature of each of the expenses covered by invoice raised by C&F agents and their coverage by provisions of Chapter XVII-B. Hence, the matter need to be set aside and restored to the file of the Assessing Officer for necessary analysis of various such expenses incurred by agent on behalf of principal and applicability of provisions of deduction of income-tax at source to these expenses to work out disallowance under section 40(a)(ia) read with provisions of Chapter XVII-B . The Assessing Officer shall de-novo adjudicate the issue on merits in accordance with law.[Para 16]

HEADNOTE: Section 194C, read with  section 40(a)(ia), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Contractors/sub-contractors, payments to [Reimbursement of expenses] - Assessment year 2005-06 - Whether where expenses were incurred by CF agents on behalf of assessee and claims were made on actual basis, assessee while making reimbursement of said expenses was not liable to deduct tax at source under section 194C - Held, yes [Para 6.4.3] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where expenses were incurred by CF agents on behalf of assessee and claims were made on actual basis, assessee while making reimbursement of said expenses was not liable to deduct tax at source under section 194C

FACT: During relevant year, assessee reimbursed certain expenses incurred by C&F agents on its behalf.

The Assessing Officer finding that assessee had not deducted tax at source while making reimbursement of expenses, disallowed said payments under section 40(a)(ia).

The Commissioner (Appeals) opined that since these payments were made on actual basis and did not contain any element of income, there was no need to deduct tax at source. He, thus, deleted the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: In terms of sub-section (2) of section 4, which is the charging section, in respect of income chargeable under sub-section (1), income tax shall be deducted at source or paid in advance, where it is so deductible or payable under any provision of this Act.

Thus, it is clear that tax is to be deducted only where element of income is a part of payment and since reimbursement of expenses does not constitute trading receipts or has any element of income therein, TDS is not liable to be made from reimbursements.

Though section 194C mentions TDS being made on 'any sum' paid to a resident in pursuance of a contract, the term 'any sum' cannot be stretched to mean even expenses incurred on behalf of the client and later recovered from them.

When a C&F agent incurs expenses like custom duty, port dues, and other sundry charges, he is merely acting as a front man of his client and on his behalf. These expenses do not normally have any nexus with the commission he is supposed to earn for his work. [Para 6.4.1]

In the case on hand, as pointed out by the Commissioner (Appeals), the expenses have been incurred by the C&F Agents on behalf of the assessee, the claims were made on actual basis and the amounts were separately shown with proper evidence.

The fact that the reimbursement of expenses have been separately billed, in the case on hand, is not disputed. The C&F Agents are appointed to provide the service of carrying out sales for which they are paid service charges on which TDS has been made and not for the purpose of incurring expenses on behalf of the assessee.

In this view of the matter, the reimbursement of expenses by C&F Agents cannot be held to be contract/service on which the provisions of section 194C of the Act would come into play and apply.

In view of the factual position as laid out above, it is held that there is no need to deduct TDS on reimbursement of expenses to C&F Agents which are separately billed and accordingly the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is upheld. [Para 6.4.3]

headnotes.text: Section 16 of the Central Goods And Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit - Period April 2006 to 2008 - Whether it could not be contended that since definition of Rule 2(e) underwent amendment with effect from 1-4-2011, whereby, it was indicated that trading activity would fall in category of services, therefore rule 6(3)(c) could apply to trading activity only after 1.4.2011 - Held, yes - During relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax - Appellant company acted as a commission agent was also engaged in trading activities - Whether since appellant was not paying service tax on trading activity, credit of tax paid on services vis-a-vis input services could only be taken on a pro-rata basis as per formula stipulated in Rule 6(3)(c) - Held, yes - Whether however, since no separate accounts were maintained by appellant with regard to taxable and non-taxable services, apportionment as provided in Rule 6(3)(c) would triggered - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in denying credit of service tax - Held, yes [Para 12][In favour of revenue]GST/Cenvat Credit: Where during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax, if appellant engaged in activities of trading and commission agency did not maintain separate accounts regarding taxable and non-taxable services, it would not be entitled to credit of service tax

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period 2005-06 and 2006-07 - Assessee under a contract with State Government laid pipelines for a canal pipeline project - Assessee by considering said service as falling under category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ paid service tax on same after availing benefit of Modvat credit - Revenue viewed that above service was not taxable and therefore held that in view of provisions of rule 6(3)(c) assessee was entitled to avail Cenvat credit to extent of 20 per cent only as it was not maintaining separate accounts for inputs and input services used for both exempted and taxable services - However, it was found that Cenvat credit accounts were being maintained separately by assessee on basis of various projects being handled by it - In fact, total amount of credit availed in respect of project of laying down of pipelines had been taken by revenue from Cenvat credit accounts maintained by assessee - Whether, in view of above, question of invocation of provisions of rule 6(3)(c) did not arise - Held, yes [Para 10]

Rule 6, read with rule 2(d) and rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was manufacturing as well as importing 'consumer goods' and selling them - Assessee took credit of input services only pro rata on turnover basis attributable to manufacturing business and did not take credit of Rs. 16 lakh relating to trading business - Department argued that 'imported goods' amounted to 'exempted goods' and since separate accounts were not maintained, assessee was liable to pay Rs. 297 crore being 10 per cent/5 per cent of value of exempted goods under rule 6(3) - HELD : 'Imported goods', which are traded, cannot be regarded as 'exempted goods' and hence, rule 6 cannot be applied thereto - Secondly, since assessee has not availed any credit in respect of input services relating to traded goods, question of maintenance of separate accounts under rule 6(2) and consequent applicability of rule 6(3) would not arise - Even otherwise, since assessee has followed formula under rule 6(3A) ab initio and has not taken any ineligible credit, rule 6(3) cannot be applied - Hence, demand was set aside [Paras 5.1 to 5.4] [In favour of assessee]

I. Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Period from April 2000 to March 2007 - Department denied credit on ground that assessee did not maintain separate accounts for input services used for taxable and exempted services and input service tax credit had been availed/utilised in excess of 20 per cent of credit taken in contravention of rule 6(3)(c) - HELD : Cap of 20 per cent was applicable on service tax payable and not on service tax credit actually availed - What was restricted was only utilisation of credit and not taking credit per se; credit taken could be carried forward - When cap was removed on 1-4-2008, assessee was eligible to utilise credit also - Further, utilising credit in excess of limit would attract only interest liability; entire service tax itself could not be denied to assessee - Hence, matter was remanded back to adjudicating authority to re-examine matter in light of CBEC circular dated 21-11-2008 [Para 5.1] [In favour of assessee]ST : Utilising Cenvat credit in excess of limit fixed under rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 would attract only interest liability; entire credit itself cannot be denied to assessee  ST : Break bulk fee and freight rebate are not, prima facie, liable to service tax under Custom House Agent's services and Business Auxiliary Services respectively  ST : Commission and incentive received from airlines for booking of cargo space is, prima facie, liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : CCX fee received from foreign principal for purpose of delivering documents to customers in India, to collect and remit freight charges due to overseas company is liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : Cenvat Credit cannot be denied for procedural violations

Cenvat credit - Trading activity - Common inputs and input services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Input services were attributable to trading activity - Assessee undertook taxable services and trading activity - Issue regarding input services used for trading activity covered by decisions in Ruchika Global Interlinks v. CESTAT 2017 (5) G.S.T.L. 225 (Mad.) and Lally Automobiles (P.) Ltd. v. Commr. (Adjudication) C.Ex. 2018 (17) G.S.T.L. 422 (Del.) - Since assessee was not paying Service Tax on trading activity, credit of services vis-a-vis input services could only be taken on pro rata basis as per formula stipulated in Rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Confirmation of demand with interest invoking extended period of limitation on Cenvat credit availed on trading activity was to be upheld - Since Cenvat credit and applicable interest were paid much before issuance of show-cause notice, assessee was entitled to benefit of 25 per cent of penalty imposed - Order to that extent was to be modified Rule 9(e), read with rule 6 and rule 15 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 7 to 9] [In favour of assessee]ST : Assessee not paying Service Tax on trading activity could take credit of tax paid on services vis-a-vis input services only on pro rata basis as per formula stipulated in rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004  ST : Availment of credit prior to registration as Input Service Distributor (ISD) being only procedural irregularity, Cenvat credit could not be denied

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Goods transport agency's service and telephone service were not covered by list of common services in respect of which credit could be admissible even if they were used for exempted as well as dutiable goods - Hence, assessee was required to maintain separate records for them - Since assessee has failed to maintain separate accounts, credit of said two services was to be disallowed [Para 4] [In favour of revenue]

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Period April, 2006 to January, 2007 - Assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax on commission paid to commission agent for receiving services of latter - Revenue denied credit on ground that benefit was liable to be restricted to procurement of purchase orders by commission agents and was not admissible insofar as collection of sale price of goods was concerned - Whether bifurcating commission agents’ function into pre-clearance and post-clearance of goods as done by lower authorities is clearly not permissible inasmuch as commission agents’ service is one integrated service and, therefore, assessee was entitled to benefit of Cenvat credit on entire amount of commission paid by it to commission agent - Held, yes [Para 3]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of taxable service - Stay Order - Period from April, 2008 to March, 2009 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture and trading of pharmaceuticals - Department argued that credit of input services used in relation to trading could not be availed - HELD : Trading activity was not a taxable service under section 65 of Finance Act, 1994 during material period; therefore, there was no question of payment of service tax on that activity by manufacturing units - Prima facie, manufacturing units could not have been expected to maintain separate accounts - Hence, stay was granted [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]ST : CENVAT - Trading activity was not an exempt service under rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit rules, 2004 prior to 1-4-2011; therefore, prima facie, there was no requirement to maintain separate accounts or payment under rule 6 on that activity by manufacturing units

Cenvat credit - Trading activity - Common inputs and input services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Input services were attributable to trading activity - Assessee undertook taxable services and trading activity - Issue regarding input services used for trading activity covered by decisions in Ruchika Global Interlinks v. CESTAT 2017 (5) G.S.T.L. 225 (Mad.) and Lally Automobiles (P.) Ltd. v. Commr. (Adjudication) C.Ex. 2018 (17) G.S.T.L. 422 (Del.) - Since assessee was not paying Service Tax on trading activity, credit of services vis-a-vis input services could only be taken on pro rata basis as per formula stipulated in Rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Confirmation of demand with interest invoking extended period of limitation on Cenvat credit availed on trading activity was to be upheld - Since Cenvat credit and applicable interest were paid much before issuance of show-cause notice, assessee was entitled to benefit of 25 per cent of penalty imposed - Order to that extent was to be modified Rule 9(e), read with rule 6 and rule 15 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 7 to 9] [In favour of assessee]  Cenvat credit - Input service distributor - Availment of credit prior to registration as Input Service Distributor (ISD) was only a procedural irregularity - Cenvat credit could not be denied - Demand to that extent was to be set aside [Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 10 and 11] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted service - Assessee had used steel and cement in pre-stressed cement for manufacturing of exempted products, as well as dutiable products without maintaining a separate account of inputs and availed Cenvat credit on inputs - Revenue denied benefit on ground that no separate account was maintained and, accordingly, demanded 10 per cent of total value of exempted final goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) after taking into account fact that assessee had reversed Cenvat credit taken on inputs used in manufacture of exempted goods, held that assessee was not required to pay 10 per cent of price of exempted final goods - Whether in view of decision of Tribunal in Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 14 STT 328 (Bom.), impugned order did not suffer from any infirmity - Held, yes [Para 5]

Rule 3, read with rule 6, of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - General - Period April, 2004 to March, 2005 - Whether trading activity merely involves purchases and sales and cannot be considered as a service/exempted service - Held, yes - Whether in cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994 and, thus, assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor an excisable goods - Held, yes - Whether, in such a case, once in a quarter or once in a six months, quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities was to be deducted according to standard accounting principles and balance only will be availed for purpose of payment of service tax of output service - Held, yes [Para 8]

I. Rule 6 of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 read with sections 65(25) and 67, of the Finance Act, 1994 - Valuation of taxable services - Inclusion of Reimbursements - Period from 16-10-1998 to 18-4-2006 - As per rule 6(8), value of Clearing and Forwarding Agent services would gross amount of remuneration or commission (by whatever name called) paid to such agent by client - Phrase 'by whatever name called' must necessarily have some link or reference or nature to receipt of remuneration or commission and, therefore, gross amount referred to in rule 6(8) would apply to receipts of such sum, which would bear character of remuneration or commission - If a receipt is for reimbursing expenditure incurred for purpose of providing services, mere act of reimbursement cannot be regarded as having character of remuneration or commission [Paras 7 to 9] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : If a receipt is for reimbursing expenditure incurred for purpose of providing services, such 'reimbursement' cannot be regarded as having character of 'remuneration or commission' received by clearing and forwarding agent and, therefore, same is not includible in value in erstwhile Rule 6(8) of Service Tax Rules

Rule 2(1), read with rules 2(d), 2(e), and 6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Commission Agent's Services - Assessee procured contract of Rs. 41.5 crore to supply pre-heaters to DC out of which goods valuing Rs. 5.5 crore were supplied out of own manufacture and balance were supplied out of purchases from market - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on commission in respect of procurement of said contract - Department allowed credit in respect of commission relating to manufacturing activity of Rs. 5.5 crore but denied credit of commission relating to 'trading activity' of Rs. 36 crore - HELD : Assessee availed credit on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products and therefore, assessee is not eligible to avail credit on commission paid on trading goods - Hence, denial of credit relating to Rs. 36 crore was in consonance with rule 2(l) [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Service tax paid on commission in respect of trading goods is not eligible for credit because same is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products  Cenvat Credit : Where credit is taken in respect of trading activity and said fact was not disclosed by assessee, same can be denied invoking extended period

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Position prior to 1-3-2008 - Assessee, a provider of both exempted service and taxable service, did not maintain separate accounts in respect of credit attributable to input and input services used in providing such taxable and exempted output services - Assessee utilised credit of inputs and input services only up to 20 per cent of service tax payable on output services as per rule 6(3)(c) - Department alleged that as credit of capital goods and inputs/input services was not separately shown by assessee, assessee had violated provisions of rule 6(3)(c) - HELD : In view of judgment in assessees own case in Idea Cellular Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 19 STT 423 (New Delhi - CESTAT) in Idea Cellular Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 19 STT 423 (New Delhi - CESTAT), credit of capital goods was not hit by restriction under rule 6(3)(c) - As prima facie case was in favour of assessee, requirement of pre-deposit waived [Paras 4 and 5] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 9 , read with rule 5 , of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Documents on which credit may be taken - Assessee, a commission agent, took credit of services of sub-agents - Department denied credit on grounds that : (a) invoice of sub-agents did not indicate all particulars; (b) there was no agreement between sub-agents and assessee, as copy of agreement was given only after issue of notice; (c) there was no methodology for quantification of commission - HELD : As regards objection (a), lower authority could call for details of purchase order and other correspondence and terms of understanding between assessee and sub-agents, and verify nature of payment effected on such services - Objection (b) is also not tenable, as genuineness of agreement/documents has not been disputed - Objection (c) is also not tenable, as long as commission paid is not disputed, which can even be verified from bank statements or certificates from bank - Hence, matter was remanded back for verification of these aspects [Paras 8 to 10] [In favour of assessee/Matter remanded]Cenvat Credit : Credit of commission paid to sub-agents cannot be denied, merely because there was no methodology to determine commission, so long as commission paid is not disputed and details are verifiable from bank certificates.  Cenvat Credit : In case of allegation as to non-realisation of remittances for export of services, lower authority should examine whether any action was taken under FEMA against assessee; in absence of any proceedings under FEMA, it cannot be presumed that remittances of export are not co-relatable.

Rule 2(1), read with Rule 2(d) and Rules 2(e) and 6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Commission Agent's Services - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on commission in respect of procurement of orders in respect of 'manufacturing activity' as well as 'trading activity' - Department allowed credit in respect of commission relating to manufacturing activity but denied credit of commission relating to 'trading activity' on ground that it was ineligible for credit - HELD : Assessee availed credit on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products and therefore, assessee is not eligible to avail credit on commission paid on trading goods - Activities not integrally connected with business of manufacture of final products would not qualify as input service - Hence, credit was rightly denied [Paras 5 to 9] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Service tax paid on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products, is not eligible for input service credit

Rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input services - Commission agent's service - Service rendered by overseas commission agent by canvassing and procuring orders and following up payments - Input service - Credit admissible (Para 6)

Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - In case of an assessee engaged in manufacture of excisable goods as well as trading activity, credit of telephone services, etc. used commonly in relation to both was required to be reversed pro rata [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Assessee utilized service tax credit for exempted as well as non-exempted category of services provided to it - Revenue denied credit on ground that assessee had not maintained separate records for services received by it for exempted and for non-exempted categories and, therefore, in terms of rule 6(3)(c), assessee was entitled to utilize only 20 per cent of amount of credit - Admittedly, assessee had availed service tax credit on services mentioned in rule 6(5) - Whether once it was established that service tax credit availed was on services as mentioned in rule 6(5), in view of clear language of rule 6(5), rule 6(3) would not be applicable and credit of entire/whole amount of service tax was allowable to assessee - Held, yes [Para 6]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period from March, 2005 to August, 2005 - Assessee was providing telephone services (both landline and mobile) - Adjudicating authority found that assessee had availed Cenvat credit on certain input services which were used for rendering both taxable and exempted output services and accordingly, in terms of rule 6(3)(c) raised demand of equivalent to credit taken in excess of 20 per cent of tax liability - Assessee submitted that it had separate registration for its mobile telephone unit and that as this unit was rendering only taxable services, there was no question of rule 6(3)(c) being invoked against it - Whether, in view of assessee’s submissions, prima facie, mobile unit of assessee with separate registration with department was liable to be treated as one service tax assessee distinct from landline unit which had separate registration with department for service tax purpose - Held, yes - Whether therefore, output service rendered by landline unit could not enter into reckoning where a demand was sought to be raised on mobile unit under rule 6(3)(c) and, therefore, matter was required to be remanded to Commissioner for fresh decision in light of plea of separate registration raised by assessee - Held, yes [Para 2]

II. rule 6, read with rule 2(d),  and rule 2(e), of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit -  Exempted and Dutiable Goods or Exempted and Taxable Services, Obligation of assessee - Rule 6 applies only where a manufacturer manufactures both excisable dutiable final products and also manufactures excisable exempted goods - Rule 6 is applicable only if a manufacturer : (i) avails CENVAT credit on any input (as defined in section 2(k)); and (ii) manufactures such final products which are chargeable to duty; and (c) also manufactures such final products which are exempted goods - Only if said conditions are satisfied, it is necessary for manufacturer to maintain separate accounts or pay amounts as specified in rule 6(3) [Paras 21 to 25] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Revenue proceeded against assessee on ground that it had not maintained separate accounts in respect of goods manufactured by it carrying nil rate of duty as well as rate of duty as required under rule 6 - Accordingly, assessee was directed to deposit 8 per cent of value of finally exempted goods - Assessee contended that it had reversed credit and, therefore, it was not required to pay 8 per cent of value - Whether in view of such reversal, impugned demand could not be sustained - Held, yes [Para 10]

Rule 6, read with rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Stay order - Assessee, a constituent of a company, entered into an agreement for sale of telecommunication equipments - Invoice for telecommunication equipments was issued from Corporate Office and invoice for services was issued from assessee-branch office - Assessee took (i) Cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in provisions of taxable output services as also (ii) cenvat credit distributed/allotted by Corporate Office i.e., Input service distributor (ISD) - Commissioner took a view that sale of telecommunication equipments from Corporate Office was a trading activity and not a taxable service, hence, exempted within meaning of rule 2(e); Commissioner held that assessee had to avail Cenvat credit only to extent of 20 per cent of amount of service tax payable and, resultantly, excess credit taken by assessee was to be recovered - However, there was no finding that assessee had provided taxable as well as exempted services - Whether, prima facie, trading activity of selling telecommunication equipments did not constitute exempted services for assessee to come within mischief of rule 6(3)(c) and, therefore, demand raised by Commissioner in that regard, prima facie, was not sustainable - Held, yes - Whether further, prima facie, adjudicating authority had no jurisdiction to raise question of admissibility or otherwise of impugned credit allotted by input service distributor and availed of by assessee, as eligibility or otherwise of service tax credit has to be examined at end of ISD only - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, there would be total waiver of pre-deposit requirement - Held, yes [Stay granted]

Rule 5 , read with rule 2(e) and rule 6 , of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Refund of - Period prior to 1-10-2014 - Assessee was a commission agent for foreign companies, which amounted to export of service - Assessee took credit of services received from sub-agents and claimed refund of such credit - Department denied refund on ground that export amounted to 'exempt service', as bank realisation certificates were not correlated with export invoices - HELD : Under rule 6(8), export of services will not be an exempted service, if conditions prescribed under clauses (a) and (b) of said rule are satisfied; however, said aspect was not examined - In event of non-realisation of remittances for export of services, which is also governed under FEMA, lower authority should have examined whether any action was taken under FEMA against assessee - In absence of any such proceedings, it cannot be presumed that remittances of export are not co-relatable - Hence, matter was remanded back for verification of these aspects [Paras 11  12] [In favour of assessee/Matter remanded]

Rule 6  of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Common imputs and input services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Assessment year 2008-09 - During year 2008-09, assessee provided taxable as well as exempted services - Adjudicating Authority having found that assessee had not maintained separate accounts, as required under rule 6(2), confirmed demand as per provisions of rule 6(3)(i) on value of exempted services - Commissioner (Appeals) having noticed that assessee had reversed proportionate credit on value of exempted services subsequently with interest held that assessee had satisfied conditions in view of retrospective amendment carried out to provisions of rule 6 by Finance Act, 2010 and accordingly set aside impugned order - Against impugned order, revenue filed appeal and assessee filed cross objections - Whether in view of fact that Commissioner (Appeals) had already allowed benefit and further in view of complexity of nature, as a special case, assessee would be eligible to reverse proportionate credit attributable to clearances to Jammu  Kashmir State alone for year 2008-09 subject to condition that it would file a letter rectifying deficiencies in letter of option given by it earlier as contemplated in rule 6(3A) - Held, yes [Paras 17 and 18][In favour of assessee]CENVAT: Where assessee, during year 2008-09, provided taxable as well as exempted services and Adjudicating Authority having noticed that it had not maintained separate accounts confirmed demand on value of exempted services and further Appellate Authority having noticed that assessee had reversed proportionate credit on value of exempted services subsequently with interest, set aside impugned order, assessee would be eligible to reverse proportionate credit attributable to clearances to Jammu  Kashmir State alone

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 - Cenvat credit - respondents did not maintain separate account of inputs used in manufacture of dutiable and exempted final products and cleared exempted final product on payment of 8% amount - credit not to be reversed even in respect of inputs exclusively used in manufacture of exempted final product only - Revenue's appeals dismissed (Para 6)

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Period 2013-2017 - Assessee was registered and holding service tax registration certificate for provider/recipient of work contract, Design Services, Business Support Services etc., and were availing the credit of the tax paid on "input services" under provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Revenue having noticed that assessee was also engaged in trading of mutual fund units and same being exempted services, raised demand of 6% of value of exempted services - Whether assessee was not engaged in business of trading in securities (Mutual Funds) but investment in Mutual Fund was an investment activity and gain from return of Mutual Fund was taxed as capital gain and not as business income and, therefore, Rule 6(3) was not applicable; impugned demand of 6% of value of exempted services was not sustainable - Held, yes [Para 5] [ In favour of assessee]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where assessee was not engaged in business of trading in securities (Mutual Funds) but investment in Mutual Fund was an investment activity and gain from return of Mutual Fund was taxed as capital gain and not as business income, Rule 6(3) was not applicable

Rule 2(p) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Output service - Assessee took Cenvat credit of service tax paid on GTA service and utilized same for payment of service tax on commission paid to its foreign agent for procurement of export orders, under head business auxiliary services - Adjudicating authority held that service tax paid on GTA service could not be taken as credit by assessee as it was not paying any excise duty on its final product and also was not providing any output service - Commissioner (Appeals) held that prior to omission of Explanation to rule 2(P) with effect from 18-4-2006, not only credit can be taken by a person who is liable to pay service tax but also same can be utilized for payment of excise duty/service tax - However, revenue contended that in view of decision of Tribunal in ITC Ltd. v. CCE [2011] 31 STT 463/11 taxmann.com 166 (Bang - CESTAT), even prior to 19-4-2006 assessee was required to pay service tax on GTA service received by him in cash but not through Cenvat credit - Whether matter was to be remanded to Commissioner (Appeals) for fresh decision - Held, yes [Para 5] [Matter remanded]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted service - Period 1-6-2001 to 30-10-2006 - Whether where a manufacture of final product has not opted to maintain separate inventory and accounts in respect of inputs intended to be used in manufacture of dutiable final product and those intended to be used in manufacture of exempted final product and has opted to pay to revenue, such amount (being a percentage of sale price of exempted goods) as prescribed under sub-rule (3) of rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2001/2002/2004, it shall not be necessary for him to reverse any CENVAT credit taken on inputs which were used in manufacture of the exempted final product - Held, yes [Para 9] Circulars & Notifications : Notification Nos. 3/2001 - CE, 6/2002 - CE and 6/2006-CE

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Period 1-9-1999 to 31-12-2002 - Assessee had entered into contracts with clients for receiving their goods, warehousing same and forwarding them to buyers - Said contracts also provided for clients (principal) directly sending goods to buyers - Service tax was demanded from assessee on commission received by it in above cases, under category of ‘Clearing and forwarding agents’ - Whether cases of transport of materials directly to buyers by principal against orders procured by assessee did not attract service tax under head ‘C&F agents’ - Held, yes - Whether where goods were received by assessee and forwarded to buyers on instructions of principal, service tax had to be paid by assessee - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned order was to be set aside and matter was to be remanded to original authority to redetermine liability of assessee to pay service tax - Held, yes [Para 3.1] Circulars & Notifications : CBEC Circular No. B43/7/97-TRU, dated 11-7-1997

II. Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Commission Agent's Services - Position prior to 1-4-2008 - Commission paid to agents causing sale of final product cannot be termed as expenditure on sales promotion - Such commission cannot be stated to be a service used directly or indirectly in or in relation to manufacture of final products or clearance of final products from place of removal - Activity of commission agent did not also fall under 'activity relating to business such as..', as it did not have any similarity to illustrative activities viz., 'accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security' in any manner - Hence, CENVAT credit would not be admissible in respect of commission paid to foreign agents [Paras 5.2(vii), 5.2(viii)  5.2(ix)] [In favour of revenue]

Section 194Q of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with rule 37BA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Deduction of tax at source - Purchase of goods (Commission agent) - Assessment year 2023-24 - Assessee was a commission agent - It claimed TDS credit of certain amount - Assessing Officer granted TDS credit only to extent of certain amount and disallowed balance amount - In case of Yagneswari General Traders v. ITO in ITA No. 39/Viz/2024 dated 18/03/2024, it was held that where assessee acted only as an agent and not as a principal, its turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of its principals, and thus assessee was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Whether, following same, assessee being a commission agent was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Held, yes [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : CBDT Circular No. 452, dated 17-03-1986

Cenvat Credit -  Common inputs used for both dutiable and exempted goods-Failure to maintain separate accounts - Credit on insurance service used both for dutiable and exempted goods - Reversed by assessee - Nothing surviving in demand - Demand set aside - Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Para 7]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Credit on insurance service used both for dutiable and exempted goods reversed by assessee, demand on account of failure to maintain separate account set aside

Cenvat Credit -  Common inputs used for both dutiable and exempted goods-Failure to maintain separate accounts - Credit on insurance service used both for dutiable and exempted goods - Reversed by assessee - Nothing surviving in demand - Demand set aside - Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Para 7]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period 1-9-2004 to 29-2-2008 - Assessee was engaged in providing various output services - Service tax was demanded from assessee on ground that it had availed Cenvat credit in respect of services which were used for providing services in J&K State and SEZ which were exempted during relevant time, and while paying service tax it was required to utilize only 20 per cent of credit available for payment of service tax on input service in accordance with provisions of rule 6(3)(c) - Assessee contended that rule 6(3)(c) was not applicable to instant case as it had not taken credit of service tax paid on all common input services - However, no verification had been conducted with respect to claim made by assessee - Whether matter was to be remitted to Commissioner for fresh consideration - Held, yes [Para 5]

Section 194Q of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with rule 37BA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Deduction of tax at source - Purchase of goods (Commission agent) - Assessment year 2023-24 - Assessee was a commission agent - It claimed TDS credit of certain amount - Assessing Officer granted TDS credit only to extent of certain amount and disallowed balance amount - In case of Yagneswari General Traders v. ITO in ITA No. 39/Viz/2024 dated 18/03/2024, it was held that where assessee acted only as an agent and not as a principal, its turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of its principals, and thus assessee was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Whether, following same, assessee being a commission agent was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Held, yes [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a licensed chillies commission agent, acted only as an agent and not as a principal, its turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of its principal, and thus it was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Stay order - Assessee was providing different services - It was also involved in activity of sale of parts relating to gas turbines - Revenue found that (i) assessee was availing Cenvat credit on service tax paid on common input services which had been used by it for taxable output service as well as sale of parts relating to gas turbines and (ii) that assessee was not maintaining separate records for common input services - Revenue held that assessee was required to utilize only 20 per cent of service tax payable from Cenvat credit and having not done so, assessee had violated provisions of rule 6(3)(c) - Accordingly, revenue raised demand from assessee - Assessee sought for waiver of a part of pre-deposit contending that it had already reversed amount in respect of Cenvat credit on common input service - Whether since such reversal was sufficient for hearing appeal application for waiver of a part of pre-deposit was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 6] [Stay granted]

Rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Periods 2004-05 and 2005-06 - Assessee, a manufacturer, paid service tax on sales commission given to its sales agents under category of ‘Business auxiliary services’ - Said sales commission was only in respect of sales made through commission agents - Whether assessee was eligible to Cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services of sales agents - Held, yes [Para 5.4]

Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods - Assessee has option either to maintain separate account of common inputs used in manufacture of dutiable and exempted final product or to pay 8% amount on exempted final product even though inputs are capable of being accounted separately - appeal allowed (Para 4)

Section 65(25) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Period 2000-04 - Whether a clearing and forwarding agent (CFA) receives commission only and that too against a service provided by it - Held, yes - Whether, where rental income, distribution charges, warehousing charges and transportation charges were collected by assessee under separate contracts, they would not represent charges for CFA services - Held, yes - Whether since Commissioner’s order suffered from various defects, matter was to be remanded for readjudication - Held, yes [Para 6] Circulars and Notifications : Board’s Circular F.No. B43/1/97-TRU, dated 6-6-1997

Section 65, read with section 76, of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Period 16-7-1997 to 31-10-1998 and 1-11-1998 to 31-8-1999 - Whether for a service provided by clearing and forwarding agent to be taxable, such service has to be relatable to clearing and forwarding operations and can be in any manner and it is not necessary that said agent must deal with goods directly - Held, yes - RZC were procuring orders for various tobacco products manufactured by appellant-company from dealers and passing on same to appellants, from whom they were receiving commission in lieu of service so provided - Whether said services were definitely connected with clearing and forwarding of various tobacco products being manufactured by appellants - Held, yes - Whether RZC were a ‘clearing and forwarding agent’ of appellants and service provided by them were liable to tax - Held, yes - Whether since appellants had already been penalised, there was no justification for imposition of separate penalty upon their director - Held, yes [Para 9] Notifications and Circulars - Trade Notice No. 59 of 1999, dated 4-10-1999 issued by Mumbai Commissionerate-I

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit Common inputs or input services for taxable and exempt final products - Central Excise (Removal of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty for Manufacture of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2001 - Notification No. 4/2006-CE dt. 1.3.2006 - Spent sulphuric acid - arising at intermediate stage of manufacture of final product - cleared under Rules of 2001 in terms of notification - not clearance at nil rate of duty or without payment of duty - amount in terms of Rule 6(3)(b) is not payable, though separate account of inputs is not maintained - Revenue's appeal dismissed. (Para 6)

Section 68 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with rule 6 of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 - Payment of service tax - Period December, 1999 to November, 2003 - Assessee, a clearing and forwarding agent, paid service tax on ‘service charges’ received by it from its clients for clearing and forwarding (C&F) services - Revenue claimed that assessee should have paid tax on amounts collected from such clients towards expenses incurred in connection with said service - Whether in view of decision of Tribunal in case of Sangamitra Services Agency v. CCE [Final Order No. 902 of 2007, dated 24-7-2007], impugned order of revenue was not justified - Held, yes [Para 3]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period June 2005 to October 2006 - Assessee, a manufacturer, was registered as an ‘input service distributor’ - It received various services and distributed same to various factories - It utilized input service credit availed at various factories for payment of excise duty liability of various factories on final products manufactured by them - Revenue denied said credit on ground that though input service credit was availed by assessee for duty paid as well as exempted final products, but it had not maintained separate records for inputs used in manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods - Whether since assessee had not maintained, separate accounts of input service separately for dutiable as well as non-dutiable exempted goods, in view of rule 6 only option left with assessee was either to reverse proportionate input service credit or to reverse 10 per cent of value of exempted final product at time of clearance - Held, yes - Whether assessee was not entitled to avail input service credit in full but it had to reverse input service credit proportionately availed for exempted final product - Held, yes [Paras 15 &16]

Section 194Q of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Purchase of goods (Commission agent) - Assessment year 2023-24 - Assessee was an individual and a licensed chillies commission agent - Assessee claimed credit for entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Assessing Officer granted TDS credit only to extent of certain amount and disallowed TDS credit of balance amount - It was noted that in case of Yagneswari General Traders v. ITO in ITA No. 39/Viz/2024 dated 18/03/2024, it was held that where assessee acted only as an agent and not as a principal and its turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of its principals, it was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Whether, following same, assessee being a commission agent was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Held, yes [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : CBDT Circular No. 452, dated 17-03-1986.

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 - Storage of inputs outside the factory of the manufacturer - Cenvat credit - Hexane - used in manufacture of dutiable final product (refined vegetable oil) and exempted by product (de-oiled cake) - in view of the process involved separate account of hexane can not be maintained - Rule 6(3) is not attracted when it is impossible to maintain separate account of common input - moreover, respondents have reversed credit taken on hexane - 8% or 10% amount not payable on de-oiled cake - Revenue's appeal dismissed (Para 4)

III. Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 105 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (Telescoping) – Assessment year 2023-24 – AO alleged that assessee had procured accommodation RTGS entries through traders and paid commission at rate of 4 per cent on RTGS amounts aggregating to about Rs. 1188 crores, and accordingly made addition of about Rs. 47.52 crores under section 69C – Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition by granting telescoping against estimated profits and treated RTGS-linked amounts as sales made through traders and recorded in books rather than accommodation entries – Tribunal observed that addition was based only on statement of an employee which was never reaffirmed by directors or principal officer of assessee-company – Tribunal further observed that once sales made to traders were treated as recorded sales, allegation regarding accommodation RTGS entries had no basis – Whether therefore, no addition could be sustained on account of alleged commission for obtaining such accommodation entries – Held, yes [Para 32] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, read with section 35F of Central Excise Act, 1944 - Cenvat Credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Stay order - Period October 2004 to September 2005 - Duty was demanded from assessee under rule 6(3), on ground that it did not maintain separate accounts and inventory in respect of inputs and input services used in, or in relation to manufacture of exempted final product and those used in, or in relation to manufacture of dutiable final product - However, assessee stated that it did maintain separate accounts and inventory, details whereof had been furnished - However, Commissioner had not accepted same to be correct accounting and confirmed demand - Whether since Commissioner had neither stated which was correct accounting, nor was there any indication in impugned order as to provisions relating to method to be adopted for separate accounts for inputs and input services by manufacturers of excisable goods and providers of output services, there would be waiver of pre-deposit requirement and stay on recovery in respect of above demand - Held, yes [Paras 1 & 2] [Stay granted]

Section 194Q of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Purchase of goods (Commission agent) - Assessment year 2023-24 - Assessee was an individual and a licensed chillies commission agent - Assessee claimed credit for entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Assessing Officer granted TDS credit only to extent of certain amount and disallowed TDS credit of balance amount - It was noted that in case of Yagneswari General Traders v. ITO in ITA No. 39/Viz/2024 dated 18/03/2024, it was held that where assessee acted only as an agent and not as a principal and its turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of its principals, it was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Whether, following same, assessee being a commission agent was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q - Held, yes [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a licensed chillies commission agent, acted only as an agent and not as a principal, his turnover would include only gross commission and not sales effected on behalf of his principals and thus, he was eligible to get credit of entire amount deducted as tax at source under section 194Q

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Period 2012-17 - Appellant was providing Commercial Training and Coaching Services and they had also invested in mutual funds and have earned profit during years 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17 which they have shown as under head 'other income' - Department considered investment in mutual fund as trading in mutual funds and issued a notice on presumption that appellant is providing exempted services which is trading in mutual funds and has not maintained separate records for common input services availed in providing output services and exempted activity i.e. trading and hence liable to pay 6 per cent/7 per cent of amount of exempted services - However, it is found that 'trading' has not been defined under service Tax but in context of securities,'trading' means an activity where a person is engaged in selling goods and occupy for purpose of making profit but certainly trading is different from redemption of mutual fund units - In instant case appellant cannot transfer mutual fund units to third party and give only by redemption to mutual fund because appellant is not permitted to trade mutual fund unit in absence of a license from SEBI - There is a restriction on right to transfer unit and appellant cannot transfer units to any other person - Further, appellant cannot be termed as service provider because he only makes an investment in mutual fund and earn profit from it which is shown in Books of Account under head 'other income' - Whether therefore, question of invoking Rule 6 did not arise and Department had wrongly invoked provisions of Rule 6(3) demanding reversal of credit on exempted service - Held, yes [Para 5]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where appellant only made investments in mutual fund and earned profit from it which was shown in Books of Account under head 'other income', he could not have been termed as 'service provider', hence, department had wrongly invoked provisions of rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 demanding reversal of credit on exempted services

facts.text:
The appellant was engaged in providing maintenance and repair services and commissioning and installation service of RO systems. It was observed that the appellants were availing the credit on advertising, security, courier, telephone and banking services which were not entirely used in providing ‘maintenance and repair’ services, but also used in trading activity and, therefore, credit of input services which were entirely used in trading activity was not available to the appellants for payment of service tax. The amounts of service tax payable for two half-yearly period were Rs. 34,143 and Rs. 27,315. Total Cenvat credit available to the appellants was Rs. 6,828, i.e., 20 per cent of Rs. 34,143 as per rule 6(3) and Rs. 8,877, i.e., 35 per cent of Rs. 25,363 as per rule 3(5). The balance amount was to be paid by the appellants in cash only.

The appellants had adjusted the service tax amount fully from Cenvat credit and wrongly availed Cenvat credit of Rs. 43,801.

The lower authorities claimed that appellant should have maintained separate accounts in respect of input services used for trading activity which were liable to service tax and the Cenvat credit availed by the appellant was demanded.

The assessee was awarded a contract by the State Government under the Sujalam Sufalam Spreading Canal Pipe Line Project for laying pipelines. The assessee by considering the said service as falling under the category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ paid the service tax on the same after availing the benefit of Modvat credit and filed due service tax returns with the department. Based upon the enquiries conducted and investigations made, the revenue entertained a view that the above laying down of pipelines did not amount to providing services under the category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’, and the service being non-taxable, the assessee was not entitled to avail the Cenvat credit. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee raising demand by invoking the provisions of rule 6(3)(c), which provide for restriction for utilizing of Cenvat credit to the extent of 20 per cent only, in the event of non-maintenance of separate accounts for inputs and input services used for both exempted and taxable services. On adjudication, the Commissioner held that inasmuch the services of laying down pipelines had been held to be a non-taxable service, the same could not be equated with exempted services and, as such, rule 6(3)(c) could not be invoked. He further held that as the assessee had maintained separate Cenvat credit accounts project wise, the allegation of maintenance of a common credit account was incorrect and, as such, rule 6(3)(c) had no applicability. He, accordingly, dropped the demand. Though in the instant appeal the assessee did not dispute service tax liability, yet challenged impugned order on ground of limitation.

The assessee was registered with the Department for providing taxable services falling under the categories of Consulting Engineer, Maintenance or Repair Services and, Erection, Commissioning and Installation Services. It had entered into a contract with ‘B’ for supply and installation of BTS, Microcell and other Microwave equipments for telecommunication network. The invoice for the supply of telecommunication equipment was issued from its corporate office and the invoice for service portion was issued from its branches. The assessee was taking the Cenvat credit of tax paid on the input services used in the provision of taxable output services as well as the Cenvat credit distributed by its Corporate Office (i.e., input service distributor). It was noticed that the Cenvat credit distributed by the corporate office also pertaining to the input services used exclusively for the procurement of telecommunication equipments. The revenue took a view that the assessee was engaged in the sale of telecommunication equipments from its Corporate Office which was a trading activity and a non-taxable service outside the scope of the Act. Therefore, the trading activity fell within the meaning of exempted services as defined under rule 2(e). According to the revenue as the assessee had not maintained separate records at its Corporate Office for the input services commonly used in the taxable output services provided from the branches or in the exempted services provided from the Corporate Office, it was liable to utilize the Cenvat credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding twenty per cent of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services in terms of rule 6(3)(c). However, the assessee had utilized the entire Cenvat credit available with it towards the discharge of service tax liability on the taxable output services. Thus, the Commissioner confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had utilized excess Cenvat credit which was liable to be recovered from it. Besides that, the Commissioner also confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had wrongly availed of the Cenvat credit on insurance service, foreign consultancy service, etc., which were used exclusively in the provision of exempted services and, were utilized towards payment of service tax. The Commissioner also confirmed the demand disallowing the Cenvat credit on the services, viz., flower arrangements, garden maintenance, outdoor catering, real estate agent’s services for residential accommodation of its employees distributed by its Corporate Office on the ground that same could not be termed as input services defined under rule 2(l).

On application :

The assessee had centralized service tax registration for providing various taxable services. It was also involved in activity of sale of parts relating to gas turbines. On verification of its records, the revenue noticed that (i) the assessee was availing Cenvat credit on the service tax paid on the input services, i.e., telephones, courier, rent-a-cab, clearing services, outdoor catering, Chartered Accountant services, business support services, manpower supply and recruitment service, etc., (ii) that these were all common inputs which had been used by it for taxable output service as well as sale of parts relating to gas turbines. The revenue, accordingly, issued a show cause alleging that the assessee was not maintaining separate records for the input services commonly used in the taxable services as well as in the sale of gas turbines and, hence, it was required to utilize only 20 per cent of the service tax payable from the Cenvat Credit and having not done so, and having utilized the Cenvat credit in excess of 20 per cent it had violated the provisions of rule 6(3)(c) and, accordingly, raised demand. The adjudicating authority confirmed the demand. The assessee filed instant application seeking waiver of a part of pre-deposit amount contending that the amount of the Cenvat credit taken on the common inputs attributable to the services of sale of parts of gas turbines had already been reversed by it and, as such, there was no need for any confirmation of the demand.

The assessee was engaged in providing various output services. The Commissioner confirmed service tax demand for relevant period on the assessee on the ground that it had availed Cenvat credit in respect of services which were used for providing services in J&K State and SEZ which were exempted during relevant time, and while paying the service tax, it was required to utilize only 20 per cent of the credit available for payment of service tax on the input service in accordance with the provisions of rule 6(3)(c ). Rule 6(3A) was amended from 1-4-2008 and he was ignorant about these provisions and continued to follow the old provision which restricted utilisation of Cenvat credit to the extent of 20 per cent.

Input services of insurance and car are used for business and expenses are reflected in the profit & loss account of the firm.

Order-in-Original and Order-in-Appeal travelled beyond the show-cause notice to the extent that the show-cause notice only sought to deny credit on the bills which were not in the name of the firm.

Extended period of limitation cannot be invoked in the absence of mens rea.

On appeal:

Facts

The assessee was a manufacturer of Grinding Media and it had :

procured orders from their purchasers Associate Cement Companies (hereinafter referred to as ACC);

forwarded the said order to their subsidiary company viz., Well Cast Steel Ltd (hereinafter referred to as WSL);

goods were delivered by WSL directly to ACC and raised the invoice in name of the assessee denoting therein 4 per cent CST and a discount amount for such sale.

Department demanded service tax on allegedly received commission by assessee classifying same under 'Business Auxiliary Services'.

The assessee argued that :

the entire transaction is of trading and

they have not acted as a commission agent ; and

entire issue is hit by limitation.

Assessee's Arguments

The goods in question were consigned by the WSL directly to ACC in Jharkhand.

The assessee being manufacturer of Grinding Media was having capacity constraint hence got the order manufactured from its own subsidiary company.

As per provisions of section 6(2) of Central Sales Tax Act, second sale can be effected by transfer of documents of titles to such goods during their movement of goods from one state to another. WSL directly delivered the goods to the customers of assessee that raised commercial invoices on the assessees' name giving him discount. Transit sale is accepted form of sale for claiming exemption from payment of CST. There is no specific condition in section 6(2) of CST Act by which exemption can be disallowed in the case of transit sales on the ground that sales are made to pre-determined buyer. In the entire transaction, the only thing that requires determination is whether the transfer of property in goods took place while the goods were in transit or not; in the given case, it is so. Benefit of section 6(2) of the CST Act cannot be denied for subsequent sale made to pre-determined buyer is the law settled by the apex court.

The assessee and WSL procured requisite valid statutory documents, i.e., E-1 Form and C-Form for claiming benefit of payment of CST under section 6(2) of the CST Act from the sales tax authorities and the said transactions have been accepted by the sales tax authorities and completed the assessments from time to time holding that there was an interstate sale. ACC the ultimate purchaser has issued C-Forms to the assessee which has been produced before the authorities.

It is the burden on the revenue to establish that assessee had provided taxable services which fall under the category of Marketing/Promoting of Goods, which has not been discharged by the revenue in the case in hand.

Discount given cannot be considered as commission.

At the most, there may have been a breach of provisions of CST Act and may not have service tax angle and definitely not a Business Auxiliary Service.

WSL had discharged Central Excise duty on the entire sale value of the goods to ACC on a price on which assessee has sold the goods, hence the same transaction cannot be taxed under Service Tax.

Revenue's Arguments

The assessee had acted as a commission agent within the definition of 'mercantile agent' as per section 2(9) of Sale of Goods Act.

The assessee having placed an order on behalf of ACC to WSL, have represented themselves as commission agent or Del Credere Agent.

The assessee had purchased the goods for their principal and supplied it in accordance with the law. Since the manufacturer is located in Karnataka and the assessee is located in Gujarat, the goods undisputedly moved from Karnataka to the purchaser who is in Jharkhand and the goods did not come to Gujarat at all. Movements of goods indicate that it was not a trading activity but an activity as mercantile agent known as commission agent as the goods are sold to the client ACC in Jharkhand, which is very evident from the fact, on reading the invoices raised by WSL which indicates direct delivery of goods to ACC Jharkhand.

Even if for argument sake, it is taken that the transactions between the assessee and WSL is a transit sale, CST should have been paid on so called sale price of WSL to assessee which is absent in the case in hand and the procedure prescribed in section 6 of CST Act, which is not done.

There are two different prices indicated on the invoices one from WSL to assessee and another from assessee to ACC. Payment of excise duty under rule 9 of the Valuation Rules does not alter the status of the assessee as the commission agent.

The entire modus operandi was unearthed only after thorough investigation and claim of the assessee as to demand hit by limitation is incorrect.

The Service-tax liability arises when there is promotion/marketing of products; which in the case in hand is very evident.

Issue Involved

The assessee-firm had availed of the Cenvat credit in terms of rule 3. The credit was disallowed by the Commissioner on the ground that the payment of service tax made by assessee under TR-6 challan could not be treated as evidence and same could not be considered as a prescribed document for the purpose of taking the Cenvat credit.
