On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee-company was assessed under section 143(3). The assessment was, however, set aside by the Commissioner under section 263 and the assessment was directed to be modified by way of additions to the total income of the amounts representing credits in 'Sales tax suspense account' and the amount lying credited in "Collector of Customers (Party) account". With regard to the deposit of sales tax appearing in the balance-sheet, the assessee contended that the assessee, at the time of sale, collected the higher sales tax which was payable by an unregistered dealer from such parties who, though registered dealers, could not produce the same later. This additional collection made for the time being was, however, to be refunded to such purchasers as and when they would furnish the requisite declaration form. The Tribunal held that the extra collection from the registered dealer treating him as unregistered dealer in the absence of declaration forms yet to forthcome, represented a deposit by the said registered dealer as caution money refundable against the declaration form eventually furnished. In such circumstances, it could not be said that such collection would form part of the trading receipts. In case of custom duty, the assessee contended that it acted as a commission agent for importing goods against letters of authority on behalf of third parties against their import licences and realized commission/service charges. The assessee received deposits against bank guarantees furnished against customs duty liability for goods so imported on behalf of the parties as per the directions of the High Court. The goods imported neither belonged to the assessee nor were they included in its turnover. As such, the provision of section 43B was not attracted. The Tribunal accepted the assessee's case and held that the said amounts could not be treated as trading receipts of the assessee.

On reference :

The assessee carried on business as commission agent of foodgrains. It purchased paddy for and on behalf of ‘S’ from ‘P’ and since ‘S’ could not make payment in time, the assessee had to make payments in cash to ‘P’ to maintain his reputation in the market. The Assessing Officer not accepting the contention of the assessee that payments had been made as commission agent and under exceptional circumstances provided in rule 6DD(j), made disallowance of those payments under section 40A(3). On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the disallowance.

On second appeal :

Tata Ltd., London and Tata Incorporated, New York, were appointed by the appellants as their buying agents and a commission of 2l/2% was paid to them for the services rendered. The issue that arises for determination is whether this commission is to be included in the assessable value of the goods. While the appellants claim that in terms of Rule 9(1)(i) of the Customs Valuation Rules, commission paid to buying agents is excluded from the assessable value of the goods, the Department contend that by raising invoices, Tata Ltd. and Tata Incorporated had lost their identity as Buying agents and are to be treated as suppliers.

Facts

The assessee gets TV sets manufactured by three manufacturers.

Three manufacturers of TV sets place orders on manufacturers of picture tubes.

The picture tubes are directly supplied by the picture tube manufacturers and payments are received from the manufacturers of TV sets directly.

The rates of picture tubes are however settled by the assessee with the supplier/manufacturers of picture tubes.

After receiving payment from the manufacturers of TV sets, manufacturers/suppliers of picture tubes pay agreed amounts as commission, to the assessee.

Department sought levy of service tax on this commission under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services'.

Issue Involved

Whether commission earned by assessee was liable to service tax under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' ?

The assessee, a rice mill, approached the regional market yard for purc- hase of rice and instead of paying cash/cheque/draft to the agent ‘K’, prepared a challan and deposited the cash in the account of ‘K’. Such challan was produced before ‘K’ and goods were purchased. The Assessing Officer on the basis of accounting entries in the books of ‘K’, noted that they had recorded the receipt by way of cash. Thus, the assessee was said to have purchased the goods by paying cash and not by way of crossed cheque/draft. Therefore, the Assessing Officer by invoking the provision of section 40A(3), disallowed the amount representing 20 per cent of the total amount paid to ‘K’. The Assessing Officer did not entertain the argument of the assessee as to the exception provided in clause (f) and clause (l) of rule 6DD. The Assessing Officer noted that ‘K’ was not an agent of assessee and he also held that the assessee did not purchase the goods from agriculturists but from ‘K’, who was a full fledged dealer and not merely an commission agent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that payment to the party by way of DD/cheque only had to be considered and if the payment was made otherwise than by cheque/draft, it was in contravention of provisions of section 40A(3). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal:

The appellant initially availed Cenvat credit on the inputs. After utilising the same in manufacture of exempted goods, it reversed the credit. However, the department on finding that the appellant had not maintained separate records regarding the various inputs, used in the manufacture of exempted as well as dutiable goods, raised demand for payment of 8 per cent of value of the clearance of the exempted goods under rule 6.

On appeal :

The assessee entered into a contract with one 'R' mainly for procurement of purchase orders from the customers for its principal 'R' on commission basis, which included to inform 'R' to dispatch the goods to the customers as per orders procured, pursuing the customers to make an early payment directly to 'R', raising debit notes to 'R' for making payment of commission, and supervising the transportation of dispatches including making necessary arrangement for transportation of the products.

The Adjudicating Authority held the contract between the assessee and 'R' was one to provide 'clearing and forwarding agent service' under section 65(105)(zzzzq).

The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the said order.

On second appeal, the Judicial Member held that the services provided by the assessee to 'R' would not fall under the category of 'clearing and forwarding agent service'. Whereas the Technical Member held that the services were in the nature of 'clearing and forwarding agent service'.

Upon such difference of opinion, the matter was referred to the Third Member, who agreed with the view taken by the Judicial Member.

On appeal to High Court by revenue:

The assessee-firm acted as a commission agent on behalf of agriculturists. Under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, if the assessee proved that it was acting on behalf of the agriculturist principals, such goods were exempted from sales tax. The assessee maintained mercantile system of accounting and its books of account indicated all details of agriculturist principals, purchasers, the quantity of goods sold, the sale proceeds and also sales tax collected from the purchasers. The sales tax collected was credited to the sales tax account and the sales tax account was debited with the payments made to Government as and when assessments were completed. At the end of the year, when the assessment was completed, if it was established that the assessee was only acting for the agriculturist principals, and if each of the agriculturist principal's turnover was less than Rs. 10,000, the amounts paid during the course of the year were refunded. The assessee, while debiting the sales tax account with the said amount of refund, credited the same to separate sales tax refund account. The assessee also maintained debtors ledger wherein each agriculturist principal's account was credited with the amount of sales tax refundable to him, so that the total of the credits given in the separate debtors ledger accounts was equal to the total of the credits standing in the refund account in the main ledger account.

The assessee claimed that the refunded sales tax amount should not be treated as trading receipt and, therefore, it should not be included in the assessee's income as it had to be made over to the agriculturist principals. The ITO, however, included the impugned amount. The Tribunal upheld the assessee's claim.

On reference :

The assessee was in the business of export of various items of iron and steel. The services of carrying and forwarding agents (C & F agents) were important in the business of export so as to make the goods available to the buyers in a short span of time as these agents possessed the required expertise in shipping the consignment to far reached places. These agents utilised the services of various shipping companies and other facilitators to whom the payments were made for respective services rendered by them in the form of Inland Haulage on export consignment.

The Assessing Officer made the addition of amount paid on account of Inland Haulage on export consignment made by the assessee to C & F agents because the assessee had not deducted TDS on the such payment as per section 194C.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition by restricting it to 10 per cent.

On cross appeal:

The appellants were engaged in the manufacture of tobacco products. They entered into an agreement with RZC, appointing the latter as their agent for the purpose of marketing their product, booking orders, managing, supervising and developing of the market. In consideration of the services rendered by the said agent, the appellants were to pay commission at the rates mentioned in the schedule to the contract on the net sale proceeds of the orders received through the agent. The appellants were issued show-cause notice, alleging that as they were availing services of RZC, who were working as ‘clearing and forwarding Agent’ on commission basis, they were liable to pay service-tax. The appellants took a stand before the adjudicating authority that the service rendered by RZC did not come under the purview of clearing and forwarding agent and the same was entirely different. As such, the question of payment of service tax did not arise. During the course of personal hearing, they contended that after the amendments in the Service Tax Rules through the Finance Bill, they should have been issued a fresh show-cause notice. The Commissioner confirmed the service tax of certain amount, not paid by the appellants. In addition, he also imposed penalty on the appellants and their director.

On appeal :

Facts

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods.

They have not maintained separate accounts in respect of inputs meant for used in the manufacture of dutiable goods and exempted goods.

They paid 10% on the value of total price of exempted final product in terms of rule 6(3)(b) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and collected the same from their customers.

The department raised demand of said recovery section 11D of Central Excise Act, 1944 along with interest and penalty.

Assessee's Arguments

Since amount recovered under rule 6(3)(b) from buyers had been paid to the department, there was no question of payment again.

Revenue's Arguments

On perusal of the invoices, it is clear that the assessee collected this amount representing as duty which is squarely covered under section 11D of the Central Excise Act. The assessee should not mention the amount in their invoices as the goods are exempted by Notification No. 3/2004-CE dated 6.1.2004.

Issue Involved

Whether section 11D would apply to amounts recovered from buyers under rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 ?

During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1962-63, BK exported tobacco to Japan and France where it was sold through the non-resident assessees, TL, a Japanese company, and SPL, a French concern. TL and SPL were operating as BK's agent and were to be paid commission on sales effected through them. BK received the entire sale proceeds in India and made credit entries in his books of account in respect of the commission payable to the TL and SPL and remitted the same to them subsequently. Though both TL and SPL rendered services as BK's selling agents outside the taxable territories, an extra feature in relation to TL was that it had been appointed as an exclusive selling agent for Japan. The ITO assessed, under section 143(3) read with section 163, the commission remitted to TL and SPL. Both the AAC and the Tribunal upheld the ITO's order. On reference, the High Court held that the assessments were not justified and set aside the Tribunal's order. On appeal by the revenue:

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and trading of synthetic fabric. During the year, it paid certain amount as agency commission and overseas commission and claimed deduction of the same. It stated that (i) the agency commission had been paid to the local agents for their services provided for introducing to overseas parties, to whom it sold the goods on principal to principal basis, (ii) in the invoices from the gross amount of sales deduction upto 12.5 per cent had been given in the name of commission, and (iii) in the books after recording gross sales, the deduction was separately recorded as overseas commission.

The Assessing Officer accepted the local commission paid, but disallowed the overseas commission under section 37(1) on the grounds that (i) no services had been rendered by the overseas agents inasmuch as no details/documents of further sales by these agents had been furnished by the assessee, (ii) from the perusal of sample contract notes furnished by the assessee with overseas agents it was evident that the same was a contract for purchase and sale of goods and commission had been merely deducted from the sales invoice at a flat rate without rendering of any services by these overseas agents, and (iii) in all such contract notes name of the Indian agents who introduced the assessee to these overseas parties had been written for which commission had already been paid by the assessee to the Indian agents. Thus, for the same invoice, commission had been paid to local agents as well as overseas agents. He, therefore, added the amount of overseas commission to the income of the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the impugned addition made by the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal:

The assessee had incurred expenditure relating to export charges for purpose of clearing and forwarding charges consisting of payments towards customs duties, transport charges, postage expenses, commission to the C&F agent and the service tax. It was also explained that all the expenses included under the head export charges except the service charges/commission to C&F agent were pertaining to reimbursement of actual expenses incurred by the C&F agent on behalf of the assessee.

The Assessing Officer (AO), during the assessment proceedings found that the assessee has debited export charges of Rs. 158 crore to the profit & loss account but not deducted the TDS. Therefore, the Assessing Officer disallowed the entire sum of Rs. 158 crore under section 40(a)(ia) and added same back to the income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that a sum of Rs. 33.76 lakhs out of the payment made to Shipping Agents was incurred towards local transportation charges and the same are excludible from the purview of deduction of tax at source under section 194C(6) and a sum of Rs. 1.23 crores was paid towards the ocean freight and TDS is not deducted since the same constitute the reimbursement of expenses. Accordingly, deleted the addition of Rs. 1.5 crores made by the Assessing Officer.

The assessee was a company engaged in the business of providing small, medium and high end enterprise solutions all over the country.

The assessee had filed its return under normal provisions. However, the return was taken up for scrutiny and the Assessing Officer had made additions to the income of assessee on both substantive and protective basis. The Assessing Officer had carried out due verification and scrutiny and was satisfied that the bifurcation/apportionment was justified and correct.

Subsequently, a notice was issued by the Commissioner under section 263. The Commissioner had issued notice by observing that commission required to be disallowed under section 36(1)(ii), as it was paid to the two Managing Directors. The Commissioner also observed that assessee had booked majority of expenses against the unit carrying out trading operations and thereby had inflated profits of the manufacturing unit for claiming exemption under section 80-IC, whereas expenses booked for eligible unit under section 80-IC were lesser than the amount as against expenses on account of trading activities.

The assessee submitted that the commission paid was duly approved by the shareholders of the company, and therefore, section 36(1)(ii) was not applicable. It was also submitted that assessee has been maintaining separate books of account for manufacturing unit receipts and expenditure which was exempt under section 80-IC and the trading activities. However, there were certain common expenses, which were to be segregated, as common expenses were not unusual, abnormal or unique in such cases. In order to carry out the said segregation, the assessee had made apportionment and the ratio thereof was indicated and informed to the Assessing Officer.

The Commissioner in his order observed that the assessment made by the Assessing officer accepting such commission payment without verifying as to whether provisions of section 36(1)(ii) are attracted was set aside on this issue with a direction to the Assessing Officer to verify as to whether the concerned directors were stake holders/shareholders in the company, entitled to profits/dividend of the company and if these facts appear to be correct then the provisions of section 36(1)(ii) may be invoked to disallow the commission payment made to the said directors and the fresh assessment order under section 143(3) may be passed accordingly.

On the second issue, the Commissioner, instead of commenting upon or giving a final finding whether aforesaid apportionment was acceptable or not, observed that it was possible that there was an attempt to inflate expenses on trading activity and an attempt might have been made to reduce actual expenses of the exempt unit. The use of the word 'possible' would indicate that there was no finding and adjudication by the Commissioner and his observations were based on mere suspicion and certainly uncertain.

On appeal, the Tribunal in its order reproduced the relevant portions of the notice under section 143(2) wherein details of the commission paid to related parties, etc. were mentioned. However, it did not notice the letters/ replies filed before the Assessing Officer and observed that the assessee was unable to furnish the details enclosed with the reply or to show that the questions in this regard were asked by the Assessing Officer.

On further appeal:

The Assessing Officer noticed that some payments exceeding Rs. 20,000 were made by the assessee in cash towards purchase of raw cotton in violation of section 40A(3). The assessee claimed that the persons to whom the disputed payments made were acting as agents of the assessee in procuring the raw cotton from the growers and, therefore, such payments are covered under rule 6DD(i), the Assessing Officer did not accept the claim of the assessee and therefore, disallowed 20 per cent of the aggregate of such payment.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) by observing either the genuineness of the transaction or the authentication of the sales tax order by the sales tax department held that the agriculture co-operative society as well as the private commission mundis to whom the assessee made payments, were acting only as agents of the assessee. He, therefore, reversed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On appeal by revenue:

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. Certain excisable goods being manufactured by the assessee were exempted from whole of the duty of excise or were chargeable to nil rate of duty of excise. The assessee had availed Cenvat credit of duty paid on inputs known as Residual Furnace Oil (RFO) being used for generation of steam within the factory premises, which was used for manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted excisable final products or the goods charged to nil rate of duty. As the assessee was not maintaining any separate records of the said inputs being used in the manufacture of exempted goods or goods charged to nil rate of duty as required under rule 6(2), the revenue took the view that it was liable to pay an amount equivalent to 8 per cent of the price of the said exempted goods in terms of rule 6(3)(b ). The Commissioner, therefore, issued a show-cause notice to the assessee raising a demand for payment of duty. Thereafter, the Commissioner vide order dated 24-7-2003 ordered for recovery of the entire amount of the Cenvat credit availed by the assessee on RFO as common input, which was used for manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods. On appeal, the Tribunal set aside the order passed by the Commissioner.

On appeal to the High Court :

■

The assessee, a Kaccha Arahtia/commission agent facilitating sale of agricultural produce for farmers, earned only commission (Adat). For AY 2022-23, he filed a return under section 139(1) declaring commission receipts of about Rs. 2.95 lakhs and claimed aggregate TDS credit of about Rs. 2.37 lakhs as per Form 26AS, comprising TDS reported under sections 194Q, 194H and 194A; TDS under section 194Q had been deducted by purchasers and was reflected in the assessee’s PAN.

■

On processing under section 143(1)(a), CPC allowed TDS credit proportionate to the commission receipts (about Rs. 0.10 lakhs) and withheld the balance on the ground that no corresponding receipts were shown other than commission.

■

In appeal, the CIT(A) confirmed denial of TDS credit insofar as section 194Q, holding under section 199 read with Rule 37BA(2) that income and TDS must be in the same person; he noted the TDS pertained to farmers’ sales and that the assessee had not filed declarations with deductors or obtained correction statements to shift the credit.

■

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal.

The assessee was engaged in the business of selling of goods on behalf of its principal on the price fixed by the principals itself. The revenue issued a show cause notice to the assessee alleging that it was performing the duties of a clearing & forwarding agent, hence, it was liable to pay service tax on the amount received as commission from its principals. On adjudication, the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the adjudication order. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it was not supplying goods to the buyers at the direction of its principal, so it was not liable to pay service tax under the category of 'clearing and forwarding agent.' On the other hand, the revenue relying upon the Board's Circular No. 59/A/2003, dated 20-6-2003 contended that as the assessee was engaged in both the activities, i.e., as commission agent as well as clearing & forwarding agent, it was liable to pay service tax.

held.text:
The goods which the assessee had traded are imported goods. As per the definition of exempted goods under rule 2(d) of CCR exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-C.E., dated 1-3-2011 is availed.

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum at the rate of 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. [Para 5.2]

Secondly, as per rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the assessee has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply.

Even assuming but not admitting that the assessee has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, rule 6(3A) which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the assessee has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the assessee has not been disputed by the revenue and the revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the assessee in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the assessee has taken ineligible credit, the question of assessee violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all. [Para 5.3]

If the assessee reversed input service tax credit attributable to trading activities according to standard accounting principles, the same would suffice for satisfying the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6. [Para 5.4]

As regards the wrong availment of credit during the period 2005-08, another show-cause notice has already been issued to the assessee which has been adjudicated and pending before Tribunal. Thus, the department was fully aware of the practices followed by the assessee and has also approved of the same. In view of the above, invocation of the extended period of time to demand service tax is also not sustainable in law. [Para 5.5]

Clearly, during the period in issue, i.e., 2006-07 and 2007-08, trading activity, which was one of the businesses, carried out by the appellant was not amenable to service tax. The amendment to rule 2(e), stated that there was no liability to pay service tax of trading activity, during the relevant period. [Para 9]

In this context, it may also be relevant to note, how exempted services was defined in rule 2(e) of the 2004 rules till 31-3-2011 and thereafter.

Both before and after amendment, 'exempted services' meant those taxable services, which were exempt from whole of service tax and, included those services on which service tax was not leviable, under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.2]

Therefore, given the rule position, what would govern the matter would be the determination of the issue as to whether or not, a particular service is amenable to service tax under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.3]

Since, the trading activity was not amenable service tax at the relevant period, surely, the apportionment as provided in rule 6(3)(c) would get triggered. [Para 10.4]

Having regard to the rule position and given the admitted fact that no separate accounts were maintained by the appellant, with regard to the taxable and non-taxable services, clause (c) of sub-rule 3 of rule 6 of 2004 rules would apply. [Para 11]

For the foregoing reasons, there was interference is called for with the order of the Tribunal. Accordingly, the questions of law framed are answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 12]

There was considerable force in the argument of the assessee that once service tax paid on input services had not been taken at all, the provisions of rule 6(3)(c ) would not be applicable. However, it was found that even though the assessee submitted a list of ten services and the credit available thereon which was not taken, yet no verification had been conducted to check whether the claim made by the assessee that it had not taken Cenvat credit in respect of the common services and, therefore, it would not be required to maintain separate accounts, was correct. In fact, the Commissioner’s view that even if Cenvat credit on common input services was not taken, the assessee was required to maintain separate accounts, could not be accepted. [Para 4]

The very beginning of the rule 6(2) shows that only where a provider of output service avails Cenvat credit in respect of input services and uses the same and he is engaged in providing exempted as well as taxable services, then only he is required to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and utilization of input services. There was no detailed discussion on applicability of the rule and the requirement of maintenance of separate accounts by the Commissioner in the impugned order. However, in view of this provision, unless the department showed that the assessee had availed credit of input services which had also been used for providing any of the exempted services, the demand could not be sustained. For this purpose, there was a need for verification of the claim made by the assessee that it had not taken credit of service tax paid on all the common input services and their number was only ten. Even though all the other points were arguable, yet if it was found that the claim made by the assessee in respect of those ten services was correct and, in such a case, the whole case made out by the department would not be sustainable, it would be appropriate to send the matter back to the Commissioner so that he could get this verified properly and thereafter consider the matter afresh. In view of the above discussion, the requirement of pre-deposit of service tax demanded, interest thereon, penalties, etc., was to be waived and the stay petition was to be allowed and the matter was to be remanded to the Commissioner for fresh adjudication. [Para 5]

P.M. Dave for the Appellant. Avinash Thete for the Respondent.

What is sought to be taxed under the rule 6(8) is service rendered by a C&F Agent to his client and the amount on which tax is leviable is the gross amount of remuneration or commission paid to such agent by the client. Prima facie, this amount does not include the actual expenses incurred by the C&F Agent for and on behalf of his client and service tax is not leviable on such expenses. In the instant case the test appeared to be settlement of the question as to whether the amount spent for the clearing and forwarding operation would have been spent by the principal had he not engaged a C&F Agent. It appeared that the amounts on which the above differential tax was sought to be levied from the assessee were amounts spent by them for and on behalf of their clients and not any remuneration or commission, nothing had been brought on record to indicate that these amounts were collected by the assessee from their clients as remuneration or commission. [Para 2]

The assessee had made out a prima facie case. Accordingly, there would be waiver of pre-deposit and stay of recovery in respect of the amounts of tax and penalty. [Para 3]

I. Trading an exempted service only from 1-4-2011

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force with effect from 16-08-2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit up to 9-09-2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10-09-2004. [Para 5]

Under the Credit Rules, 2002 input service is defined in rule 2(c) as any taxable service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service. Rule 3(1) provided that an output service provider shall be allowed to take credit (service tax credit) of the service tax paid on input service, in the enumerated manner. Sub-clause (a) of this Rule provides that where an input service falls in the same category of taxable service as the output service, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 16-08-2002; sub-clause (b) stipulates that in any other case, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 14-05-2003. Sub rule (2) of Rule 3 provides that for the purpose of these rules, two services shall be deemed to be falling in the same category of taxable service, if the input service or output service fall in the same sub-clause of clause (105) of Section 65 of the Act.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 3 states that where a service provider avails credit on any input service and renders output services which are chargeable to service tax as well as exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be, he shall maintain separate accounts for receipt and consumption of input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of taxable output services and input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be. Sub-rule (5) of rule 3 enacts that where a service provider opts not to maintain separate accounts, as stipulated in sub-rule (4), he shall be allowed to utilize service tax credit for payment of service tax on any output service only to an extent of an amount not exceeding 35 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on such output services. [Para 6]

On a true and fair construction of the relevant provisions of the Credit Rules, 2002, it is apparent that credit could be taken on an input service falling in the same category of taxable service as the output service in respect of which the service tax liability arises and discharged from the available credit. It is axiomatic that trading in goods is neither a taxable service and could not, in the absence of a legislative/statutory fiction provided, capable of being construed as an exempted service. [Para 7]

Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, 2004 sets out the obligations of a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) provides that no cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) enjoins maintenance of separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input or input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service; and the quantity of input spent for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and authorizes taking of cenvat credit only on that quantity of input or input services which are intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing taxable output services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 carves out specified exclusions to the requirements set out in sub-rule (2). Sub-clause (c) of rule 6(3) stipulates that the provider of an output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The 2004 Credit Rules were amended with effect from 01-04-2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an Explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'. [Para 9]

Trading activity - Whether a service

As regards the issue as to whether trading activity can be called a service, it is quite clear that since trading activity is nothing but purchase and sales and is covered under Sales Tax Law, it may not be appropriate to call it a service. Trading activity cannot be called a service and, therefore, it cannot be considered as an exempted service also. [Para 5]

Applicability of Cenvat Credit Rules (and Service Tax Credit Rules) on trading activity

Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 provides that where output service provider does not maintain separate account, he is to follow the procedure or avail the options available under that rule. Rule 6 is applicable only when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation in rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity was not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions. [Para 7]

Eligibility for availing input service tax credit

In cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, there arises a situation where an assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable goods. There is no provision to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that the appellant choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what will be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appeared to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles was deducted and the balance only will be availed for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition was not against the law in view of the fact the there were several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal, wherein a view had been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit. [Para 8]

♦ Rule 3(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 permits utilization of CENVAT Credit for payment of service tax and excise duty. [Para 5]

♦ There is no provision for segregation of CENVAT credit for payment of excise duty and for payment of service tax. There is no requirement for one to one correlation of CENVAT credit availed on input services towards payment of output services. [Para 6]

EDITOR'S NOTE

♦ A question of day-to-day importance stands raised in this judgment.

♦ The requirement to maintain separate accounts exists under Rule 6 only in case where a manufacturer is engaged in manufacture of dutiable and exempt goods or a provider of output services is engaged in provision of taxable and exempt services.

♦ Though CENVAT Credit Rules contain separate provision in respect of manufacturer of excisable goods and provider of services, it must be noted that once CENVAT Credit is validly availed, there is no restriction on its utilization except as stated in Rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

On a plain reading of rule 6(1), it is obvious that if inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted goods, credit is not allowed except in the circumstances mentioned under sub-rule (2). A manufacturer who avails of the Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of final products which are chargeable to duty as also exempted goods, the manufacturer has to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products and the quantity of inputs used for the manufacture of exempted goods and take the Cenvat credit only on that quantity of inputs which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. A plain reading of this rule does not lead to any ambiguity, absurdity or defeat the provisions of the Act. Rule 6(2) and rule 6(3), read together mean that in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted products no Cenvat credit is allowed. It may, however, happen that the inputs are used in the manufacture of both exempted and dutiable goods, in which event if the register as required is maintained the credit can be taken for the quantity of inputs used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. If records are not maintained as required, the duty has to be paid in terms of rule 6(3). The presumptive tax payable in terms of rule 6(3) has been recognized and accepted by the Supreme Court in CCE v. Ballarpur Industries Ltd. 2007 (215) ELT 489. Rule 6(1) does not lead to the construction that if the manufacturer without maintaining the books, does not take credit for the duty paid on inputs for manufacture of exempted goods, rule 6(1) is satisfied. Rule 6(1) is satisfied only when the requirements of the rule 6(2) are satisfied, which requires register to be maintained for separate accounts of receipt, consumption and inventory of the inputs. Rule 6(3) provides that if separate accounts are not maintained then the amount has to be paid by a manufacturer. [Para 18]

The rule has to be read together to understand its object. Once a manufacturer manufactures from common inputs two final products, one dutiable and the other exempted, rule 6(2) would be attracted and on failure to maintain separate records, rule 6(3) would apply. Rule 6(1) in such an event would result in denying to the manufacturer Cenvat credit. Once the inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted goods irrespective of whether such inputs are used in the manufacture of dutiable goods, such manufacturer can avail of credit only in terms of rule 6(3). [Para 19]

A power to give benefit encompasses within itself the power to put conditions and restrictions under which credit is available. Power to give benefit also carries with it power to take it back or withdraw it. The rule if properly read starts with the words ‘Cenvat credit shall not be allowed’. Therefore, rule 6 makes it clear that insofar as inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods are concerned, no Cenvat credit is allowed. The rule making authority, however, noting that inputs may be used both for manufacturing final products which may be dutiable and other final products which are exempt, has provided that such manufacturer will be given credit insofar as inputs used for manufacturing of dutiable goods are concerned, if accounts are maintained in terms of the rules. Therefore, merely because the assessee contended that he was willing to forego credit on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final product it does not warrant a departure from the requirements of rule 6(2) and 6(3). The rules contemplate that on failure to maintain accounts in terms of rule 6(2) the consequences would be in terms of rule 6(3)(a) or (b). It is not possible to read down the rule as ‘amount not exceeding’ as was sought to be contended on behalf of the assessee. [Para 24]

Rule 6(1) is clear; the Cenvat credit cannot be availed of on inputs used in the manufacturing of exempted goods. It then adds the words except in the circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). A Court cannot read into the said rule something different or render otiose the words. The rule mandates specifically that an assessee seeking to avail Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, the only method by which he can avail of the credit is by following sub-rule (2). [Para 26]

In terms of sub-section (2) of section 4, which is the charging section, in respect of income chargeable under sub-section (1), income tax shall be deducted at source or paid in advance, where it is so deductible or payable under any provision of this Act.

Thus, it is clear that tax is to be deducted only where element of income is a part of payment and since reimbursement of expenses does not constitute trading receipts or has any element of income therein, TDS is not liable to be made from reimbursements.

Though section 194C mentions TDS being made on 'any sum' paid to a resident in pursuance of a contract, the term 'any sum' cannot be stretched to mean even expenses incurred on behalf of the client and later recovered from them.

When a C&F agent incurs expenses like custom duty, port dues, and other sundry charges, he is merely acting as a front man of his client and on his behalf. These expenses do not normally have any nexus with the commission he is supposed to earn for his work. [Para 6.4.1]

In the case on hand, as pointed out by the Commissioner (Appeals), the expenses have been incurred by the C&F Agents on behalf of the assessee, the claims were made on actual basis and the amounts were separately shown with proper evidence.

The fact that the reimbursement of expenses have been separately billed, in the case on hand, is not disputed. The C&F Agents are appointed to provide the service of carrying out sales for which they are paid service charges on which TDS has been made and not for the purpose of incurring expenses on behalf of the assessee.

In this view of the matter, the reimbursement of expenses by C&F Agents cannot be held to be contract/service on which the provisions of section 194C of the Act would come into play and apply.

In view of the factual position as laid out above, it is held that there is no need to deduct TDS on reimbursement of expenses to C&F Agents which are separately billed and accordingly the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is upheld. [Para 6.4.3]

In the case of Raja Rajeshwari Intl. Polymers (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (180) ELT 448 (Bang.-Trib.), it was held that dealer agent does not fall within the purview of clearing and forwarding operation and no service tax is payable on commission received on account of Del credere agency. Even Commissioner (Appeals) in the impugned order had observed that said services of the appellants were not liable to service tax and they were not liable to pay tax on the commission received by them. Therefore, confirmation of levy of service tax on that count on the appellants was not maintainable. [Para 3]

The facts were that on the basis of a letter dated 19-11-2008 from ‘R’ Ltd. to the assessee, it claimed to be an agent of the former in respect of sale made to the Indian Navy and Coast Guards. The enclosure to this letter, forwarded by the assessee to ‘R’ Ltd. in regard to services rendered by four sub-agents in the relevant year, had also been confirmed by ‘R’ Ltd. The paperbook contained evidence regarding payment of commissions to these parties and accounting for the same in their returns of income. ‘K’ had confirmed that it displayed a small version of RO system of ‘R’ Ltd. in its shop and it used to provide information to persons or concerns through the assessee. Further, ‘E’ stated to the effect that it was passing on information in regard to prospective buyers to the assessee for following up the orders and the commission was received on completion of the orders, i.e., on receipt of payments. The same statement of the proprietor of ‘B’ was recorded, who confirmed business dealings with the assessee for the years 2003 to 2005. In the case of ‘M’ Ltd. there was an agreement dated 10-4-2004 in force and said firm also confirmed the receipt of commission from the assessee. As against the aforesaid, evidence was found in the course of survey of ‘R’ Ltd. which was interpreted by its Assessing Officer to mean that payments were made to the assessee by cheques and after retaining its commission, the balance amount was returned to ‘R’ Ltd. The evidence produced by the assessee in the course of assessment led to a conclusion that the sub-agents had provided some information regarding prospective buyers, for which the commission was paid to them. The evidence seized from ‘R’ led to a conclusion that the assessee was used as a conduit for passing on the money to it after retaining commission for providing bogus bills. However, both sets of evidences did show that the assessee was paid at the rate of 5 per cent of the value of the order, out of which it paid an amount at the rate of 3.75 per cent either to the sub-agents or to ‘R’ Ltd. The whole of the evidence, including the bills raised by ‘R’ Ltd. on its clients, showed that the assessee and its sub-agents were in the same position insofar as the mentioning of the names in the bills of ‘R’ Ltd. was concerned, i.e., neither the name of the assessee nor of the sub-agent appeared on the bills. The assessee did not claim to have dealt with the Government departments directly. It had dealt with sub-agents and ‘R’ Ltd. for communication of information about prospective buyers. The revenue had also not been able to prove that the payments were against the public policy. The provision contained in the Explanation to section 37(1) uses the words ‘which is an offence or which is prohibited by law’. No evidence had been produced to show that payment of commission to the sub-agents was either an offence or it was prohibited by law. [Para 5]

■

Rule 37BA envisages allowance of TDS credit in proportion to the income declared by the assessee. This proportion needs to be established for every nature of receipt on which TDS has been claimed by the assessee. Therefore, while allowing TDS claimed under each section, it has to be ascertained that entire income on which TDS has been claimed is duly offered in the ITR by the assessee and in case the income so declared for each nature of receipt on which TDS has been claimed is lesser than that appearing in Form No. 26AS then only CPC may deny the credit of TDS for relevant nature of receipt. Since the receipts of interest and commission on which TDS has been claimed under sections 194A and 194H are fully declared in ITR, the entire TDS claimed under sections 194A and 194H needs to be fully allowed. Hence the proportionate TDS disallowed is absolutely unjustified and, therefore, deserves to be allowed. [Para 2.6]

■

As regards the disallowance of TDS credit under section 194Q is concerned, the Bench found that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia. Therefore, the turnover on which tax is deducted under section 194Q is not the turnover of the assessee. Hence has rightly not been shown as such by the assessee. Moreover a Kachha Arhatia acts only as an agent for his constituent and never acts as principal. Therefore, the remuneration of Kachha Arhatia consists solely of commission and he has no control on the profit and losses made by his constituents.

■

The assessee has drawn attention of the Bench to sample invoices on which TDS was deducted under section 194Q by the principal buyer and the corresponding vikray parchi issued by the Mandi to the respective farmers. These documents clearly show that the amount invoiced by the assessee to the principal buyer and the value of goods transferred by assessee to the farmer is exactly the same. Therefore, turnover of the Kachha Arhatia is merely the commission paid by principal buyer on which the principal buyer deducts TDS under section 194H and which has been duly shown as income in the ITR by the assessee. Therefore, the TDS deducted by such principle buyers by virtue of provisions of section 194Q is eligible to be claimed by the Kachha Arhatia in his ITR on the grounds that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia and is duly registered as such with the Mandi. Perusal of the vikray parchi issued at the Mandi to the farmers and the corresponding invoice raised by the assessee to the principal buyer undoubtedly establishes the fact that the assessee has no control or margin in the sale facilitated by him and earns merely commission from such transactions.

■

The assessee has no domain over the goods sold to the principle buyers. As clarified by Central Board of Direct Taxes in its Circular No. 452 of 1986), so far as Kachha Arhatias are concerned the turnover does not include the sales effected on behalf of principals and only commission (gross) has to be considered for the purpose of income tax. Therefore, TDS deducted under section 194Q by the principle buyers cannot be refused by invoking rule 37BA read with section 199.

■

As the sale facilitated by the assessee for the farmers is not the turnover of the assessee and the income from such transaction (commission) being duly offered for tax by the assessee in his ITR, the TDS deducted both under sections 194H and 194Q deserves to be fully allowed. Further the Form No. 26AS also depicts that the invoices on which TDS has been deducted under section 194Q also has TDS deducted under section 194H. Thus the contention of the assessee that he is merely a Kachha Arhatia is potrayed beyond all doubts and needs to be accepted.

■

Therefore, the Assessing Officer is to be directed to allow TDS claimed under section 194Q by the assessee. [Para 2.7]

Rule 6 speaks about obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) of rule 6 states that cenvat credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input or input services which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or for providing exempted services. Sub-rule (2) of rule 6 states that in case the manufacture or service provider uses common inputs/input services, then such manufacturer or service provider has to maintain separate accounts and credit is to be taken only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for manufacture of dutiable goods or providing taxable services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 speaks about the situation when such manufacturer or service provider does not maintain separate accounts. It provides for two options. It was amended vide Notification No. 10/2008-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2008 with effect from 1-4-2008. As per the new sub-rule (3) of rule 6, the manufacturer/service provider opting not to maintain separate account has to follow either of the following two options:-

A manufacturer shall pay 10 per cent (5 per cent with effect from 7-7-2009) of sale price of the exempted goods and an output service provider shall pay 8 per cent (6 per cent with effect from 7-7-2009) of the value of the exempted services; or

Reverse the credit on inputs and input services pertaining to exempted goods and exempted services as per the procedure and conditions prescribed in rule 6(3A). [Para 5]

The rule 6(3A) states that while exercising the option, the manufacturer of goods or the provider of output service shall intimate in writing the department regarding the option exercised. In the instant case, admittedly there is no intimation given by the assessee informing its exercise of option. The contention of the department is that when the assessee has not intimated its option in writing then the assessee is bound to pay the duty amount calculated under the first option. The said rule does not say that on failure to intimate, the manufacturer/service provider would lose his choice to avail second option of reversing the proportionate credit. Rule 6(3A) is nothing but a procedure contemplated for application of rule 6(3). Therefore, the argument of the revenue that the requirement to intimate the department about the option exercised is mandatory and on failure the assessee has no other option but to accept and comply rule 6(3)(i) and make payment of 5 per cent/10 per cent of sale price of exempted goods/value of exempted services is not acceptable or convincing. The rule 6(3A) does not lay down any such restriction. The procedure and conditions laid in rule 6(3A) is intended to make rule 6(3)workable and not to take away the option available to the assessee. In any case, at no stretch of imagination can it be said that on failure to intimate the department, rule 6(3)(i) would automatically come into application. [Para 6]

Therefore, the impugned demand raised against the assessee was not legal and proper. [Para 7]

It cannot be said that the commission that the air travel agents get from the airlines is independent of and distinct from the services that they provide to the air-travellers and is relatable to the business that they provide to the airlines. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle was cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case was gone.

From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l), the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided that it is made taxable. Therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. It may also be said that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air travellers. If in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-travellers. On the other hand, it may be said that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited. The tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the petitioners that because of section 67(k), the nature of the tax itself changes was incorrect. Section 67(k), which provides the ‘measure of the tax’, is not unconnected with the main levy of the tax. The provision of section 67(k ) does not in any manner alter the nature of tax and does not shift it from the service rendered to the customer to the service rendered to the airlines. The contention, therefore, was clearly incorrect on facts.

The further argument that the notification dated 26-6-1997 restricts the tax to the commission alone and is repugnant to the scheme of the tax was obviously incorrect. The basis of the argument that the commission received from the airlines by the air travel agent is taken a measure for imposing a levy on a different service rendered to the customer by the agent, was itself incorrect. Therefore, the argument that the impugned provision of section 67(k) is repugnant to the general scheme of the Act was to be rejected.

As far as the second contention of the petitioner with regard to rule 6(7) was concerned, the language of rule 6(7) itself suggests that it is an optional matter. Therefore, the members of the petitioner-association, who had not exercised the option would had no concern with the validity of that rule while those who had opted for it, and majority of them having done so, could also not challenge the said validity.

In fact, it was not necessary for the High Court to take stock of the petitioners’ contention regarding the unconstitutionality of the rules but, even otherwise, there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found with that rule much less in the light of the submission made by the petitioners. The High Court was in complete agreement with the department that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration section 93 and section 94(2)(a) jointly. Indeed, there is a specific power under section 93 to grant exemption in any manner. Section 94(2)(a) speaks of the rule-making power on the subject of collection and recovery of service tax under section 66 and section 68. What is suggested by rule 6(7) is nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations. It was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule- making power. It does not amount to an independent levy again. Therefore, it was to be held that there was nothing wrong with the rule in question. This rule provides for an independent measure as the basic airfare. For this reason, no merit was found in the writ which was liable to be dismissed.

The assessee had been authorised different parties of Northern India to purchase rubber on their behalf. As per the terms and conditions of these agreement, the assessee had been appointed as buying agent for the purchase of rubber and other commodities in the State of Kerala on behalf of the respective parties. It was also stipulated that purchase would be made on behalf of principals and despatched to them. The principals, agreed to give commission of 1 per cent of the purchase price besides the reimbursement of expenses incurred for the purpose of purchasing rubber and other commodities. The assessee was buying rubber and latex from the agricultures from Keral for and on behalf of its principal as their agent. The dealings in rubber are controlled by the Rubber Board. The Rubber Board had also intimated the principals that the assessee had been recognised as their agent to purchase and despatch rubber on their behalf.

The CBDT in Circular No. 452, dated 17-3-1987 has laid down the principles of distinction between kutcha arhatiya and pucca arhatiya. On a perusal of distinctions between kutcha arhatiya and pucca arhativa as enumerated in the above circular and further illustrations given by the CBDT Circular Nos. 564&572, dated 5-7-1990 respectively wherein it has been made clear that turnover and sales are interchangeable and sole reliance cannot be placed on the definition of ‘turnover’ under section 2(o ) of the Haryana General Sales-tax Act, the contrary definition as contained in the Central Sales-tax Act cannot be ignored Since the assessee was receiving commission @1% of purchase value besides reimbursement of expenses incurred for the purposes of purchase and if the Assessing Officer’s contention was accepted that the assessee was trading in these items, there was no question of receiving fixed commission and there should, in fact, be bearing of profit or loss in each separate transaction depending on market conditions but this was not the case of the assessing authority nor it was borne out from the record. The Assessing Officer had not worked out the profit as such earned by the assessee from trading in rubber and latex. Therefore, taking into consideration the facts that the Rubber Board had registered the assessee as an authorised agent to purchase and despatch rubber on behalf of different principals no sales as such had been effected by the assessee, the goods purchased were transferred to the principals at the cost price, the goods were transferred not against ‘C Form’ but against ‘F From’ of sales tax issued by the transferee, the commission agency agreement between the principals and the assessee etc., the role of assessee was that of agent and not of trader. Secondly, according to the CBDT Circular Nos. 564&572 dated 5-7-1990. The turnover and sales are interchangeable and as the assessee had not made any sale rubber or latex, the total transaction conducted to earn commission would not be regarded as ‘sale’ or ‘turnover’ of the assessee. In view of the above facts and circumstances, for working out 80HHC deduction, it was the commission earned which was to be considered for working out the said deduction and not the aggregate transaction made to earn commission and, hence, no interference was needed with the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

P.K. Sahu for the Appellant. Rakesh Gupta for the Respondent.

The denial in the case of Cadila Healthcare Ltd. (supra) to the commission paid to the overseas agents shall apply to this category of service, where the service is rendered for overseas commission. The sales tax collections could be taken to be a trust fund in which the assessee had no interest. As a matter of fact the primary liability to pay sales tax on sales effected by the assessee was independent of the fact whether he collected sales tax from his buyers or not. The statute enabled the dealers to collect sales tax with a view to pass on their liability to their buyers. Therefore, if the sales tax collected by the assessee from his buyers during the year of account is in excess of his actual liability towards sales tax for that period, such excess would go only for his benefit. Therefore, the Tribunal was not correct in holding that the excess collections were not trading receipts of the assessee.

The decision of the Supreme Court in Chowringhee Sales Bureau (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1973] 87 ITR 542, fully supported the revenue’s stand that sales tax collections should be taken to be trading receipts and as and when the amounts are paid to discharge the sales tax liability, such amounts will have to be deducted.

So far as the separate accounts maintained by the assessee were concerned, they had been kept only on cash basis, that was, the sales tax collections made had been credited and the actual sales tax payments had been debited on the respective dates of collection and payment. Neither the sales tax collections nor the payments made by the assessee which had been recorded in the separated accounts had gone into the general accounts maintained by the assessee for his business, as the assessee had always been contending that he had been making collections as an agent of the Government and even the excess collection would have ultimately to be paid to the Government. In these separate accounts as and when the amounts had been paid to the sales tax authorities, they had been debited. An assessee may employ one method of accounting for one part of his business or one class of customers, and a different method for another part of his business or another class of customers. He may also keep accounts in respect of different parts of the same business on different basis. If such different methods are employed regularly and consistently the profits have to be computed in accordance with the respective methods, provided it results in a proper determination of the true profits. The assessee should, therefore, be taken to have adopted the cash basis so far as the sales tax collections were concerned and, therefore, the principle of the decision in Chowringhee Sales Bureau P. Ltd. v. CIT [1973] 87 ITR 542 (SC) would stand attracted. Therefore, it was held that the assessee had maintained his accounts in relation to the sales tax collections only on cash basis and, therefore, only when he pays out the amount for discharging his sales tax liability, he can claim deduction.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

While gone through Circular no. 715, dated 8-8-1995. It was noted that in reply to question no. 7 the CBDT has opined as under (relevant extract is reproduced):

'Question 7: Whether a travel agent/clearing and forwarding agent would be required to deduct tax at source from the sum payable by the agent to an airline or other carrier of goods or passengers?

Answer: The travel agent, issuing tickets on behalf of the airlines for travel of individual passengers, would not be required to deduct tax at source as he acts on behalf of the airlines. The position of clearing and forwarding agents is different. They act as independent contractors. Any payment made to them would, hence, be liable for deduction of tax at source. They would also be liable to deduct tax at source while making payments to a carrier of goods.'

This question relates to a situation where the C&F agent makes the payment to the airlines or other carrier of goods or passenger. This question, is not relevant to decide whether the assessee is required to deduct tax at source when payment is made to C&F agent. Question no. 6 deals with a case where the payment is made for carriage of the goods or passenger by any mode of transport to C&F agent. In reply to this question, the Board has clearly laid down in Circular no. 715, dated 8-8-1995 that 'As regards payments made to clearing and forwarding agents for carriage of goods, the same shall be subjected to tax deduction at source under section 194C of the Act.' The assessee could also not adduce any evidence that the C&F agent deducted tax at source while making payment to the carrier so as to prove that the amount which was paid by the assessee to the C&F agent represents reimbursement of the freight paid by the C&F agent on behalf of the assessee to the airlines. It is not the intention of the Legislature that neither the C&F agent deducts the tax when it makes the payment to the carrier nor the assessee deducts the tax at source when it makes payment to C&F agent. If the assessee claims that the amount paid to the C&F agent by the assessee represents reimbursement, the onus is on the assessee to prove that it represents the reimbursement of the claim. Hence, provisions of section 194C are clearly applicable in the case of the assessee. [Para 6]

In the instant case the assessee was following mercantile system of accounting. As per the agreement the sales made by the assessee were as distributor/ commission agent of the principal. The property remained with the principal till the goods were sold by the assessee. In the circumstances the mere fact that the assessee had accounted for the purchase and sales in its final accounts would make no difference. The mere existence of accounting entries in the books of the assessee were not decisive of the fact that the sales and purchases belonged to the assessee. It was true that the sales tax collected would be a part of trading receipt but such trading receipt would be of that of the principal and not of the assessee-distributor/commission agent. Merely because the liability to pay sales tax was on the agent, it would not convert the receipt of the sales tax collected as trading receipt of the assessee.

It was only for the purposes of collection of tax under the Sales Tax Act that the commission agent was made liable to pay sales tax jointly and severally along with the principal. In those circumstances though the assessee was jointly and severally liable under the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, the sales tax collected would not form part of the assessee’s trading receipts and consequently, not even the expenditure. In fact the assessee had not claimed the expenditure in its profit and loss account and the receipts of the sales tax collection as well as the payments made therefrom were directly shown in the balance sheet under the head ‘Sales tax collection account’.

The assessee’s claim was, therefore, allowed and directions were issued not to disallow sales tax liability under section 43B.

Commission on purchase not covered under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' :

The conjunctive 'and' between the words 'clearing' and 'forwarding' indicate and mean that where clearing operations are separate from forwarding operations, levy of tax would not be attracted i.e. there would be no charge of tax if the transaction involved only one of the two components of the conjuncted service namely 'clearing' and 'forwarding'. The expression a clearing and forwarding agent in relation to clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner' contemplates only one person operating both as the clearing and the forwarding agent; and if a person has rendered service as forwarding agent without rendering any service as 'clearing agent' he could not be considered to have rendered both services as a 'clearing and forwarding agent'. [Para 2]

'Clearing and forwarding operations' would be various activities having a bearing on clearance of goods and would normally involve documentary processes and arrangements for transfer of goods to their destination; and may also involve clearance at subsequent stages during forwarding operations. A clearing and forwarding agent normally undertakes the following activities :-

(a)

Receiving goods from the factories or premises of the principal or his agents;

(b)

Warehousing these goods;

(c)

Receiving despatch orders from the principal;

(d)

Arranging despatch of goods as per the directions of the principal by engaging transport on his own or through the authorised transporters of the principal;

(e)

Maintaining records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; and

(f)

Preparing invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 3]

Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of the enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of goods, the service would not be a taxable service as defined in section 65(105)(j) read with section 65(25) which defines a clearing and forwarding agent. [Para 4]

In this case, assessee neither receives goods from the factory premises of the principal; warehouses such goods; receives despatch orders from the principal; arranges despatch of goods as per directions of the principal by engaging a transport on its own or through authorised transporters of the principal; nor maintains records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; nor even prepares invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 5]

Hence, assessee, in no manner, engages in any of the six enumerated activities which constitute clearing and forwarding operations. It never has custody of the picture tubes; does not receive them from manufacturers of the tubes; does not warehouse the picture tubes; does not receive despatch orders from manufacturers of picture tubes which are directly forwarded to manufacturers of the TV sets; does not arrange despatch of goods as per directions either of the manufacturers of picture tubes or manufacturers of TV sets; nor engages transport on its own or through authorised transporters of manufacturers of picture tubes or manufacturers of TV sets; and does not maintain records of the receipt and despatch of picture tubes and the stock available at the warehouse; nor prepares invoices either on behalf of the principal manufacturers or manufacturers of TV sets. [Para 6]

There is neither the conjunctive service of clearing and forwarding provided by the assessee nor either of the services of clearing or forwarding. As the assessee has not provided any of the core enumerated activities of clearing and forwarding operations, it has not directly or indirectly provided any service connected with clearing and forwarding operations in any manner to any other person. That the assessee was not a consignment agent is also not in dispute. [Para 7]

Therefore, assessee is not liable to Service Tax under the taxable head 'clearing and forwarding agency'. Even otherwise, commission agents were exempt from service tax vide Notification No. 13/2003 dated 20-5-2003 from 1-7-2003 upto 9-9-2004. Revenue proceeded on the basis that the assessee had provided 'clearing and forwarding agency' service, contrary to the distinct classification w.e.f. 1-7-2003; the services provided by it constituted Business Auxiliary Service. [Para 8]

Since the assessee has considered only commission income as its income and, after relevant expenditure, offered net profit for taxation, it claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders in terms of sections 194Q and 194A. In total, the Assessing Officer allowed proportionate credit for TDS on the ground that the assessee has offered only the part of the income, whereas it claimed TDS on the entire sales value. It is found that, once the assessee is operating as a commission agent, then the income of the assessee is net commission income received from the farmers, but not the total sales value of the farmers. Since the law provides for TDS under section 194Q on total sales value, and further, the assessee has raised sales invoices in its name, the traders have deducted TDS on the entire sales value, but the fact remains that, the assessee has considered the total income accrued on the total sales value being commission received from the farmers, as its income. Therefore, the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A, has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee and thus, the provisions of section 199 read with rule 37BA(2) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 are complied with. Therefore, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) that Assessing Officer has rightly allowed proportionate credit as per section 199 read with rule 37BA(2), is incorrect, going by the facts, because, there is no finding from the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) that, the income on which TDS has been deducted under sections 194Q and 194A has not suffered tax in the hands of the assessee. Since the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194A and 194Q has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee, the assessee has righty claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders and reported in Form 26AS. The Assessing Officer, without appreciating relevant facts, allowed proportionate credit for TDS, even though the assessee is entitled for credit for the entire TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A.
