Control on clearing, forwarding or booking agent and any person transporting goods and furnishing of information by such agent or person

62. (1) Every clearing, forwarding or booking agent or broker or a person transporting goods who in the course of his business handles documents of title to goods or transports goods or takes delivery of goods for or on behalf of a dealer and having his place of business in the State of Chhattisgarh shall furnish information about his place of business to such authority, within such time, in such form as may be prescribed.

(2) Every such agent or person shall maintain true and complete accounts, registers and documents in respect of the goods handled by him and the documents of title relating thereto and shall furnish true and complete particulars and information relating to the transaction of goods of any dealer to any officer appointed under section 3, not below the rank of an Assistant 1[Commercial Tax] Officer as and when required by him and shall produce the said accounts, registers and documents before such officer as and when required by him.

(3) Any agent or person referred to in sub-section (1) who contravenes the provisions of the said sub-section or sub-section (2), the Commissioner may, after giving such agent or person an opportunity of being heard, direct him to pay by way of penalty—

(i)

one thousand rupees if the contravention is of the provisions of sub-section (1) on each occasion of inspection by any officer referred to in sub-section (2); and

(ii)

not less than three times but not exceeding five times of the amount of tax payable in respect of the goods involved in the transactions of a dealer which appears to have been evaded by such dealer, if the contravention pertains to the provisions of sub-section (2).

Explanation : For the purpose of this section,—

(i)

"Clearing, forwarding, booking agent or broker" shall include a person who renders his services for clearing, forwarding or booking of or taking delivery of consignment of goods at railway premises, air cargo, complex, containers depot, booking agency, goods transport company office or any place of loading or unloading of goods or contrives, makes and concludes, bargains and contracts for or on behalf of any dealer for a fee, reward, commission, remuneration or other valuable consideration or otherwise.

(ii)

"Person transporting goods" shall, besides the owner, include manager, agent, driver, employee of the owner, a person in-charge of a place of loading or unloading of goods or in-charge of a goods carrier carrying such goods for dispatch to other places or gives delivery of any consignment of such goods to the consignee.

Tax credit

11. (1)(a) A registered dealer who has purchased the taxable goods (hereinafter referred to as the "purchasing dealer") shall be entitled to claim tax credit equal to the amount of,—

1[(i)

tax collected from the purchasing dealer, by a registered dealer from whom he has purchased such goods or the tax payable by the purchasing dealer to a registered dealer who has sold such goods to him during the tax period; or]

(ii)

tax paid by him during the tax period under 2[sub-section (1), (2), (5) or (6)] of 3[section 9; or]

4[(iii)

tax paid by the purchasing dealer under the Gujarat Tax on Entry of Specified Goods into Local Areas Act, 2001 (Guj. 22 of 2001);]

(b) The tax credit to be so claimed under this sub-section shall be subject to the provisions of sub-sections (2) to (12); and the tax credit shall be calculated in such manner as may be prescribed.

(2) The registered dealer who intends to claim the tax credit shall maintain the register and the books of accounts in such manner as may be prescribed.

(3) (a) Subject to the provisions of this section, tax credit to be claimed under sub-section (1) shall be allowed to a purchasing dealer on his purchase of taxable goods which are intended for the purpose of—

(i)

sale or re-sale by him in the State;

(ii)

sale in the course of inter-State trade and commerce;

(iii)

branch transfer or consignment of taxable goods to other States (subject to the provision of sub-clause (b) below);

(iv)

sales in the course of export out of the territory of India;

(v)

sales to export oriented units or the units in Special Economic Zones for sale in the course of export out of the territory of India;

(vi)

use as raw material in the manufacture of taxable goods intended for (i) to (v) above or in the packing of the goods so manufactured;

Composition of tax on agricultural produce

14B. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, the Commissioner may, in such circumstances and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, permit a Commission Agent engaged in the business of agricultural produce, to pay at his option in lieu of the amount of tax leviable from him under this Act, a lump sum tax by way of composition at such rate as may be fixed by the State Government by notification in the Official Gazette.

(2) The permission to pay lump sum tax under sub-section (1) shall be granted by the Commissioner to a Commission Agent who,—

(a)

exclusively carries on a business of agricultural produce, and

(b)

is licensed as general commission agent with a market committee established under the Gujarat Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1963.

(3) The Commissioner shall not grant permission to pay lump sum tax under sub-section (1) to a Commission agent who,—

(a)

sells the goods in the course of inter-State trade and commerce or exports goods out of the territory of India,

purchases the goods in the course of inter-State trade and commerce or imports goods from a place out of the territory of India,

(c)

dispatches the goods to his branch or his consigning agent outside the State or receives the goods from his branch situated outside the State or from consigning agent outside the State,

(d)

sells the goods to a person who is not a registered dealer, or

(e)

sells the goods to a dealer who is permitted to pay lump sum tax under section 14.

(a)

be entitled to claim tax credit in respect of tax paid by him on his purchases,

(b)

charge any tax under this Act in his sales bill or sales invoices in respect of the sales on which lump sum tax is payable, and

(c)

issue tax invoice to any dealer who has purchased the goods from him.

(6) The permission granted under sub- section (1) shall remain valid so long as the provisions of this section and rules made in this behalf are complied with; and in case of breach of any of the provisions of this section or rules, the commission agent shall be liable to pay tax under sections 7 and 9 for such tax period as may be prescribed.

Certain agents liable to tax for sales on behalf of principal

68. (1) Where any person sells or purchases any taxable goods on behalf of his principal then such person and his principal shall both be jointly and severally liable to pay tax on the turnover of such sales or purchases.

(2) If the principal, on whose behalf a commission agent has sold or purchased any goods, shows to the satisfaction of the Prescribed Authority that tax has been paid by the commission agent on such goods under sub-section (1), the principal shall not be liable to pay tax again in respect of the same transaction.

(3) Where a manager or an agent of a non-resident dealer sells or purchases any goods on behalf of the non-resident dealer in the State, then the non-resident dealer and the manger or agent residing in the State, shall be jointly and severally liable to pay tax on the turnover of such sales or purchases:

Provided that, if the non-resident dealer shows to the satisfaction of the Prescribed Authority that the tax payable in respect of any sale or purchase has been paid by the manager or agent residing in the State, then the non-resident dealer shall not be liable to pay tax in respect of the same transaction.

Keeping of accounts and records

Keeping of accounts

33. (1) Every registered dealer and every person liable to be registered under the Act shall keep and maintain a true and correct account of his daily transactions showing the goods produced, manufactured, bought and sold by him and the value thereof separately together with invoices and bills.

(2) Every such dealer or person shall keep separate purchase, sale and disposal accounts in respect of each commodity, whether taxable or not, dealt with by him 1[and the account in respect of purchase made within the State shall be in Form VAT 170].

2[(3) Every dealer other than a dealer opting to pay tax by way of composition under section 15, shall maintain a VAT account containing details of input and output tax, together with credit and debit notes issued during any tax period.]

(4) Every such dealer or person shall keep current books of accounts at the place or places of business entered on his certificate of registration, and every purchase and sale shall be brought to account as soon as the purchase or sale is made.

(5) The registers, accounts and documents maintained shall be sequentially numbered, and where the registers and other documents are maintained by means of a computer or any other similar mechanical device, the dealer shall maintain copies in paper of such registers and other documents printed on a monthly basis.

(6) Any entry in such registers, accounts and documents shall not be erased, effaced or overwritten, and all incorrect entries shall be scored out under attestation and correct entry recorded and where the registers, accounts and documents are maintained by means of a computer or any other similar mechanical device, the dealer shall also maintain a record of correction or change of any entry.

(7) For the purpose of sub-rule (4), current books of accounts shall include computer hardware and software used in connection with business activities of the dealer or person.

(8) The accounts maintained by dealers together with all invoices, bills, declarations, way-bills and delivery notes relating to stocks, deliveries, purchases, output and sales shall be preserved by them for the time specified under section 32 or for any further period as may be notified by the Commissioner and shall be kept at the place of business, mentioned in the registration certificate.

(9) Every commission agent, broker, del credere agent, auctioneer or any other mercantile agent shall maintain accounts showing—

(a)

particulars or authorisation received by him from each principal to purchase or sell goods on behalf of each principal separately;

(b)

particulars of goods purchased or goods received for sale on behalf of each principal each day;

(c)

particulars of purchases or sales effected on behalf of each principal each day;

(d)

details of accounts furnished to each principal each day; and

(e)

the tax paid on purchases or on sales effected on behalf of each principal and the challan number and date of remittance of the tax into the Government Treasury.

(10) Every purchasing agent shall keep particulars of the names and addresses of the dealers or persons from whom he purchased the goods, and every selling agent shall keep the particulars of the names and addresses of the dealers or persons to whom he sold the goods.

(11) Every wholesale dealer, importer, exporter and manufacturer shall maintain monthly stock accounts in respect of each commodity dealt with by him, and such stock account shall contain particulars of purchases or receipts, sales, deliveries and balance of stock.

(12) Every manufacturer of goods shall maintain monthly production of accounts, showing quantitative details of the various raw materials used in the manufacture and the quantitative details of the goods so manufactured.

(13) Every dealer who is required to maintain stock accounts shall maintain subsidiary accounts for each godown if there is more than one godown for keeping his stocks.

(14) Every dealer or person executing works contract shall keep separate accounts showing—

(a)

the particulars of the names and addresses of the persons for whom and on whose behalf he carried on the execution of works contract in respect of each works contract;

(b)

the particulars of goods procured by way of purchase or otherwise for the execution of works contract;

(c)

the particulars of goods to be utilized in execution of each works contract; and

(d)

the details of payment received in respect of each works contract.

(15) Every dealer or person engaged in the transfer of a right to use any goods shall keep—

(a)

particulars of the names and addresses of the persons to whom he delivered the goods for use;

(b)

details of amounts received in respect of each transaction; and

(c)

monthly stock accounts in respect of each commodity dealt with by him and such stock account shall contain particulars of purchases or receipts, deliveries and balance of stock.

CHAPTER VI

INSPECTION OF BUSINESS PLACES AND ACCOUNTS AND ESTABLISHMENT OF CHECK POSTS

Maintenance and preservation of accounts

58. (1) Every person registered under the Act, every dealer liable to get himself registered under the Act and every other dealer who is so required by an assessing authority, shall keep and maintain the following books of accounts disclosing true and complete accounts of his daily transactions in Malayalam or in English together with the vouchers and bills:—

(i)

a daily cash book, that is to say, a record of all cash receipts and payments, kept and maintained from day to day indicating the cash balance in hand at the end of each day;

(ii)

a journal, if the accounts are maintained according to mercantile system of accounting;

(iii)

a ledger;

(iv)

a purchase register showing date wise details of the person from whom goods are purchased indicating the registration number, if the purchase is from a registered dealer, details of goods, quantity and value of goods purchased, freight, delivery charges or cost of installation which are separately charged, other charges, if any, paid, and input tax for such purchases;

(v)

a sales register showing date wise details of sales effected to registered dealers indicating the registration number of the purchasing dealer, quantity and value of each class of goods sold, freight, delivery charges or cost of installation separately charged, other charges, if any, received and output tax for such sales;

(vi)

a stock register showing date wise details of in-out- balance position of goods indicating opening stock, goods purchased, goods received otherwise than by way of purchase, goods received on stock transfer, goods sold or used for manufacturing, goods disposed of otherwise than by way of sale or manufacturing, consignment or stock transfer, goods bought or sold in the course of inter State trade or commerce or in the course of export out of or import into the territory of India, and the closing stock. 1[Where goods are disposed of in different ways, local sales, inter-State sale, export, use in manufacture etc., the quantitative details of goods disposed of under each category shall be separately furnished in the register;]

2[(vii)

a dealer who is a whole saler-cum-retailer, shall maintain a day-to-day stock register as specified under clause (vi) only in respect of the wholesale transactions which shall show clearly the quantitative details of goods taken from the wholesale section to the retail section each day. In respect of the retail section the dealer shall maintain a closing stock inventory for the year;

(viii)

a dealer who is having only retail business and is paying tax under sub-section (5) of section 6 need maintain only the records mentioned in clauses (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) and a closing stock inventory for the year;

(ix)

where any dealer sends any goods to any place within the State or outside the State for processing, repairs, maintenance, testing or any other similar purposes and return, he shall maintain separate accounts showing the particulars of the goods, documents accompanying the consignment, name and address of the person to whom sent, purpose for which the goods are sent, the date on which the goods are received back, the quantity and nature of goods received back and document accompanying the consignment;

(x)

where a dealer is undertaking job works in relation to any goods received from any other person, he shall keep accounts showing the particulars of the goods received from such other person nature of job works undertaken, the quantity and nature of the goods returned and the date of return.]

(2) Every dealer shall keep separate purchase and sales accounts for different goods liable to tax at different rates of tax. Separate accounts shall be kept for the purchases in respect of which the dealer is eligible to claim input tax credit showing the purchase price and the tax paid on such purchase separately. Purchase price shall not include the tax collection on such purchase.

(3) Every registered dealer, every dealer liable to get himself registered under the Act and every other dealer who is required so to do by the assessing authority shall keep the books of accounts, in the case of a registered dealer, at the place or places of business entered in the certificate of registration and in the case of others at the place where the dealer carries on his business. Every purchase and every sale shall be brought to account as soon as the purchase or sale, as the case may be, is effected. 1[Every contractor, including a contractor who has opted for payments of tax at compounded rate, shall keep the books of accounts relating to each contract at the work site.]

(4) Every dealer shall keep separate accounts in respect of sales or purchases in the course of export or import and in respect of inter-State sales or purchases.

(a)

Tax credit in respect of transactions between commission agent and principal and in case of transfer of business

17. (1) When a commission agent receives taxable goods from his principal for the sale on behalf of such principal, the principal shall issue tax invoice equivalent to the purchase price of the goods so transferred.

(2) The principal shall indicate the amount of tax separately in the tax invoice referred to in sub-rule (1).

(3) The tax to be indicated separately under sub-rule (2) shall be the amount which the selling dealer had charged on the goods purchased by the principal which is transferred to the commission agent.

(4) The liability of the principal to pay tax on such transfer of goods to the agent shall be as if it is a sale, and provisions of section 11 and the rules made thereunder shall apply, mutatis mutandis.

(5) The commission agent when selling the goods transferred to him by the principal, he shall be liable to pay tax under the Act on the sale price of such goods.

(6) The commission agent shall be entitled to claim tax credit under section 11 and the rules made thereunder to the extent the amount of tax charged separately in the tax invoice referred to in sub-rule (2).

(7) When the commission agent has sold the goods on behalf of the principal, the commission agent shall send to his principal a monthly statement showing the following particulars:—

(i)

value (showing separately the amount of tax charged) of goods transferred by the principal,

(ii)

sale price with amount of tax charged separately on the goods sold by the commission agent,

(iii)

amount of the commission charged by the commission agent in respect of such goods sold by him on behalf of his principal.

(8) On receipt of statement referred to in sub-rule (7), the principal may include in his total turnover of sale, the difference of the amount referred to in clauses (i) and (ii) of sub-rule (7) and may deduct the similar amount from his turnover liable to tax under section 7 of the Act.

(9) When a commission agent purchases taxable goods on behalf of his principal, he shall issue to his principal a tax invoice indicating the value of the goods purchased and indicating separately the amount of tax charged in the original tax invoice of the goods so purchased and shall be liable to pay the tax under section 7 accordingly:

Provided that the commission agent may claim tax credit of the amount of tax charged separately on such purchase by the selling dealer in his tax period in which a tax invoice under this sub-rule is issued by him to his principal.

(10) The principal on receipt of the tax invoice referred to in sub-rule (9) shall show such purchases in his total turnover of purchases and section 11 of the Act and the rules made thereunder shall apply mutatis mutandis in respect of such purchases made by the commission agent.

(11) Where a dealer liable to pay tax under the Act transfers his business in whole or part as provided in section 51, the transferee of the business may claim the tax credit in the manner as under:—

(i)

in case where business has been transferred in whole, then the amount of balance of tax credit on the day of such transfer shall be deemed to be transferred to the transferee subject to the provisions of section 11 and the rules made thereunder,

(ii)

in case where business has been transferred in part, then the balance of the tax credit as admissible under the rules on the day of transfer shall be deemed to be transferred to the transferee subject to the provisions of section 11 and the rules made thereunder:

Provided that the transferor shall reduce such amount of tax credit transferred to the transferee under this clause in the tax period in which such transfer has taken place.

Accounts of agents

47. (1) A dealer carrying on business as an agent, shall furnish along with his monthly tax return, a statement, showing separately the description of each category of goods purchased or sold for each principal and the turnover and tax due thereon.

Explanation : For the purpose of this rule, the term 'agent' means an agent as defined under sub-clause (iii) of clause (n) of section 2.

(2) Such dealer shall maintain—

(i)

accounts showing separately the particulars of each category of goods purchased or received for sale, in respect of each principal;

(ii)

the original or copy of the written contracts, entered into with the principal or letters of authorisation received from the principals ;

(iii)

Accounts of dealer carrying business as principal and agent

48. A dealer carrying on business both as principal as well as agent shall maintain, in addition to the accounts prescribed in rules 45, 46 and 47, separate stock account as follows,—

(i)

stock accounts of goods dealt by him on his own account, and

(ii)

CHAPTER VIII

ACCOUNTS & RECORDS

Nature of accounts to be maintained

62. (1) Every registered dealer and every person liable to be registered under the Act shall keep and maintain a true and correct account of his daily transactions showing the goods produced, manufactured, bought and sold by him and the value thereof separately with invoices and bills.

(2) Every such dealer or person, shall keep separate account of every purchase and sale made in the State, in the course of inter-State trade or commerce, in the course of import into India and in the course of export out of India.

(3) Every dealer shall maintain account of purchases and sales made in the State in respect of different classes of goods liable to tax at different rates of tax separately. He shall maintain—

(a)

an Input Tax Register in Form VAT-48 recording therein in chronological order all purchases made;

(b)

an Output Tax Register in Form VAT-49 recording therein in chronological order all sales made;

(c)

details of credit and debit notes issued during any period.

(4) Every such dealer or person shall keep current books of accounts at the place or places of business entered in his certificate of registration and every purchase and sale must be brought to account as soon as the purchase or sale is made.

Explanation : For the purpose of this sub-rule, current books of accounts shall include Computer Hardware and Software used in connection with business activities of the dealer or person.

(5) The registers, accounts and documents maintained shall be sequentially numbered and where the registers and documents are maintained by means of a Computer or any other similar mechanical devise, the dealer shall maintain copies in paper of such registers and other documents printed on a monthly basis.

(6) Any entry in such registers, accounts and documents shall not be erased, effaced or overwritten and all incorrect entries shall be scored out under attestation and correct entry recorded and where the registers, accounts and documents are maintained by means of a Computer or any other similar mechanical devise, the dealer shall also maintain a record of correction or change of any entry.

(7) Every commission agent, broker, del-credere agent, auctioneer or any other mercantile agent doing business as a dealer, shall maintain following accounts showing—

(a)

particulars of authorizations received by him to purchase or sell goods on behalf of each principal separately;

(b)

particulars of goods purchased or if goods received for sale on behalf of each principal each day;

(c)

details of purchases or sales effected on behalf of each principal each day; and

(d)

details of accounts furnished to each principal each day.

(8) Every wholesale dealer, importer, exporter and manufacturer shall maintain monthly stock account in respect of commodities dealt with by him, and such stock account shall contain particulars of purchases or receipts, sales, deliveries and balance of stock.

(9) Every manufacturer of goods shall maintain monthly production of accounts showing quantitative details of the various raw materials used in the manufacture and the quantitative details of the goods so manufactured.

(10) Every dealer or person who is required to maintain stock accounts shall maintain subsidiary accounts for each godown for keeping the stocks.

(11) Every dealer or person shall also maintain annual accounts including trading, profit and loss account and balance sheet.

(12) Every dealer or person required to keep or maintain books of accounts or other record including tax invoices relating to his purchases and sales shall retain them until the expiration of eight years after the end of the year to which they relate.

Maintenance and preservation of accounts and records

45. (1) Every registered dealer and every person liable to be registered under the Act shall keep and maintain a true and correct account of his all transactions showing the goods produced, manufactured, bought, transferred, purchased or procured, imported, supplied and sold by him and the value thereof separately, together with delivery challans, invoices and bills. Every such dealer or person shall maintain accounts relating to purchase, sale and disposal in respect of each commodity, whether taxable or not, dealt with by him.

(2) Every dealer shall maintain records of collection and payment of tax and the claim of tax credit during any period. Every dealer shall maintain a register of delivery challan, tax invoice, credit note and debit note issued by him and he shall enter therein the details of tax invoices, credit notes and debit notes as prescribed in rules 42 and 43.

(3) (a) Every dealer who is liable to pay tax under the Act, shall exempt the dealer who has been granted permission to pay lump-sum tax under section 14, maintain monthly stock accounts in respect of each commodity dealt with by him, and such stock account shall contain particulars of purchases or receipts, sales, deliveries and balance of stock, 5[xxx].

(b) Every dealer dealing in commodities mentioned in Schedule III shall keep and maintain daily accounts separately over and above monthly account under clause (a) in Form 213.

(4) Every manufacturer of goods shall maintain monthly production of accounts showing quantitative details of various raw materials used in the manufacture and the quantitative details of the goods so manufactured.

(5) Every purchasing dealer shall keep particulars of names and addresses of dealers or persons from whom he has purchased the goods and particulars of names and addresses of the dealers to whom he has sold the goods as also the complete address of the premises wherein goods transacted during the tax period are kept or stored by the dealer:

Provided that in case such goods are found either kept or stored at any place otherwise than the place referred to above, after giving an opportunity of being heard to such person under whose possession such goods are found, it shall be presumed that tax payable under the Act on such goods is attempted to evade and the assessing authority shall seize such goods and give receipt thereof to the person from whose possession or control such goods are seized:

Provided further that the assessing authority may release the goods on furnishing security in the manner referred to in rule 12 of the amount equivalent to fair market price of such goods seized.

(6) Every dealer shall keep the records and particulars of the goods which are disposed of without any consideration.

(7) Every commission agent, broker, del credere agent, auctioneer or any mercantile agent shall maintain accounts showing,—

(a)

particulars of authorization given to him by each principal to purchase or sell goods on behalf of such principal separately;

(b)

particulars of goods purchased or goods received for sale on behalf of each principal each day;

(c)

particulars of purchases or sales effected on behalf of each principal;

(d)

details of accounts furnished to each principal;

(e)

details of transactions referred to in rule 17;

(f)

tax paid on purchases or on sales effected on behalf of each principal and the challan number and date of remittance of the tax into the Government Treasury.

(8) Every dealer or person executing works contract shall keep separate account showing,—

(a)

the particulars of names and addresses of the persons for whom and on whose behalf he carried on the execution of works contract;

(b)

the particulars of goods procured by way of purchases or otherwise for the execution of works contract;

(c)

the particulars of goods to be utilized in execution of each works contract;

(d)

the details of payment received in respect of each works contract; and

(e)

the particulars of charges towards labour service and other like charges which are deductible under sub-clause (c) of clause (30) of section 2:

Provided that such amount shall be reasonable with regards to the nature of the respective works contract.

(9) Every dealer or person engaged in the transfer of right to use any goods shall keep—

(a)

particulars of names and addresses of the persons to whom he has delivered the goods for use,

(b)

details of amounts received in respect of each transaction, and

(c)

monthly stock accounts in respect of each commodity dealt with by him and such stock account shall contain particulars of purchases or receipts, deliveries and balance of stock.

(10) Every dealer or person liable under the Act shall keep books of accounts at the place or places of business mentioned in the certificate of registration and every purchase and sale shall be brought to account as soon as possible the purchase or sale is effected.

Accounts of dealers transacting through agents

46. (1) A dealer, transacting business through agents, shall furnish along with his monthly tax return, a statement, showing separately the description of each category of goods purchased or sold through each agent; and the turnover and tax due thereon; and designation of the assessing authority to whom the tax is paid by the agent.

Explanation: For the purpose of this rule, the term 'agent' means an agent as defined under sub-clause (iii) of clause (n) of section 2.

(2) Such dealer shall also furnish the following, as and when demanded by the assessing authority:—

(i)

the originals of the written contract, entered into with the agents or the authorisation letters issued to the agent;

(ii)

accounts showing the description, quantity and the value of the goods despatched to each agent on each occasion with proof of movement of goods;

(iii)

copies of the tax invoice issued by the agents to the purchasers;

(iv)

accounts rendered by the agents to the dealer from time to time.

Manner of proving payment of tax by the contractor and the principal or the commission agent

7. (1) A claim made by a contractor under clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 6 shall be supported by a declaration in Form 3 to be issued by the sub-contractor and shall be admitted in proof of such claim.

(2) A claim made by a principal under sub-clause (i) of clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 6 shall be supported by an adat patti or sale account issued by the commission agent in accordance with the system prevalent in the market and shall be admitted in proof of such claim.

(3) A claim made by a commission agent under sub-clause (ii) of clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 6 shall be supported by a declaration in Form 4 issued by the principal and shall be admitted as proof in support of such claim.

(3) Such registered dealer who has a taxable turnover relating to goods taxable at different rates shall—

(a)

record the daily total sales of goods taxable at different rates, including exempt sales, at the end of the day; and

(b)

at the end of the month, based on daily taxable sales, calculate the tax con ten t using the tax fraction or fractions for the rate or rates of tax in force and include the amount in the return for that period.

(4) Such registered dealer, who has a taxable turnover relating to goods which are taxable at different rates and cannot be identified separately, shall—

(a)

record daily total sales at the end of the day;

(b)

at the end of the month, calculate daily total sales for that month;

(c)

apportion those total sales into taxable sales in the same proportion as the value of purchases of taxable goods made in the month out of the value of total purchases in that month; and

(d)

from the apportioned taxable sales, calculate the tax for the month using the tax fraction or fractions for the rate or rates of tax in force and include the amount in the return for the month.

Maintenance of records

43. Records to be maintained by registered dealers.

(1) Every registered dealer shall keep and maintain a true and correct account of his business transactions.

(2) The following records in particular shall be maintained:—

(a)

A monthly account specifying total output tax, input tax and net tax payable or the tax credit due for refund including carried forward of such balance from the preceding month.

(b)

Purchase records, such as, purchase invoices, cash and credit invoices with despatch challans and transport and courier documents/receipts wherein tax has been charged and all purchases made without charge of tax including import of goods from other States or countries or from unregistered dealers.

(c)

Sales records showing separately sales made at each rate of tax, zero rate and exempt sales.

(d)

The copies of tax invoices related to taxable sales and invoices related to exempt sales in chronological and numerical order.

(e)

Credit and debit note issued/received, in chronological and numerical order.

(f)

Records of all zero rated exports of goods together with copies of custom clearance certificates, invoices issued to the foreign purchasers, transport documentation, Form 'FT prescribed under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, orders or contracts for with the foreign purchasers and evidence of payment by bank, transfer through a bank or by a letter of credit payable by bank.

(g)

Records of inter-State sales and inter-State transfer supported by 'C Forms, 'F' Forms, waybills and stock transfer vouchers.

(h)

Cash records maintained by retailers, viz. cash book, petty cash vouchers, and other accounting records including cash registers, machine rolls details in the daily takings.

(i)

Details of input tax calculation where the registered dealer is making both taxable and exempt sales.

(j)

The registers, accounts and documents maintained shall be sequentially numbered and where the register and other documents are maintained by means of a computer or any other similar mechanical device, the dealer shall maintain copies in paper of such registers and other documents printed on a monthly basis.

(k)

Documentation, records and claims eligible for all transitional tax credit in respect of stock held on the appointed day or on first registration.

(l)

Stock records showing stock receipts, returns, deliveries and balances ratewise.

(m)

Manufacturing records including records of capital goods and raw materials.

(n)

Annual accounts including Trading, Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet, with Schedules.

(o)

Order records, delivery notes/challans and waybills.

(p)

Records of the bank transactions.

(3) A dealer opting for composition of tax under section 7 of the Act and an unregistered dealer shall maintain a daily record of his gross sale and purchase details.

(4) All records maintained in course of business shall be retained for a period of six years from the expiry of the year to which they relate.

CHAPTER VII

RECORDS AND INVESTIGATION

Maintenance of accounts by dealers

45. (1) Where any dealer keeps and maintains his accounts in a language other than English, he shall adopt international numerals in the maintenance of such accounts.

(2) Every dealer shall keep accounts showing separately for each category of goods produced or manufactured; bought or received; sold, supplied or distributed by him and the quantity and value thereof together with the voucher.

(3) Every dealer, except the dealer opted to pay tax at compounded rate as provided under sections 19 and 15(2), shall keep separate purchase and sales accounts for each category of goods, showing the input tax and output tax. The input tax column of the purchase account shall be totalled taking into account of disallowance, restriction, partial-reversal and reversal of input tax credit as contemplated under rule 17 and output tax column shall also be totalled taking into account of exclusions and deductions contemplated under rules 15 and 16. All the purchase and sales accounts shall be closed on monthly basis for the purpose of reporting the turnover in the return.

(4) A dealer paying tax in compounded rate shall maintain purchase account and sales account preserving the tax invoice of purchase and sales.

(5) Further the accounts of purchase and sales shall be maintained separately when such purchases and sales take place within the Union territory, in the course of inter-State trade or commerce and in the course of import or export.

(6) Every registered dealer who manufactures or produces shall maintain a production-cum-stock register in Form-H.

(7) Every dealer executing works contract shall keep separate accounts for each contract specifying the particulars of the names and addresses of the persons for whom he has executed works contract.

(8) Every dealer executing works contract and opting to pay tax by way of composition shall maintain records of

(a)

payments received from the contractee;

(b)

records of entry in Form-L Return; and

(c)

records of tax deduction at source.

(9) Every dealer executing works contract and not opting to pay tax by way of composition shall keep the following records, namely:—

(a)

the particulars of goods procured by way of purchase or otherwise for the execution of works contract;

(b)

the particulars of goods to be used or used in the execution of each works contract;

(c)

the details of payment received in respect of each works contract; and

(d)

the details of:

(i)

labour charges for works executed;

(ii)

amount paid to sub-contractor for labour and services;

(iii)

charges for planning, designing and architect's fee;

(iv)

charges for obtaining on hire or otherwise machinery and tools used for the execution of the works contract;

(v)

cost of consumables such as water, electricity, fuel etc., used in the execution of the works contract; the property in which is not transferred in the course of execution of a works contract;

(vi)

cost of establishment of the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services;

(vii)

other similar expenses relatable to the supply of labour and services;

(viii)

profit earned by the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services;

(ix)

all amounts for which goods exempted are transferred in execution of works contract; and

(x)

turnover of the goods involved in the execution of works contract which are transferred in the course of inter-State trade or commerce under section 3 of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 (Central Act 74 of 1956) or transferred outside the Union territory under section 4 or transferred in the course of import or export under section 5 of the said Act.

SERVICE TAX - SMALL SERVICE PROVIDER EXEMPTION - CLUBBING OF PARTNER'S RECEIPTS WITH THAT OF FIRM

1. Our partnership is registered under service tax and has been paying service tax under commercial coaching services. Now, the partners are also individually providing the same services however their receipts are less then Rs. 9 Lakhs. Please clarify whether partners are liable to pay service tax on the basis of their relation with firm and whether partners' receipts can be clubbed with that of the firm ?

As per definition of 'person' under section 65B(37), person is defined to include firm as a separate category of persons. Therefore, for purpose of service tax, firm is a separate person from its partners and same view would apply in respect of claim of small service provider's exemption.

However, creation of bogus entities or bogus separation of receipts in order to claim SSI-exemption has been held to be impermissible under Central Excise and same attracts clubbing of turnover.

In short, if resources are same (i.e., infrastructure, finance, staff, management, branding, control are same), then, clubbing would get attracted.

SERVICE TAX - COMMISSION FROM FOREIGN COMPANIES - LIABILITY TO SERVICE TAX

2. We are providing services of commission agent to Singapore based foreign company for the sale of iron ore. The commission is received in foreign exchange. Please clarify whether this would be liable to service tax ? Can there be any tax planning ?

As per rule 2(f) of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012, intermediary is defined to mean "intermediary" means a broker, an agent or any other person, by whatever name called, who arranges or facilitates a provision of a service (hereinafter called the 'main' service) or a supply of goods, between two or more persons, but does not include a person who provides the main service or supplies the goods on his account. As per rule 9(c), the Place of Provision of services of an intermediary would be location of such intermediary (w.e.f. 1-10-2014).

In view of definition under Rule 2(f), commission agents and other agents, or the like would be liable to service tax on their location basis. Accordingly, Indian commission agents of foreign companies are liable to service tax w.e.f. 1-10-2014, even if the commission is earned by them in the foreign exchange.

Hence, it appears that your services are liable to service tax. We would suggest of any tax planning in view of very wide words used.

Nevertheless, if it can be shown that the services being provided are consultancy services, not relatable to supply/sale of goods, then only, rule 9(c) read with rule 2(f) would not apply.

CENVAT CREDIT - WORKS CONTRACT SERVICES v. TRADING SERVICE

3. We are having 2 divisions : trading division and service division (works contract services). Can we take credit of input services received from sub-contractor which is used exclusively to provide works contract service ?

Since trading activity is also an exempted service under rule 2(e) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004; hence, you become provided for taxable as well as exempt service and have to comply with the provisions of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Therefore, you should either maintain separate accounts and, if not, pay 7% (6% up to 18-5-2015) of the value of exempted services of trading as per rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

The provisions of rule 6 override provisions of all other rules.

SERVICE TAX - DISTRIBUTORS v. COMMISSION AGENTS

4. We are distributors of products of Johnson & Johnson. The following is the procedure :

J&J supplies to us @ Rs. 100 (invoiced) ;

We sells to our customer @ Rs. 100 ;

Bad debts, if any, are borne by us ;

We raise a debit note of Rs. 10 towards profit margin on sales ;

On confirmation J & J raises credit note of Rs. 10 on us.

Thus, we end up paying Rs. 90 to J&J.

Whether we are liable to pay service tax ? Whether our practice needs amends ?

In our considered view, your practice is very well in order. There is no service tax liability, as you are not an agent of J&J; in fact, you buy from J&J and sell to the customers. The fact that J&J invoices you first and title apparent gets transferred would show that there is pure sale of goods to you and by you to your customers.

It appears that this practice is being adopted by J&J to control your profit margin.

EXPERTS’ OPINION : CENVAT CREDIT

Thus Spake Experts

An assessee is pro-viding both taxable and exempt services. He utilises various input services for providing his output services. In respect of some of the input services, he is in a position to establish direct correlation between his input service and taxable output service. In respect of general (common input services like telephone, courier, manpower supply, bank services etc., he is not able to establish direct relation with either exempt output service or taxable output service. He is utilising full Cenvat credit in respect of input services where he is able to establish direct relation between input service and output taxable service, as per rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules. In addition, in respect of common input services where he is not able to establish any direct relation with output service, he is availing Cenvat credit to the extent of 20% of amount of service tax payable on taxable output service, as provided in rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

For example, service tax payable by him is Rs. 100. Service tax paid on his common input services is Rs. 25. Service tax paid on services where he can directly establish relation with his taxable output service is Rs. 10. He is availing Cenvat credit of Rs.10 [rule 6(2)] plus Rs. 20 [rule 6(3)(c)]. Is it legally correct? In short, whether rules 6(2) and 6(3)(c) are mutually exclusive or they can be used simultaneously.

V.S. DATEY

The issue will arise in due course and it appears to be a borderline case. There is no specific prohibition in simultaneous availment of credit under rules 6(2) and 6(3). Hence, it can be argued that what is not prohibited is deemed to have been permitted and hence simultaneous availment of rules 6(2) and 6(3) is permissible. This is also justifiable on the principle that ambiguity in taxation provision should be resolved in favour of tax payer.

Counter View - Rule 6(3) starts with the words ‘notwithstanding anything contained in rules 6(1) and 6(2)’. Thus, rule 6(3) overrides provisions of rules 6(1) and 6(2). From this, it appears that assessee has to follow either rule 6(2) [which allows full credit if he can maintain separate accounts of input service] or rule 6(3)(c) [which allows use of common input services for providing dutiable as well as exempted/excluded taxable services].

In other words, if he is not able to maintain separate accounts even in respect of some of the input services, he has to either completely forego input credit on those services and go under rule 6(2) for services where he can identify separately, or avail rule 6(3)(c ) in respect of all input services and take credit to the extent of 20% of service tax payable on output services.

However, there is no clear provision that these are mutually exclusive and assessee cannot avail partially rule 6(2) and partially rule 6(3)(c).

Hence, if assessee is slightly risk taking type, he may avail simultaneously rules 6(2) and 6(3), as one never knows which view will ultimately prevail in such borderline cases.

We are providing both taxable and exempt services. Taxable services are to the tune of Rs. 45 lakhs and exempt services are Rs. 30 lakhs. Total input service tax paid is Rs. 3,00,000 which includes Rs. 1,00,000 which is directly related to taxable services. Balance Rs. two lakhs relates to common input services like telephone, rent, etc. We would like to know whether provision of proportionate credit under rule 6(3) applies to entire input credit of Rs. three lakhs or whether we can take full credit of Rs. one lakh and apply ratio to balance credit of Rs. two lakhs ?

Basic issue is whether rule 6(2) and 6(3) are mutually exclusive or whether they are complimentary. Of course, applying the ratio to entire credit is a safer option and in second case, some litigation is possible and, hence, it should be taken only after disclosing all details to the Department and after considering possible cost of litigation (after making full disclosure). However, my views are as follows—

Rule 6(2) and 6(3) should be taken as complimentary and not mutually exclusive. The words used in rule 6(3) are ‘notwithstanding anything contained in rule 6(1) and 6(2), the manufacturer of goods or provider of output service, opting not to maintain separate accounts, shall follow either of the following options as applicable to him’.

This sub-rule can be interpreted to mean that the assessee can follow rule 6(2) for inputs and input services for which he can maintain separate records and accounts and follow rule 6(3) in respect of inputs and input services for which the assessees opts not to maintain separate accounts.

In my view, fair interpretation is that rule 6(3) should apply to cases of common inputs and common input services where the assessee is not in a position to maintain separate accounts. Thus, rule 6(2) and 6(3) are complimentary.

In costing, there are concepts of ‘allocation’ and ‘apportionment’. The costs which can be allocated directly to a particular product should be so allocated, while costs which cannot be directly allocated to any particular product/service, should be apportioned on a reasonable basis. This principle can be applied here.

The input goods/services which can be directly allocated to taxable goods/services and exempt goods/services should be allocated under rule 6(2). Full credit should be allowed of the Cenvat credit allocable to taxable goods/services and no credit should be allowed for the Cenvat credit allocable to exempt goods/services. The remaining input credit/input services should be apportioned between taxable goods/services and exempt goods/services on the basis of formulae given in rule 6(3A). This should give best possible and most fair results. Of course, this should be done after making full disclosure to the Department, to avoid charge of suppression of facts.

"‘Commission agent’ means any person who acts on behalf of another person and causes sale or purchase of goods, or provision or receipt of services, for a consideration and includes any person who, while acting on behalf of another person—

Commercial concern and commission agent

9. When the service was notified, the individual commission agents were taking a stand that they are not ‘Commercial Concern’, but proprietors. However, going by the definition, the word ‘Commercial Concern’ does not figure in the definition nor in the exemption notification and, hence, this stand taken by the commission agents turned out to be futile exercise.

An ‘Agent’ is defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which refers to ‘A person employed to do any act for another; or to represent another in dealings with third persons’.

In the light of the above, other than those commission agents representing the foreign principals and canvassing their orders for the goods in India, the other commission agents accepted the levy and started complying with the provisions of service tax and payment of the same effective from July 9, 2004.

CENVAT credit

10. The new CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 came into effect from September 10, 2004, which gave an interesting relief under the term ‘Inter-sectoral Credit’ which enabled the service providers to take credit not only on service tax paid on input services, but also excise duty paid on inputs and capital goods, which is used for providing taxable output service. Thus, all the service providers who are paying service tax are granted CENVAT credit facility announced under the abovesaid Rules so that to a great extent the service tax liability is reduced. Those who are availing exemption of Rs.4 lakhs are certainly not eligible for CENVAT credit, which is a pre-condition for any exemption from payment of service tax granted to the service provider.

Additional responsibility handled by commission agents

11. In the present business scenario, some of the commission agents undertake additional responsibility as part of their agreement with the principals, such as erection, installation and commissioning of the goods ordered by the Indian customer on behalf of the foreign principal. In such scenario, since erection, installation, commissioning is also one of the notified services, and since such services are rendered/provided and used/consumed within India, a liability to pay service tax will arise. However, the foreign principals do not pay any separate amount to the Indian commission agents towards erection, installation and commissioning and, the amount is arrived at after taking into account this service as well.

Though the commercial agreement between the foreign principal and the Indian commission agent is in order, yet it will pose a problem for arriving at the value of taxable service, when it comes to payment of service tax on erection, installation and commissioning portion. Unfortunately, the commission agents cannot avail abatement of 67 per cent granted under Notification No. 19/2003-ST, dated August 20, 2003, which applies only to those composite contracts involving supply of machinery and erection, installation and commissioning of the same.

In the scenario discussed above, the machinery is supplied by the foreign principal, whereas the erection, installation, commissioning activity is taking place in India and, therefore, the department is bound to insist for payment of service tax on the gross amount received as commission. Therefore, the commission agents should enter into the agreement in such a manner that the commission amount is split into a major portion towards commission for sale of goods and balance portion towards erection, installation and commissioning. In such situation, the service tax liability on erection, installation and commissioning will be only on the reduced quantum of amount received specifically towards the above service. It is also a choice of the commission agent to arrive at a fixed amount required for erection, installation and commissioning so that the fixed amount is taken into account to arrive at the value of taxable service. Unfortunately, service tax so paid towards erection, installation and commissioning cannot be availed as CENVAT credit since it is not required for rendering the output service of commission agent and it is a helpless situation of grin and bear it. In other words, it is an additional cost to be provided for in business.

Services exported and embargo under rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, assigns an obligation on the manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods as well as the provider of taxable and exempted service, as stipulated therein. This article examines as to under what circumstances the provisions of rule 6(3)(c) can be applied restricting the service provider to utilize only 20 per cent of credit, especially with reference to the phrase ‘exempted services’.

Introduction

1. Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 (the CCR), assigns an obligation on the manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods as well as the provider of taxable and exempted service, as stipulated therein. In terms of rule 6(2), the provider of output service who avails cenvat credit in respect of any input or input service has to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption, and inventory of input and input service meant for use in providing output service on which service tax is payable. In other words, the service provider is to maintain records separately for receipt, consumption, inventory of each of the input/input service which are (a) relatable to taxable output service and (b) exempted service. If for any reason such maintenance of accounts is neither possible nor feasible, in terms of provisions of rule 6(3)(c), the provider of output service shall utilize credit only to extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the service tax payable on taxable input service. On the contrary, the credit can be utilized fully under the following circumstances :

uIf the entire services are taxable service on which service tax is paid (no exempted service) (or)

uIf separate accounts are maintained as above.

New Cenvat Credit Rules

2. In the Budget 2004-05, credit of service tax and excise duty was extended across goods and services. The concept of inter-sectoral credit or credit across goods and services was brought into force, followed by introduction of new Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

As per rule 2(e) of the CCR, ‘exempted service’ means taxable services which are exempt from the whole of duty leviable thereon and includes services on which no service tax is leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994.

As per rule 2(d), ‘exempted goods’ means excisable goods which are exempt from whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to ‘NIL’ rate of duty.

The definitions are similar except that in respect of ‘exempted goods’ it includes goods which are chargeable to ‘NIL’ rate of duty for the reason that duty as per section 3 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 shall be levied on all excisable goods manufactured or produced in India at the rates set forth in the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985, and for some goods the tariff rate itself is ‘NIL’, while in respect of taxable services charge of service tax at 12 per cent is as per the provisions of section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994.

In terms of rule 6(1) of the CCR, the CENVAT credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input service which is used in ‘exempted services’ except under circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2) . Therefore, a service provider who provides ‘taxable service’ and ‘exempted service’ but does not maintain separate set of accounts in terms of rule 6 (2), is permitted to utilize the input credit only to the tune of 20 per cent of service tax payable in view of the embargo in rule 6(3)(c).

Let us assume that a service provider renders only two categories of service (a) taxable services and (b) services which are exported but exempt by virtue of the Export of Services Rules, 2005 (the ESR). Now the moot question is whether taxable services which are exempted by virtue of the ESR are to be treated as taxable service or exempted service within the meaning of rule 2(e) of the CCR, to attract the mischief of rule 6(3)(c).

Rule 3 of the ESR contains provisions relating to export of services which have to be fulfilled to deem such services as export of services. Further, as per rule 4 of the ESR, any service which is taxable under clause (105) of section 65 of the Act, may be exported without payment of tax.

Another important condition is that the goods or services so procured are in addition to that of services provided to the service recipient.

From the above we can see that the common thing in both the conditions and definition is that the agent who is a service provider in this case shall receive the actual amount towards procurement of goods or services to be paid to the third party.

Sub-rule (2) deals with the cases where the service is provided partly in India and partly outside India. According to the said sub-rule, in this case the value for charging service tax shall include the value of service partly provided in India.

Conclusion

4. After going through these Rules and new section 67 any ordinary prudent man having little knowledge of the service tax will come to conclusion that the litigation is bound to proliferate. This reminds one of the old days of section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944. It is said that the laws are made for the people’s convenience but it is also well said that more you go deep in any law the same Acts against the interest of the common persons. This set of Rules along with the new section 67 is the best example for that.

CREDIT OF INPUT SERVICE TAX USED AS COMMON SERVICES

A manufacturing company manufactures twisted and texturising yarn. It pays excise duty on such yarn. It is also appointed dealer of POY/PFY of a Ltd. Co. Some quantity of above yarn (raw-material yarn) is consumed in manufacture of excisable yarn and he does trading for rest of the quantity. He receives commission on whole quantity of yarn purchased as a dealer. Service tax is paid on commission received on whole lot of yarn received as a dealer. The same company also manufactures machines for own use and for public sale. Excise duty is paid on manufacturing of final machines. It pays service tax on job charges paid in manufacture of making machines and also on repairs and maintenance on machines. The company is registered under excise and service tax provisions. Query - (a) Whether service tax paid on (input services) relating to job work and R and M can be set-off against service tax payable by company on output service tax on yarn commission? (b) It is said that with Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, across the board sectorial credit can be enjoyed by manufacturer-cum-service provider? (c) What are restrictions for a manufacturer-cum-service tax provider in Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004?

Basically, Cenvat provisions do not require one to one relationship. Cenvat is a common pool of credit of all duties as specified in rule 3(1). This credit can be utilised for payment of any duty or tax, as specified in rule 3(4), subject to restrictions as specified in rule 3(7). Thus, except restrictions under rule 3(7), the credit is completely inter-changeable.

Moreover, definition of input service is very wide. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’. Any relation with manufacture or provision of service is not required. Hence, in my view, Cenvat credit of any input service is available for payment of service tax on any output service.

Of course, department may not easily agree to this but I think legal position is quite clear.

Is he entitled to utilise Credit of the duties paid on ‘inputs’ or ‘capital goods’ for paying the service tax?

The question is raised only in light of the fact that the inputs/capital goods have no relationship at all with rendering of the service of Commission Agent.

The principle discussed above will apply here also.

CENVAT CREDIT – OPTION TO MAINTAIN SEPARATE ACCOUNTS

1. We are providing works contract services and job-work services where both services are liable for service tax one is at full rate and another is at abatement rate with reverse charge. Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, as it stood before 1-4-2016, mandated maintenance of separate books of account for taxable and exempted activities, failing which credit was liable to be reversed as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 (viz. 6 or 7 per cent; or pro rata).

Now, the requirement to maintain separate accounts has been done away within. In case of exempted as well as taxable activities, the credit cannot be taken for exempted activities and said credit is to be computed as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The said rule provides for percentage-based payment or pro rata reversal, as opted for by the assessee.

Hence, you have options :

Do not take credit of common inputs and input services

If credit is taken of common inputs and input services, then, —

either opt for percentage-based reversal or

opt for pro rata reversal.

2. One of my client has availed CENVAT credit on input service on the entire amount of the bill. Subsequently service provider has given the discount on the bill. Whether proportionate CENVAT credit to be reversed on the portion of the amount of discount received ?

Assuming no reverse charge case, credit can be taken on receipt of invoice. Further, payment of value of service and service tax should be made to the service provider within 3 months of date of invoice, failing which credit has to be reversed and can be re-taken only after full such payment.

As regards Part/Discounted Payment, it is provided in Circular No. 122/3/2010-S.T., dated 30-4-2010 that, in cases where receiver of service makes part/discounted payment only after 3 months, then, he is entitled to take full or pro rata credit provided he has also paid the amount of service tax, (whether proportionately reduced or the original amount) to the service provider.

Going by the Circular, if original amount of service tax is paid to the service provider, then, credit would not be touched. Accordingly, we opine as under :

[a]

If service tax amount is not changed and only value is reduced/negotiated, then, full credit may be taken [full and final settlement towards value would amount to 'payment of value' and would suffice requirements of rule 4(7)].

[b]

Alternatively, if service tax amount is also changed [say, original service tax is Rs. 14 and service tax as per revised value is Rs. 9.8], then, service provider may take benefit of rule 6(3) [credit of Rs. 4.2 may be taken by service provider] and service receiver may take credit of Rs. 9.8.

SERVICE TAX – GOVERNMENT/LOCAL AUTHORITY CAN BE BUSINESS ENTITY

3. Can Government/Local Authority be Business Entity for the purpose of section 65B of the Finance Act, 1994 ?

All services by government or local authority to any business entity are liable to service tax. Business Entity [Section 65B(17)]means any person ordinarily carrying out any activity relating to industry, commerce or any other business or profession. Since even government or local authority can be carrying out any activity relating to industry, commerce or any other business or profession, hence, they can also be business entity. Accordingly, the services might be liable to service tax.

However, by virtue of Entry 54 of Mega Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012, services provided —

by Government or a local authority

to another Government or local authority

falling under section 66D(a)(iv),

are exempt from service tax.

Hence, even if government or local authority is business entity, services availed by it from another government or local authority falling under section 66D(a)(iv) are exempt.

INPUT SERVICES USED FOR SELF-MANUFACTURED AS WELL AS TRADED GOODS

We are manufacturers of engineering products. We also are traders of those products, i.e., we procure these goods under our brand name and sale. We have appointed selling agents for sale of our products (both self-manufactured and traded). We pay selling commission to our indenting agents. The selling agents charge service tax on the commission. We avail Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission paid by us on traded goods as well as self-manufactured goods, and utilise the same for payment of excise duty on our self-manufactured products. Department has issued a show-cause notice to us, informing that we are not eligible for service tax paid by us on commission attributable to traded goods. Please advise.

You are eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax paid both on self-manufactured goods and traded goods, for the following reasons -

(1)Definition of ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is very wide. As per inclusive part of the definition, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’, since the words used are ‘such as’ and not ‘viz.’.

(2)The inclusive part of definition clearly covers ‘sales promotion’. The inclusive part of definition does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’.

(3)Cenvat Credit Rules do not require any one to one relation between input and output.

(4)Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not require distribution of Cenvat credit in any particular ratio. Entire credit of service tax at HO or depot or branch offices can be transferred to any unit without any restriction. The rule makes no distinction between services used for manufacture and services used for other activities like trading, financing, etc.

(5)The Finance Minister in para 148 of his Budget Speech on 8-7-2004 has stated as follows, "I propose to take a major step towards integrating tax on goods and services. Accordingly, I propose to extend credit of service tax and excise duty across goods and services".

(6)Thus, the Cenvat Credit Rules have to be interpreted keeping this goal in mind and, hence, cannot be interpreted narrowly. As per doctrine of purposive interpretation, an interpretation which advances purpose of the Statute should be preferred over an interpretation which defeats the purpose.

(7)It is clear that after introduction of the Cenvat Credit Rules, the whole company is treated as one single entity for Cenvat credit. The definition of ‘input service’ and ‘input service distributor’ has abolished distinction between ‘goods’, ‘manufacture’ and ‘services’. Entire company is treated as one unit for purpose of Cenvat credit, as is the position under ‘Goods and Service Tax’ (GST) which has been set as the goal. Even concept of ‘LTU’ (Large Taxpayer Unit) is a step in that direction.

(8)Even assuming that there is some ambiguity (though really there is none), it is well-settled principle that the benefit of doubt goes to assessee.

Thus, Cenvat credit availed by you is legally correct.

However, you must keep in mind that current decisions of Tribunal are highly conservative and, hence, ultimate result is uncertain. You should be mentally prepared to pay interest @ 13%, if final decision goes against you.

Therefore, unless the air travel agents book the tickets and thereby unless they provide the services to the customers, they do not become entitled to any commission. It cannot, therefore, be said that the commission that the air travel agents get from the airlines is independent of and distinct from the services that they provide to the air-travellers and are relatable to the business that they provide to the airlines. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process, the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle is cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case goes away. From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l), the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided which is made taxable. In our opinion, therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. We may also say that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air-travellers. If, in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission, that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-traveller. On the other hand, we may say that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited, the tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which, there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the learned counsel that because of section 67(k) the nature of the tax itself changes, is incorrect." (p. 305)

12. Like Indian commission agents are representing the foreign principals and canvassing the product and obtaining the orders, it is also a common commercial scenario for the Indian companies to employ commission agents abroad who can move around and obtain orders based on which the goods can be exported from India to the customer identified by the foreign commission agents. The commission so paid to the foreign agents is for the services rendered outside India. However, with the introduction of new set of Rules ‘Service Tax (Provided from Outside India and received in India) Rules, 2006, which came into effect from April 19, 2006, it is an unfortunate situation that the commission so paid by Indian principals to the foreign commission agent will be treated as a taxable service under the newly introduced section 66A read with the above-mentioned new Rules. As a result, the Indian principals will be deemed to be the service provider and, accordingly, service tax is payable on the commission amount remitted by them outside India since the same is paid for the services provided from outside India by the foreign commission agent, but received in India by the Indian principal.

If a foreign commission agent undertakes the job of erection, installation and commissioning of the goods imported by the Indian principal and charges the customer separately, question of service tax liability will not arise on Indian principal, since such services are rendered/provided and used/consumed outside India, which will not attract service tax. If, however, foreign commission agent raises separate bill on the Indian principals for such activities or for undertaking maintenance or repair work during warranty period, such service will attract service tax under the new Rules and Indian principal will be liable to pay such service tax.

Reimbursement of expenses

13. Normally, commission agents obtain reimbursement of expenses from their principals based on the terms of contract and till the introduction of new Valuation Rules, 2006, not only the commission agents, but also other service providers were not including such expenses reimbursed by the service receiver in the value of taxable service and this has resulted in a heavy loss of revenue to the Government. However, the valuation concept has undergone a sea change with effect from April 18, 2006 with the introduction of substituted section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994 and introduction of a new set of Rules titled Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, which came into effect from April 19, 2006.

Rule 5 of the above rules clearly indicates that any expenses incurred by the service provider during the course of rendering the service will form part of the value of taxable service and service tax payable on such amount. As a result of this stringent provision, the reimbursement concept has undergone a major change and only when a service provider acts as a Pure Agent, and fulfils all the eight conditions laid down under Rule 5(2) of the Valuation Rules, 2006, such amount can be excluded from the value of taxable service. Thus, there is no more free lunch to the service providers and service tax is now payable on the value of taxable service which should include, inter alia, any expenses incurred for rendering the output service. For example, if a chartered accountant in Mumbai undertakes the audit of his clients in Chennai, the air travel expenses, hotel expenses, taxi expenses, etc., cannot be excluded as a reimbursement of expenses on actuals, but are to be included in the value of taxable service since these are incurred for rendering his output service.

(1)Mere receipt of benefit of service in India does not mean service is provided in India.
