Para 4.1-8- The service provider in the course of providing any taxable service may incur certain expenditure or cost as a pure agent of the client. The service provider seeks to exclude such expenditure or cost incurred by him as a pure agent of his client (generally known as reimbursable expenditure) from the value of the taxable services. Para 4.1-9There could be situations where the client of the service provider specifically engages the service provider, as his agent, to contract with the third party for supply of any goods or services on his behalf. In those cases such goods or services so procured are treated as supplied to the client rather than to the contracting agent. The service provider in such cases incurs the expenditure purely on behalf of his client in his capacity as agent of the client. Amounts paid to the third party by the service provider as a pure agent of his client can be treated as reimbursable expenditure and not includible in the taxable value. However, if the service provider acts as an undisclosed agent i.e. acting in his own name without disclosing that he is actually acting as an agent of his client, he cannot claim the expenditure incurred by him as reimbursable expenditure. Whether the expenditure or cost incurred by the service provider in his capacity as a pure agent of the client or incurred on his own account is a question of fact and law and is to be determined carefully.

Para 4.1-10Indication of different elements of the transaction in the invoice or bill could often be misleading. One has to carefully examine the exact legal nature of the transactions and other material facts before taking a view as to whether or not the expenditure sought to be excluded from the value is reimbursable expenditure. Not only the form, but also the substance of the transaction should be duly taken into account.

Para 4.1-11Rule 5 pertains to reimbursable expenditure incurred by the service provider as a pure agent of his client. Explanation (1) to rule 5(2) clearly specifies the criteria to decide whether the service provider acts as a pure agent or not in a given situation. In the case of agency function, the agent neither intends to hold nor holds any title to the goods or services and also never uses such goods or services so procured. It is also important to note that the service provider only receives the actual amount incurred to procure such goods or services.

Para 4.1-12The service provider who seeks to claim exclusion of certain value from the taxable value should also fulfil all the conditions specified in rule 5(2).

10.8-6 Service provider must disclose that he is acting only as agent?

The departmental clarifications are generally in line with statutory provisions. However, para 4.1-9 of the departmental clarification envisages that the service provider should disclose that he is acting merely as agent of principal for purpose of payment of these expenses. Otherwise, he cannot claim the expenditure incurred by him as reimbursable expenditure. This view does not seem to be correct for following reasons -

Rule 5(2) of Valuation Rules does not stipulate such a provision.

Contract Act does not require that Agent must disclose that he is acting purely as Agent.

An Agency need not be necessarily by express agreement. It can be by implication, ratification or even by estoppel.

Whether payment is as agent is question of fact and law - Para 4.1-9 of Press release (II) F. No. B1/4/2006-TRU, dated 19-4-2006 further states that whether the expenditure or cost incurred by the service provider in his capacity as a pure agent of the client or incurred on his own account is a question of fact and law and is to be determined carefully.

There can be no quarrel about this proposition.

10.8-7 Only actual amount should be recovered?

One of the conditions for exemption of payment as 'pure agent' is that only actual amount should be recovered from the customer. The service provider should recover only actual amounts which he has incurred on behalf of service receiver. These should be indicated separately in his invoice and of course, proper documentary evidence should be available. If the service provider charges some amount for making such payments, service tax will be payable on such service charges. It is advisable to show such service charges separately in invoice, to avoid fruitless litigation.

Even if such service charges are not shown separately, it does not mean that entire amount will be subjected to service tax. For example, if actual expenses incurred are Rs. 10,000 and the service provider charges Rs. 11,000, in my view, at the most, he will be liable to pay service tax on Rs. 1,000 and not on Rs. 11,000. This is because, concept of 'pure agent' is subsidiary to basic section 67 which says that service tax is payable only on gross value of services.

In U.M. Thariath v. CCE (2008) 12 STT 378 (CESTAT), it was held that service tax is not payable on commission collected on behalf of Principal.

There are many contrary views also. However, since GST is on 'supply of service', aforesaid judgments are likely to held valid in GST also. Toll charges paid by transporter of goods includible - In Premier Vigilance & Security P Ltd. In re (2018) 99 taxmann.com 79 = 71 GST 76 (AAR-WB), the taxable person was providing service of transport of cash in specially built vehicles. He was paying toll charges at on highways and recovering the same from customer. It was held that the applicant is not acting as pure agent. Hence, value of service will include toll charges also [There can be different view, if the contract is only for transport of goods or persons].

7.9-3 Problems arising out of concept of pure agent due to ITC provision

The concept of 'pure agent' will be difficult in GST. In GST, ITC is available only if tax invoice contains GSTIN of recipient and the invoice is uploaded. The pure agent has to ensure that invoices of supplier are in name of Principal with his GSTN number.

In many cases, the supplier issues tax invoice in name of pure agent with his GSTIN. In such case, the only option is to include that amount in the invoice of agent and charge GST on total amount, including amount paid as pure agent.

7.10 GST on Reimbursement of expenses

Reimbursements of expenses received by supplier of goods or services from the recipient of goods or services are of two types. One type of expenses are those which are not part of his scope of supply, but paid by supplier of goods or services on behalf of recipient of services or goods for administrative convenience and then recovered from service receiver - e.g. port expenses incurred by Customs Broker, air ticket charges paid by air travel agent, advertisement bill paid by advertising agency etc. These are not part of value of service.

Other type of expenses are incurred by the supplier for supply of services or goods and recovered from recipient of service separately on actual basis e.g. travelling expenses by market survey agency, out of pocket expenses of auditors, consulting engineer or maintenance engineer, design charges for special purpose of machinery etc.

These are essential for supplying the goods or services as goods or services cannot be supplied without such expenses. In my view, these are part of value of goods or services.

Really, this aspect is directly linked with concept of 'pure agent'.

As per section 2(31) of CGST Act. 'Consideration' includes any payment made or to be made, in respect of, in response to, or for the inducement of, the supply of goods or services or both, whether by the said person or by any other person.

Thus the payment made for travelling expenses, hotel expenses, etc., are in respect of supply of service and should be includible.

However, in Intercontinental Consultants & Technocrats (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2012] 28 taxmann.com 213 = 38 STT 75 = 59 VST 487 (Del HC DB), it was held that service tax is payable 'for such service'. The reimbursable expenses are not charges for 'such service' and hence are not includible in value. The rule 5(1) providing for inclusion of such expenses is ultra vires and sections 66 and 67 of Finance Act, 1994 - followed in ESPN Software India (P.) Ltd. v. CST [2014] 70 VST 205 (CESTAT) * Aashita International v. CST [2014] 73 VST 195 (CESTAT) * C.J. Shah v. CCE [2015] 77 VST 378 (CESTAT) - view confirmed in UOI v. Intercontinental Consultants [2018] 66 GST 450 = 91 taxmann.com 67 (SC).

This decision should apply in GST also.

Thus, in view of judgment of Delhi High Court upheld by Supreme Court, GST should not be payable on reimbursement of expenses.

This can be justified on the basis that tax is payable on 'supply' and scope of 'supply' of any service is on basis of mutual agreement between supplier and recipient of service.

This can also be justified on the well settled principle that ambiguity in tax law, if any, should be resolved in favour of taxable person

In Text Hundred India (P.) Ltd v. Commissioner of Service Tax, Delhi [2018] 94 taxmann.com 170 (CESTAT), assessee was providing service under category of event management. It received reimbursable expenses from client on actual basis. It was held that such amount not includible in gross value for purpose of payment of service tax.

Commission to local agent - Exporters from abroad often appoint local agents in India to promote their sales in India. These agents get commission in Indian Rupees which is paid directly by Indian Importer. (Amount net of commission is paid to foreign exporter in foreign currency.) However, if the local agent himself imports goods, there is no question of adding indenting agent's commission as the commission is payable only when he imports on behalf of others - Mittal International v. CC (2002) 50 RLT 382 = 145 ELT 667 (CEGAT).

Customs duty is leviable on commission payable to Indian agent in Rupees. This should also be calculated on basis of rate of exchange as in force when Bill of Entry is presented, as announced u/s 14. Service charges paid to canalising agency includible - In some cases, when imports are made by canalising agency, goods are sold to Indian buyer on 'high sea sale' basis. The imported goods are cleared by Indian buyer. In such cases, 'service charges' payable to the canalizing agency have to be included for calculation of 'Assessable Value'. These charges are incurred before clearance of goods and these cannot be termed as 'buying commission'. The canalising agency is not 'agent' of the importer and 'service charge' is not 'buying commission' - Hyderabad Industries Ltd. v. CC 2001(135) ELT 960 (CEGAT) - also followed in Gupta Chemicals v. CC 2002(148) ELT 535 (CEGAT).

Brokerage is paid to third party - Brokerage is paid either by buyer or seller to third party. Similarly, commission (which are clearly distinct from discounts) are payable only to a third party - CC v. Hewlett Packard Ltd. 1999(108) ELT 221 = 29 RLT 290 (CEGAT).

5.5-2 Packing cost is includible

Cost of containers which are treated as being part of goods for customs purposes are addible for valuation purposes (e.g. * cases for camera, necklaces etc. especially shaped for the article suitable for long term * packing materials are classified along with that article. Hence, its cost will be includible). Similarly, cost of packing - both labour and material is to be included. [Rules 10(1)(a)(ii) and 10(1)(a)(iii) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007] - upheld in Garden Silk Mills Ltd. v. UOI 1999(8) SCC 744 = 1999 AIR SCW 4150 = 113 ELT 358 = AIR 2000 SC 33 (SC 3 member bench).

Cost of Packing done in customs area not includible in customs valuation - In CC v. Indian Potash (2009) 234 ELT 507 (CESTAT), packing of imported goods was done in customs area to meet requirements of Fertilizer Price Control Order. It was held that this packing cost is not includible as taxable event has reached when goods reached customs barrier and bill of entry filed. Hence cost incurred after landing of goods is not includible.

Cost of durable and re-usable containers not to be added : Modern trend is to pack goods in containers for convenience of transport. These containers are durable and re-usable. Hence, cost of such containers is not added for Customs Valuation, if importer agrees to execute a bond to re-export the containers within six months.

5.2-4 Toll charges

Even otherwise, in CCE v. Toll is actually covered under List II i.e. State List and hence service tax cannot be imposed.

10.9

Specific cases in which the commission, costs, etc., will be included or excluded

Earlier section 67 had made specific provisions in respect of inclusion/exclusion of certain commission, costs, payments etc. New section 67 does not make provisions of these. These have been now included in rule 6.

Inclusions in value of taxable services - As per rule 6(1), subject to the provisions of section 67 of the Act, the value of the taxable services shall include the following -

(i)

the commission or brokerage charged by a broker on the sale or purchase of securities including the commission or brokerage paid by the stock-broker to any sub-broker

(ii)

the adjustments made by the telegraph authority from any deposits made by the subscriber at the time of application for telephone connection or pager or facsimile or telegraph or telex or for leased circuit

(iii)

the amount of premium charged by the insurer from the policy holder

(iv)

the commission received by the air travel agent from the airline

(v)

the commission, fee or any other sum received by an actuary, or intermediary or insurance intermediary or insurance agent from the insurer

(vi)

the reimbursement received by the authorised service station, from manufacturer for carrying out any service of any motor car, light motor vehicle or two wheeled motor vehicle manufactured by such manufacturer

(vii)

the commission or any amount received by the rail travel agent from the Railways or the customer

(viii)

the remuneration or commission, by whatever name called, paid to such agent by the client engaging such agent for the services provided by a clearing and forwarding agent to a client rendering services of clearing and forwarding operations in any manner

(ix)

the commission, fee or any other sum, by whatever name called, paid to such agent by the insurer appointing such agent in relation to insurance auxiliary services provided by an insurance agent.

(x)

the amount realised as demurrage or by any other name whatever called for the provision of a service beyond the period originally contracted or in any manner relatable to the provision of service [this clause inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012]

Explanation 1 to earlier section 67 (existing upto 18-4-2006) also provided that these are includible in 'value' for purpose of service tax. Only clauses (viii) and (ix) have been newly added in rule 6(1).

10.9-1 Exclusions from value of taxable services

Rule 6(2) states that subject to the provisions contained in rule 6(1), the value of any taxable service does not include the following -

(i)

initial deposit made by the subscriber at the time of application for telephone connection or pager or facsimile (FAX) or telegraph or telex or for leased circuit;

(ii)

the airfare collected by air travel agent in respect of service provided by him;

(iii)

the rail fare collected by rail travel agent in respect of service provided by him;

(iv)

interest on delayed payment of any consideration for the provision of services or sale of property, whether movable or immovable [amended w.e.f. 1-7-2012. Earlier, the words used were as follows - 'interest on loans']. - - However,Interest paid to Government or local authority by business entity for delayed payment for any services provided by Government or local authority would form part of value of taxable service. Thus, service tax will be payable on such interest also [but not on interest for delayed payment of taxes or penalties] - proviso to rule 6(2)(iv) of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, inserted w.e.f. 13-4-2016.

(v)

taxes levied by any Government on any passenger travelling by air, if shown separately in ticket issued to passenger (inserted w.e.f. 27-2-2010)

(vi)

accidental damages due to unforeseen actions not relatable to the provision of service [inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012].

(vii)

subsidies and grants disbursed by the Government, not directly affecting the value of service [inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012].

Explanation 1 to earlier section 67 (existing upto 18-4-2006) also provided that these are excludible in 'value' for purpose of service tax.

10.9-2 No service tax on interest on delayed payment but service tax should be payable on penalty

Foreign Money Transfer Service Operator (MTSO) (like Western Union) provide service of transferring money from outside India to Indian recipient in India. This is similar to Money Order service. The facility is used by persons outside India for remitting money from outside to India to their relatives in India.

Remitter located outside India (say A) approaches Money Transfer Service Operator (MTSO) (say B) located outside India for remitting money to a beneficiary in India (say E). A pays money to B. For this service, B receives fee/commission from A.

B appoints agents in India (say C) (who is usually a Bank or post office or some financial entity) for delivery of money to E. C is paid fee/commission from B for providing this service. C may deliver money directly to E or C may appoint sub-agent (say D) for this purpose. Usually no fee is charged from E but sometimes, some fee/charges may be recovered from E also.

ANNEXURES TO CHAPTER NINE

ANNEX 9.1

[PARA 9.2-6]

CIRCULAR NO. 754/70/2003-CX, DATED 9-10-2003

AVAILMENT TO CREDIT ON INPUTS USED EXCLUSIVELY FOR THE MANUFACTURE OF EXEMPTED FINISHED GOODS

I am directed to say that Board's attention has been drawn to the availment of credit on inputs falling under Chapters 28 and 29 used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods by certain assessees manufacturing finished goods falling under Chapter 30 of Schedule to Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. It has been reported that these assessees are subsequently reversing an amount @ 8% of the price of the exempted goods under clause (b) of sub-rule (3) of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002.

2. The matter has examined in Board in the context of admissibility of such credit or otherwise. In this connection, your attention is invited to sub-rule (1) of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 which prescribes that no Cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of inputs which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The said sub-rule makes an exception of the circumstances in which such credit on inputs used for the exempted goods can be availed. Sub-rule (2) of the said rule gives an option to the manufacturer to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in for the manufacture of exempted and dutiable goods and in case, he does not opt for the separate records, clause (b) of sub-rule (3) requires a manufacturer to pay an amount equal to 8% of the total price of the exempted goods excluding sales tax and other taxes as paid. Thus, it is clear that the option to maintain the separate accounts or payment of 8% of the price of the exempted goods can be exercised only in respect of common inputs used for the manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods. Where any inputs are clearly identifiable as used only in or in relation to the manufacture of final products which are exempt from payment of duty, CENVAT credit is not admissible on such inputs which are used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted final products. The circumstances specified in sub-rule (2), sub-rule (3) do not cover, or envisage availment of credit on inputs used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted final products.

3. It is therefore, clarified that no credit can be taken on inputs which are used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted final products. It may also be seen that this position was the same in erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944 and there has been no change in this principle. The procedural facility is prescribed to take care of the practical difficulties which may be faced by the manufacturers using the same inputs in both dutiable and exempted final products. Necessary action to recover the credit wrongly availed of, if any, may be taken at your end.

HEADNOTE: Section 16 of the Central Goods And Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit - Period April 2006 to 2008 - Whether it could not be contended that since definition of Rule 2(e) underwent amendment with effect from 1-4-2011, whereby, it was indicated that trading activity would fall in category of services, therefore rule 6(3)(c) could apply to trading activity only after 1.4.2011 - Held, yes - During relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax - Appellant company acted as a commission agent was also engaged in trading activities - Whether since appellant was not paying service tax on trading activity, credit of tax paid on services vis-a-vis input services could only be taken on a pro-rata basis as per formula stipulated in Rule 6(3)(c) - Held, yes - Whether however, since no separate accounts were maintained by appellant with regard to taxable and non-taxable services, apportionment as provided in Rule 6(3)(c) would triggered - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in denying credit of service tax - Held, yes [Para 12][In favour of revenue]GST/Cenvat Credit: Where during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax, if appellant engaged in activities of trading and commission agency did not maintain separate accounts regarding taxable and non-taxable services, it would not be entitled to credit of service tax

FACT: The appellant was engaged in trading activities as well as in commission business. The appellant obtained centralized registration with the service tax department under the category "Business Ancillary Services".

Evidently, the appellant's records were examined by the internal audit party of the department. The audit carried out revealed that the appellant had been claiming credit of service tax on various common input services which were used both for its trading activity and its business of commission agent.

As far as the commission agency business was concerned, service tax was paid by the appellant, while no service tax was paid for trading activity. Thus, the audit party came to the conclusion that excess credit of service tax had been claimed by the assessee.

The stand taken by the appellant was that during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax. It was alleged that due to an incorrect audit objection to the alleged utilization of cenvat credit qua the exempted services, the appellant had paid up the purportedly excess amount, which was, otherwise not payable.

The Adjudicating Authority, however, was not impressed with the stand taken by the appellant and, therefore, proceeded to reject its claim for refund.

The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order passed by Adjudicating Authority.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: Clearly, during the period in issue, i.e., 2006-07 and 2007-08, trading activity, which was one of the businesses, carried out by the appellant was not amenable to service tax. The amendment to rule 2(e), stated that there was no liability to pay service tax of trading activity, during the relevant period. [Para 9]

In this context, it may also be relevant to note, how exempted services was defined in rule 2(e) of the 2004 rules till 31-3-2011 and thereafter.

Both before and after amendment, 'exempted services' meant those taxable services, which were exempt from whole of service tax and, included those services on which service tax was not leviable, under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.2]

Therefore, given the rule position, what would govern the matter would be the determination of the issue as to whether or not, a particular service is amenable to service tax under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.3]

Since, the trading activity was not amenable service tax at the relevant period, surely, the apportionment as provided in rule 6(3)(c) would get triggered. [Para 10.4]

Having regard to the rule position and given the admitted fact that no separate accounts were maintained by the appellant, with regard to the taxable and non-taxable services, clause (c) of sub-rule 3 of rule 6 of 2004 rules would apply. [Para 11]

For the foregoing reasons, there was interference is called for with the order of the Tribunal. Accordingly, the questions of law framed are answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 12]

; therefore, allegation of suppression was invalid.

Revenue argued that activity of trading could be considered as services and since during material time, it was not a taxable service, it should be construed as 'exempted service'. Since assessee has not maintained any separate account in respect of the dutiable/taxable goods/services and exempted goods/services, payment at 10 per cent/ 5 per cent of the value of the exempted services was to be made under rule 6(3). Assessee argued that trading was deemed as exempted service only from 1-4-2011; hence, demand for period prior thereto cannot be made on that count.

HELD: The goods which the assessee had traded are imported goods. As per the definition of exempted goods under rule 2(d) of CCR exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-C.E., dated 1-3-2011 is availed.

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum at the rate of 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. [Para 5.2]

Secondly, as per rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the assessee has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply.

Even assuming but not admitting that the assessee has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, rule 6(3A) which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the assessee has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the assessee has not been disputed by the revenue and the revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the assessee in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the assessee has taken ineligible credit, the question of assessee violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all. [Para 5.3]

If the assessee reversed input service tax credit attributable to trading activities according to standard accounting principles, the same would suffice for satisfying the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6. [Para 5.4]

As regards the wrong availment of credit during the period 2005-08, another show-cause notice has already been issued to the assessee which has been adjudicated and pending before Tribunal. Thus, the department was fully aware of the practices followed by the assessee and has also approved of the same. In view of the above, invocation of the extended period of time to demand service tax is also not sustainable in law. [Para 5.5]

service only from 1-4-2011

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force with effect from 16-08-2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit up to 9-09-2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10-09-2004. [Para 5] Under the Credit Rules, 2002 input service is defined in rule 2(c) as any taxable service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service. Rule 3(1) provided that an output service provider shall be allowed to take credit (service tax credit) of the service tax paid on input service, in the enumerated manner. Sub-clause (a) of this Rule provides that where an input service falls in the same category of taxable service as the output service, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 16-08-2002; sub-clause (b) stipulates that in any other case, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 14-05-2003. Sub rule (2) of Rule 3 provides that for the purpose of these rules, two services shall be deemed to be falling in the same category of taxable service, if the input service or output service fall in the same sub-clause of clause (105) of Section 65 of the Act.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 3 states that where a service provider avails credit on any input service and renders output services which are chargeable to service tax as well as exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be, he shall maintain separate accounts for receipt and consumption of input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of taxable output services and input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be. Sub-rule (5) of rule 3 enacts that where a service provider opts not to maintain separate accounts, as stipulated in sub-rule (4), he shall be allowed to utilize service tax credit for payment of service tax on any output service only to an extent of an amount not exceeding 35 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on such output services. [Para 6]

On a true and fair construction of the relevant provisions of the Credit Rules, 2002, it is apparent that credit could be taken on an input service falling in the same category of taxable service as the output service in respect of which the service tax liability arises and discharged from the available credit. It is axiomatic that trading in goods is neither a taxable service and could not, in the absence of a legislative/statutory fiction provided, capable of being construed as an exempted service. [Para 7]

Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, 2004 sets out the obligations of a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) provides that no cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) enjoins maintenance of separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input or input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service; and the quantity of input spent for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and authorizes taking of cenvat credit only on that quantity of input or input services which are intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing taxable output services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 carves out specified exclusions to the requirements set out in sub-rule (2). Sub-clause (c) of rule 6(3) stipulates that the provider of an output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The 2004 Credit Rules were amended with effect from 01-04-2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an Explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'. [Para 9]

From the provisions of both, the Credit Rules, 2002 and the Credit Rules, 2004 it is clear that trading is neither a service nor an exempted service. Therefore no credit of the service tax paid on taxable input services used for trading could be taken and utilized for remittance of service tax on taxable services provided by the assessee, even for discharging a percentage (35 per cent or 20 per cent, as a case may be) of the service tax liability on the taxable service provided.

HEADNOTE: Rule 2(d), read with rule  6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted Goods - Exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty - Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods - Imported goods, which are traded, cannot be considered as exempted goods and rule 6 would not apply thereto [Para 5.2] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Exempted goods have to be excisable goods; hence, imported goods, which are traded, cannot be considered as exempted goods and rule 6 of CENVAT Credit rules, 2004 would not apply thereto

Rule 6, read with rule 2(d) and rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was manufacturing as well as importing 'consumer goods' and selling them - Assessee took credit of input services only pro rata on turnover basis attributable to manufacturing business and did not take credit of Rs. 16 lakh relating to trading business - Department argued that 'imported goods' amounted to 'exempted goods' and since separate accounts were not maintained, assessee was liable to pay Rs. 297 crore being 10 per cent/5 per cent of value of exempted goods under rule 6(3) - HELD : 'Imported goods', which are traded, cannot be regarded as 'exempted goods' and hence, rule 6 cannot be applied thereto - Secondly, since assessee has not availed any credit in respect of input services relating to traded goods, question of maintenance of separate accounts under rule 6(2) and consequent applicability of rule 6(3) would not arise - Even otherwise, since assessee has followed formula under rule 6(3A) ab initio and has not taken any ineligible credit, rule 6(3) cannot be applied - Hence, demand was set aside [Paras 5.1 to 5.4] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11A, of the Central Excise Act, 1944, read with section 73, of the Finance Act, 1994 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Invocation of Extended Period of Limitation - Department invoked extended period to deny credit - Assessee argued that procedure adopted by it was known to department while taking action for earlier period; hence, invocation of extended period on allegation of suppression was invalid - HELD : For earlier period, a show-cause notice had already been issued to assessee and matter was pending before Tribunal - Thus, department was fully aware of practices followed by assessee and had also approved of same - Hence, extended period is not invocable [Para 5.5] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: Assessee was manufacturing TV, washing machines, AC, etc. and was also importing said goods for resale.

Assessee took credit of input services pro rata based on turnover ratio attributable to manufacturing business.

Department argued that since 'imported goods' were 'exempted goods', assessee was liable to pay 10 per cent 5 per cent 6 per cent of value of said exempted goods. Department issued notice dated 7-10-2011 invoking extended period to seek demand.

Assessee argued that —

since he was not taking credit relating to 'trading business', rule 6(2) or rule 6(3) were inapplicable ;

since credit as per formula under Rule 6(3A) was merely Rs. 16 lakh, which was not taken; demand of Rs. 297 crore was invalid ;

its procedure of taking credit only on dutiable goods based on turnover ratio was known to department when audit was conducted in 2008 and furthermore, for earlier period, proceedings on same ground had been initiated and were pending before Tribunal; therefore, allegation of suppression was invalid.

Revenue argued that activity of trading could be considered as services and since during material time, it was not a taxable service, it should be construed as 'exempted service'. Since assessee has not maintained any separate account in respect of the dutiable/taxable goods/services and exempted goods/services, payment at 10 per cent/ 5 per cent of the value of the exempted services was to be made under rule 6(3).

them. The principals, agreed to give commission of 1 per cent of the purchase price besides the reimbursement of expenses incurred for the purpose of purchasing rubber and other commodities. The assessee was buying rubber and latex from the agricultures from Keral for and on behalf of its principal as their agent. The dealings in rubber are controlled by the Rubber Board. The Rubber Board had also intimated the principals that the assessee had been recognised as their agent to purchase and despatch rubber on their behalf. The CBDT in Circular No. 452, dated 17-3-1987 has laid down the principles of distinction between kutcha arhatiya and pucca arhatiya. On a perusal of distinctions between kutcha arhatiya and pucca arhativa as enumerated in the above circular and further illustrations given by the CBDT Circular Nos. 564&572, dated 5-7-1990 respectively wherein it has been made clear that turnover and sales are interchangeable and sole reliance cannot be placed on the definition of ‘turnover’ under section 2(o ) of the Haryana General Sales-tax Act, the contrary definition as contained in the Central Sales-tax Act cannot be ignored Since the assessee was receiving commission @1% of purchase value besides reimbursement of expenses incurred for the purposes of purchase and if the Assessing Officer’s contention was accepted that the assessee was trading in these items, there was no question of receiving fixed commission and there should, in fact, be bearing of profit or loss in each separate transaction depending on market conditions but this was not the case of the assessing authority nor it was borne out from the record. The Assessing Officer had not worked out the profit as such earned by the assessee from trading in rubber and latex. Therefore, taking into consideration the facts that the Rubber Board had registered the assessee as an authorised agent to purchase and despatch rubber on behalf of different principals no sales as such had been effected by the assessee, the goods purchased were transferred to the principals at the cost price, the goods were transferred not against ‘C Form’ but against ‘F From’ of sales tax issued by the transferee, the commission agency agreement between the principals and the assessee etc., the role of assessee was that of agent and not of trader. Secondly, according to the CBDT Circular Nos. 564&572 dated 5-7-1990. The turnover and sales are interchangeable and as the assessee had not made any sale rubber or latex, the total transaction conducted to earn commission would not be regarded as ‘sale’ or ‘turnover’ of the assessee. In view of the above facts and circumstances, for working out 80HHC deduction, it was the commission earned which was to be considered for working out the said deduction and not the aggregate transaction made to earn commission and, hence, no interference was needed with the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

P.K. Sahu for the Appellant. Rakesh Gupta for the Respondent.

an airline or other carrier of goods or passengers?

Answer: The travel agent, issuing tickets on behalf of the airlines for travel of individual passengers, would not be required to deduct tax at source as he acts on behalf of the airlines. The position of clearing and forwarding agents is different. They act as independent contractors. Any payment made to them would, hence, be liable for deduction of tax at source. They would also be liable to deduct tax at source while making payments to a carrier of goods.' This question relates to a situation where the C&F agent makes the payment to the airlines or other carrier of goods or passenger. This question, is not relevant to decide whether the assessee is required to deduct tax at source when payment is made to C&F agent. Question no. 6 deals with a case where the payment is made for carriage of the goods or passenger by any mode of transport to C&F agent. In reply to this question, the Board has clearly laid down in Circular no. 715, dated 8-8-1995 that 'As regards payments made to clearing and forwarding agents for carriage of goods, the same shall be subjected to tax deduction at source under section 194C of the Act.' The assessee could also not adduce any evidence that the C&F agent deducted tax at source while making payment to the carrier so as to prove that the amount which was paid by the assessee to the C&F agent represents reimbursement of the freight paid by the C&F agent on behalf of the assessee to the airlines. It is not the intention of the Legislature that neither the C&F agent deducts the tax when it makes the payment to the carrier nor the assessee deducts the tax at source when it makes payment to C&F agent. If the assessee claims that the amount paid to the C&F agent by the assessee represents reimbursement, the onus is on the assessee to prove that it represents the reimbursement of the claim. Hence, provisions of section 194C are clearly applicable in the case of the assessee. [Para 6]

to purchasers/traders/exporters, and the same has been offered as income in the financial statements and paid relevant taxes. The buyers/traders/exporters deducted TDS under section 194Q in respect of sales on the total sale value and reported in the PAN number of the assessee. Similarly, the buyers/traders/exporters had deducted TDS under section 194A in respect of interest payment on delayed payments and reported in the PAN number of the assessee. [Para 7]

■ Since the assessee has considered only commission income as its income and, after relevant expenditure, offered net profit for taxation, it claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders in terms of sections 194Q and 194A. In total, the Assessing Officer allowed proportionate credit for TDS on the ground that the assessee has offered only the part of the income, whereas it claimed TDS on the entire sales value. It is found that, once the assessee is operating as a commission agent, then the income of the assessee is net commission income received from the farmers, but not the total sales value of the farmers. Since the law provides for TDS under section 194Q on total sales value, and further, the assessee has raised sales invoices in its name, the traders have deducted TDS on the entire sales value, but the fact remains that, the assessee has considered the total income accrued on the total sales value being commission received from the farmers, as its income. Therefore, the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A, has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee and thus, the provisions of section 199 read with rule 37BA(2) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 are complied with. Therefore, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) that Assessing Officer has rightly allowed proportionate credit as per section 199 read with rule 37BA(2), is incorrect, going by the facts, because, there is no finding from the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) that, the income on which TDS has been deducted under sections 194Q and 194A has not suffered tax in the hands of the assessee. Since the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194A and 194Q has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee, the assessee has righty claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders and reported in Form 26AS. The Assessing Officer, without appreciating relevant facts, allowed proportionate credit for TDS, even though the assessee is entitled for credit for the entire TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A. The Commissioner (Appeals), without appreciating relevant facts, simply sustained additions made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 8]

■

This issue is squarely covered by the decision of Tribunal, Visakhapatnam Bench, in the case of Bala Krishna Traders v. ITO [ITA No.302/Viz/2025, dated 18-7-2025] where, under identical set of facts, the Tribunal has allowed credit for TDS as claimed by the assessee, on the basis of Form No.26AS filed for the relevant assessment year. A similar view has been taken by the Coordinate Bench of the Tribunal, Visakhapatnam, in the case of Gorla Srinivasa Reddy v. ITO [ITA No.503/Viz/2024, dated 20-12-2024], where, under identical set of facts, allowed credit for TDS as claimed by the assessee. In this view of the matter, considering the facts and circumstances of the case and also by following the decisions relied upon by the assessee, the Assessing Officer is directed to allow credit for TDS, as claimed by the assessee, on the basis of Form No. 26AS filed for the assessment year under consideration. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle was cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case was gone. From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l), the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided that it is made taxable. Therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. It may also be said that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air travellers. If in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-travellers. On the other hand, it may be said that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited. The tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the petitioners that because of section 67(k), the nature of the tax itself changes was incorrect. Section 67(k), which provides the ‘measure of the tax’, is not unconnected with the main levy of the tax. The provision of section 67(k ) does not in any manner alter the nature of tax and does not shift it from the service rendered to the customer to the service rendered to the airlines. The contention, therefore, was clearly incorrect on facts.

The further argument that the notification dated 26-6-1997 restricts the tax to the commission alone and is repugnant to the scheme of the tax was obviously incorrect. The basis of the argument that the commission received from the airlines by the air travel agent is taken a measure for imposing a levy on a different service rendered to the customer by the agent, was itself incorrect. Therefore, the argument that the impugned provision of section 67(k) is repugnant to the general scheme of the Act was to be rejected.

As far as the second contention of the petitioner with regard to rule 6(7) was concerned, the language of rule 6(7) itself suggests that it is an optional matter. Therefore, the members of the petitioner-association, who had not exercised the option would had no concern with the validity of that rule while those who had opted for it, and majority of them having done so, could also not challenge the said validity.

In fact, it was not necessary for the High Court to take stock of the petitioners’ contention regarding the unconstitutionality of the rules but, even otherwise, there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found with that rule much less in the light of the submission made by the petitioners. The High Court was in complete agreement with the department that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration section 93 and section 94(2)(a) jointly. Indeed, there is a specific power under section 93 to grant exemption in any manner. Section 94(2)(a) speaks of the rule-making power on the subject of collection and recovery of service tax under section 66 and section 68. What is suggested by rule 6(7) is nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations. It was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule- making power. It does not amount to an independent levy again. Therefore, it was to be held that there was nothing wrong with the rule in question. This rule provides for an independent measure as the basic airfare. For this reason, no merit was found in the writ which was liable to be dismissed.

It has, further, been clarified that under section 65A of the Finance Act, 1994, it has also been provided that in case of overlap, a service would be classified under the head, (a ) which provides most specific description, (b) in case of a composite service, having combination of different taxable services, the service which give them their essential character and (c ) in case the test of (a) and (b ) does not resolve it, the service which comes earlier in the clauses of section 65, i.e., the service that was subjected to service tax earlier. Since insurance services and C & F services are more specific in description and were also subjected to service tax prior to imposition of tax on business auxiliary service, the insurance agents, C & F agents working on commission basis would fall under those respective categories. From this, it follows that a particular service can be taxed only under one head of service. [Para 6]

1 and rule 8 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether cess on green leaves is a part of expenditure incurred in business of growing and manufacture of tea and it is allowable as a business expenditure - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, while computing composite income derived from sale of tea grown and manufactured by assessee entire cess would be claimed against taxable income - Held, yes [In favour of assessee] FACT: The assessee filed a return of income of Rs. 661.15 crores and claimed a deduction in the amount of Rs. 11.41 crores under section 80-I, Rs. 218.62 crores under section 80-IA and Rs. 20.20 crores under section 80-HH. The Assessing Officer assessed the income under section 143(3) at Rs. 814.66 crores and restricted the deduction claimed under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH to Rs. 11.06 crores, Rs. 201.08 crores and Rs. 18.57 crores respectively. The Commissioner issued a notice under section 263 stating that on verification of the records, it was revealed that the following expenditure, though having a bearing on the profits of the units, had not been considered for allocation, i.e., (i) Research and Development (R & D) revenue expenditure - Rs. 33,95,42,336; (ii) R & D Capital expenditure - Rs. 12,39,73,377; (iii) Interest paid - Rs. 32,16,45,000; (iv) Agency commission - Rs. 35,59,51,682 (including Miscellaneous expenditure). The Commissioner stated that as this expenditure had a bearing on the profits of the units, it should have been allocated proportionately. An excess allowance, the notice stated, had resulted in an under-assessment of Rs. 9.87 crores. The Commissioner by his order, came to the conclusion that the research expenditure incurred by the assessee is inextricably linked with the business of the assessee, including business in those products which are manufactured in the units entitled to a deduction under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH. The expenditure as noted by the Commissioner, had been allowed in computing the income under the head 'profits and gains from business or profession' for the whole of the business of the assessee, including of those units which were entitled to the aforesaid deductions. The logical corollary was held to be that in computing the profits derived from an eligible unit for the purpose of the aforesaid deductions, an appropriate part of the expenditure would have to be allocated to the units. As regards agency commission, the assessee had stated that an amount of Rs. 35.59 crores had already been allocated in arriving at the profit derived from the eligible units that was included under the head of advertisement. The assessee stated that there was no omission on its part and the amount should not once again be allocated in arriving at the profits of the units in respect of which a deduction was sought under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH. The Commissioner held that the interest and agency commission which relate to the whole of the business would have to be allocated to the eligible units. During the course of the hearing before the Commissioner, pursuant to the notice under section 263, a query was raised to the effect that cess which had been imposed on green leaf tea was required to be claimed entirely against the agricultural income in view of the decision of the Gauhati High Court in Jorehaut Group Ltd. v. Agrl. ITO [1997] 226 ITR 622. The assessee relied upon the provisions of rule 8 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and submitted that in the case of an assessee, who is engaged in growing and manufacturing tea, the composite income calculated in accordance with the provisions of the Act, is required to be apportioned between the income on the manufacture of tea and income from agriculture in the ratio of 40 : 60. According to the assessee, cess on green leaves is a part of the expenditure incurred in the business of growing and manufacture of tea. The Commissioner in his order under section 263 relied upon the judgment of the Gauhati High Court while coming to the conclusion that cess on green leaves was liable to be claimed entirely against agricultural income. On further appeal, Tribunal set aside order of Commissioner. It held that that the jurisdiction under section 263 had not been invoked properly and the entire cess could be claimed against taxable income.

Since the receipts of interest and commission on which TDS has been claimed under sections 194A and 194H are fully declared in ITR, the entire TDS claimed under sections 194A and 194H needs to be fully allowed. Hence the proportionate TDS disallowed is absolutely unjustified and, therefore, deserves to be allowed. [Para 2.6]

■ As regards the disallowance of TDS credit under section 194Q is concerned, the Bench found that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia. Therefore, the turnover on which tax is deducted under section 194Q is not the turnover of the assessee. Hence has rightly not been shown as such by the assessee. Moreover a Kachha Arhatia acts only as an agent for his constituent and never acts as principal. Therefore, the remuneration of Kachha Arhatia consists solely of commission and he has no control on the profit and losses made by his constituents.

■

The assessee has drawn attention of the Bench to sample invoices on which TDS was deducted under section 194Q by the principal buyer and the corresponding vikray parchi issued by the Mandi to the respective farmers. These documents clearly show that the amount invoiced by the assessee to the principal buyer and the value of goods transferred by assessee to the farmer is exactly the same. Therefore, turnover of the Kachha Arhatia is merely the commission paid by principal buyer on which the principal buyer deducts TDS under section 194H and which has been duly shown as income in the ITR by the assessee. Therefore, the TDS deducted by such principle buyers by virtue of provisions of section 194Q is eligible to be claimed by the Kachha Arhatia in his ITR on the grounds that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia and is duly registered as such with the Mandi. Perusal of the vikray parchi issued at the Mandi to the farmers and the corresponding invoice raised by the assessee to the principal buyer undoubtedly establishes the fact that the assessee has no control or margin in the sale facilitated by him and earns merely commission from such transactions.

■

The assessee has no domain over the goods sold to the principle buyers. As clarified by Central Board of Direct Taxes in its Circular No. 452 of 1986), so far as Kachha Arhatias are concerned the turnover does not include the sales effected on behalf of principals and only commission (gross) has to be considered for the purpose of income tax. Therefore, TDS deducted under section 194Q by the principle buyers cannot be refused by invoking rule 37BA read with section 199.

■

As the sale facilitated by the assessee for the farmers is not the turnover of the assessee and the income from such transaction (commission) being duly offered for tax by the assessee in his ITR, the TDS deducted both under sections 194H and 194Q deserves to be fully allowed. Further the Form No. 26AS also depicts that the invoices on which TDS has been deducted under section 194Q also has TDS deducted under section 194H. Thus the contention of the assessee that he is merely a Kachha Arhatia is potrayed beyond all doubts and needs to be accepted.

■

Therefore, the Assessing Officer is to be directed to allow TDS claimed under section 194Q by the assessee. [Para 2.7]

FACT: ■

The assessee was an individual and carrying business as a commission agent by selling chillies on behalf of farmers to registered dealers (GST Dealers). The assessee filed the return of income for the assessment year 2022-23 admitting a total income of Rs. 10.51 lakhs.

■

The CPC processed the return of income under section 143(1) wherein it was observed that the CPC had allowed the tax credit amounting to Rs. 10,271 as against Rs. 48,593 claimed by the assessee in the return of income.

■

The assessee also filed a petition under section 154 seeking re-processing of the return by allowing the correct TDS credit claimed by the assessee, wherein the CPC had rejected the petition filed under section 154.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The CBDT Circular No. 452, dated 17-3-1986 relied on by the assessee and the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Thota Venkateswarlu v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 290 (Viz) of 2024, dated 27-8-2024] wherein the Tribunal has relied on the decision of this Bench in the case of Yegneswari General Traders v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 39(Viz) of 2024, dated 18-3-2024] have been gone through. From the above it is clear that Kaccha Arahtias turnover includes only the gross commission and not the sales effected on behalf of their principals. In the present case, it is a fact that the assessee is only a licensed commission agent in Agricultural Market Committee Yard, Guntur. Therefore, the Circular issued by the CBDT (supra) squarely applies to the assessee and hence the assessee is acted only as an agent (kaccha arahtia) and therefore it is eligible to get credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source and there is no short fall of TDS as concluded by the revenue authorities. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to grant credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source in the case of the assessee. [Para 7]

■

Considering the identical facts and circumstances of the assessee's case with that of the appeal decided by the Tribunal in the case of Yegneswari General Traders (supra) wherein the Tribunal has relied on the decision of this Bench in the case of Thota Venkateswarlu (supra) and Subba Reddy Mareddy v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 96(VIZ) of 2024, dated 25-11-2024], following the principle of consistency, there is no hesitation to set-aside the orders of the revenue authorities and direct the Assessing Officer - CPC to grant credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source in the case of the assessee. Thus, the grounds raised by the assessee are allowed. [Para 8]

■

In the result, appeal of the assessee is allowed.[Para 9]

On revenue’s appeal : HELD: The facts were that on the basis of a letter dated 19-11-2008 from ‘R’ Ltd. to the assessee, it claimed to be an agent of the former in respect of sale made to the Indian Navy and Coast Guards. The enclosure to this letter, forwarded by the assessee to ‘R’ Ltd. in regard to services rendered by four sub-agents in the relevant year, had also been confirmed by ‘R’ Ltd. The paperbook contained evidence regarding payment of commissions to these parties and accounting for the same in their returns of income. ‘K’ had confirmed that it displayed a small version of RO system of ‘R’ Ltd. in its shop and it used to provide information to persons or concerns through the assessee. Further, ‘E’ stated to the effect that it was passing on information in regard to prospective buyers to the assessee for following up the orders and the commission was received on completion of the orders, i.e., on receipt of payments. The same statement of the proprietor of ‘B’ was recorded, who confirmed business dealings with the assessee for the years 2003 to 2005. In the case of ‘M’ Ltd. there was an agreement dated 10-4-2004 in force and said firm also confirmed the receipt of commission from the assessee. As against the aforesaid, evidence was found in the course of survey of ‘R’ Ltd. which was interpreted by its Assessing Officer to mean that payments were made to the assessee by cheques and after retaining its commission, the balance amount was returned to ‘R’ Ltd. The evidence produced by the assessee in the course of assessment led to a conclusion that the sub-agents had provided some information regarding prospective buyers, for which the commission was paid to them. The evidence seized from ‘R’ led to a conclusion that the assessee was used as a conduit for passing on the money to it after retaining commission for providing bogus bills. However, both sets of evidences did show that the assessee was paid at the rate of 5 per cent of the value of the order, out of which it paid an amount at the rate of 3.75 per cent either to the sub-agents or to ‘R’ Ltd. The whole of the evidence, including the bills raised by ‘R’ Ltd. on its clients, showed that the assessee and its sub-agents were in the same position insofar as the mentioning of the names in the bills of ‘R’ Ltd. was concerned, i.e., neither the name of the assessee nor of the sub-agent appeared on the bills. The assessee did not claim to have dealt with the Government departments directly. It had dealt with sub-agents and ‘R’ Ltd. for communication of information about prospective buyers. The revenue had also not been able to prove that the payments were against the public policy. The provision contained in the Explanation to section 37(1) uses the words ‘which is an offence or which is prohibited by law’. No evidence had been produced to show that payment of commission to the sub-agents was either an offence or it was prohibited by law. [Para 5]

From these facts of the case, it was noticed that the accounting entries passed by the assessee in its books of account were not in accordance with the principles of accountancy. As per the Accounting Principles, commission expenses requires to directly debited to commission account and it should be shown in the profit and loss account along with other heads of expenditures. Thus, there was a direct attempt to hide correct facts regarding commission expenditures from the return of income filed and from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. The Assessing Officer examined the contentions of the assessee that the recipients, sister concerns were offered the said commission in their hands by higher rate of tax than the rate of tax which was to be paid by the assessee-company in the assessment order and found that the effective tax rate in the hands of the sister concerns came to only 4.73 per cent. In the light of above facts couple with the fact that the commission paid without rendering any services, the action of the assessee was covered by main section 271(1)(c ). That the assessee had concealed the particulars regarding the commission which was not directly accounted for in commission account and profit and loss account. The profit and loss account was the part of the return of income filed by the assessee. The accounting entries passed in books of account was with the intention to avoid direct flash on the commission payments to sister concerns particularly when services were not rendered against commission payments amount to concealment of particulars. The particular of a commission furnished by the assessee were also inaccurate in the sense that the assessee claimed the commission expenditure against which no services were rendered. The commission expenditure claim of the assessee was not accordingly true claim, not accurate, not exact or correct; it was an erroneous and it was an inaccurate statement of the commission claim. It was neither a case of interpretation of any provision of the statutes nor it was case of two views on the issue. There was no force in the submissions of the assessee, that in earlier years penalty under section 271(1)(c) were initiated on the similar disallowance but the Assessing Officer himself had dropped those penalties. It was found that in those years the Assessing Officer dropped the penalty proceeding as the assessments were quested by the Tribunal on the ground that notices under section 148 were not in accordance with law. When the assessee furnished inaccurate particulars of the income, such case was squarely covered by the provisions of section 271(1)(c) and penalty was accordingly, leviable. In the return of income, it was the claim of the assessee that the assessee had incurred commission expenses. The heavy burden was on assessee particularly when the commissions were paid to sister concerns. The assessee had failed to discharge its burden as no materials were produced to show that the commission paid against the services rendered. Thus, the assessee had failed to substantiate its claim both in quantum matters as well as in penalty proceedings. The Assessing Officer had examined the commission payment in detail by exercising his power provided in the Act by examining books of account at the time of assessment proceedings, by making survey, by taking statements and other examination of post survey proceedings. The claim of commission expenditures of the assessee was found false. There was substance in the submissions of the department that the top executive officers of the assessee had admitted that those sister concerns companies existed only on paper and accommodative bills were issued. He further submitted that the assessee did not make any attempt to show the genuineness of the payments at the time of survey or at the time of assessment or at the time of appellate proceedings or at the time of penalty proceedings. The assessee had failed to submit any material basis on which it could be said that the claim of the assessee was a bona fide claim. Under the circumstances, the case of the assessee was also covered by Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c). Once the case was covered by section 271(1)(c) penalty was leviable. Accordingly, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals), was to be upheld. [Para 9.5]

It was further, noted that commission had been paid on export of diamond stating details of exports made by assessee, respective commission and details of service tax collected thereon and assessee had also produced details of other commission expenditure incurred by assessee which were also identical - Whether in view of above facts, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure in question as non-genuine and bogus - Held, yes [Para 26] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds. It filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year declaring it's total income.

Subsequently information was received from Investigation wing that assessee-company had made bogus payment to 'R' and 'RS' which were paper companies without having any business activities. These companies were engaged in providing accommodation entries or sending bogus foreign remittances to entities based in Hong Kong and UAE in guise of bogus import purchases. Further information was received from investigation directorate Mumbai that an action under section 133A was carried out wherein it was found that assessee had debited expenses in the form of commission from four different parties. The enquiries were conducted and found that all the 4 companies have the same address and they were not available on the addresses mentioned in the income tax return and no business activity was being carried out from those premises. Based on the above information, the Assessing Officer made additions on account of (i) bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods and (ii) bogus commission payment made by assessee during the year under consideration.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted said additions.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: Issue relating to bogus purchases

The Commissioner (Appeals) has categorically noted that assessee has submitted the evidences with respect to the Ledger accounts of the transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of the assessee showing the payment made to the parties. Assessee has also shown the mapping of corresponding purchases and sales. The argument of the department is that one-to-one mapping shown by the assessee is not correct for the reason that in the purchase bills of these parties there is no narration with respect to the quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as the colour etc. To support the same, the assessee has submitted the other beans of the other parties, which have been accepted by the Assessing Officer as genuine purchases. On perusal of those bills, also there is no mention of number of diamonds as well as the colour of the diamonds. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the purchase bills the assessee should have mentioned this details as that is not the trade practice and that is also not the reason why the Assessing Officer has rejected those purchases. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with rule 6(8) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 - Valuation of taxable service - Department raised demand of service tax on appellants, clearing and forwarding agents, on gross amount charged by them from clients - Appellant contended that tax was to be levied only on standard commission - Relevant rule 6(8) was found to be ambiguous - However, section 67 provides that taxable value of service would be gross amount charged by service provider - Whether no prima facie case had been made out by appellants for waiver of pre-deposit requirements - Held, yes Circulars and Notifications : Board’s Circular dated 11-7-1997

FACT: The department taking into consideration the gross amount received by the appellant-clearing and forwarding agent as taxable value, raised demand of service tax. The appellant contended that the amount collected as service charges was in fact, commission and as per rule 6(8), the same alone was the taxable ingredient of gross amount collected from the clients.

On application :

HELD: Rule 6(8) was found to be ambiguous. The Board Circular dated 11-7-1997 appears to have clarified the position in terms of section 67. The section will prevail over the rule. The appellants had not made out a prima facie case. They had not pleaded financial hardship in the instant application. Therefore, the appellants were directed to pre-deposit a part of demand raised. [Para 2]

Consequently whether the demands are sustainable and whether penalties are imposable. [Para 8] It is true that the services which the assessee rendered with respect to handling of cargo and processing, etc. are classifiable as cargo handling services if it had rendered them in isolation. However, custom house agent himself also renders these services in addition to the services under CHA Regulations, 1984. It has been recognised by the CBEC that all these activities are part of the custom house agent activities. If these activities are considered as part of custom house agent services, then the amount charged by the assessee should form part of the assessable value for the custom house agent services. However, in the instant case, the assessee claims that it has rendered the services through other agencies and it has only collected the amounts from its clients to the extent the service providers charged from it. In other words, it has not charged anything extra for these services over and above what the service providers have charged from it. As per rule 5 of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, any expenditure or costs incurred by the service provider should be treated as consideration. However, this rule has been run down by the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Intercontinental Consultants & Technocrats (P.) Ltd. [2018] 91 taxmann.com 67/66 GST 450. Therefore reimbursable expenses cannot be included in the value of the taxable services rendered by the assessee. However, it needs to be ascertained whether the amounts it has collected from its clients are the same as they were charged by the service providers. Otherwise the remaining amount becomes the consideration for their services as Custom House Agency and needs to be included in the value of taxable services and service tax to be recomputed. [Para 9]

In view of the aforesaid, the services rendered by the assessee during the course of custom house agency services in the form of handling of cargo, etc. do not form a separate taxable service falling under 'cargo handling services' or 'port services'. It is a composite service rendered by the custom house agent. The amounts charged by the assessee from its clients do not get included in the value of taxable services rendered to the extent that they are reimbursable expenses. This is a fact to be verified from the invoices and accounts. Therefore, the matter required to be remanded back to the Original Authority for the sole purpose of computing the duty liability after deducting the value of reimbursable expenses from the invoices. [Para 10]
