HEADNOTE: Section  199  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with rule  37BA  of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Credit for tax deducted  (Illustrations) - Assessment year  2023-24  - Assessee was acting as an agent for a foreign shipping company - It raised invoices on importers/exporters/ freight forwarders for ocean freight, terminal handling charges, documentation charges, etc. - A part of amount received from importer/exporter/ freight forwarder was retained by assessee and balance part was transferred to account of its principal - However, assessee could not have divulged this information with importers/exporters/ freight forwarders as otherwise, customers would push it for a better deal - In such circumstances, concerned importer/exporter/ freight forwarder had deducted tax at source on entire amount of invoice raised by assessee on them - In turn, foreign shipping line deposited due taxes - Assessee had been filing its return of income, declaring such gross receipts as its income which it was entitled to receive - Assessing Officer allowed TDS credit proportionately - Whether since on account of business expediency, assessee could not have divulged this information with importers/exporters/ freight forwarders but information relating to deduction of tax was furnished by deductor to Income-tax authority and same was contained in Form 26AS of assessee, assessee should be allowed credit in respect of entire amount of TDS as reflected in such Form - Held, yes [Paras 9, 10 and 13] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was acting as an agent for a foreign company who was a resident of Hong Kong. It raised invoices on importers/exporters/freight forwarders for ocean freight, terminal handling charges, documentation charges, etc. A part of this amount received from the importer/exporter/freight forwarder was retained by the assessee and the balance part was transferred to the account of its principal.

■

The assessee filed its return of income and claimed credit for TDS as per Form 26AS. However, the Assessing Officer allowed TDS credit to the extent of receipts offered to tax by the assessee in its return of income and disallowed the balance TDS credit.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal of the assessee by relying upon section 199 read with rule 37BA(2).

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

Section 199(3) enables the CBDT to make such rules for the purposes of giving such credit including the rules for grant of such credit to a person other than that referred to in sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) thereof. Pursuant thereto, rule 37BA has been notified by the CBDT. [Para 8]

■

According to sub-rule (1) of rule 37BA, such credit for TDS has to be allowed to the person to whom payment has been made or credit has been given on the basis of information relating to deduction of tax furnished by the deductor to the Income-tax authority. As in the instant case, such information is contained in Form 26AS which is also according to the said rule, thus the assessee should be allowed credit in respect of the entire amount of TDS as reflected in such Form. [Para 9]

■

Although sub-rule (2) of rule 37BA enables the recipient of income to file a declaration with the deductor to the effect that such TDS may be reflected in the name of the other person. But this enabling provision is not mandatory. However, if the necessary requirement in the rule is fulfilled, then, the deductor has to reflect the TDS in the name of the other person in which event the said person would get credit in respect of such TDS. Otherwise, TDS credit has to be allowed to the person from whose payment such TDS has been deducted. As in the instant case on account of business expediency, the assessee could not have divulged this information with the importers/exporters/freight forwarders. [Para 10]

■

The assessee has also ensured that the foreign shipping line has deposited due taxes on the payment made by it to the non-resident shipping line. It also understands that, the said non-resident shipping line is complying with the obligations under the Act including filing of its return of income in India. Moreover it is not the case of the revenue that the assessee has not offered the correct income to tax as well as there is no qualification by its Auditor in the audit report. [Para 12]

■

Therefore considering the totality of the facts and circumstances, the balance tax credit in respect to TDS is to be allowed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 65, read with section 76, of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Period 16-7-1997 to 31-10-1998 and 1-11-1998 to 31-8-1999 - Whether for a service provided by clearing and forwarding agent to be taxable, such service has to be relatable to clearing and forwarding operations and can be in any manner and it is not necessary that said agent must deal with goods directly - Held, yes - RZC were procuring orders for various tobacco products manufactured by appellant-company from dealers and passing on same to appellants, from whom they were receiving commission in lieu of service so provided - Whether said services were definitely connected with clearing and forwarding of various tobacco products being manufactured by appellants - Held, yes - Whether RZC were a ‘clearing and forwarding agent’ of appellants and service provided by them were liable to tax - Held, yes - Whether since appellants had already been penalised, there was no justification for imposition of separate penalty upon their director - Held, yes [Para 9] Notifications and Circulars - Trade Notice No. 59 of 1999, dated 4-10-1999 issued by Mumbai Commissionerate-I

FACT: The appellants were engaged in the manufacture of tobacco products. They entered into an agreement with RZC, appointing the latter as their agent for the purpose of marketing their product, booking orders, managing, supervising and developing of the market. In consideration of the services rendered by the said agent, the appellants were to pay commission at the rates mentioned in the schedule to the contract on the net sale proceeds of the orders received through the agent. The appellants were issued show-cause notice, alleging that as they were availing services of RZC, who were working as ‘clearing and forwarding Agent’ on commission basis, they were liable to pay service-tax. The appellants took a stand before the adjudicating authority that the service rendered by RZC did not come under the purview of clearing and forwarding agent and the same was entirely different. As such, the question of payment of service tax did not arise. During the course of personal hearing, they contended that after the amendments in the Service Tax Rules through the Finance Bill, they should have been issued a fresh show-cause notice. The Commissioner confirmed the service tax of certain amount, not paid by the appellants. In addition, he also imposed penalty on the appellants and their director.

On appeal :

HELD: In the Trade Notice No. 59 of 1999, dated 4-10-1999, issued by the Mumbai Commissionerate-I, the clearing and forwarding agent has been defined as ‘any person who is engaged in providing any service, either directly or indirectly, connected with clearing and forwarding operations in any manner to any other person and includes a consigning agent’. The details of the activities given in the said Trade Notice are only few of the activities undertaken by clearing and forwarding agent, as is apparent by the use of the expression ‘normally’. As such, it is clear that the activities given in the said Trade Notice are not exhaustive but are inclusive in nature and describes the jobs to be normally undertaken by the clearing and forwarding agent. As per the definition of clearing and forwarding agent, he is a person who is engaged in providing ‘any’ service, either directly or ‘indirectly’ connected with clearing and forwarding operations, in ‘any’ manner to any other person. The use of expression ‘any’ and ‘indirectly’ in the said definition of clearing and forwarding agent, is indicative of the fact, that the scope of the services to be provided by clearing and forwarding agent is quite wide. He is not only the person who is actually dealing with the goods who has to be termed as clearing and forwarding agent. Even if the services are indirect, but the same are connected with the clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner, of the other persons, he would be covered by the definition of clearing and forwarding agent. In the instant case, admittedly, RZC was procuring orders from the dealer and passing on the same to the appellant, from whom they were receiving the commission, in lieu of services so provided. The said services were definitely connected with the clearing and forwarding operations of the various tobacco products being manufactured by the appellant. It is further seen that the taxable service has been defined as any service provided by clearing and forwarding agent ‘in relation’ to clearing and forwarding operations in ‘any manner’. From the above, it is clear that the service has to be relatable to the clearing and forwarding operations and can be in any manner and it is not necessary that the said agent must deal with the goods directly. As such, the lower authority had rightly concluded that RZC was a clearing and forwarding agent and services provided by them were liable to tax. [Para 9]

FACT: ■

With effect from assessment year 2017-18, pursuant to Ind AS-19, the assessee split the gratuity charge between the profit and loss account and Other Comprehensive Income. The gratuity contribution was paid within the time prescribed under section 43B.

■

The Assessing Officer did not allow deduction of the portion routed through OCI.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the deduction, holding that the change was only in presentation due to accounting standards and that the payment having been made within the prescribed time, deduction was allowable under section 43B.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service or used by the manufacturer whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal and includes services used in relation to various activities of the description provided therein including advertisement or sales promotion.

Commission paid to the various agents cannot be stated to be a service used directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products or clearance of final products from the place of removal. In the absence of any material on record, as noted above to indicate that such commission agents were involved in the activity of sales promotion as explained earlier, the commission agent is directly concerned with the sales rather than sales promotion and as such the services provided by such commission agent would not fall within the purview of the main or inclusive part of the definition of input service as laid down in rule 2(l) of the rules. [Para 5.2(viii)]

Commission agent's services were also not 'activities relating to business' :

The includes part of the definition of 'input service' includes "activities relating to the business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security". The words "activities relating to business" are followed by the words "such as". Therefore, the words "such as" must be given some meaning.

The words "such as" indicate that what are mentioned thereafter are only illustrative and not exhaustive. Thus, the activities that follow the words "such as" are illustrative of the activities relating to business which are included in the definition of input service and are not exhaustive. Therefore, activities relating to business could also be other than the activities mentioned in the sub-rule.

However, that does not mean that every activity related to the business of the assessee would fall within the inclusive part of the definition. For an activity related to the business, it has to be an activity which is analogous to the activities mentioned after the words "such as". What follows the words "such as" is "accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security".

The activity of commission agent, therefore, should bear some similarity to the illustrative activities. None of the illustrative activities, viz., "accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security" is in any manner similar to the services rendered by commission agents nor are the same in any manner related to such services. Under the circumstances, though the business activities mentioned in the definition are not exhaustive, the service rendered by the commission agents not being analogous to the activities mentioned in the definition, would not fall within the ambit of the expression "activities relating to business".

Consequently, CENVAT credit would not be admissible in respect of the commission paid to foreign agents. [Para 5.2(ix)]

research and development and on scientific capital expenses should not be allocated, the reply of the assessee contained virtually no material or details to establish that there was no direct nexus between the expenditure incurred under the head in question and the business of the undertakings with reference to which the deduction was claimed. As noted earlier, all that the assessee stated was that the capital expenditure on scientific research had not been incurred at the undertakings and is not directly linked with the operations of the undertakings. Besides this statement, the assessee within whose knowledge, the facts pertaining to the business of the undertaking and the nature of the research expenditure rested, came forth with no detailed explanation. As a matter of fact, in the course of the proceedings under section 263, the explanation which was tendered by the assessee, was not that the research was not undertaken at the units, but that the products which were being manufactured by the units were those in respect of which the company already possessed the requisite know-how. Be that as it may, the fundamental basis on which the Tribunal has proceeded which is that there was due application of mind by the Assessing Officer during the course of the enquiry is erroneous. As a matter of fact, the Assessing Officer ought to have considered whether in computing profits derived from the industrial undertaking, the expenditure incurred by the assessee inter alia on research and development was proximately and directly connected with the business of the undertaking. The Assessing Officer's order shows that he failed to do so. Consequently, the Commissioner was justified in taking recourse to his power under section 263. The order passed by the Assessing Officer was without application of mind. The crucial issue namely, as to whether the expenses in question, bore a direct nexus with the undertaking in respect of which the deduction was sought under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH so as to warrant an allocation of expenditure between the units was not considered by the Assessing Officer. Even if the Assessing Officer were to be regarded as having proceeded on a certain hypothesis, he has acted on an incorrect assumption of the fact without a due and proper application of mind. That certainly, would warrant the exercise of the revisional jurisdiction under section 263. [Para 17]

On the issue of allocation of cess on green leaves, it seems that rule 8 stipulates that income derived from the sale of tea grown and manufactured by the seller in India shall be computed as if it were income derived from business, and forty per cent of such income shall be deemed to be income liable to tax. Rule 8 provides for a legal fiction for determining what part of the income of an assessee, who is engaged in the growing of tea leaves and the manufacture of tea, would be regarded as being attributable to income from the manufacturing operations and liable to tax. As a result of the fiction brought in by Rule 8, the entire income which is derived from the sale of tea grown and manufactured by the seller is required to be computed, in the first instance, as if it is an income derived from business. 40 per cent of the income which is so derived, is then deemed to be income which is liable to tax. The expenditure which was incurred by the assessee on the payment of cess on green leaves, is expenditure which is liable to be taken into account in computing the income of the assessee from the business. As a matter of fact, this view has been taken by the Calcutta High Court in the case of the assessee itself, i.e., Hindustan Lever Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 11 taxmann.com 64 (Cal.). The Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court relied upon the decision in CIT v. AFT Industries Ltd. [2004] 270 ITR 167 / 141 Taxman 433 and held that the amount of cess so payable was deductible. In view of the fact that the decision of the Calcutta High Court holds the field now insofar as the assessee is concerned, there was no merit in the challenge which has been advanced on behalf of the revenue to that aspect of the order passed by the Tribunal. The Tribunal rightly held that the entire cess can be claimed against taxable income. [Para 19]

On the issue of agency commission and on the issue of interest, there are no reasons in the order of the Commissioner for taking recourse to the revisional jurisdiction under section 263. As regards agency commission, the assessee had stated before the Commissioner that the agency commission has already been factored in while computing the profits of the eligible units. Similarly, as regards the element of interest, the assessee disclosed before the Commissioner that it had not depended upon borrowed funds and that there was sufficient accruals in the eligible units themselves. The assessee stated before the Commissioner that it had not borrowed funds for setting up of the units and units had been set up with internal accruals. The assessee has placed reliance on the fact that on the date of the balance-sheet, the assessee had invested an aggregate of Rs. 739 crores and that since each of the units in respect of whom the deduction is claimed had earned substantial profits they were not in need of borrowed funds for their operations. There is no finding to the contrary in the order passed by the Commissioner. [Para 20]

HEADNOTE: Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods - Appellant initially took Cenvat credit on inputs - Subsequently, they were used in manufacture of exempted goods and so credit was reversed - Department on finding that no separate record for various inputs used in manufacture of exempted goods was maintained by appellant, raised a demand of duty on exempted goods cleared - However, Commissioner in his order observed that appellant was maintaining separate records of inputs on which it had initially taken credit - Whether appellant had a very strong case on merits for waiver of pre-deposit of duty and penalty - Held, yes

FACT: The appellant initially availed Cenvat credit on the inputs. After utilising the same in manufacture of exempted goods, it reversed the credit. However, the department on finding that the appellant had not maintained separate records regarding the various inputs, used in the manufacture of exempted as well as dutiable goods, raised demand for payment of 8 per cent of value of the clearance of the exempted goods under rule 6.

On appeal :

HELD: The adjudicating authority of the impugned order had observed that there exists no specific condition in rule 6(2) for keeping the separate stock/storage of common inputs to be used for manufacture of exempted goods and dutiable goods, but keeping of separate accounts is necessary. However, he had observed that at the time of personal hearing, the noticees produced copies of invoices under which the noticees had purchased inputs and in respect of which they had availed Cenvat credit and maintained separate accounts. He had also recorded that the scrutiny of the records and the reports from the field formation revealed that they were not keeping separate account in respect of some of inputs, viz., felts, wires, oil and greases. But from the observations of the Commissioner, it was found that the Assistant Commissioner reported to him that the assessee was maintaining separate records of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods. In the instant case also the assessee has incurred various expenses on behalf of clients and while billing to the clients for services rendered a separate bill/debit note has been issued to recover various expenses incurred on behalf of the clients. The assessee in the books of account has accounted services charges/commission received from the clients for rendering C&F agent service as its income but reimbursement of expenses has been squared off in the parties account. On the other hand, the clients have deducted TDS on total payments made to the assessee including reimbursement of expenses. Thus obviously there will be a difference between total payments made by the clients and TDS deducted thereon as per Form no. 26AS and gross receipt booked by the assessee in its books of account. The Assessing Officer has noted difference in gross receipt as per books of account of the assessee and gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS. The assessee has explained difference between gross receipt and claimed that said difference is on account of reimbursement of expenses. The assessee had filed reconciliation explaining difference with party wise service charges received and reimbursement of amount received towards reimbursement of expenses. The Assessing Officer never disputed these facts. However, he rejected reconciliation filed by the assessee only for the reason that the assessee could not prove with sufficient documents that reimbursement of expenses was accounted in the books of clients. The reason given by the Assessing Officer to make addition towards difference in gross receipt appears to be baseless and incorrect because the assessee can file whatever evidence the Assessing Officer wants to prove its financial transactions with its clients but it is incorrect on the part of the Assessing Officer to expect the assessee to produce books of account of its clients. The only reason for the Assessing Officer to make addition towards difference in gross receipt is doubt and suspicion on expenses booked by the clients in their books of account. The Assessing Officer is miserably failed to understand the concept of accounting because deduction of TDS on total payments including reimbursement of expenses itself is a sufficient proof that the clients have accounted expenses incurrred by the assessee on behalf of the clients. The clients have deducted TDS on total payments including reimbursement of expenses because of this there is difference between gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS reported by the clients while deducting TDS under sections 194J and 194C, when compared to gross receipt reported in the books of account of the assessee. The assessee is following the method of accounting as per which it was accounting service charges received from the clients towards rendering various services as its income and reimbursement of expenses is squared off in the parties account. The assessee has filed a party wise reconciliation along with ledger account explaining the difference. As per chart filed by the assessee the gross receipt towards C&F service charges and other income exactly matches with gross receipt booked by the assessee in its books of account. The assessee had also reconciled difference between reimbursement of expenses and as per bills filed by the assessee amount received from clients towards reimbursement of expenses is more than the amount of difference noticed by the Assessing Officer from Form No. 26AS. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making addition towards difference in gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS and as per books of account of the assessee.

Since this condition was not satisfied, he confirmed the levy of duty, penalty, etc. The finding of the Commissioner of Central Excise was not in consonance with the observations made and the ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (81) ELT 3. [Para 5] In this case, Court’s attention was drawn to the departmental circular according to which in a case where the manufacturer produces dutiable final products and also final goods which are exempt from duty, it is not reasonably possible to segregate inputs utilised in manufacture of the dutiable final products from the final products which are exempt from duty. Based on this, the Court held that the manufacturer may take credit of duty paid on all the inputs used in the manufacture of final products, on which duty will have to be paid and in view of this clarification by the Departmental circular, the Court saw no reason as to why the assessee should not make a debit entry in the credit account before removal of the exempted final product; and, hence, it cannot be said that the assessee had taken credit for the duty paid on the inputs utilised in the manufacture of the final exempted product under rule 57A. The Court, therefore, took the view that the claim for exemption of duty on the disputed goods cannot be denied on the plea that the assessee had taken the credit of the duty paid on the inputs used in manufacture of these goods. The ratio laid down in this decision was squarely applicable to the facts of the instant case and maintenance of separate books of account at the initial stage cannot be considered to be a condition precedent for the purpose of claiming the benefit of exemption to the respondent-assessee. [Para 6]

Even rule 6(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 says that notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rules (1) and (2), the manufacturer or the provider of output service, opting not to maintain separate accounts, shall follow either of the following conditions, as applicable to him. Even otherwise rule 3 says that the manufacturer or producer of the final product or provider of output services shall be allowed to take credit on various items enumerated therein. This issue had come up for consideration before the Allahabad High Court in the case of Hello Minerals Water (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India 2004 (174) ELT 422, wherein it is held that reversal of Modvat credit amounts to non-taking of credit on the inputs. Hence, the benefit of the notification granting exemption/rate of duty has to be given on the final products since the reversal of credit on the input was done. Accordingly, the Tribunal’s order in the instant case was justified. [Para 7]

Therefore, same were liable to be considered in the hands of the assessee as per provisions of section 68. [Para 7] In the instant case, the assessee was Katcha Arhatia. The role of Katcha Arhatia is to provide a platform to the sellers to sell their produce in the market. The transactions of purchase and sale made at the business premises of the Katcha Arhatia do not represent his own purchases and sales. He only acts as a commission agent on behalf of the seller and the buyer. The documentary evidence, in the instant case, established beyond doubt that agricultural produce in the form of kapas and narma, equal to the quantity shown, was indeed purchased/sold on the respective dates. [Para 7.1]

However, what the assessee had not been able to establish but the revenue had been able to establish, was that the produce in the form of kapas and narma was indeed purchased from 51 parties mentioned in the assessment order, for which addition was made by the Assessing Officer. That finding was supported by the enquiries made by the Assessing Officer during the course of the assessment proceedings, i.e., the non-service of enquiry letters by postal authorities on 12 persons, the statements of the two persons and the village sarpanches, recorded by the inspectors during the conduct of enquiries and inability of the assessee to produce any of the 51 parties before the Assessing Officer. Moreover, it was not a case where the identity of only a few persons was not established, the number was 51 out of 52, which was too large. Identity of only one person was established. Besides, the assessee had not been able to produce any documentary evidence in the form of stamped receipts/simple receipts as to when amounts covered by the purchase of agricultural produce were paid to the parties in the subsequent assessment year. The payments for purchases had not been made by cheques through banking channels. Besides, the assessee had not produced any evidence, nor placed any material to show that those parties/farmers existed in the respective villages. [Para 7.2]

Two sister concerns of the assessee had purchased the agricultural produce in auction through the assessee. The purchases made by them in the presence of the officials, supported by documentary evidence were genuine. It was a fact that the amounts due from the two sister concerns had been shown outstanding and the nature of such credits was purchases of cotton and narma from the assessee and such entries appeared in their books of account. The assessee, in his books, had shown the amounts due from his sister concerns as sundry debtors and the corresponding credit entries in their books of account justified such action. Therefore, no fault could be found with the entries made in the books of account of the sister concerns, because their balance sheets depicted correct position about their assets and liabilities. But if the credits appearing in the balance sheet remained unexplained, the same would warrant addition in the instant case, because the credits appeared in the balance sheet of the assessee. If those credits were not genuine, the balance sheet would show the difference on asset side, higher than the total of liabilities. Therefore, the addition under section 68 would be called for in the instant case, and not in the cases of sister concerns. [Paras 7.3]

In the instant case, the assessee had not carried on any trading on its own. He had earned income by way of Dami on the transactions effected through him as a commission agent. Income received by way of Dami was fully supported by documentary evidence. Therefore, the question of rejection of book results did not arise in the instant case. Moreover, there is nothing in section 68 that the books of account must be rejected before making an addition under this section.This is an independent and deeming provision and will apply if the assessee fails to offer an explanation of the source of particular receipt/credit appearing in the books of account or if the explanation given by the assessee is found to be not satisfactory by the Assessing Officer. [Para 7.4]

It is not correct to say that the inspector cannot record the statement of any person. The Assessing Officer made enquiries through his inspectors in exercise of the powers conferred under the Act. Moreover, such enquiries only confirmed the fact that the persons had not been found existing at the given villages and obviously they had not sold the cotton and narma through the assessee. No material had been placed by the assessee to controvert such findings. In fact, when the assessee was confronted with the results of such enquiries and given copies of statements recorded by the inspector, no request was made to the Assessing Officer for allowing an opportunity of cross-examination. Thus, the objection raised in that regard was untenable. [Para 7.5]

The assessee was required to establish the factum of existence and identity of the parties and the fact that those persons had actually sold the produce to the assessee. [Para 7.7]

Ltd. (supra ). [Para 11] In view of the above reasoning, it could be held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are not applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. [Para 12]

HELD (PER TECHNICAL MEMBER)

It is seen that rule 6(1) specifically prohibits Cenvat credit being allowed on such quantity of inputs as used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Therefore, there is no authority in law for availing Cenvat credit on the quantity of inputs intended or used for the manufacture of exempted goods except in terms of rule 6(2), which allows the manufacturer to avail the Cenvat credit only in respect of that particular quantity of inputs, which is intended to be used in the manufacture of dutiable goods subject to their maintaining separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of final products. But if separate accounts are not maintained, though Cenvat credit is availed, then sub-rule 3 of rule 6 provides for payment of amount equal to Cenvat credit on dutiable inputs for cases covered under sub-rule (3)(a ) and in respect of all other inputs, sub-rule (3)(b) of rule 6 provides for payment of an amount of 8 per cent or 10 per cent of total price (excluding sales tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods), of the exempted final products charged by the manufacturer for the sale of such goods at the time of their clearance from the factory. Thus, reversal of the credit taken or availed under rule 6 is not contemplated by the rules. [Para 15]

If the interpretation put by the majority order is held to be correct, it will render the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) ibid providing for payment of an amount equal to 8 per cent or 10 per cent rather otiose. This militates against an interpretation, which renders it superfluous and is of no significance. [Para 16]

It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacturer of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts had to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It cannot be given, as the amount of reversal of credit has to be worked out in a manner prescribed in the Rules. There was no such prescription prior to the amendment. This decision of the majority will make the amendment superfluous. Such interpretation has to be avoided. [Para 23]

In the light of the aforesaid discussions, it was held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. [Para 26]
