Maintenance of records

43. Records to be maintained by registered dealers.

(1) Every registered dealer shall keep and maintain a true and correct account of his business transactions.

(2) The following records in particular shall be maintained:—

(a)

A monthly account specifying total output tax, input tax and net tax payable or the tax credit due for refund including carried forward of such balance from the preceding month.

(b)

Purchase records, such as, purchase invoices, cash and credit invoices with despatch challans and transport and courier documents/receipts wherein tax has been charged and all purchases made without charge of tax including import of goods from other States or countries or from unregistered dealers.

(c)

Sales records showing separately sales made at each rate of tax, zero rate and exempt sales.

(d)

The copies of tax invoices related to taxable sales and invoices related to exempt sales in chronological and numerical order.

(e)

Credit and debit note issued/received, in chronological and numerical order.

(f)

Records of all zero rated exports of goods together with copies of custom clearance certificates, invoices issued to the foreign purchasers, transport documentation, Form 'FT prescribed under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, orders or contracts for with the foreign purchasers and evidence of payment by bank, transfer through a bank or by a letter of credit payable by bank.

(g)

Records of inter-State sales and inter-State transfer supported by 'C Forms, 'F' Forms, waybills and stock transfer vouchers.

(h)

Cash records maintained by retailers, viz. cash book, petty cash vouchers, and other accounting records including cash registers, machine rolls details in the daily takings.

(i)

Details of input tax calculation where the registered dealer is making both taxable and exempt sales.

(j)

The registers, accounts and documents maintained shall be sequentially numbered and where the register and other documents are maintained by means of a computer or any other similar mechanical device, the dealer shall maintain copies in paper of such registers and other documents printed on a monthly basis.

(k)

Documentation, records and claims eligible for all transitional tax credit in respect of stock held on the appointed day or on first registration.

(l)

Stock records showing stock receipts, returns, deliveries and balances ratewise.

(m)

Manufacturing records including records of capital goods and raw materials.

(n)

Annual accounts including Trading, Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet, with Schedules.

(o)

Order records, delivery notes/challans and waybills.

(p)

Records of the bank transactions.

(3) A dealer opting for composition of tax under section 7 of the Act and an unregistered dealer shall maintain a daily record of his gross sale and purchase details.

(4) All records maintained in course of business shall be retained for a period of six years from the expiry of the year to which they relate.

SERVICE TAX - SMALL SERVICE PROVIDER EXEMPTION - CLUBBING OF PARTNER'S RECEIPTS WITH THAT OF FIRM

1. Our partnership is registered under service tax and has been paying service tax under commercial coaching services. Now, the partners are also individually providing the same services however their receipts are less then Rs. 9 Lakhs. Please clarify whether partners are liable to pay service tax on the basis of their relation with firm and whether partners' receipts can be clubbed with that of the firm ?

As per definition of 'person' under section 65B(37), person is defined to include firm as a separate category of persons. Therefore, for purpose of service tax, firm is a separate person from its partners and same view would apply in respect of claim of small service provider's exemption.

However, creation of bogus entities or bogus separation of receipts in order to claim SSI-exemption has been held to be impermissible under Central Excise and same attracts clubbing of turnover.

In short, if resources are same (i.e., infrastructure, finance, staff, management, branding, control are same), then, clubbing would get attracted.

SERVICE TAX - COMMISSION FROM FOREIGN COMPANIES - LIABILITY TO SERVICE TAX

2. We are providing services of commission agent to Singapore based foreign company for the sale of iron ore. The commission is received in foreign exchange. Please clarify whether this would be liable to service tax ? Can there be any tax planning ?

As per rule 2(f) of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012, intermediary is defined to mean "intermediary" means a broker, an agent or any other person, by whatever name called, who arranges or facilitates a provision of a service (hereinafter called the 'main' service) or a supply of goods, between two or more persons, but does not include a person who provides the main service or supplies the goods on his account. As per rule 9(c), the Place of Provision of services of an intermediary would be location of such intermediary (w.e.f. 1-10-2014).

In view of definition under Rule 2(f), commission agents and other agents, or the like would be liable to service tax on their location basis. Accordingly, Indian commission agents of foreign companies are liable to service tax w.e.f. 1-10-2014, even if the commission is earned by them in the foreign exchange.

Hence, it appears that your services are liable to service tax. We would suggest of any tax planning in view of very wide words used.

Nevertheless, if it can be shown that the services being provided are consultancy services, not relatable to supply/sale of goods, then only, rule 9(c) read with rule 2(f) would not apply.

CENVAT CREDIT - WORKS CONTRACT SERVICES v. TRADING SERVICE

3. We are having 2 divisions : trading division and service division (works contract services). Can we take credit of input services received from sub-contractor which is used exclusively to provide works contract service ?

Since trading activity is also an exempted service under rule 2(e) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004; hence, you become provided for taxable as well as exempt service and have to comply with the provisions of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Therefore, you should either maintain separate accounts and, if not, pay 7% (6% up to 18-5-2015) of the value of exempted services of trading as per rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

The provisions of rule 6 override provisions of all other rules.

SERVICE TAX - DISTRIBUTORS v. COMMISSION AGENTS

4. We are distributors of products of Johnson & Johnson. The following is the procedure :

J&J supplies to us @ Rs. 100 (invoiced) ;

We sells to our customer @ Rs. 100 ;

Bad debts, if any, are borne by us ;

We raise a debit note of Rs. 10 towards profit margin on sales ;

On confirmation J & J raises credit note of Rs. 10 on us.

Thus, we end up paying Rs. 90 to J&J.

Whether we are liable to pay service tax ? Whether our practice needs amends ?

In our considered view, your practice is very well in order. There is no service tax liability, as you are not an agent of J&J; in fact, you buy from J&J and sell to the customers. The fact that J&J invoices you first and title apparent gets transferred would show that there is pure sale of goods to you and by you to your customers.

It appears that this practice is being adopted by J&J to control your profit margin.

EXPERTS’ OPINION : CENVAT CREDIT

Thus Spake Experts

An assessee is pro-viding both taxable and exempt services. He utilises various input services for providing his output services. In respect of some of the input services, he is in a position to establish direct correlation between his input service and taxable output service. In respect of general (common input services like telephone, courier, manpower supply, bank services etc., he is not able to establish direct relation with either exempt output service or taxable output service. He is utilising full Cenvat credit in respect of input services where he is able to establish direct relation between input service and output taxable service, as per rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules. In addition, in respect of common input services where he is not able to establish any direct relation with output service, he is availing Cenvat credit to the extent of 20% of amount of service tax payable on taxable output service, as provided in rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

For example, service tax payable by him is Rs. 100. Service tax paid on his common input services is Rs. 25. Service tax paid on services where he can directly establish relation with his taxable output service is Rs. 10. He is availing Cenvat credit of Rs.10 [rule 6(2)] plus Rs. 20 [rule 6(3)(c)]. Is it legally correct? In short, whether rules 6(2) and 6(3)(c) are mutually exclusive or they can be used simultaneously.

The issue will arise in due course and it appears to be a borderline case. There is no specific prohibition in simultaneous availment of credit under rules 6(2) and 6(3). We are providing both taxable and exempt services. Taxable services are to the tune of Rs. 45 lakhs and exempt services are Rs. 30 lakhs. Total input service tax paid is Rs. 3,00,000 which includes Rs. 1,00,000 which is directly related to taxable services. Balance Rs. two lakhs relates to common input services like telephone, rent, etc. We would like to know whether provision of proportionate credit under rule 6(3) applies to entire input credit of Rs. three lakhs or whether we can take full credit of Rs. one lakh and apply ratio to balance credit of Rs. two lakhs ?

Basic issue is whether rule 6(2) and 6(3) are mutually exclusive or whether they are complimentary. Of course, applying the ratio to entire credit is a safer option and in second case, some litigation is possible and, hence, it should be taken only after disclosing all details to the Department and after considering possible cost of litigation (after making full disclosure). However, my views are as follows—

Rule 6(2) and 6(3) should be taken as complimentary and not mutually exclusive. The words used in rule 6(3) are ‘notwithstanding anything contained in rule 6(1) and 6(2), the manufacturer of goods or provider of output service, opting not to maintain separate accounts, shall follow either of the following options as applicable to him’.

This sub-rule can be interpreted to mean that the assessee can follow rule 6(2) for inputs and input services for which he can maintain separate records and accounts and follow rule 6(3) in respect of inputs and input services for which the assessees opts not to maintain separate accounts.

In my view, fair interpretation is that rule 6(3) should apply to cases of common inputs and common input services where the assessee is not in a position to maintain separate accounts. Thus, rule 6(2) and 6(3) are complimentary.

In costing, there are concepts of ‘allocation’ and ‘apportionment’. The costs which can be allocated directly to a particular product should be so allocated, while costs which cannot be directly allocated to any particular product/service, should be apportioned on a reasonable basis. This principle can be applied here.

The input goods/services which can be directly allocated to taxable goods/services and exempt goods/services should be allocated under rule 6(2). Full credit should be allowed of the Cenvat credit allocable to taxable goods/services and no credit should be allowed for the Cenvat credit allocable to exempt goods/services. The remaining input credit/input services should be apportioned between taxable goods/services and exempt goods/services on the basis of formulae given in rule 6(3A). This should give best possible and most fair results. Of course, this should be done after making full disclosure to the Department, to avoid charge of suppression of facts.

Commercial concern and commission agent

9. When the service was notified, the individual commission agents were taking a stand that they are not ‘Commercial Concern’, but proprietors. However, going by the definition, the word ‘Commercial Concern’ does not figure in the definition nor in the exemption notification and, hence, this stand taken by the commission agents turned out to be futile exercise.

An ‘Agent’ is defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which refers to ‘A person employed to do any act for another; or to represent another in dealings with third persons’.

In the light of the above, other than those commission agents representing the foreign principals and canvassing their orders for the goods in India, the other commission agents accepted the levy and started complying with the provisions of service tax and payment of the same effective from July 9, 2004.

CENVAT credit

10. The new CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 came into effect from September 10, 2004, which gave an interesting relief under the term ‘Inter-sectoral Credit’ which enabled the service providers to take credit not only on service tax paid on input services, but also excise duty paid on inputs and capital goods, which is used for providing taxable output service. Thus, all the service providers who are paying service tax are granted CENVAT credit facility announced under the abovesaid Rules so that to a great extent the service tax liability is reduced. Those who are availing exemption of Rs.4 lakhs are certainly not eligible for CENVAT credit, which is a pre-condition for any exemption from payment of service tax granted to the service provider.

Additional responsibility handled by commission agents

11. In the present business scenario, some of the commission agents undertake additional responsibility as part of their agreement with the principals, such as erection, installation and commissioning of the goods ordered by the Indian customer on behalf of the foreign principal. In such scenario, since erection, installation, commissioning is also one of the notified services, and since such services are rendered/provided and used/consumed within India, a liability to pay service tax will arise. However, the foreign principals do not pay any separate amount to the Indian commission agents towards erection, installation and commissioning and, the amount is arrived at after taking into account this service as well.

Though the commercial agreement between the foreign principal and the Indian commission agent is in order, yet it will pose a problem for arriving at the value of taxable service, when it comes to payment of service tax on erection, installation and commissioning portion. Unfortunately, the commission agents cannot avail abatement of 67 per cent granted under Notification No. 19/2003-ST, dated August 20, 2003, which applies only to those composite contracts involving supply of machinery and erection, installation and commissioning of the same.

In the scenario discussed above, the machinery is supplied by the foreign principal, whereas the erection, installation, commissioning activity is taking place in India and, therefore, the department is bound to insist for payment of service tax on the gross amount received as commission. Therefore, the commission agents should enter into the agreement in such a manner that the commission amount is split into a major portion towards commission for sale of goods and balance portion towards erection, installation and commissioning. In such situation, the service tax liability on erection, installation and commissioning will be only on the reduced quantum of amount received specifically towards the above service. It is also a choice of the commission agent to arrive at a fixed amount required for erection, installation and commissioning so that the fixed amount is taken into account to arrive at the value of taxable service. Unfortunately, service tax so paid towards erection, installation and commissioning cannot be availed as CENVAT credit since it is not required for rendering the output service of commission agent and it is a helpless situation of grin and bear it. In other words, it is an additional cost to be provided for in business.

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, assigns an obligation on the manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods as well as the provider of taxable and exempted service, as stipulated therein. This article examines as to under what circumstances the provisions of rule 6(3)(c) can be applied restricting the service provider to utilize only 20 per cent of credit, especially with reference to the phrase ‘exempted services’.

Introduction

1. Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 (the CCR), assigns an obligation on the manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods as well as the provider of taxable and exempted service, as stipulated therein. In terms of rule 6(2), the provider of output service who avails cenvat credit in respect of any input or input service has to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption, and inventory of input and input service meant for use in providing output service on which service tax is payable. In other words, the service provider is to maintain records separately for receipt, consumption, inventory of each of the input/input service which are (a) relatable to taxable output service and (b) exempted service. If for any reason such maintenance of accounts is neither possible nor feasible, in terms of provisions of rule 6(3)(c), the provider of output service shall utilize credit only to extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the service tax payable on taxable input service. On the contrary, the credit can be utilized fully under the following circumstances :

uIf the entire services are taxable service on which service tax is paid (no exempted service) (or)

uIf separate accounts are maintained as above.

New Cenvat Credit Rules

2. In the Budget 2004-05, credit of service tax and excise duty was extended across goods and services. The concept of inter-sectoral credit or credit across goods and services was brought into force, followed by introduction of new Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

As per rule 2(e) of the CCR, ‘exempted service’ means taxable services which are exempt from the whole of duty leviable thereon and includes services on which no service tax is leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994.

As per rule 2(d), ‘exempted goods’ means excisable goods which are exempt from whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to ‘NIL’ rate of duty.

The definitions are similar except that in respect of ‘exempted goods’ it includes goods which are chargeable to ‘NIL’ rate of duty for the reason that duty as per section 3 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 shall be levied on all excisable goods manufactured or produced in India at the rates set forth in the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985, and for some goods the tariff rate itself is ‘NIL’, while in respect of taxable services charge of service tax at 12 per cent is as per the provisions of section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994.

In terms of rule 6(1) of the CCR, the CENVAT credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input service which is used in ‘exempted services’ except under circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2) . Therefore, a service provider who provides ‘taxable service’ and ‘exempted service’ but does not maintain separate set of accounts in terms of rule 6 (2), is permitted to utilize the input credit only to the tune of 20 per cent of service tax payable in view of the embargo in rule 6(3)(c).

Let us assume that a service provider renders only two categories of service (a) taxable services and (b) services which are exported but exempt by virtue of the Export of Services Rules, 2005 (the ESR). Now the moot question is whether taxable services which are exempted by virtue of the ESR are to be treated as taxable service or exempted service within the meaning of rule 2(e) of the CCR, to attract the mischief of rule 6(3)(c).

Rule 3 of the ESR contains provisions relating to export of services which have to be fulfilled to deem such services as export of services. Further, as per rule 4 of the ESR, any service which is taxable under clause (105) of section 65 of the Act, may be exported without payment of tax.

2. One of my client has availed CENVAT credit on input service on the entire amount of the bill. Subsequently service provider has given the discount on the bill. Whether proportionate CENVAT credit to be reversed on the portion of the amount of discount received ?

Assuming no reverse charge case, credit can be taken on receipt of invoice. Further, payment of value of service and service tax should be made to the service provider within 3 months of date of invoice, failing which credit has to be reversed and can be re-taken only after full such payment.

As regards Part/Discounted Payment, it is provided in Circular No. 122/3/2010-S.T., dated 30-4-2010 that, in cases where receiver of service makes part/discounted payment only after 3 months, then, he is entitled to take full or pro rata credit provided he has also paid the amount of service tax, (whether proportionately reduced or the original amount) to the service provider.

Going by the Circular, if original amount of service tax is paid to the service provider, then, credit would not be touched. Accordingly, we opine as under :

[a]

If service tax amount is not changed and only value is reduced/negotiated, then, full credit may be taken [full and final settlement towards value would amount to 'payment of value' and would suffice requirements of rule 4(7)].

[b]

Alternatively, if service tax amount is also changed [say, original service tax is Rs. 14 and service tax as per revised value is Rs. 9.8], then, service provider may take benefit of rule 6(3) [credit of Rs. 4.2 may be taken by service provider] and service receiver may take credit of Rs. 9.8.

According to the respondents, they had surrendered the credit going into the exempted final product at the earliest available opportunity. The respondents, thus, had not taken advantage of the credit availed on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final product and, thus, were not liable to pay any amount on removal of exempted final product. The revenue’s case was that the respondents had to pay as set out under rule 6(3), as no separate accounts, etc., were maintained by them. Thus, demand was raised and penalty was imposed. u On a plain reading of rule 6(1), it is obvious that if inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted goods, credit is not allowed except in the circumstances mentioned under sub-rule (2). Rule 6(1) does not lead to the construction that if the manufacturer without maintaining the books, does not take credit for the duty paid on inputs for manufacture of exempted goods, rule 6(1) is satisfied. Rule 6(1) is satisfied only when the requirements of the rule 6(2) are satisfied, which requires register to be maintained for separate accounts of receipt, consumption and inventory of the inputs. Rule 6(3) provides that if separate accounts are not maintained then the amount has to be paid by a manufacturer.

REVERSAL OF CENVAT WHEN RECEIVABLES WRITTEN-OFF

This query is in respect of my client who is providing Mobile Phone service in Mumbai. It has shown certain amounts of dues pertaining to post paid services billed for against customers but not realized for the period 2004-05 to 2006-07. Subsequently, it had fully written-off such dues as they became irrecoverable and the amount written-off during said period amounts to Rs. 412 lakhs. The CERA audit group during the course of an audit has asked my client to reverse the credit attributable to input service against the above written-off amount on a proportionate basis. Kindly let me have your guidance in the matter.

Issue is interesting. Really the audit point cannot be said to be baseless. As per rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, "exempted services" means taxable services which are exempt from the whole of the service tax leviable thereon, and includes services on which no service tax is leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act. Thus, services for which no payment is received might fall in the aforesaid decision and, hence, may attract rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules.

However, till 31-3-2008, there was no provision of ‘proportionate reversal’. In case of Cenvat credit of input services, as per rule 6 as then existing (up to 31-3-2008), the Cenvat credit was to be restricted to 20 per cent of service tax payable on output service. From the figures you have indicated, I think that your credit should fall within 20 per cent limit and in that case, Cenvat credit would not be reversible at all. Just check.

INPUT SERVICES USED FOR SELF-MANUFACTURED AS WELL AS TRADED GOODS

We are manufacturers of engineering products. We also are traders of those products, i.e., we procure these goods under our brand name and sale. We have appointed selling agents for sale of our products (both self-manufactured and traded). We pay selling commission to our indenting agents. The selling agents charge service tax on the commission. We avail Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission paid by us on traded goods as well as self-manufactured goods, and utilise the same for payment of excise duty on our self-manufactured products. Department has issued a show-cause notice to us, informing that we are not eligible for service tax paid by us on commission attributable to traded goods. Please advise.

You are eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax paid both on self-manufactured goods and traded goods, for the following reasons -

(1)Definition of ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is very wide. As per inclusive part of the definition, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’, since the words used are ‘such as’ and not ‘viz.’.

(2)The inclusive part of definition clearly covers ‘sales promotion’. The inclusive part of definition does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’.

(3)Cenvat Credit Rules do not require any one to one relation between input and output.

(4)Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not require distribution of Cenvat credit in any particular ratio. Entire credit of service tax at HO or depot or branch offices can be transferred to any unit without any restriction. The rule makes no distinction between services used for manufacture and services used for other activities like trading, financing, etc.

(5)The Finance Minister in para 148 of his Budget Speech on 8-7-2004 has stated as follows, "I propose to take a major step towards integrating tax on goods and services. Accordingly, I propose to extend credit of service tax and excise duty across goods and services".

(6)Thus, the Cenvat Credit Rules have to be interpreted keeping this goal in mind and, hence, cannot be interpreted narrowly. As per doctrine of purposive interpretation, an interpretation which advances purpose of the Statute should be preferred over an interpretation which defeats the purpose.

(7)It is clear that after introduction of the Cenvat Credit Rules, the whole company is treated as one single entity for Cenvat credit. The definition of ‘input service’ and ‘input service distributor’ has abolished distinction between ‘goods’, ‘manufacture’ and ‘services’. Entire company is treated as one unit for purpose of Cenvat credit, as is the position under ‘Goods and Service Tax’ (GST) which has been set as the goal. Even concept of ‘LTU’ (Large Taxpayer Unit) is a step in that direction.

(8)Even assuming that there is some ambiguity (though really there is none), it is well-settled principle that the benefit of doubt goes to assessee.

Thus, Cenvat credit availed by you is legally correct.

However, you must keep in mind that current decisions of Tribunal are highly conservative and, hence, ultimate result is uncertain. You should be mentally prepared to pay interest @ 13%, if final decision goes against you.

Relevant case law 4. The validity of rule 6(7) was challenged in the case of Airlines Agents Association v. Union of India [2002] 121 Taxman 298 (Mad.). The High Court upheld the validity of rule 6(7). The High Court held (i) that there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found in that rule, (ii) that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration sections 93 and 94(2)(a) jointly, (iii) that what was suggested by rule 6(7) was nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations, and (iv ) that it was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule-making power.

In Airlines Agents Association’s case (supra), it was contended that the commission paid by the airlines is in respect of services to the airlines and not services to the customer and, therefore, the said commission should not be taxed. The High Court rejected that contention and held as under:

". . . It is not as if the air travel agents get a fixed commission or income from the airlines irrespective of the passages booked by them in favour of the customers in the nature of a ‘retainer fee’ or ‘guarantee money’, at least that is not the case pleaded before us. Therefore, unless the air travel agents book the tickets and thereby unless they provide the services to the customers, they do not become entitled to any commission. Their commission is entirely dependent on and connected with the passage they book for the customers. It cannot, therefore, be said that the commission that the air travel agents get from the airlines is independent of and distinct from the services that they provide to the air-travellers and are relatable to the business that they provide to the airlines. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process, the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle is cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case goes away. From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l), the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided which is made taxable. In our opinion, therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. We may also say that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air-travellers. If, in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission, that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-traveller. On the other hand, we may say that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited, the tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which, there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the learned counsel that because of section 67(k) the nature of the tax itself changes, is incorrect." (p. 305)

3.3 Treatment of traded goods - A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods. The sale may be within India or outside. Obviously, there will be many common input services. Now, traded goods are not ‘exempt goods’. It is also not ‘service’, since one is not providing services to anyone else. Further, one cannot provide service to oneself.

Including the entire value of turnover of traded goods into dividend (above line) will be highly unfair to the assessee since the services attributable to such traded goods will certainly not be proportional to value of the traded goods, in cases where the assessee is both manufacturer as well as trader.

As the formulae stand today, turnover of traded goods can neither be included in divisor (below the line) nor the dividend (above the line). This would give higher Cenvat credit to the assessee. It would be fair to provide some percentage of turnover of traded goods (by way of rules), which should be added to dividend (above the line) to give fair results.

Import of service and commission agents

12. Like Indian commission agents are representing the foreign principals and canvassing the product and obtaining the orders, it is also a common commercial scenario for the Indian companies to employ commission agents abroad who can move around and obtain orders based on which the goods can be exported from India to the customer identified by the foreign commission agents. The commission so paid to the foreign agents is for the services rendered outside India. However, with the introduction of new set of Rules ‘Service Tax (Provided from Outside India and received in India) Rules, 2006, which came into effect from April 19, 2006, it is an unfortunate situation that the commission so paid by Indian principals to the foreign commission agent will be treated as a taxable service under the newly introduced section 66A read with the above-mentioned new Rules. As a result, the Indian principals will be deemed to be the service provider and, accordingly, service tax is payable on the commission amount remitted by them outside India since the same is paid for the services provided from outside India by the foreign commission agent, but received in India by the Indian principal.

If a foreign commission agent undertakes the job of erection, installation and commissioning of the goods imported by the Indian principal and charges the customer separately, question of service tax liability will not arise on Indian principal, since such services are rendered/provided and used/consumed outside India, which will not attract service tax. If, however, foreign commission agent raises separate bill on the Indian principals for such activities or for undertaking maintenance or repair work during warranty period, such service will attract service tax under the new Rules and Indian principal will be liable to pay such service tax.

Reimbursement of expenses

13. Normally, commission agents obtain reimbursement of expenses from their principals based on the terms of contract and till the introduction of new Valuation Rules, 2006, not only the commission agents, but also other service providers were not including such expenses reimbursed by the service receiver in the value of taxable service and this has resulted in a heavy loss of revenue to the Government. However, the valuation concept has undergone a sea change with effect from April 18, 2006 with the introduction of substituted section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994 and introduction of a new set of Rules titled Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, which came into effect from April 19, 2006.

Rule 5 of the above rules clearly indicates that any expenses incurred by the service provider during the course of rendering the service will form part of the value of taxable service and service tax payable on such amount. As a result of this stringent provision, the reimbursement concept has undergone a major change and only when a service provider acts as a Pure Agent, and fulfils all the eight conditions laid down under Rule 5(2) of the Valuation Rules, 2006, such amount can be excluded from the value of taxable service. Thus, there is no more free lunch to the service providers and service tax is now payable on the value of taxable service which should include, inter alia, any expenses incurred for rendering the output service. Whether Cenvat Credit can be availed on the basis of bills submitted for reimbursements. For example, when a consultant claims reimbursement for local conveyance by Taxi to his client, whether the client can take the Cenvat credit of service tax paid by the Consultant on the taxi hire charges. If you see the Service Tax Valuation Rules, these are really part of service of the consultant and the consultant should include in his Bill and charge service tax on it. He can take credit of the service tax. Legally, this is safe and better and indeed legally correct way.

Of course, Cenvat credit cannot be denied simply because Bill is in name of consultant, but this legal fact is not accepted by department and you may end up into costly litigation.

Whether service tax paid on the telephone expenses & courier charges at the marketing offices of a company can be claimed as Cenvat Credit.(If the bill is in the name of the company, but the address is of that marketing office).

If you are maintaining centralised accounting at HO and all bills and records are available in main office/factory, you can take credit.

Further, sub-rule (3)(c) of the above said rules reads as under : "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) and sub-rule (2), the manufacturer or the provider of output service opting not to maintain separate accounts shall follow either of the following conditions as applicable to him, namely :

The provider of output service shall utilize the credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services."

From the above-said provision, it is clear that where an output service provider is availing credit on inputs and input services and providing taxable as well as exempted services without opting to maintain separate account of inputs and input services received and used for the exempted services and refrains to avail Cenvat Credit on such inputs/input services, he has no other option but to use Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on the output services. Therefore, the intention of the law is, the assessee shall either maintain separate account of input and input services for exempted output services and not to avail Cenvat Credit thereon or to utilize Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the service tax payable on output services. Therefore, if the assessee decides to avail Cenvat Credit directly related to the taxable output services and utilizes the same fully for payment of service tax on output services and simultaneously avails Cenvat Credit on common inputs and input services without maintaining separate account and utilizing such credit only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable, it will defeat the intention of the legal provision which is explained in the example given below :

Let the input service credit availed on input services used exclusively for taxable output service is Rs. 10,000.

Common input services which are used partly for taxable and partly for exempted services, credit availed fully of Rs. 20,000.

Let service tax payable on the taxable output service be Rs. 50,000.

The correct way to utilize the Cenvat Credit for the above said situation would be 20% of Rs. 50,000, i.e., Rs. 10,000 which can be utilized out of the total credit of Rs. 30,000 (Rs. 10,000 related to the taxable output services and Rs. 20,000 credit on common input services used for taxable as well as exempted output service). Therefore, the balance amount, i.e., Rs. 50,000 minus Rs. 10,000 Cenvat Credit utilized = Rs. 40,000 has to be used as to be paid through TR-6 challan.

Had Cenvat Credit been utilized as explained in the query, the assessee can utilize the credit of Rs. 10,000 which is directly related to taxable output service plus another Rs. 10,000 i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 service tax payable on output service = Rs. 20,000 and the balance amount of Rs. 30,000 would have been paid through TR-6 challan.

However, it may be noted that the provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, do not provide for more than one set of Cenvat Credit record for input service credit i.e. one for the input service credit related to taxable output service and second common input services credit account which are partly used for taxable output service and party for exempted services nor this sort of arrangement is prohibited, but considering the practice followed under Central Excise, I am of the opinion, that under above stated example, the assessee can avail total credit on Rs. 30,000 (10,000 + 20,000), but utilization will be restricted to 10% of service tax payable i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 = Rs. 10,000 and balance amount of Cenvat Credit unutilized (Rs. 30,000 total Cenvat Credit minus Rs. 10,000 credit utilized = Rs. 20,000) will be carried forward to the next month. It is further clarified that the law does not restrict the assessee to take Cenvat Credit on common input service only to the extent of 20% of service tax paid.

In the above said example the common input service credit of entire Rs. 20,000 can be availed and it is not restricted for availment of credit upto 20% of Rs. 20,000 i.e. Rs. 4,000.

Opinion : In short, if the assessee does not opt for separate account as envisaged under Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, he can avail the credit on the common inputs services fully but he can utilize the total credit available at the end of the month not exceeding 20% of service tax payable.

u A power to give benefit encompasses within itself the power to put conditions and restrictions under which credit is available. Power to give benefit also carries with it power to take it back or withdraw it. The rule if properly read starts with the words ‘Cenvat credit shall not be allowed’. Therefore, rule 6 makes it clear that insofar as inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods are concerned, no Cenvat credit is allowed. The rule making authority, however, noting that inputs may be used both for manufacturing final products which may be dutiable and other final products which are exempt, has provided that such manufacturer will be given credit insofar as inputs used for manufacturing of dutiable goods are concerned, if accounts are maintained in terms of the rules. Therefore, merely because the assessee contended that he was willing to forego credit on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final product it does not warrant a departure from the requirements of rule 6(2) and 6(3). The rules contemplate that on failure to maintain accounts in terms of rule 6(2) the consequences would be in terms of rule 6(3)(a) or (b). It is not possible to read down the rule as ‘amount not exceeding’ as was sought to be contended on behalf of the assessee.

u Rule 6(1) is clear; the Cenvat credit cannot be availed of on inputs used in the manufacturing of exempted goods. It then adds the words ‘except in the circumstances mentioned’ in sub-rule (2). A Court cannot read into the said rule something different or render otiose the words. The rule mandates specifically that an assessee seeking to avail Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, the only method by which he can avail of the credit is by following sub-rule (2).

u In our opinion, the taxing machinery has to follow the method provided more so by the Assessing Officer. He cannot disregard a rule. It is not open to an assessee to contend that because he has chosen not to maintain the records as required, revenue authorities even against the grain of the language of the rule, must estimate the inputs used in the manufacture of final dutiable products and, accordingly, pass necessary orders. It is also not possible to accept the contention that because they are familiar with the procedure of ascertaining the amount of credit, that by itself makes rule 6(3)(b) directory.

u Once the law itself has laid down the circumstances under which credit can be availed, it is that method by which the credit can alone be availed. It is not open to an assessee to contend that some other method is also available and the assessee has the choice of claiming credit or reversing the same. Such an argument is devoid of merits considering the clear language of rule 6(1).

Decision in the case of National Engineering Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 21 STT 188 (New Delhi - CESTAT) 4.2 The assessee was an agent of a foreign company, i.e., GMC. It procured orders/contracts from Indian Railways for GMC and received commission on which service tax had been paid under the category of ‘Business auxiliary services’. The commission, however, was not received directly from GMC, but was received through Indian Railways in Indian currency. As per understanding between GMC and Indian Railways, GMC received payment from Indian Railways after deducting the commission payable to the assessee. The assessee filed refund claim on the ground that the services provided by it to GMC on which service tax had been paid were export of services in terms of rule 3(3). The Assistant Commissioner rejected the refund claim on the ground that since the commission was received in non-convertible Indian currency, in view of the proviso to sub-rule (3) of rule 3, same could not be treated as export of services. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assistant Commissioner. The appellant pleaded that when the Business Auxiliary Service, taxable under section 65(105)(zzb ) of the Finance Act, 1994 is provided by a service provider in India to a recipient located outside India and service is used in or in relation to commerce or industry of the recipient, the same has to be treated as export of the service in terms of sub-rule (3) of rule 3 of Export of Services Rules, 2005. That the conditions (a), (b) and (c) of the proviso to sub-rule (3) are applicable only in a situation where the service recipient abroad has any commercial or industrial establishment or any office relating thereto, in India, and only in such a situation the conditions mentioned in clauses (a ), (b) and (c) of the proviso have to be satisfied. One of such condition being that the payment for such service is received by the service provider in convertible foreign exchange; that GMC, did not have any commercial establishment or office in India and therefore, the proviso to sub-rule (3) of rule 3 was not applicable; that in view of this, the business auxiliary service provided by the appellant to GMC had to be treated as service export and, therefore, no service tax was payable in respect of services and the appellant was eligible of the refund of the service tax paid by it.

The Tribunal held that just because commission was received by the appellant through Indian Railways in Indian Rupees as Indian Railways made payment to GMC in foreign currency after deducting the commission payable to GMC, it could not be said that the service provided by the appellant to GMC, USA was not export of service under rule 3(3) of the Export of Services Rules and, therefore, the appellants were held eligible for refund of the service tax paid on such service exported to GMC, USA.

The Tribunal further held that in the case of ETA Travel Agency (P.) Ltd. (supra) cited by Ld. DR, the offshore service receiver had an office in India and the commission had been received from the bank account of such local office of the offshore service receiver and in view of the facts of the case, the Tribunal held that the service had been provided and received in India and it was not a case of export of service. Therefore, as per Tribunal, this judgment of the Tribunal was not applicable to the facts of this case and, therefore, the Tribunal held that the service provided by the appellant to GMC, USA had to be treated as ‘export of service’ under rule 3(3) of the Export of Services Rules. The Tribunal also followed the decision of National Engg. Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 17 STT 398 (New Delhi - CESTAT), given in the appellant’s own case even the reasoning were different.

6. Though the issues are numerous which still need clarity since the statute is still in its nascent stage, some of the identified issues are as under :

(i) Rule 6(3), Opt in - your choice, Opt out - no choice during the financial year

The sub-rule clarifies that an option would be exercisable both in the case of goods and services as manufactured or provided by the assessee. He cannot opt for Option 1 for goods and option 2 for services or vice versa. Also, exercise of such option cannot be withdrawn at any point of time during the financial year. He may change his option from the next year onwards. Thus, though the choice of opting in for the non-maintenance of separate books of account is open during the financial year, yet the option to opt out of it is unavailable to the manufacturer of service provider for that financial year.

(ii) Meaning of the term - ‘exempt’

The sub-rule does not define the term ‘exempt’ for the purpose of this sub-rule. Technically speaking, exempted goods/services are a sub-set of taxable goods/services. Exempted goods/services are specified by a notification by the Central Government and, accordingly, no duty/tax is leviable on them. However, there are other goods or services which are non-taxable and cannot be called ‘exempt’ technically. For example services of an advocate.

Having said this, the interpretation of the term ‘exempt’ is important for the calculation of duty/tax in respect of the Cenvat credit attributable towards exempted goods/services. Thus, extension of the term ‘exempt’ on non-taxable goods/services or otherwise would change the entire computation. For example when a provider of taxable services is providing exempt services and also is engaged in trading of goods (non-taxable), whether he needs to pay an amount equal to Cenvat credit attributable towards trading activity also, as he has to do in the case of exempt services. The answer is in affirmative when we equate trading to an exempt service and not otherwise.

Further, a larger question would be whether in case of an assessee engaged in the provision of taxable service and non-taxable service, would the computation under rule 6(3A) be applicable on him ? The question would be answered as ‘YES’ when non-taxable is equated as ‘exempt’ otherwise the answer is ‘NO’.

The more logical calculation would be to take out the Cenvat credit attributable towards non-taxable activities and then apply rule 6(3) on the balance Cenvat credit. Thus, the assessee should avail only the credit excluding that which is attributable towards non-taxable activities.

(iii) Choice of option - whether premises-wise or assessee-wise

Further, another point worth mentioning here is that the term used by the statute for availment of choice is manufacturer/service provider and not premises of manufacturer (factory) or service provider. Even the definition of ‘manufacturer’ under central excise uses the word ‘person’ and not ‘factory’. Accordingly, one school of thought might interpret that the availment of the options above should be same throughout all locations across India and the option cannot be availed of differently for different premises.

Expressing it with an example, Mr. X is a service provider having offices in Delhi, Mumbai and Pune, all three offices being separately registered with service tax department. Mr. X is providing taxable services under the category of ‘chartered accountant services’ and also availing the exemption provided thereunder. Thus, he is the provider of both taxable as well as exempt services. Now, the question is whether he can opt for option I for his Delhi and Mumbai offices and option II for Pune or will he have to opt for a single option for all his offices since the sub-rule uses the words ‘service provider’ when offering the choice.

CLARIFICATION ON AMENDMENTS TO RULE 6 EFFECTED FROM 1-4-2008

In the Budget 2008-09, certain amendments have been carried out in the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 pertains to an assessee who manufactures dutiable and exempted goods and provision of taxable and exempted services. As a general principle, CENVAT credit is not allowed on input or input service used for the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services [refer Rule 6(1)]. Exception to Rule 6(1) is contained in rule 6(3), 6(5) and 6(6).

Rule 6(2) : Provides facility to an assessee to maintain separate Cenvat credit account for dutiable and exempted goods or services (hereinafter referred to as outputs) and take credit only on inputs and input services meant for use in dutiable outputs.

Rule 6(3) : Pertains to an assessee opting not to maintain separate Cenvat credit accounts for dutiable and exempted outputs. Such assessee has to opt for one of the following two options :

(i)

Pay an amount equal to 10% of the value of the exempted goods or 8% of the value of the exempted services. Exempted service includes non-taxable service also.

OR

(ii)

Pay an amount equivalent to the CENVAT credit attributable to inputs and input services used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or for provision of exempted services. Rule 6(3A) prescribes the conditions and procedure to determine the amount of CENVAT credit attributable to exempted outputs.

Schemes under rule 6(3) are optional and each individual scheme is comprehensive and self-contained. An assessee can exercise the option in relation to all his activities as an assessee and the option is not available only in relation to a part of his activity and the option once exercised cannot be withdrawn during the said financial year.

Distributive Trade Services

25.1 Trading and Hospitality Services

Distributive trade services and hospitality services fall under section 6 of Classification of Services.

Headings for distributive trade are - (a) wholesale trade (9961) (b) Retail Trade (9962).

Heading for hospitality services (Accommodation food and beverage services) is 9963. Groups in this heading are - Accommodation Service (of hotel, campsite) (99631), Accommodation service (rooms, hostels) (99632) and Food, edible preparation and beverage services (99633).

25.2 Services of commission agent

Services of commission agent in wholesale trade fall under 99611.

Services of commission agent in retail trade fall under 99621.

Note that services of Clearing and Forwarding Agent (C&F) do not fall under this head.

The GST rate is 18% (CGST 9% and SGST 9%) or IGST 18%.

Commission Agent is not required to register if his receipts of commission are less than Rs 20/10 lakhs per annum - Persons who supply goods or services or both on behalf of other taxable persons whether as an agent or otherwise require registration under GST even if his turnover is below Rs 20/10 lakhs per annum- section 24(1)(vii) of CGST Act.

There was misunderstanding that all commission agents require mandatory registration under GST irrespective of his commission income (i.e. even if income from commission is below 20/10 lakhs per annum).

Now it has been clarified that such registration is required only by C&F agents who stock and sale goods on behalf of Principal. Registration is not required by ordinarily commission agents who do not deal in goods or services themselves, if their annual turnover is less than Rs 20/10 lakhs - CBI&C Circular No. 57/31/2018-GST dated 4-9-2018.

Position in respect of del credere agent - Del credere agent is similar to commission agent. The only difference is that he guarantees payment to supplier of goods or services, if recipient does not pay. In some cases, the del credere agent himself pays to supplier and then recovers amount from recipient. In some case, the del credere agent advances short term loan to buyer and then buyer pays to the supplier.

CBI&C, vide circular No. 73/47/2018-GST dated 5-11-2018, has clarified that if del credere agent is like ordinary commission agent, there is no impact on GST liability.

However, if the del credere agent (DCA) received the goods and then supplies as per para 3 of Schedule I of CGST Act (i.e. he is C&F Agent), the value of interest will be included in the value of supply of goods by DCA to the recipient as per section 15(2)(d) of CGST Act. [Note that in this case, there are two separate transactions and tax invoices. The first transaction is when supplier raises tax invoice on DCA (who is similar to C&F Agent in this case) and second is when the DCA (who is similar to C&F Agent in this case) issues tax invoice on buyer].

Del credere agent passing early payment bonus to buyer - In K K Polymers, In re (2019) 72 GST 41 = 100 taxmann.com 17 (AAR-Rajasthan), the applicant, a Del credere agent, was getting bonus for early payment which he was passing on to customer. It was held that this not a service.

Service of arranging trucks to GTA for commission is service as agent under heading 9967 - Service of arranging trucks to GTA for commission is service as agent under heading 9967 [support service to transport] and GST rate is 18% - Deeraj Goyal In re (2021) 88 GST 327 = 131 taxmann.com 85 (AAR-AP).

Value of taxable supply of commission agent includes all incidental charges received - Consideration received by commission agent in respect of elements like agent's commission, agent's transport charges, stationery charges, compensation on handling and evaporation loss shall form part of value of taxable supply - Provat Kumar Kundu, In re [2022] 142 taxmann.com 76 (AAR-WB).

25.2-1 Exemption to services of Fair Price Shops to Central/State Government or Union Territory

Service provided by Fair Price Shops to Central Government by way of sale of wheat, rice and coarse grains under Public Distribution System (PDS) against consideration in the form of commission or margin are exempt.

Rule 6(3) has been radically changed w.e.f. 1-4-2008. Provisions upto 31-3-2008 are summarised below.

If assessee opts not to maintain separate accounts in respect of inputs and input services utilised for exempted goods/exempted output services as required under rule 6(2), he has to pay ‘amount’ of 10% of total price (excluding taxes) of exempted final product [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

In case of output services, he could utilise credit only upto 20% of service tax on output services. [He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services].

The third option i.e. proportionate reversal of Cenvat credit was not available upto 31-3-2008.

Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services — Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/output services and partly for exempted goods/services. In such cases, the manufacturer/service provider has two options — (a) Maintain separate inventory and accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services. In such cases, he should not avail Cenvat credit of the inputs and input services which are used in exempted final services at all — Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules (b) Pay 10% ‘amount’ if he does not maintain separate inventory and records, if he is a manufacturer — Rule 6(3)(b) [If he is service provider, his credit is restricted to 20% of tax payable, as explained later] [provision upto 31-3-2008]

‘Amount’ if separate inventory and records not maintained - If the manufacturer opts not to maintain such separate accounts, he has to pay an amount equal to 10% of the ‘price’ of such exempted goods. Such payment can be made by debit to Cenvat credit account or PLA [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

Reversal of Cenvat credit in case of some exempted goods - In case of some specified exempted goods, the manufacturer of these final products only has to reverse Cenvat credit they had taken on inputs and input services, which were used for manufacture of exempted final product. - Rule 6(3)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Cenvat credit on capital goods — If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and party for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products [rule 6(4)] — confirmed in Idea Cellular v. CCE (2009) 19 STT 423 = 36 VST 217 (CESTAT).

No reversal or payment of amount in certain cases — If excisable goods are removed to SEZ unit, SEZ developer, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting, payment of 10% ‘amount’ is not required [rule 6(6)].

Cenvat credit of service tax in case of supplies made by DTA to EOU - Supplies from DTA to EOU are entitled to Cenvat credit of service tax paid — para 6.11(v) of FTP.

Proportional Cenvat in case of general insurance companies providing taxable as well as exempt services - Rule 6(3)(d) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2007 provided an option to general insurance service providers providing taxable as well as exempted insurance schemes and who do not maintain separate input/input services credit accounts, to utilise Cenvat credit proportionate to the inputs and input services used in providing output services. The scheme was applicable only to general insurance services referred to in section 65(105)(d) and is optional - para 11.1 of D.O. F. No. 334/1/2007-TRU dated 28-2-2007 issued by Shri R Sekar, Joint Secretary (TRU). Now this specific provision has been deleted w.e.f. 1-4-2008.

22.4 Some case law relating to definition of 'input service' has become inapplicable after amendment to definition of 'input service' w.e.f. 1-4-2011. However, major part of case law is still relevant. The case law, which in my view is still relevant, is given below.

22.4-1 There were disputes about eligibility of Cenvat credit on servicers provided by commission agent. Hence, following explanation has been added to rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, w.e.f. 3-2-2016 after sub-clause (C) -

Explanation - For the purpose of this clause, sales promotion includes services by way of sale of dutiable goods on commission basis.

The drafting of the explanation is faulty. Firstly, it is not clear what is meant by 'this clause', since firstly, any of sub-clauses (A), (B) and (C) of definition of 'input service' has no relation with 'sales commission'. Secondly, commission agent really never sales the goods. He only 'facilitates' sales. Thirdly, the explanation only refers to sale of dutiable goods. What about commission agents of services like hotels, travel of passengers, food etc.?

Be as it may, at least issue of eligibility of input service of commission agent of goods has been sorted out.

The explanation has retrospective effect - In Essar Steel India v. CCE (2016) 335 ELT 660 (CESTAT), it has been rightly held that this explanation is clarificatory in nature and has retrospective effect.

In my view, this decision is correct, for reasons stated below.

Right from beginning, department has consistently held (as per circulars/instructions discussed below) that input service of service tax paid by commission agents is eligible 'input service'. Tribunal and one High Court (Punjab and Haryana HC) have also consistently held the same view. Problems were created only because one adverse decision of Gujarat High Court in case of Cadila Healthcare delivered in year 2013.

Departmental circular - Para 5 of CBE&C circular No. 943/04/2011-CX, dated 29-4-2011 has specifically clarified that even under new definition of input service, service tax on sales commission is eligible as input service.

It can be argued that canteen is not 'outdoor catering' as per trade parlance, even if run by outside contractor.

The question does not arise if (a) canteen is as per statutory requirements under Factories Act, as that service is exempt from service and hence no question of Cenvat credit (b) Canteen is not air conditioned.

In that case, service tax is not payable at all.

Goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-CE, dated the 1st March, 2011 is availed are exempted goods [Rule 2(d)]. The expression "no relationship whatsoever with the manufacture of a final pro-duct" must be interpreted and applied strictly and not loosely. The expression does not include any goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. Only credit of goods used in the factory but having absolutely no relationship with the manufacture of final product is not allowed. Supply of goods— (a) by a principal to his agent where the agent undertakes to supply such goods on behalf of the principal, or (b) by an agent to his principal where the agent undertakes to receive such goods on behalf of the principal, will be subject to GST, even if there is no consideration - clause 3 of Schedule I of CGST Act.

'Agent' means a person, including a factor, broker, commission agent, arhatia, del credere agent, an auctioneer or any other mercantile agent, by whatever name called, who carries on the business of supply or receipt of goods or services or both on behalf of another - section 2(6) of CGST Act.

Liability only of C&F Agents, not of commission agents - As per aforesaid clause (a), the agent will be liable for GST on value goods or services only if he undertakes to supply any goods or services or both on behalf of any principal (like consignment agent). The judgment of Gujarat High Court in case of Cadila was discussed at the Central Excise Tariff Conference on Tariff Matters organized by CBE&C on 28 and 29 October 2015. Minutes of the conference and decisions taken have been circulated vide CBE&C instruction F No. 96/85/2015-CX.1 dated 7-12-2015.

As per Para B.30 of aforesaid instruction dated 7-12-2015, the conference noted that in case of Cadila, the sales commission agent was only trading in goods i.e. buying and selling the goods without undertaking any sales promotion or advertising. If activity of sales commission agent involves an element of sales promotion, Cenvat credit of service tax paid on commission agent is available.

Full extract of para B.30 of the CBE&C instruction dated 7-12-2015 is given below.

B.30 Meerut Zone - Cenvat Credit - Admissibility of Cenvat Credit on Service Tax Paid on Sales Agency Commission Service:

Issue - CBEC vide its Circular No. 943/4/2011-CX dated 29.04.2011 at point No.5 has clarified that credit of service tax paid on sales commission services (Business auxiliary services) used in 28 relation to manufacture/sale of finished goods is admissible under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. However, there are conflicting judgments of Hon'ble High Courts in this regard. Hon'ble High Court of Gujarat in case of Cadila Health Care [2013 (30) STR 0003] has disallowed the said Cenvat credit whereas Hon'ble Tribunal in case of Birla Corporation Ltd. [2014 (35) STR977] followed the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Bombay and allowed the credit. Board may be requested by the conference to issue necessary clarification on the subject to avoid further litigation and to achieve uniformity in the practice of assessment.

Discussion & Decision

The conference discussed the issue in detail and the facts of both the cases where apparently conflicting judgments have been delivered. It was noted that the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Gujarat was in a very specific set of circumstances where the sales commission agent seemed to be only trading in the goods i.e. buying and selling the goods without undertaking any sales promotion or advertising. In the said judgment, Hon'ble court noted that "there is nothing to indicate that such commission agents were actually involved in any sales promotion activities as envisaged under the said expression. Obviously, commission paid to the various agents would not be covered in this expression since it cannot be stated to be a service used directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products or clearance of final products from the place of removal". Board Circular No. 943/4/2011-CX., dated 29-4-2011 at point No. 5 on the other hand has explained the situation where the commission agent renders the service of sales promotion in following words -"....... Moreover the activity of sale promotion is specifically allowed and on many occasions the remuneration for same is linked to actual sale.......". Board circular directs that input service credit would be available when there is a element of sales promotion as sales promotion is a service. Thus, the conflict between the judgment and the circular is not as large as is perceived. Both the Board circular and case laws on the subject allow credit of input services, when the activity of the sales commission agent involves an element of sales promotion.

Impact of decision of Gujarat High Court - Assessees and Tribunal benches within jurisdiction of Gujarat High Court were bound by decision of Gujarat High Court. However, even these assessees could take Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission, if there agreement is properly worded to establish that the agent is not simply trading but is also doing additional work of sales promotion and advertising.

Assessees outside jurisdiction of Gujarat High Court could take a stand that in view of contrary decision of Punjab and Haryana High Court, they are not bound by decision of Gujarat High Court.

For example, assume that service tax payable on output service is Rs 100. Service tax paid on input service is Rs 15. These input services are used both for taxable output services and exempt/non-taxable output services. In such case, assessee can avail and utilise credit of entire Rs 15. He will have to pay balance in cash, even if credit of Rs 55 is still available in his books.

He may take credit of Rs 75 in his Service Tax (Receivable) Account, but can utilise credit of Rs 20.

The balance may remain in his Service Tax Credit Account. He can utilise it in future if opportunity arises.

Explanation 1.—For the purposes of sub-rule (2), "pure agent" means a person who—

(a)

enters into a contractual agreement with the recipient of service to act as his pure agent to incur expenditure or costs in the course of providing taxable service;

(b) neither intends to hold nor holds any title to the goods or services so procured or provided as pure agent of the recipient of service;

(d)

receives only the actual amount incurred to procure such goods or services.

Explanation 2.—For the removal of doubts it is clarified that the value of the taxable service is the total amount of consideration consisting of all components of the taxable service and it is immaterial that the details of individual components of the total consideration is indicated separately in the invoice.

Illustration 1.—X contracts with Y, a real estate agent to sell his house and thereupon Y gives an advertisement in television. Y billed X including charges for television advertisement and paid service tax on the total consideration billed. In such a case, consideration for the service provided is what X pays to Y. Y does not act as an agent on behalf of X when obtaining the television advertisement even if the cost of television advertisement is mentioned separately in the invoice issued by X. Advertising service is an input service for the estate agent in order to enable or facilitate him to perform his services as an estate agent.

Illustration 2.—In the course of providing a taxable service, a service provider incurs costs such as travelling expenses, postage, telephone, etc., and may indicate these items separately on the invoice issued to the recipient of service. In such a case, the service provider is not acting as an agent of the recipient of service but procures such inputs or input service on his own account for providing the taxable service. Such expenses do not become reimbursable expenditure merely because they are indicated separately in the invoice issued by the service provider to the recipient of service.

Illustration 3.—A contracts with B, an architect for building a house. During the course of providing the taxable service, B incurs expenses such as telephone charges, air travel tickets, hotel accommodation, etc., to enable him to effectively perform the provision of services to A. In such a case, in whatever form B recovers such expenditure from A, whether as a separately itemised expense or as part of an inclusive overall fee, service tax is payable on the total amount charged by B. Value of the taxable service for charging service tax is what A pays to B.

Illustration 4.—Company X provides a taxable service of rent-a-cab by providing chauffeur-driven cars for overseas visitors. The chauffeur is given a lump sum amount to cover his food and overnight accommodation and any other incidental expenses such as parking fees by the Company X during the tour. At the end of the tour, the chauffeur returns the balance of the amount with a statement of his expenses and the relevant bills. Company X charges these amounts from the recipients of service. The cost incurred by the chauffeur and billed to the recipient of service constitutes part of gross amount charged for the provision of services by the Company X.

15.10-2 Services of freight forwarder

Para 5.9.6 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 gives following illustration.

Illustration - A freight forwarder arranges for export and import shipments. There could be two possible situations here- one when he acts on his own account, and the other, when he acts as an intermediary.

When the freight forwarder acts on his own account (say, for an export shipment)

A freight forwarder provides domestic transportation within taxable territory (say, from the exporter's factory located in Pune to Mumbai port) as well as international freight service (say, from Mumbai port to the international destination), under a single contract, on his own account (i.e. he buys-in and sells freight transport as a principal), and charges a consolidated amount to the exporter. This is a service of transportation of goods for which the place of supply is the destination of goods. Since the destination of goods is outside taxable territory, this service will not attract service tax. Here, it is presumed that ancillary freight services (i.e. services ancillary to transportation- loading, unloading, handling etc.) are "bundled" with the principal service owing to a single contract or a single price (consideration).

On an import shipment with similar conditions, the place of supply will be in the taxable territory, and so service tax will be attracted.

When he acts as an intermediary

Where the freight forwarder acts as an intermediary, the place of provision will be his location. Service tax will be payable on the services provided by him. However, when he provides a service to an exporter of goods, the exporter can claim refund of service tax paid under notification for this purpose.

Similarly, persons such as call centres, who provide services to their clients by dealing with the customers of the client on the client's behalf, but actually provided these services on their own account, will not be categorized as intermediaries.

15.10-3 Service on principal to principal basis is not intermediary service

Service provided to foreign Principal on principal to principal basis is not intermediary service.

For example, service of marketing consultant is not 'intermediary service', if he gets his fees at fixed rate and not on basis of turnover achieved.

In addition to providing marketing and promotion service, assessee was also providing services of supervision of call centre services and payment processing services. It was held that the place of supply of service is outside taxable territory and hence service tax is not applicable.

Assessee received commission from its Singapore subsidiary. It was held that service was delivered to subsidiary. It cannot be said that service is delivered in India.

15.10-4 Ironical situation - Receiving foreign exchange is taxed

This provision has created an ironical situation. If Indian commission agent provides service to Principal outside India, he is required to pay IGST, though he is receiving payment in foreign exchange. On the other hand, if a foreign commission agent provides service to Indian Principal, the Indian Principal has to pay him in foreign exchange but no IGST is payable.

Thus, a transaction where actually India received foreign exchange is subjected to IGST, while transaction where there is outflow of foreign exchange from India is not subject to IGST.

No IGST and no reverse charge on services provided by foreign Commission Agents to Indian Principals - In case of foreign commission agents providing service to Indian Principal, the place of supply of service is outside India. Hence, no IGST is payable even under reverse charge.

This has been confirmed in Midas Foods P Ltd. In re (2021) 128 taxmann.com 360 (AAR-Uttarakhand).
