Relevant case law 4. The validity of rule 6(7) was challenged in the case of Airlines Agents Association v. Union of India [2002] 121 Taxman 298 (Mad.). The High Court upheld the validity of rule 6(7). The High Court held (i) that there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found in that rule, (ii) that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration sections 93 and 94(2)(a) jointly, (iii) that what was suggested by rule 6(7) was nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations, and (iv ) that it was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule-making power.

In Airlines Agents Association’s case (supra), it was contended that the commission paid by the airlines is in respect of services to the airlines and not services to the customer and, therefore, the said commission should not be taxed. The High Court rejected that contention and held as under:

". . . It is not as if the air travel agents get a fixed commission or income from the airlines irrespective of the passages booked by them in favour of the customers in the nature of a ‘retainer fee’ or ‘guarantee money’, at least that is not the case pleaded before us. Therefore, unless the air travel agents book the tickets and thereby unless they provide the services to the customers, they do not become entitled to any commission. Their commission is entirely dependent on and connected with the passage they book for the customers. It cannot, therefore, be said that the commission that the air travel agents get from the airlines is independent of and distinct from the services that they provide to the air-travellers and are relatable to the business that they provide to the airlines. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process, the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle is cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case goes away. From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l), the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided which is made taxable. In our opinion, therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. We may also say that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air-travellers. If, in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission, that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-traveller. On the other hand, we may say that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited, the tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which, there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the learned counsel that because of section 67(k) the nature of the tax itself changes, is incorrect." (p. 305)

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force w.e.f. 16.08.2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit upto 10.09.2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10.09.2004. 6. Under the Credit Rules, 2002 input service is defined in Rule 2(c) as any taxable service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service. Rule 3(1) provided that an output service provider shall be allowed to take credit (service tax credit) of the service tax paid on input service, in the enumerated manner. Sub-clause (a) of this Rule provides that where an input service falls in the same category of taxable service as the output service, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 16.08.2002; sub-clause (b) stipulates that in any other case, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 14.05.2003. Sub rule (2) of Rule 3 provides that for the purpose of these rules, two services shall be deemed to be falling in the same category of taxable service, if the input service or output service fall in the same sub-clause of clause (105) of Section 65 of the Act (the Finance Act, 1994). Sub-rule (4) of Rule 3 states that where a service provider avails credit on any input service and renders output services which are chargeable to service tax as well as exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be, he shall maintain separate accounts for receipt and consumption of input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of taxable output services and input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be. Sub-rule (5) of Rule 3 enacts that where a service provider opts not to maintain separate accounts, as stipulated in sub-rile (4), he shall be allowed to utilize service tax credit for payment of service tax on any output service only to an extent of an amount not exceeding 35% of the amount of service tax payable on such output services.

7. On a true and fair construction of the relevant provisions of the Credit Rules, 2002, it is apparent that credit could be taken on an input service falling in the same category of taxable service as the output service in respect of which the service tax liability arises and discharged from the available credit. It is axiomatic that trading in goods is neither a taxable service and could not, in the absence of a legislative/statutory fiction provided, capable of being construed as an exempted service.

8. Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, 2004 sets out the obligations of a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) provides that no cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) enjoins maintenance of separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input or input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service; and the quantity of input spent for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and authorizes taking of cenvat credit only on that quantity of input or input services which are intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing taxable output services. Sub-rule (3) of Rule 6 carves out specified exclusions to the requirements set out in sub-rule (2). Sub-clause (c) of Rule 6(3) stipulates that the provider of an output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service.

9. The 2004 Credit Rules were amended w.e.f. 01.04.2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'.

10. From the provisions of both, the Credit Rules, 2002 and the Credit Rules, 2004 it is clear that trading is neither a service nor an exempted service. Therefore no credit of the service tax paid on taxable input services used for trading could be taken and utilized for remittance of service tax on taxable services provided by the assessee, even for discharging a percentage (35% or 20%, as a case may be) of the service tax liability on the taxable service provided.

However, in case of export of services, these are ‘exempt services’ since, as per rule 2(e) service on which no tax is payable is also ‘exempt service’. It can be said that both export of goods and export of services should be taken in denominator (divisor), i.e., below the line to give correct and fair results. If these are taken in dividend (above the line), it will amount to reversal of Cenvat credit attributable to these services, which certainly is illogical.

3.2 Calculation of value of common inputs in case of exempted final products - The formulae as given in rule 6(3A) are only in respect of Cenvat credit attributable to (a ) inputs used for provision of exempted services and (b) input services used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services.

There is no formula to calculate Cenvat credit attributable to value of inputs used in manufacture of exempted final product, when inputs are common. In any case, consumables, fuel, dies, toolings, etc., will be ‘common inputs’ in most of the cases.

In absence of any formula, the only option with the assessee is to calculate the same either on basis of input-output ratio, or on the basis of formula similar to the one applicable for calculation of inputs used for provision of exempted services.

3.3 Treatment of traded goods - A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods. The sale may be within India or outside. Obviously, there will be many common input services. Now, traded goods are not ‘exempt goods’. It is also not ‘service’, since one is not providing services to anyone else. Further, one cannot provide service to oneself.

Including the entire value of turnover of traded goods into dividend (above line) will be highly unfair to the assessee since the services attributable to such traded goods will certainly not be proportional to value of the traded goods, in cases where the assessee is both manufacturer as well as trader.

As the formulae stand today, turnover of traded goods can neither be included in divisor (below the line) nor the dividend (above the line). This would give higher Cenvat credit to the assessee. It would be fair to provide some percentage of turnover of traded goods (by way of rules), which should be added to dividend (above the line) to give fair results.

If no such provision is made in rules, there is a strong case to argue that it is not includible in divisor as well as dividend at all, since it is neither exempted goods nor exempted service (rather it is not ‘service’ at all).

3.4 Supplies to EOU, SEZ, etc. - Rule 6(6) states that provisions of rules 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply in case of excisable goods removed to SEZ, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting.

According to strict interpretation, this turnover shall not come either in denominator or in dividend. This would be unfair. It will give absurd results, particularly when sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., are large, as amount to be reversed will be very heavy. Sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., should appear in denominator, as per correct VAT principles.

3.5 Services specified in rule 6(5) - As per rule 6(5) in case of specified 16 services, full Cenvat credit of input service is available even if these services are partly used in manufacture of exempted final product/output services. This rule has not been amended even if rule 6(3) has been recast with effect from April 1, 2008. Cenvat credit in relation to these services should be outside the calculations made as per rule 6(3A) and entire credit will be available, without any reversal.

3.6 Treatment of opening balance - An assessee always tries to utilise Cenvat credit first and then pay through PLA/GAR-7. However, despite his efforts, some opening balance is possible, particularly in initial stages of production/provision of services.

Principally, the formula should apply to opening balances also.

3.7 Service tax paid under reverse charge method - In cases where service tax is paid under reverse charge method (particularly GTA services and sponsorship services), what would be the treatment ? As per amended rules, in case of GTA service, this amount should be paid by GAR-7 challan and not by cash with effect from March 1, 2008. However, this is not ‘output service’ as per amended rule 2(p). Hence, it appears that this amount is ‘input service’ and will be ‘service tax paid’. It will neither appear in divisor nor in dividend, but proportional reversal will have to be made.

choice of the commission agent to arrive at a fixed amount required for erection, installation and commissioning so that the fixed amount is taken into account to arrive at the value of taxable service. Unfortunately, service tax so paid towards erection, installation and commissioning cannot be availed as CENVAT credit since it is not required for rendering the output service of commission agent and it is a helpless situation of grin and bear it. In other words, it is an additional cost to be provided for in business. Some commission agents also undertake on behalf of the foreign principals, the maintenance and repair work of the goods so supplied within the warranty period for which no charges are collected from the Indian customer though the commission agents rendering such service may be paid an agreed amount. Such amount will also attract service tax since management, maintenance and repair is also one of the notified service. If the commission paid by the foreign principal covers, inter alia, maintenance and repair during the warranty period, then the department is bound to insist for service tax on the entire commission amount in the absence of any specific split up of the amount towards the same. Thus, it is imperative that such commission agent who enters into the contract with the foreign principal, quantifies the amount payable towards maintenance and repair.

After warranty period, if the maintenance and repair work is undertaken by way of annual maintenance contract or otherwise, that will be a contract between the Indian service provider and Indian service receiver and the tax is payable on the amount so realized from the Indian customer towards the above service.

Import of service and commission agents

12. Like Indian commission agents are representing the foreign principals and canvassing the product and obtaining the orders, it is also a common commercial scenario for the Indian companies to employ commission agents abroad who can move around and obtain orders based on which the goods can be exported from India to the customer identified by the foreign commission agents. The commission so paid to the foreign agents is for the services rendered outside India. However, with the introduction of new set of Rules ‘Service Tax (Provided from Outside India and received in India) Rules, 2006, which came into effect from April 19, 2006, it is an unfortunate situation that the commission so paid by Indian principals to the foreign commission agent will be treated as a taxable service under the newly introduced section 66A read with the above-mentioned new Rules. As a result, the Indian principals will be deemed to be the service provider and, accordingly, service tax is payable on the commission amount remitted by them outside India since the same is paid for the services provided from outside India by the foreign commission agent, but received in India by the Indian principal.

If a foreign commission agent undertakes the job of erection, installation and commissioning of the goods imported by the Indian principal and charges the customer separately, question of service tax liability will not arise on Indian principal, since such services are rendered/provided and used/consumed outside India, which will not attract service tax. If, however, foreign commission agent raises separate bill on the Indian principals for such activities or for undertaking maintenance or repair work during warranty period, such service will attract service tax under the new Rules and Indian principal will be liable to pay such service tax.

Reimbursement of expenses

13. Normally, commission agents obtain reimbursement of expenses from their principals based on the terms of contract and till the introduction of new Valuation Rules, 2006, not only the commission agents, but also other service providers were not including such expenses reimbursed by the service receiver in the value of taxable service and this has resulted in a heavy loss of revenue to the Government. However, the valuation concept has undergone a sea change with effect from April 18, 2006 with the introduction of substituted section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994 and introduction of a new set of Rules titled Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, which came into effect from April 19, 2006.

Rule 5 of the above rules clearly indicates that any expenses incurred by the service provider during the course of rendering the service will form part of the value of taxable service and service tax payable on such amount. As a result of this stringent provision, the reimbursement concept has undergone a major change and only when a service provider acts as a Pure Agent, and fulfils all the eight conditions laid down under Rule 5(2) of the Valuation Rules, 2006, such amount can be excluded from the value of taxable service. Thus, there is no more free lunch to the service providers and service tax is now payable on the value of taxable service which should include, inter alia, any expenses incurred for rendering the output service. For example, if a chartered accountant in Mumbai undertakes the audit of his clients in Chennai, the air travel expenses, hotel expenses, taxi expenses, etc., cannot be excluded as a reimbursement of expenses on actuals, but are to be included in the value of taxable service since these are incurred for rendering his output service.

Billing

14. It is a common commercial practice in respect of services received from commission agent, that generally neither bill nor debit note is raised by commission agents on the principals. On the contrary, periodically, the principals either issue credit notes and account the commission payable or as and when payment is made to the Commission Agent, the same is accounted in the books of account.

abroad but utilised/received in India - As regards second type of services, there does not seem to be any constitutional difficulty in imposing tax on services provided abroad but utilised/consumed in India, as it will have territorial nexus in India. However, it can be argued that at least till June 16, 2005, there was no provision to impose such tax on import of services. Till June 16, 2005, only services ‘provided in India’ are taxable. Are services of commission agent provided in India ? - During the period July 9, 2004 to June 15, 2005, Indian service receiver would be liable to pay service tax on these services if these were ‘provided in India’. The issue involved is whether services of foreign Commission Agents can be said to be ‘provided in India’ ? There is no doubt that benefit of the service is received in India. It also cannot be said that these services were consumed by Indian service receiver abroad, since he never went abroad to ‘receive’ these services. Hence, the services can be said to be ‘received in India’. Department may argue that ‘provision’ of service is not complete unless it is ‘received’. Hence, service is provided in India. As against this, following arguments support the view that no service tax is payable, at least till June 16, 2005 -

(1)Mere receipt of benefit of service in India does not mean service is provided in India. For example, receiving telephone call or courier from abroad does not mean that telephone or courier service is provided in India. Using imported goods in India does not mean that goods were ‘manufactured’ in India.

(2)Very fact that Explanation has been added with effect from June 16, 2005 means that prior to that, such services were not taxable.

(3)Assuming that there is some ambiguity, the Supreme Court has consistently held that in case of ambiguity, decision should be in favour of assessee.

(4)Finance Act, 1994 does not have extra-territorial jurisdiction.

(5)Such tax is indirect tax on foreign resident, which is prohibited under DTAA.

Chances of getting favourable decision on this issue are good in case of the Tribunal and very good in case of the Supreme Court. However, the fact remains that final outcome of the stand is uncertain. Hence, in my view, company has to make cost benefit analysis and decide strategy.

Cenvat credit of service tax paid - Definition of ‘input service’ is very wide. All services ‘relating to business’ are input services. Services of commission agent are certainly relating to business of Indian service receiver. TR-6 challan by which service tax paid is eligible document for availing Cenvat credit. However, the service tax should not be paid through other Cenvat credit, since service of commission agent is your ‘input service’ and not ‘output service’.

TR-6 challan is a valid document for availing Cenvat credit, as per rule 9(1)(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Advisable to pay service tax if service receiver is in a position to avail Cenvat Credit - Constitutional validity of a provision can be challenged only by writ petition in High Court. Costs are heavy and result is uncertain. Even if favourable decision is obtained, it can be nullified by the Government by making retrospective amendments. Hence, it may be advisable to pay tax and avail credit.

However, the costs involved in this ‘short cut’ are - ( a) Mandatory interest and (b) No Cenvat credit of service tax for the period July 9, 2004 to September 10, 2004. If these costs are heavy, the issue is worth contesting.

Taxability after June 16, 2005 - In view of explanation added with effect from June 16, 2005 to section 65(105), service tax is certainly payable. The only escape route is challenging constitutional validity by way of a writ petition. The result is completely unpredictable and costs are high. It may be advisable to take ‘easy route’ of paying service tax and availing Cenvat credit.

Possibility of clashing with DTA provisions - There is general impression that Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) is applicable only to income-tax. Though DTAA is made specifically applicable to income-tax, it is not restricted to tax under the Income-tax Act alone. Article 2(2) of Convention with USA, gazetted vide Notification No. GSR 990(E), dated December 20, 1990, reads as follows, ‘The Convention shall apply also to any identical or substantially similar taxes which are imposed after the date of signature of the Convention in addition to, or in place of, the existing taxes’. Identical provision is made in Article 2(2) of Convention with UK, gazetted vide Notification No. GSR 91(E), dated February 11, 1994 and Article 2(4) of Convention with China, gazetted vide Notification No. GSR 331(E), dated April 5, 1995. Other Conventions also have similar provision.

It was found that these provisions are in pari materia with the provisions of rule 57CC and rule 57AD of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. Combined reading of rule 57CC (1) and 57CC (9) would indicate that rule 6(3)(b) has been carved out of a combination of the said sub-rule of rule 57CC. It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts has to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods by way of formula as provided in the rule itself; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It is the settled law that reversal of the credit taken on the inputs is as good as non-availment of the credit on the inputs.

Under the Central Excise Act, 1944, levy is on manufacture but payment is at the time of clearance. It has been decided by the Board that credit of the duty paid on common inputs is admissible when used in the manufacturer of the final product (exempted and dutiable) provided the said credit of duty paid on inputs going into the exempted category of the final product is debited in the RG 23A-Part II account before the removal of exempted final product on actual or pro rata (estimated) basis. The facility of reversing the credit taken is neither explicitly given nor necessarily implied in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002. It was held in that context that the credit taken but before utilization reversed, will amount to not taking the credit and the benefit of exemption cannot be denied.

In view of the above reasoning, the Tribunal held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are not applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. In other words, it is equivalent to reversal of credit on inputs. Therefore, according to Tribunal, the appellant had satisfied the requirement of not taking Modvat Credit on the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Their case is specifically covered by rule 57CC as well as the decision of Supreme Court with regard to not availing of Modvat Credit on inputs in the case of Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. 6. The next question that arises is whether Cenvat Credit Rules and Service Tax Credit Rules would be applicable. Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules is reproduced below :

"Where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails of CENVAT CREDIT in respect of any inputs or input services, [***], and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, the manufacturer or provider of output service shall maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and take CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing output service on which service tax is payable."

7. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 provides that where output service provider does not maintain separate account, he has to follow the procedure or avail the options available under that Rule. But this rule is applicable only when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation when we examine rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity is not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions.

8. Then the question arises as to whether the appellant would be eligible for the full amount of service tax credit taken by them on input services can be used for payment of service on output service provided the input services have been used for providing the output services. No doubt there is no one to one correlation required. This is the reason why provisions have been made in Cenvat Credit Rules and Service Tax Credit Rules to cover such situations where an assessee is providing both exempted and taxable services. In cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both Central Excise Act as well as Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, we have a situation where an assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable goods and at the same time there is no provision to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that it is for the appellant to choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what would be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appears to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles is deducted and the balance only availed for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition is not against the law in view of the fact that there are several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal wherein a view has been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit.

9. I am conscious of the fact that the decision or the conclusion reached by me above is not what was proposed in the show-cause notice or what was desired by the appellants. But here I find that the procedure adopted by the department is also not correct and at the same time as per law assessee is not eligible for service tax paid on input services attributable to trading activity. Obviously, the only solution that could be thought of what has been discussed above. In view of the above discussion, the matter is remanded to the Original Adjudicating Authority before whom the appellants shall present the details relating to service tax paid on input services attributable to trading activity and other services separately and after verification if felt necessary, the adjudicating authority shall quantify the amount to be reversed or payable by the appellant. It is made clear that if the Original Adjudicating Authority is not satisfied with the report given by the appellants and proposes any revision, such revision shall be made only after giving an opportunity to the appellants.

Further, sub-rule (3)(c) of the above said rules reads as under : "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) and sub-rule (2), the manufacturer or the provider of output service opting not to maintain separate accounts shall follow either of the following conditions as applicable to him, namely :

The provider of output service shall utilize the credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services."

From the above-said provision, it is clear that where an output service provider is availing credit on inputs and input services and providing taxable as well as exempted services without opting to maintain separate account of inputs and input services received and used for the exempted services and refrains to avail Cenvat Credit on such inputs/input services, he has no other option but to use Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on the output services. Therefore, the intention of the law is, the assessee shall either maintain separate account of input and input services for exempted output services and not to avail Cenvat Credit thereon or to utilize Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the service tax payable on output services. Therefore, if the assessee decides to avail Cenvat Credit directly related to the taxable output services and utilizes the same fully for payment of service tax on output services and simultaneously avails Cenvat Credit on common inputs and input services without maintaining separate account and utilizing such credit only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable, it will defeat the intention of the legal provision which is explained in the example given below :

Let the input service credit availed on input services used exclusively for taxable output service is Rs. 10,000.

Common input services which are used partly for taxable and partly for exempted services, credit availed fully of Rs. 20,000.

Let service tax payable on the taxable output service be Rs. 50,000.

The correct way to utilize the Cenvat Credit for the above said situation would be 20% of Rs. 50,000, i.e., Rs. 10,000 which can be utilized out of the total credit of Rs. 30,000 (Rs. 10,000 related to the taxable output services and Rs. 20,000 credit on common input services used for taxable as well as exempted output service). Therefore, the balance amount, i.e., Rs. 50,000 minus Rs. 10,000 Cenvat Credit utilized = Rs. 40,000 has to be used as to be paid through TR-6 challan.

Had Cenvat Credit been utilized as explained in the query, the assessee can utilize the credit of Rs. 10,000 which is directly related to taxable output service plus another Rs. 10,000 i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 service tax payable on output service = Rs. 20,000 and the balance amount of Rs. 30,000 would have been paid through TR-6 challan.

However, it may be noted that the provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, do not provide for more than one set of Cenvat Credit record for input service credit i.e. one for the input service credit related to taxable output service and second common input services credit account which are partly used for taxable output service and party for exempted services nor this sort of arrangement is prohibited, but considering the practice followed under Central Excise, I am of the opinion, that under above stated example, the assessee can avail total credit on Rs. 30,000 (10,000 + 20,000), but utilization will be restricted to 10% of service tax payable i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 = Rs. 10,000 and balance amount of Cenvat Credit unutilized (Rs. 30,000 total Cenvat Credit minus Rs. 10,000 credit utilized = Rs. 20,000) will be carried forward to the next month. It is further clarified that the law does not restrict the assessee to take Cenvat Credit on common input service only to the extent of 20% of service tax paid.

In the above said example the common input service credit of entire Rs. 20,000 can be availed and it is not restricted for availment of credit upto 20% of Rs. 20,000 i.e. Rs. 4,000.

Opinion : In short, if the assessee does not opt for separate account as envisaged under Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, he can avail the credit on the common inputs services fully but he can utilize the total credit available at the end of the month not exceeding 20% of service tax payable.

When the expenditure/payment does not relate to the assessee, merely because the assessee has made payments on behalf of its client would not attract the liability of deduction of tax on the assessee. More so, when the assessee has not claimed such payments as expenditure by debiting to its Profit & Loss account. When the payments were made by the assessee on behalf of the importer and subsequently the assessee has raised bills for such payments on actual basis apart from separate bills raised for agency commission and it is evident that importers have reimbursed such expenditure to the assessee on actual basis and has also separately paid agency commission as per the bills raised, the payment to CFS/ICD logically has to be treated as expenditure of importers and not the assessee. Therefore, as a natural corollary if there was any default in deduction of tax on such payments, made to the CFS/ICDs, the liability should be on the person claiming the payment as expenditure. The assessee having never claimed these payments as expenditure, provisions of section 40(a)(ia) are not attracted. Even otherwise also, if the entire issue is looked at rationally and dispassionately it is to be noticed that during the relevant previous year, assessee has earned gross commission income of Rs. 83,47,952, which has been shown in the Profit & Loss account and the Assessing Officer has also not disputed the income shown by the assessee. 4. Rule 5 enunciates the taxability or otherwise of any expenditure incurred by a service provider in the course of providing a service, as part of taxable value. The position is briefly stated as under :

(1)All expenditure or costs incurred by the service provider in the course of providing a taxable service forms an integral part of the taxable value, irrespective of whether separately indicated in the invoice or bill issued by the service provider to his client.

(2)Expenditure or cost incurred by a service provider as a pure agent of his client (generally known as reimbursable expenditure) is not includible in the taxable value.

(3)However, if the service provider acts as an undisclosed agent, i.e., acting in his own name without disclosing that he is actually acting as an agent of his client, he cannot claim the expenditure incurred by him as reimbursable expenditure.

Meaning of various terms relevant for computing refund of the Cenvat credit: Whether a service provider who is engaged in providing only exempted service can claim Cenvat credit?

No Cenvat credit is available on inputs and input services which are used in providing output services which are exempt from levy of service tax [Refer to Rule 6(1) of the Credit Rules]. It is, however, relevant to mention here that services which qualify as export of services as per Rule 6A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 do not fall within the definition of exempt services.

What are the Cenvat credit restrictions which apply to a service provider who is engaged in providing both taxable and exempt services?

As per Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, a service provider of both exempt and taxable services shall have following two options for claiming the Cenvat credit on inputs and input services:

Option A [Rule 6(2)] – Maintenance of separate records - The service provider shall maintain separate accounts for receipts, consumption/use and inventory of inputs and input services which are used in providing services other than exempted services. The Cenvat credit shall be available only on those inputs and input services which are used for provision of output services, excluding exempted services.

Option B [Rule 6(3)] – Non maintenance of separate records - Where a service provider opts for not maintaining separate records, the Cenvat credit can be paid under any of the following three methods:

pay an amount equal to 6% of the value of exempted services;

pay an amount equal to the Cenvat credit on inputs and input services attributable to exempted services, as determined under sub-rule (3A) of Rule 6; or

maintain separate accounts for the receipt, consumption, inventory of inputs and take the Cenvat credit only on inputs used for the provision of output services, excluding exempted services and pay an amount equal to the Cenvat credit on input services attributable to the exempted services as determined under sub-rule (3A) of Rule 6.

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Credit of whole service tax paid on taxable services specified in rule 6(5)

4.17 The assessee was a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. The assessee utilized service tax credit for exempted as well as non-exempted category of services provided to it. The revenue denied credit on ground that the assessee had not maintained separate records for services received by it for exempted and for non-exempted categories and, therefore, in terms of rule 6(3)(c ), the assessee was entitled to utilize only 20 per cent of amount of credit. The revenue filed an appeal aggrieved by the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) on the ground that the Commissioner (Appeals) has not considered the provisions of the Cenvat Credit Rules 6(3) and 6(5). The adjudicating authority after examining in depth rule 6(5) has said that it is clear that a service provider, who provides taxable and exempted services, shall be allowed, credit of the whole of service tax paid on taxable services specified in the said rule 6(5) unless the said service is exclusively used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or providing exempted services although no separate amounts for receipt/consumption of the input services are maintained. In rule 6(5) the important word is ‘notwithstanding’. The very use of this word means that rule 6(3) is not applicable to the input services mentioned under rule 6(5). The credit which has been taken by the party is on some of the 17 services, which are covered under rule 6(5) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. This rule does not talk about taking or utilization, so the credit is allowed to both taken and utilized services.

The Tribunal held that impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is correct and does not suffer from any infirmity.

u Exclusive usage of services for manufacture of exempted goods or providing exempted services: No credit is allowed.

In the case of GOI v. Indian Tobacco Association (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that "the word "substitute" ordinarily would mean "to put (one) in place of another"; or "to replace". In Black's Law Dictionary, Fifth Edition, at page 1281, the word "substitute" has been defined to mean "To put in the place of another person or thing", or "to exchange". In Collins English Dictionary, the word "substitute" has been defined to mean "to serve or cause to serve in place of another person or thing"; "to replace (an atom or group in a molecule) with (another atom or group)"; or "a person or thing that serves in place of another, such as a player in a game who takes the place of an injured colleague". By the reason of the amendment, no substantive right has been taken away nor any penal consequence has been imposed. Only an obvious mistake was sought to be removed thereby." As per this interpretation of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the sub-rule (3A) being substitution shall have a retrospective effect and will be applicable for all time since when the Rule was enacted. Therefore, for this reason also, for the purpose of calculation of Cenvat credit reversal, in the formula, total Cenvat credit shall mean credit of only common input service and not of input service exclusively used for the manufacture of dutiable product on which the Cenvat credit is eligible to the respondent in its entirety.

Rule 6(1) of the Rules curtails the service provider from availing Cenvat credit on input services used for exempted services. This clearly means that credit is allowed to be taken only on input services pertaining to taxable services. In other words, wherever exempted services are rendered, the credit pertaining to such exempted service is not admissible and is required to be reversed. Rule 6(2) provides that wherever exempted service is rendered, then such service provider has to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of various input services used for rendering such service and that Cenvat credit should be availed only in respect of input services used in rendering taxable service. Rule 6(3) provides an elaborate procedure for reversal of credit on a proportionate basis in respect of those service providers opting not to maintain separate accounts. Rule 6(3A) provides for a procedure for calculating proportionate credit admissible to an assessee. A service provider can avail the entire credit of input services and at the end of every month reverse a provisional amount of credit based on the preceding financial year's turnover for different services, but at the end of the year, the service provider is required to calculate final credit based on the current year's actual turnover figures and make the adjustments. What transpires, therefore, is that in terms of Rule 6(3A), a provider of output service can take only proportionate credit that is attributable to the taxable service.

17. The dispute in the appeal is regarding the interpretation of the term total Cenvat credit provided in the formula in Rule 6(3A)(b)(ii). According to the Department, the total Cenvat credit should include even those services used exclusively in taxable services, including the common service while according to the appellant it should include only common input services and services used in exempted services and not the services used exclusively in rendering taxable output service.

18. It would be clear from a conjoint reading of sub-rules 6(1), (2) and (3) of Rule 6 that the total Cenvat credit for the purpose of formula under Rule 6(3A) is only total Cenvat credit of common input service and cannot include Cenvat credit on input service exclusively used for the manufacture of dutiable goods.

19. This position is also clear from the underlying object of the amendment made in Rule 6(3A) of the Rules by Notification dated March 1, 2016, to consider only common input services and not total input service credit, for the purpose of computing the amount of reversal.

20. Such amendment was also clarified by the Tax Research Unit Circular dated February 29, 2016 to apply retrospectively inasmuch as the clarification clearly mentions that the provisions of Rule 6 providing for reversal of credit in respect of input services used in exempted services, is being redrafted with the objective to simplify and rationalize the same without altering the established principles of reversal of such credit. It has been further clarified at paragraph (iv) of the Circular that the purpose of the rule is to deny credit of such part of the total credit taken, as is attributable to the exempted services and under no circumstances this part can be greater than the whole credit.

As per the provisions of the new rule 6(3), when the manufacturer or service provider opts not to maintain separate books of account and still wants to avail credit on input and input services, he has been provided with two options : The choice of option for goods and services has to be consistent and it is not open to the assessee to opt for option 1 for goods and option 2 for services or vice versa. Further, rule 6(3) provides for certain common clauses for both the options, which are as follows :

(i)The assessee may opt for either of the option and would have to continue with that option for the rest of the financial year.

(ii)Rule specifically disallows the credit on inputs and input services used for the manufacture of exempted goods or for the provision of exempted services.

(iii)The term ‘Value’ for the purpose of sub-rules (3) and (3A) shall have the same meaning assigned to it under section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994 read with rules made thereunder or, as the case may be, the value determined under section 4 or 4A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 read with rules made thereunder.

(iv)The sub-rule also clarifies that the amount mentioned above can be paid either by utilizing Cenvat credit or by cash.

Having said this, the specific provisions in respect of each option are as follows:

u Mode of Computation : Option 1

Option 1 provides that the assessee would pay service tax at the rate of 8 per cent of value of the exempted services and 10 per cent of value of the exempted goods.

For example value of taxable services and exempt services provided by Mr. X from Delhi office is Rs. 1 lakh and Rs. 50,000, respectively. Thus, Mr. X if opting for option 1, he would pay Rs. 4,000 as service tax on exempt service and avail whole of the credit which is attributable to the taxable service or is common to both, taxable as well as exempt services.

u Mode of Computation : Option 2

If the assessee opts for option 2, he would have to pay an amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to inputs and input services used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted goods or for provision of exempted services subject to the conditions and procedure specified in sub-rule (3A). Accordingly, the rule has called for the payment of Cenvat credit attributable to exempted goods/services.

If the assessee wants to opt for this option, he would have to inform his Superintendent of Central Excise with certain factual information as prescribed in rule 6(3A).

The statute has provided that the computation of the Cenvat credit would be made in accordance with rule 6(3A). Rule 6(3A) provides that the assessee would first determine the payment on account of such Cenvat credit provisionally on a monthly/quarterly basis and then would determine the final liability before 30th of succeeding year and pay accordingly.

u Mode of Provisional Payment: to be computed on monthly/quarterly basis

Provisional payment of Cenvat credit attributable to exempted goods/services = (i) + (ii), where,

‘(i )’denotes the payment of Cenvat Credit on inputs attributable to exempted services during the month and;

‘(ii )’denotes the payment of Cenvat Credit on input services attributable to exempted goods/services during the month.

Further, the rule has provided the formula for the payment of Cenvat Credit on inputs attributable to exempted services during the month which is as follows :

Total value of Cenvat credit taken on inputs less input attributable to the manufacture of exempted goods multiplied by value of exempted services provided during the preceding financial year divided by total value of dutiable goods, taxable services and exempted services provided during the last financial year.

Similarly, for the purpose of calculating the payment of Cenvat Credit on input services attributable to exempted services during the month which is as follows :

Total value of Cenvat credit taken on input services multiplied by value of all exempted goods/service produced or provided during the preceding financial year divided by Total Value of dutiable goods, taxable services and exempted goods and services provided during the last financial year.

This calculation has to be made for all the months/quarter and tax has to be paid, accordingly, before the corresponding due date.

u Mode of Final Payment: to be computed on yearly basis

For the calculation of Cenvat credit attributable to exempted goods/services for the financial year, the above formula is same only with the difference that in place of figures of preceding year, the figures of financial year for which the calculation is being done would be substituted.

For execution of such contracts the appellant-company uses goods which are manufactured by it and also goods manufactured from other manufacturers.

no service tax is paid for the value of material supplied. In respect of Civil Construction they were paying tax on 33% of the consideration received availing benefit of Notification 1/2006-S.T. They were paying tax on the consideration received for Erection and Commissioning.

3. For procuring such contracts the appellant uses the services of Commission Agents. This commission is paid on the full value of contracts that is for both material value and service value. Insurance premiums are also paid for the full value of the contracts.

4. The dispute involved in this case is whether the appellant is eligible to take credit for the full amount of tax paid on the commission paid to the Agents and for the full amount of tax paid on insurance premium paid. While the appellant claims that they should be allowed to take credit of the full amounts of such taxes paid, the Revenue contests that the commission paid should be split into that relating to procurement of goods and that relating to services by dividing the total commission and insurance premium in the ratio of value of materials supplied and value of services rendered and credit should be allowed only on service tax paid on commission and insurance relatable to value of services. Since the appellant had taken credit for full amounts of taxes the Revenue has issued a show cause notice dated 26-6-2008 demanding the excess credit taken which stands confirmed along with interest and penalties. The tax amount so demanded is Rs. 1,32,69,499/- for the period April, 2006 to Dec., 2007.

5. The Counsel for the appellant argues that valuation for the purpose of charging tax and allowing credit are two different issues and the Revenue has made a mistake by seeing the latter in the context of the former. They argue that they are eligible for exemption under Notification 12/2003-S.T., dated 20-6-2003 for the value of the project corresponding to the value of materials supplied and that should not be reason to deny credit in relation to tax paid on services relating to procurement of materials because procurement of materials is a necessary input service for erection and commissioning.

6. The Counsel for appellants also contest the demand on grounds of limitation. They contend that credit taken was declared in their ST-3 return and therefore there is no ground for invoking extended period of limitation.

7. The Revenue on the other hand submits that the appellant had two distinct contracts with their clients for supply of materials and for Erection and Commissioning. Just because commission and insurance premium are paid on the sum of the values of the two contracts it does not mean that services for executing the first contract is input service for executing the second contract.

8. We have considered arguments on both sides.

9. The matter is contentious. Under Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules credit can be taken only on tax paid on any input service received by a provider of output services. (For sake of clarity the portion of the rule dealing with inputs, excise duty thereon and final products is not being discussed since that situation is not dealt with here). Output service itself is defined under Rule 2(p) as a taxable service. When the contract for supply of material is a separate contract the service used for executing the contract cannot be considered as used in providing output service. A reading of the provisions of Rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules along with Rule 3 prima facie suggests strength in the stand of the department.

10. However the objection of the appellant that extended period of time cannot be invoked in this case prima facie is in appellant’s favour because the details of credit taken were being reported in ST-3 returns. We note that the demand which is within the period of one year is about Rs. Thirty lakhs. Having regard to this we order that the appellant should deposit an amount of Rs. 30 lakhs within eight weeks of receipt of this order for admission of the appeal. Subject to such deposit the balance dues arising out of the impugned order shall be waived and there shall be stay on collection of such amounts during the pendency of the appeal. Sr. Advocate is that the said explanation only provides that procedure for computation and since this change is procedural in nature it will have a retrospective effect. Ld. Sr. Advocate also argued that in case of traded goods, the value addition by the appellant is only the difference between the sale price and the purchase price of the goods which is not so in the case of manufactured goods. On a query by the Bench that since Ld. Sr. Advocate is arguing that only the value addition should be taken in respect of the traded goods, then why the same criteria should not be applied in the case of manufactured goods i.e. take the differential amount between the selling price and cost of various raw materials. Sr. Advocate stated that in case of manufactured goods so many things go into production process like labour, electricity and many other services and it will not be appropriate to take the value addition. In support of his contention that in case of traded goods only value addition should be taken, Ld. Sr. Advocate took us through the judgment of the Court (5th Chamber) dated 14-7-1998 in case C-172/96 which was passed on a reference under Article 177 of the EC Treaty by the High Court of Justice of England and Wales, Queen's Bench Division. We have gone through the said judgment carefully. In the said case, the issue was how to determine the turnover for purpose of value added tax in case of transactions in different currencies by the First National Bank of Chicago. The Bank used to purchase various currencies at a certain rate in other currencies. Similarly, the Bank used to sell various currencies in other currencies. The difference between the two is generally understood as spread and would be the income of the Bank. The question was what should be considered as the turnover for purpose of VAT. It is in that context, the said court has held that the spread the difference between the selling price and purchase price should be taken for the purpose of VAT. In the present case, the dispute is not relating to computation of turnover for purpose of charging a tax as there is no tax liability in case of traded goods. The question is how to apportion the credit of tax on the input service between the manufactured goods and the traded goods, whether we should take the turner of the manufactured goods and traded goods for apportioning the credit of the service tax on input services or some other criteria should be followed. We, therefore, do not find any applicability whatsoever of the said judgment in the facts and circumstances of the present case. Another judgment quoted by the Ld. Sr. Advocate is the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Meerut V. Sharvan Kumar Swarup & Sons reported in (1994) 6 SCC 623. In this case, wealth-tax was applicable on various assets. A new rule was inserted with effect from 1-4-1979 to determine the market value of properties. The question was whether the new inserted rule can be used for determining the value of properties for earlier period and hence determine the wealth-tax. It is in this context that the Hon'ble Supreme Court has taken a view that the same would be applicable to all the proceedings pending at the time of its enactment. In the present case, as mentioned earlier, it is not the computation of tax but apportionment of the credit of service tax on input services availed for manufactured goods and traded goods. As we have already held that trading was not a service and therefore cannot be considered as an exempted service before 1-4-2011, therefore, the substantive provision itself did not exist before the said date. Under the circumstances, we are of the view that the said judgment is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case."

In terms of sub-section (2) of section 4, which is the charging section, in respect of income chargeable under sub-section (1), income tax shall be deducted at source or paid in advance, where it is so deductible or payable under any provision of this Act.

Thus, it is clear that tax is to be deducted only where element of income is a part of payment and since reimbursement of expenses does not constitute trading receipts or has any element of income therein, TDS is not liable to be made from reimbursements.

When a C&F agent incurs expenses like custom duty, port dues, and other sundry charges, he is merely acting as a front man of his client and on his behalf. These expenses do not normally have any nexus with the commission he is supposed to earn for his work. [Para 6.4.1]

In the case on hand, as pointed out by the Commissioner (Appeals), the expenses have been incurred by the C&F Agents on behalf of the assessee, the claims were made on actual basis and the amounts were separately shown with proper evidence.

The fact that the reimbursement of expenses have been separately billed, in the case on hand, is not disputed. The C&F Agents are appointed to provide the service of carrying out sales for which they are paid service charges on which TDS has been made and not for the purpose of incurring expenses on behalf of the assessee.

In this view of the matter, the reimbursement of expenses by C&F Agents cannot be held to be contract/service on which the provisions of section 194C of the Act would come into play and apply.

In view of the factual position as laid out above, it is held that there is no need to deduct TDS on reimbursement of expenses to C&F Agents which are separately billed and accordingly the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is upheld. [Para 6.4.3]

Decision in the case of National Engineering Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 21 STT 188 (New Delhi - CESTAT) 4.2 The assessee was an agent of a foreign company, i.e., GMC. It procured orders/contracts from Indian Railways for GMC and received commission on which service tax had been paid under the category of ‘Business auxiliary services’. The commission, however, was not received directly from GMC, but was received through Indian Railways in Indian currency. As per understanding between GMC and Indian Railways, GMC received payment from Indian Railways after deducting the commission payable to the assessee. The assessee filed refund claim on the ground that the services provided by it to GMC on which service tax had been paid were export of services in terms of rule 3(3). The Assistant Commissioner rejected the refund claim on the ground that since the commission was received in non-convertible Indian currency, in view of the proviso to sub-rule (3) of rule 3, same could not be treated as export of services. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assistant Commissioner. The appellant pleaded that when the Business Auxiliary Service, taxable under section 65(105)(zzb ) of the Finance Act, 1994 is provided by a service provider in India to a recipient located outside India and service is used in or in relation to commerce or industry of the recipient, the same has to be treated as export of the service in terms of sub-rule (3) of rule 3 of Export of Services Rules, 2005. That the conditions (a), (b) and (c) of the proviso to sub-rule (3) are applicable only in a situation where the service recipient abroad has any commercial or industrial establishment or any office relating thereto, in India, and only in such a situation the conditions mentioned in clauses (a ), (b) and (c) of the proviso have to be satisfied. One of such condition being that the payment for such service is received by the service provider in convertible foreign exchange; that GMC, did not have any commercial establishment or office in India and therefore, the proviso to sub-rule (3) of rule 3 was not applicable; that in view of this, the business auxiliary service provided by the appellant to GMC had to be treated as service export and, therefore, no service tax was payable in respect of services and the appellant was eligible of the refund of the service tax paid by it.

The Tribunal held that just because commission was received by the appellant through Indian Railways in Indian Rupees as Indian Railways made payment to GMC in foreign currency after deducting the commission payable to GMC, it could not be said that the service provided by the appellant to GMC, USA was not export of service under rule 3(3) of the Export of Services Rules and, therefore, the appellants were held eligible for refund of the service tax paid on such service exported to GMC, USA.

The Tribunal further held that in the case of ETA Travel Agency (P.) Ltd. (supra) cited by Ld. DR, the offshore service receiver had an office in India and the commission had been received from the bank account of such local office of the offshore service receiver and in view of the facts of the case, the Tribunal held that the service had been provided and received in India and it was not a case of export of service. Therefore, as per Tribunal, this judgment of the Tribunal was not applicable to the facts of this case and, therefore, the Tribunal held that the service provided by the appellant to GMC, USA had to be treated as ‘export of service’ under rule 3(3) of the Export of Services Rules. The Tribunal also followed the decision of National Engg. Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 17 STT 398 (New Delhi - CESTAT), given in the appellant’s own case even the reasoning were different.

Rule 37BA envisages allowance of TDS credit in proportion to the income declared by the assessee. This proportion needs to be established for every nature of receipt on which TDS has been claimed by the assessee. Therefore, while allowing TDS claimed under each section, it has to be ascertained that entire income on which TDS has been claimed is duly offered in the ITR by the assessee and in case the income so declared for each nature of receipt on which TDS has been claimed is lesser than that appearing in Form No. 26AS then only CPC may deny the credit of TDS for relevant nature of receipt. Since the receipts of interest and commission on which TDS has been claimed under sections 194A and 194H are fully declared in ITR, the entire TDS claimed under sections 194A and 194H needs to be fully allowed. Hence the proportionate TDS disallowed is absolutely unjustified and, therefore, deserves to be allowed. [Para 2.6]

■

As regards the disallowance of TDS credit under section 194Q is concerned, the Bench found that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia. Therefore, the turnover on which tax is deducted under section 194Q is not the turnover of the assessee. Hence has rightly not been shown as such by the assessee. Moreover a Kachha Arhatia acts only as an agent for his constituent and never acts as principal. Therefore, the remuneration of Kachha Arhatia consists solely of commission and he has no control on the profit and losses made by his constituents.

■

The assessee has drawn attention of the Bench to sample invoices on which TDS was deducted under section 194Q by the principal buyer and the corresponding vikray parchi issued by the Mandi to the respective farmers. These documents clearly show that the amount invoiced by the assessee to the principal buyer and the value of goods transferred by assessee to the farmer is exactly the same. Therefore, turnover of the Kachha Arhatia is merely the commission paid by principal buyer on which the principal buyer deducts TDS under section 194H and which has been duly shown as income in the ITR by the assessee. Therefore, the TDS deducted by such principle buyers by virtue of provisions of section 194Q is eligible to be claimed by the Kachha Arhatia in his ITR on the grounds that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia and is duly registered as such with the Mandi. Perusal of the vikray parchi issued at the Mandi to the farmers and the corresponding invoice raised by the assessee to the principal buyer undoubtedly establishes the fact that the assessee has no control or margin in the sale facilitated by him and earns merely commission from such transactions.

■

The assessee has no domain over the goods sold to the principle buyers. As clarified by Central Board of Direct Taxes in its Circular No. 452 of 1986), so far as Kachha Arhatias are concerned the turnover does not include the sales effected on behalf of principals and only commission (gross) has to be considered for the purpose of income tax. Therefore, TDS deducted under section 194Q by the principle buyers cannot be refused by invoking rule 37BA read with section 199.

■

As the sale facilitated by the assessee for the farmers is not the turnover of the assessee and the income from such transaction (commission) being duly offered for tax by the assessee in his ITR, the TDS deducted both under sections 194H and 194Q deserves to be fully allowed. Further the Form No. 26AS also depicts that the invoices on which TDS has been deducted under section 194Q also has TDS deducted under section 194H. Thus the contention of the assessee that he is merely a Kachha Arhatia is potrayed beyond all doubts and needs to be accepted.

■

Therefore, the Assessing Officer is to be directed to allow TDS claimed under section 194Q by the assessee. [Para 2.7]

Certain identified issues in Rule 6(3) and 6(3A):

6. Though the issues are numerous which still need clarity since the statute is still in its nascent stage, some of the identified issues are as under :

(i) Rule 6(3), Opt in - your choice, Opt out - no choice during the financial year

The sub-rule clarifies that an option would be exercisable both in the case of goods and services as manufactured or provided by the assessee. He cannot opt for Option 1 for goods and option 2 for services or vice versa. Also, exercise of such option cannot be withdrawn at any point of time during the financial year. He may change his option from the next year onwards. Thus, though the choice of opting in for the non-maintenance of separate books of account is open during the financial year, yet the option to opt out of it is unavailable to the manufacturer of service provider for that financial year.

(ii) Meaning of the term - ‘exempt’

The sub-rule does not define the term ‘exempt’ for the purpose of this sub-rule. Technically speaking, exempted goods/services are a sub-set of taxable goods/services. Exempted goods/services are specified by a notification by the Central Government and, accordingly, no duty/tax is leviable on them. However, there are other goods or services which are non-taxable and cannot be called ‘exempt’ technically. For example services of an advocate.

Having said this, the interpretation of the term ‘exempt’ is important for the calculation of duty/tax in respect of the Cenvat credit attributable towards exempted goods/services. Thus, extension of the term ‘exempt’ on non-taxable goods/services or otherwise would change the entire computation. For example when a provider of taxable services is providing exempt services and also is engaged in trading of goods (non-taxable), whether he needs to pay an amount equal to Cenvat credit attributable towards trading activity also, as he has to do in the case of exempt services. The answer is in affirmative when we equate trading to an exempt service and not otherwise.

Further, a larger question would be whether in case of an assessee engaged in the provision of taxable service and non-taxable service, would the computation under rule 6(3A) be applicable on him ? The question would be answered as ‘YES’ when non-taxable is equated as ‘exempt’ otherwise the answer is ‘NO’.

The more logical calculation would be to take out the Cenvat credit attributable towards non-taxable activities and then apply rule 6(3) on the balance Cenvat credit. Thus, the assessee should avail only the credit excluding that which is attributable towards non-taxable activities.

(iii) Choice of option - whether premises-wise or assessee-wise

Further, another point worth mentioning here is that the term used by the statute for availment of choice is manufacturer/service provider and not premises of manufacturer (factory) or service provider. Even the definition of ‘manufacturer’ under central excise uses the word ‘person’ and not ‘factory’. Accordingly, one school of thought might interpret that the availment of the options above should be same throughout all locations across India and the option cannot be availed of differently for different premises.

Expressing it with an example, Mr. X is a service provider having offices in Delhi, Mumbai and Pune, all three offices being separately registered with service tax department. Mr. X is providing taxable services under the category of ‘chartered accountant services’ and also availing the exemption provided thereunder. Thus, he is the provider of both taxable as well as exempt services. Now, the question is whether he can opt for option I for his Delhi and Mumbai offices and option II for Pune or will he have to opt for a single option for all his offices since the sub-rule uses the words ‘service provider’ when offering the choice.

Rule 6 speaks about obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) of rule 6 states that cenvat credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input or input services which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or for providing exempted services. Sub-rule (2) of rule 6 states that in case the manufacture or service provider uses common inputs/input services, then such manufacturer or service provider has to maintain separate accounts and credit is to be taken only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for manufacture of dutiable goods or providing taxable services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 speaks about the situation when such manufacturer or service provider does not maintain separate accounts. It provides for two options. It was amended vide Notification No. 10/2008-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2008 with effect from 1-4-2008. As per the new sub-rule (3) of rule 6, the manufacturer/service provider opting not to maintain separate account has to follow either of the following two options:-

A manufacturer shall pay 10 per cent (5 per cent with effect from 7-7-2009) of sale price of the exempted goods and an output service provider shall pay 8 per cent (6 per cent with effect from 7-7-2009) of the value of the exempted services; or

Reverse the credit on inputs and input services pertaining to exempted goods and exempted services as per the procedure and conditions prescribed in rule 6(3A). [Para 5]

The rule 6(3A) states that while exercising the option, the manufacturer of goods or the provider of output service shall intimate in writing the department regarding the option exercised. In the instant case, admittedly there is no intimation given by the assessee informing its exercise of option. The contention of the department is that when the assessee has not intimated its option in writing then the assessee is bound to pay the duty amount calculated under the first option. The said rule does not say that on failure to intimate, the manufacturer/service provider would lose his choice to avail second option of reversing the proportionate credit. Rule 6(3A) is nothing but a procedure contemplated for application of rule 6(3). Therefore, the argument of the revenue that the requirement to intimate the department about the option exercised is mandatory and on failure the assessee has no other option but to accept and comply rule 6(3)(i) and make payment of 5 per cent/10 per cent of sale price of exempted goods/value of exempted services is not acceptable or convincing. The rule 6(3A) does not lay down any such restriction. The procedure and conditions laid in rule 6(3A) is intended to make rule 6(3)workable and not to take away the option available to the assessee. In any case, at no stretch of imagination can it be said that on failure to intimate the department, rule 6(3)(i) would automatically come into application. [Para 6]

Therefore, the impugned demand raised against the assessee was not legal and proper. [Para 7]

It is found that, once the assessee is operating as a commission agent, then the income of the assessee is net commission income received from the farmers, but not the total sales value of the farmers. Since the law provides for TDS under section 194Q on total sales value, and further, the assessee has raised sales invoices in its name, the traders have deducted TDS on the entire sales value, but the fact remains that, the assessee has considered the total income accrued on the total sales value being commission received from the farmers, as its income.
