It cannot be said that the commission that the air travel agents get from the airlines is independent of and distinct from the services that they provide to the air-travellers and is relatable to the business that they provide to the airlines. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle was cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case was gone.

From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l), the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided that it is made taxable. Therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. It may also be said that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air travellers. If in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-travellers. On the other hand, it may be said that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited. The tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the petitioners that because of section 67(k), the nature of the tax itself changes was incorrect. Section 67(k), which provides the ‘measure of the tax’, is not unconnected with the main levy of the tax. The provision of section 67(k ) does not in any manner alter the nature of tax and does not shift it from the service rendered to the customer to the service rendered to the airlines. The contention, therefore, was clearly incorrect on facts.

The further argument that the notification dated 26-6-1997 restricts the tax to the commission alone and is repugnant to the scheme of the tax was obviously incorrect. The basis of the argument that the commission received from the airlines by the air travel agent is taken a measure for imposing a levy on a different service rendered to the customer by the agent, was itself incorrect. Therefore, the argument that the impugned provision of section 67(k) is repugnant to the general scheme of the Act was to be rejected.

As far as the second contention of the petitioner with regard to rule 6(7) was concerned, the language of rule 6(7) itself suggests that it is an optional matter. Therefore, the members of the petitioner-association, who had not exercised the option would had no concern with the validity of that rule while those who had opted for it, and majority of them having done so, could also not challenge the said validity.

In fact, it was not necessary for the High Court to take stock of the petitioners’ contention regarding the unconstitutionality of the rules but, even otherwise, there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found with that rule much less in the light of the submission made by the petitioners. The High Court was in complete agreement with the department that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration section 93 and section 94(2)(a) jointly. Indeed, there is a specific power under section 93 to grant exemption in any manner. Section 94(2)(a) speaks of the rule-making power on the subject of collection and recovery of service tax under section 66 and section 68. What is suggested by rule 6(7) is nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations. It was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule- making power. It does not amount to an independent levy again. Therefore, it was to be held that there was nothing wrong with the rule in question. This rule provides for an independent measure as the basic airfare. For this reason, no merit was found in the writ which was liable to be dismissed.

It cannot be said that the commission that the air travel agents get from the airlines is independent of and distinct from the services that they provide to the air-travellers and is relatable to the business that they provide to the airlines. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle was cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case was gone.

From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l),the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided that it is made taxable. Therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. It may also be said that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air travellers. If in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-travellers. On the other hand, it may be said that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited. The tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the petitioners that because of section 67(k ), the nature of the tax itself changes was incorrect. Section 67(k), which provides the ‘measure of the tax’, is not unconnected with the main levy of the tax. The provision of section 67(k ) does not in any manner alter the nature of tax and does not shift it from the service rendered to the customer to the service rendered to the airlines. The contention, therefore, was clearly incorrect on facts.

The further argument that the notification dated 26-6-1997 restricts the tax to the commission alone and is repugnant to the scheme of the tax was obviously incorrect. The basis of the argument that the commission received from the airlines by the air travel agent is taken a measure for imposing a levy on a different service rendered to the customer by the agent, was itself incorrect. Therefore, the argument that the impugned provision of section 67(k) is repugnant to the general scheme of the Act was to be rejected.

As far as the second contention of the petitioner with regard to rule 6(7) was concerned, the language of rule 6(7) itself suggests that it is an optional matter. Therefore, the members of the petitioner-association, who had not exercised the option would had no concern with the validity of that rule while those who had opted for it, and majority of them having done so, could also not challenge the said validity.

In fact, it was not necessary for the High Court to take stock of the petitioners’ contention regarding the unconstitutionality of the rules but, even otherwise, there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found with that rule much less in the light of the submission made by the petitioners. The High Court was in complete agreement with the department that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration section 93 and section 94(2)(a ) jointly. Indeed, there is a specific power under section 93 to grant exemption in any manner. Section 94(2)(a) speaks of the rule-making power on the subject of collection and recovery of service tax under section 66 and section 68. What is suggested by rule 6(7) is nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations. It was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule-making power. It does not amount to an independent levy again. Therefore, it was to be held that there was nothing wrong with the rule in question. This rule provides for an independent measure as the basic airfare. For this reason, no merit was found in the writ which was liable to be dismissed.

Tax on commission and also on reimbursable expenses like godown rent, loading/unloading, freight, telephone, rent, salary etc.

The assessee had been authorised different parties of Northern India to purchase rubber on their behalf. As per the terms and conditions of these agreement, the assessee had been appointed as buying agent for the purchase of rubber and other commodities in the State of Kerala on behalf of the respective parties. It was also stipulated that purchase would be made on behalf of principals and despatched to them. The principals, agreed to give commission of 1 per cent of the purchase price besides the reimbursement of expenses incurred for the purpose of purchasing rubber and other commodities. The assessee was buying rubber and latex from the agricultures from Keral for and on behalf of its principal as their agent. The dealings in rubber are controlled by the Rubber Board. The Rubber Board had also intimated the principals that the assessee had been recognised as their agent to purchase and despatch rubber on their behalf.

The CBDT in Circular No. 452, dated 17-3-1987 has laid down the principles of distinction between kutcha arhatiya and pucca arhatiya. On a perusal of distinctions between kutcha arhatiya and pucca arhativa as enumerated in the above circular and further illustrations given by the CBDT Circular Nos. 564&572, dated 5-7-1990 respectively wherein it has been made clear that turnover and sales are interchangeable and sole reliance cannot be placed on the definition of ‘turnover’ under section 2(o ) of the Haryana General Sales-tax Act, the contrary definition as contained in the Central Sales-tax Act cannot be ignored Since the assessee was receiving commission @1% of purchase value besides reimbursement of expenses incurred for the purposes of purchase and if the Assessing Officer’s contention was accepted that the assessee was trading in these items, there was no question of receiving fixed commission and there should, in fact, be bearing of profit or loss in each separate transaction depending on market conditions but this was not the case of the assessing authority nor it was borne out from the record. The Assessing Officer had not worked out the profit as such earned by the assessee from trading in rubber and latex. Therefore, taking into consideration the facts that the Rubber Board had registered the assessee as an authorised agent to purchase and despatch rubber on behalf of different principals no sales as such had been effected by the assessee, the goods purchased were transferred to the principals at the cost price, the goods were transferred not against ‘C Form’ but against ‘F From’ of sales tax issued by the transferee, the commission agency agreement between the principals and the assessee etc., the role of assessee was that of agent and not of trader. Secondly, according to the CBDT Circular Nos. 564&572 dated 5-7-1990. The turnover and sales are interchangeable and as the assessee had not made any sale rubber or latex, the total transaction conducted to earn commission would not be regarded as ‘sale’ or ‘turnover’ of the assessee. In view of the above facts and circumstances, for working out 80HHC deduction, it was the commission earned which was to be considered for working out the said deduction and not the aggregate transaction made to earn commission and, hence, no interference was needed with the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

9.11 Provisions upto 31-3-2008

Rule 6(3) has been radically changed w.e.f. 1-4-2008. Provisions upto 31-3-2008 are summarised below.

If assessee opts not to maintain separate accounts in respect of inputs and input services utilised for exempted goods/exempted output services as required under rule 6(2), he has to pay ‘amount’ of 10% of total price (excluding taxes) of exempted final product [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

In case of output services, he could utilise credit only upto 20% of service tax on output services. [He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services].

The third option i.e. proportionate reversal of Cenvat credit was not available upto 31-3-2008.

Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services — Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/output services and partly for exempted goods/services. In such cases, the manufacturer/service provider has two options — (a) Maintain separate inventory and accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services. In such cases, he should not avail Cenvat credit of the inputs and input services which are used in exempted final services at all — Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules (b) Pay 10% ‘amount’ if he does not maintain separate inventory and records, if he is a manufacturer — Rule 6(3)(b) [If he is service provider, his credit is restricted to 20% of tax payable, as explained later] [provision upto 31-3-2008]

‘Amount’ if separate inventory and records not maintained - If the manufacturer opts not to maintain such separate accounts, he has to pay an amount equal to 10% of the ‘price’ of such exempted goods. Such payment can be made by debit to Cenvat credit account or PLA [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

Reversal of Cenvat credit in case of some exempted goods - In case of some specified exempted goods, the manufacturer of these final products only has to reverse Cenvat credit they had taken on inputs and input services, which were used for manufacture of exempted final product. - Rule 6(3)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Cenvat credit on capital goods — If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and party for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products [rule 6(4)] — confirmed in Idea Cellular v. CCE (2009) 19 STT 423 = 36 VST 217 (CESTAT).

No reversal or payment of amount in certain cases — If excisable goods are removed to SEZ unit, SEZ developer, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting, payment of 10% ‘amount’ is not required [rule 6(6)].

Cenvat credit of service tax in case of supplies made by DTA to EOU - Supplies from DTA to EOU are entitled to Cenvat credit of service tax paid — para 6.11(v) of FTP.

Proportional Cenvat in case of general insurance companies providing taxable as well as exempt services - Rule 6(3)(d) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2007 provided an option to general insurance service providers providing taxable as well as exempted insurance schemes and who do not maintain separate input/input services credit accounts, to utilise Cenvat credit proportionate to the inputs and input services used in providing output services. The scheme was applicable only to general insurance services referred to in section 65(105)(d) and is optional - para 11.1 of D.O. F. No. 334/1/2007-TRU dated 28-2-2007 issued by Shri R Sekar, Joint Secretary (TRU). Now this specific provision has been deleted w.e.f. 1-4-2008.

The sales tax collections could be taken to be a trust fund in which the assessee had no interest. As a matter of fact the primary liability to pay sales tax on sales effected by the assessee was independent of the fact whether he collected sales tax from his buyers or not. The statute enabled the dealers to collect sales tax with a view to pass on their liability to their buyers. Therefore, if the sales tax collected by the assessee from his buyers during the year of account is in excess of his actual liability towards sales tax for that period, such excess would go only for his benefit. Therefore, the Tribunal was not correct in holding that the excess collections were not trading receipts of the assessee.

The decision of the Supreme Court in Chowringhee Sales Bureau (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1973] 87 ITR 542, fully supported the revenue’s stand that sales tax collections should be taken to be trading receipts and as and when the amounts are paid to discharge the sales tax liability, such amounts will have to be deducted.

So far as the separate accounts maintained by the assessee were concerned, they had been kept only on cash basis, that was, the sales tax collections made had been credited and the actual sales tax payments had been debited on the respective dates of collection and payment. Neither the sales tax collections nor the payments made by the assessee which had been recorded in the separated accounts had gone into the general accounts maintained by the assessee for his business, as the assessee had always been contending that he had been making collections as an agent of the Government and even the excess collection would have ultimately to be paid to the Government. In these separate accounts as and when the amounts had been paid to the sales tax authorities, they had been debited. An assessee may employ one method of accounting for one part of his business or one class of customers, and a different method for another part of his business or another class of customers. He may also keep accounts in respect of different parts of the same business on different basis. If such different methods are employed regularly and consistently the profits have to be computed in accordance with the respective methods, provided it results in a proper determination of the true profits. The assessee should, therefore, be taken to have adopted the cash basis so far as the sales tax collections were concerned and, therefore, the principle of the decision in Chowringhee Sales Bureau P. Ltd. v. CIT [1973] 87 ITR 542 (SC) would stand attracted. Therefore, it was held that the assessee had maintained his accounts in relation to the sales tax collections only on cash basis and, therefore, only when he pays out the amount for discharging his sales tax liability, he can claim deduction.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle was cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case was gone. From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l),the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided that it is made taxable. Therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. It may also be said that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air travellers. If in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-travellers. On the other hand, it may be said that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited. The tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the petitioners that because of section 67(k ), the nature of the tax itself changes was incorrect. Section 67(k), which provides the ‘measure of the tax’, is not unconnected with the main levy of the tax. The provision of section 67(k ) does not in any manner alter the nature of tax and does not shift it from the service rendered to the customer to the service rendered to the airlines. The contention, therefore, was clearly incorrect on facts.

The further argument that the notification dated 26-6-1997 restricts the tax to the commission alone and is repugnant to the scheme of the tax was obviously incorrect. The basis of the argument that the commission received from the airlines by the air travel agent is taken a measure for imposing a levy on a different service rendered to the customer by the agent, was itself incorrect. Therefore, the argument that the impugned provision of section 67(k) is repugnant to the general scheme of the Act was to be rejected.

As far as the second contention of the petitioner with regard to rule 6(7) was concerned, the language of rule 6(7) itself suggests that it is an optional matter. Therefore, the members of the petitioner-association, who had not exercised the option would had no concern with the validity of that rule while those who had opted for it, and majority of them having done so, could also not challenge the said validity.

In fact, it was not necessary for the High Court to take stock of the petitioners’ contention regarding the unconstitutionality of the rules but, even otherwise, there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found with that rule much less in the light of the submission made by the petitioners. The High Court was in complete agreement with the department that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration section 93 and section 94(2)(a ) jointly. Indeed, there is a specific power under section 93 to grant exemption in any manner. Section 94(2)(a) speaks of the rule-making power on the subject of collection and recovery of service tax under section 66 and section 68. What is suggested by rule 6(7) is nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations. It was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule-making power. It does not amount to an independent levy again. Therefore, it was to be held that there was nothing wrong with the rule in question. This rule provides for an independent measure as the basic airfare. For this reason, no merit was found in the writ which was liable to be dismissed.

On revenue's appeal:

Case law relating to specific services

22.4 Some case law relating to definition of 'input service' has become inapplicable after amendment to definition of 'input service' w.e.f. 1-4-2011. However, major part of case law is still relevant. The case law, which in my view is still relevant, is given below.

Services of Commission agent

22.4-1 There were disputes about eligibility of Cenvat credit on servicers provided by commission agent. Hence, following explanation has been added to rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, w.e.f. 3-2-2016 after sub-clause (C) -

Explanation - For the purpose of this clause, sales promotion includes services by way of sale of dutiable goods on commission basis.

The drafting of the explanation is faulty. Firstly, it is not clear what is meant by 'this clause', since firstly, any of sub-clauses (A), (B) and (C) of definition of 'input service' has no relation with 'sales commission'. Secondly, commission agent really never sales the goods. He only 'facilitates' sales. Thirdly, the explanation only refers to sale of dutiable goods. What about commission agents of services like hotels, travel of passengers, food etc.?

Be as it may, at least issue of eligibility of input service of commission agent of goods has been sorted out.

The explanation has retrospective effect - In Essar Steel India v. CCE (2016) 335 ELT 660 (CESTAT), it has been rightly held that this explanation is clarificatory in nature and has retrospective effect.

In my view, this decision is correct, for reasons stated below.

Right from beginning, department has consistently held (as per circulars/instructions discussed below) that input service of service tax paid by commission agents is eligible 'input service'. Tribunal and one High Court (Punjab and Haryana HC) have also consistently held the same view. Problems were created only because one adverse decision of Gujarat High Court in case of Cadila Healthcare delivered in year 2013.

Departmental circular - Para 5 of CBE&C circular No. 943/04/2011-CX, dated 29-4-2011 has specifically clarified that even under new definition of input service, service tax on sales commission is eligible as input service.

Canteen services as input service

22.4-2 There is some dispute relating to canteen services.

As per exclusion clause (C) of Rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, services in relation to outdoor catering is not eligible for Cenvat credit if such service is primarily used for personal use or consumption of employee.

The issue is whether the canteen is primarily for personal use or consumption of employee.

In Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages v. CCE (2015) 51 GST 126 = 56 taxmann.com 378 (CESTAT), it has been held that if cost is borne by company and if canteen service is used by all employees in general, it is not 'primarily for personal use or consumption of employee' and is eligible for Cenvat credit (even after 1-4-2011).

However, this view has not been accepted in Applied Micro Circuits v. CCE (2016) 54 GST 159 = 66 taxmann.com 103 (CESTAT SMB). In this case, it was held that Cenvat credit of service tax paid on outdoor catering and insurance of employees is not available.

It can be argued that canteen is not 'outdoor catering' as per trade parlance, even if run by outside contractor.

The question does not arise if (a) canteen is as per statutory requirements under Factories Act, as that service is exempt from service and hence no question of Cenvat credit (b) Canteen is not air conditioned.

In that case, service tax is not payable at all.

Goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-CE, dated the 1st March, 2011 is availed are exempted goods [Rule 2(d)]. Taxable services whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services, used for providing such taxable service, shall be taken, are exempted services [Rule 2(e)]. Hence credit of capital goods used exclusively in manufacture of such goods or in providing such service is not allowed. |
| 2. | Is the credit of only specified goods and services listed in the definition of inputs and input services not allowed such as goods used in a club, outdoor catering etc., or is the list only illustrative? | The list is only illustrative. | 3. | How is the "no relationship whatsoever with the manufacture of a final product" to be determined? | Credit of all goods used in the factory is allowed except insofar as it is specifically denied. The expression "no relationship whatsoever with the manufacture of a final pro-duct" must be interpreted and applied strictly and not loosely. The expression does not include any goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. Only credit of goods used in the factory but having absolutely no relationship with the manufacture of final product is not allowed. Goods such as furniture and stationery used in an office within the factory are goods used in the factory and are used in relation to the manufacturing business and hence the credit of same is allowed. |
| 4. | Is the credit of input services used for repair or renovation of factory or office available? | Credit of input services used for repair or renovation of factory or office is allowed. Services used in relation to renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, are specifically provided for in the inclusive part of the definition of input services. |
| 5. | Is the credit of Business Auxiliary Service (BAS) on account of sales commission now disallowed after the deletion of expression "activities related to business"? | The definition of input services allows all credit on services used for clearance of final products upto the place of removal. Moreover activity of sale promotion is specifically allowed and on many occasions the remuneration for same is linked to actual sale. Reading the provisions harmoniously it is clarified that credit is admissible on the services of sale of dutiable goods on commission basis. |
| 6. | Can the credit of input or input services used exclusively in trading, be availed? | Trading is an exempted service. Hence the credit of any inputs or input services used exclusively in trading cannot be availed. |
| 7. | What shall be the treatment of credit of input and input services used in trading before 1-4-2008? | Trading is an exempted service. Hence credit of any inputs or input services used exclusively in trading cannot be availed. | 8. | While calculating the value of trading what principle to follow- FIFO, LIFO or one to one correlation? | The method normally followed by the concern for its accounting purpose as per generally accepted accounting principles should be used. |
| 9. | Are the taxes and year end discounts to be included in the sale price and cost of goods sold while calculating the value of trading? | Generally accepted accounting principles need to be followed in this regard. 3.3-5 Transaction between principal and agent

Supply of goods— (a) by a principal to his agent where the agent undertakes to supply such goods on behalf of the principal, or (b) by an agent to his principal where the agent undertakes to receive such goods on behalf of the principal, will be subject to GST, even if there is no consideration - clause 3 of Schedule I of CGST Act.

'Agent' means a person, including a factor, broker, commission agent, arhatia, del credere agent, an auctioneer or any other mercantile agent, by whatever name called, who carries on the business of supply or receipt of goods or services or both on behalf of another - section 2(6) of CGST Act.

'Principal' means a person on whose behalf an agent carries on the business of supply or receipt of goods or services or both - section 2(88) of CGST Act.

Liability only of C&F Agents, not of commission agents - As per aforesaid clause (a), the agent will be liable for GST on value goods or services only if he undertakes to supply any goods or services or both on behalf of any principal (like consignment agent). However, if the agent does not supply goods or services, he is not liable for GST on value of goods or services. In case of commission agent, he does not undertake supply of goods or services. He will be liable for GST only on his commission.

Clause (b) will cover cases where agent returns goods to Principal.

Commission Agent is not required to register if his receipts of commission are less than Rs. 20/10 lakhs per annum - Persons who supply goods or services or both on behalf of other taxable persons whether as an agent or otherwise require registration under GST even if his turnover is below Rs. 20/10 lakhs per annum- section 24(1)(vii) of CGST Act.

There was misunderstanding that all commission agents require mandatory registration under GST irrespective of his commission income (i.e. even if income from commission is below 20/10 lakhs per annum).

Now it has been clarified that such registration is required only by C&F agents who stock and sale goods on behalf of Principal. Registration is not required by ordinarily commission agents who do not deal in goods or services themselves, if their annual turnover is less than Rs. 20/10 lakhs - CBI&C Circular No. 57/31/2018-GST dated 4-9-2018.

In case of commission agent of agricultural produce, the commission agent is not a taxable person and agriculturist is also not a taxable person. Hence, the commission agent does not require registration under GST. However, if he is liable to pay GST under reverse charge, he will be liable to be registered under section 24(iii) of CGST Act - - CBI&C Circular No. 57/31/2018-GST dated 4-9-2018, as amended vide corrigendum dated 5-11-2018.

Position in respect of del credere agent - Del credere agent is similar to commission agent. The only difference is that he guarantees payment to supplier of goods or services, if recipient does not pay. In some cases, the del credere agent himself pays to supplier and then recovers amount from recipient. In some case, the del credere agent advances short term loan to buyer and then buyer pays to the supplier.

Since the receipts of interest and commission on which TDS has been claimed under sections 194A and 194H are fully declared in ITR, the entire TDS claimed under sections 194A and 194H needs to be fully allowed. Hence the proportionate TDS disallowed is absolutely unjustified and, therefore, deserves to be allowed. [Para 2.6]

■ As regards the disallowance of TDS credit under section 194Q is concerned, the Bench found that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia. Therefore, the turnover on which tax is deducted under section 194Q is not the turnover of the assessee. Hence has rightly not been shown as such by the assessee. Moreover a Kachha Arhatia acts only as an agent for his constituent and never acts as principal. Therefore, the remuneration of Kachha Arhatia consists solely of commission and he has no control on the profit and losses made by his constituents.

■

The assessee has drawn attention of the Bench to sample invoices on which TDS was deducted under section 194Q by the principal buyer and the corresponding vikray parchi issued by the Mandi to the respective farmers. These documents clearly show that the amount invoiced by the assessee to the principal buyer and the value of goods transferred by assessee to the farmer is exactly the same. Therefore, turnover of the Kachha Arhatia is merely the commission paid by principal buyer on which the principal buyer deducts TDS under section 194H and which has been duly shown as income in the ITR by the assessee. Therefore, the TDS deducted by such principle buyers by virtue of provisions of section 194Q is eligible to be claimed by the Kachha Arhatia in his ITR on the grounds that the assessee is a Kachha Arhatia and is duly registered as such with the Mandi. Perusal of the vikray parchi issued at the Mandi to the farmers and the corresponding invoice raised by the assessee to the principal buyer undoubtedly establishes the fact that the assessee has no control or margin in the sale facilitated by him and earns merely commission from such transactions.

■

The assessee has no domain over the goods sold to the principle buyers. As clarified by Central Board of Direct Taxes in its Circular No. 452 of 1986), so far as Kachha Arhatias are concerned the turnover does not include the sales effected on behalf of principals and only commission (gross) has to be considered for the purpose of income tax. Therefore, TDS deducted under section 194Q by the principle buyers cannot be refused by invoking rule 37BA read with section 199.

■

As the sale facilitated by the assessee for the farmers is not the turnover of the assessee and the income from such transaction (commission) being duly offered for tax by the assessee in his ITR, the TDS deducted both under sections 194H and 194Q deserves to be fully allowed. Further the Form No. 26AS also depicts that the invoices on which TDS has been deducted under section 194Q also has TDS deducted under section 194H. Thus the contention of the assessee that he is merely a Kachha Arhatia is potrayed beyond all doubts and needs to be accepted.

■

Therefore, the Assessing Officer is to be directed to allow TDS claimed under section 194Q by the assessee. [Para 2.7]

The assessee filed a return of income of Rs. 661.15 crores and claimed a deduction in the amount of Rs. 11.41 crores under section 80-I, Rs. 218.62 crores under section 80-IA and Rs. 20.20 crores under section 80-HH. The Assessing Officer assessed the income under section 143(3) at Rs. 814.66 crores and restricted the deduction claimed under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH to Rs. 11.06 crores, Rs. 201.08 crores and Rs. 18.57 crores respectively. The Commissioner issued a notice under section 263 stating that on verification of the records, it was revealed that the following expenditure, though having a bearing on the profits of the units, had not been considered for allocation, i.e., (i) Research and Development (R & D) revenue expenditure - Rs. 33,95,42,336; (ii) R & D Capital expenditure - Rs. 12,39,73,377; (iii) Interest paid - Rs. 32,16,45,000; (iv) Agency commission - Rs. 35,59,51,682 (including Miscellaneous expenditure). The Commissioner stated that as this expenditure had a bearing on the profits of the units, it should have been allocated proportionately. An excess allowance, the notice stated, had resulted in an under-assessment of Rs. 9.87 crores. The Commissioner by his order, came to the conclusion that the research expenditure incurred by the assessee is inextricably linked with the business of the assessee, including business in those products which are manufactured in the units entitled to a deduction under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH. The expenditure as noted by the Commissioner, had been allowed in computing the income under the head 'profits and gains from business or profession' for the whole of the business of the assessee, including of those units which were entitled to the aforesaid deductions. The logical corollary was held to be that in computing the profits derived from an eligible unit for the purpose of the aforesaid deductions, an appropriate part of the expenditure would have to be allocated to the units. As regards agency commission, the assessee had stated that an amount of Rs. 35.59 crores had already been allocated in arriving at the profit derived from the eligible units that was included under the head of advertisement. The assessee stated that there was no omission on its part and the amount should not once again be allocated in arriving at the profits of the units in respect of which a deduction was sought under sections 80-I, 80-IA and 80HH. The Commissioner held that the interest and agency commission which relate to the whole of the business would have to be allocated to the eligible units. During the course of the hearing before the Commissioner, pursuant to the notice under section 263, a query was raised to the effect that cess which had been imposed on green leaf tea was required to be claimed entirely against the agricultural income in view of the decision of the Gauhati High Court in Jorehaut Group Ltd. v. Agrl. ITO [1997] 226 ITR 622. The assessee relied upon the provisions of rule 8 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and submitted that in the case of an assessee, who is engaged in growing and manufacturing tea, the composite income calculated in accordance with the provisions of the Act, is required to be apportioned between the income on the manufacture of tea and income from agriculture in the ratio of 40 : 60. According to the assessee, cess on green leaves is a part of the expenditure incurred in the business of growing and manufacture of tea. The Commissioner in his order under section 263 relied upon the judgment of the Gauhati High Court while coming to the conclusion that cess on green leaves was liable to be claimed entirely against agricultural income. On further appeal, Tribunal set aside order of Commissioner. It held that that the jurisdiction under section 263 had not been invoked properly and the entire cess could be claimed against taxable income.

The judgment of Gujarat High Court in case of Cadila was discussed at the Central Excise Tariff Conference on Tariff Matters organized by CBE&C on 28 and 29 October 2015. Minutes of the conference and decisions taken have been circulated vide CBE&C instruction F No. 96/85/2015-CX.1 dated 7-12-2015.

As per Para B.30 of aforesaid instruction dated 7-12-2015, the conference noted that in case of Cadila, the sales commission agent was only trading in goods i.e. buying and selling the goods without undertaking any sales promotion or advertising. If activity of sales commission agent involves an element of sales promotion, Cenvat credit of service tax paid on commission agent is available.

Full extract of para B.30 of the CBE&C instruction dated 7-12-2015 is given below.

B.30 Meerut Zone - Cenvat Credit - Admissibility of Cenvat Credit on Service Tax Paid on Sales Agency Commission Service:

Issue - CBEC vide its Circular No. 943/4/2011-CX dated 29.04.2011 at point No.5 has clarified that credit of service tax paid on sales commission services (Business auxiliary services) used in 28 relation to manufacture/sale of finished goods is admissible under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. However, there are conflicting judgments of Hon'ble High Courts in this regard. Hon'ble High Court of Gujarat in case of Cadila Health Care [2013 (30) STR 0003] has disallowed the said Cenvat credit whereas Hon'ble Tribunal in case of Birla Corporation Ltd. [2014 (35) STR977] followed the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Bombay and allowed the credit. Board may be requested by the conference to issue necessary clarification on the subject to avoid further litigation and to achieve uniformity in the practice of assessment.

Discussion & Decision

The conference discussed the issue in detail and the facts of both the cases where apparently conflicting judgments have been delivered. It was noted that the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Gujarat was in a very specific set of circumstances where the sales commission agent seemed to be only trading in the goods i.e. buying and selling the goods without undertaking any sales promotion or advertising. In the said judgment, Hon'ble court noted that "there is nothing to indicate that such commission agents were actually involved in any sales promotion activities as envisaged under the said expression. Obviously, commission paid to the various agents would not be covered in this expression since it cannot be stated to be a service used directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products or clearance of final products from the place of removal". Board Circular No. 943/4/2011-CX., dated 29-4-2011 at point No. 5 on the other hand has explained the situation where the commission agent renders the service of sales promotion in following words -"....... Moreover the activity of sale promotion is specifically allowed and on many occasions the remuneration for same is linked to actual sale.......". Board circular directs that input service credit would be available when there is a element of sales promotion as sales promotion is a service. Thus, the conflict between the judgment and the circular is not as large as is perceived. Both the Board circular and case laws on the subject allow credit of input services, when the activity of the sales commission agent involves an element of sales promotion.

Impact of decision of Gujarat High Court - Assessees and Tribunal benches within jurisdiction of Gujarat High Court were bound by decision of Gujarat High Court. However, even these assessees could take Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission, if there agreement is properly worded to establish that the agent is not simply trading but is also doing additional work of sales promotion and advertising.

Assessees outside jurisdiction of Gujarat High Court could take a stand that in view of contrary decision of Punjab and Haryana High Court, they are not bound by decision of Gujarat High Court.

It was found that there are bills of Jet Airways raised by Jet Air Freighters to the assessee. It was found that from the covering of the bill that the bills issued by Jet Air Freighters and not by the C&F agent as contended by the assessee. The amount paid by the assessee through the cheque is also Rs. 2,05,660 and not Rs. 1,25,272. The invoice nowhere states that it represents reimbursement of the air freight but it is the invoice made by Jet Air Freighters. This document, does not prove that the assessee has reimbursed the air freight paid by the C&F agent. The bills raised by Jet Air Freighters are directly in the name of the assessee. While gone through Circular no. 715, dated 8-8-1995. It was noted that in reply to question no. 7 the CBDT has opined as under (relevant extract is reproduced):

'Question 7: Whether a travel agent/clearing and forwarding agent would be required to deduct tax at source from the sum payable by the agent to an airline or other carrier of goods or passengers?

Answer: The travel agent, issuing tickets on behalf of the airlines for travel of individual passengers, would not be required to deduct tax at source as he acts on behalf of the airlines. The position of clearing and forwarding agents is different. They act as independent contractors. Any payment made to them would, hence, be liable for deduction of tax at source. They would also be liable to deduct tax at source while making payments to a carrier of goods.'

This question relates to a situation where the C&F agent makes the payment to the airlines or other carrier of goods or passenger. This question, is not relevant to decide whether the assessee is required to deduct tax at source when payment is made to C&F agent. Question no. 6 deals with a case where the payment is made for carriage of the goods or passenger by any mode of transport to C&F agent. In reply to this question, the Board has clearly laid down in Circular no. 715, dated 8-8-1995 that 'As regards payments made to clearing and forwarding agents for carriage of goods, the same shall be subjected to tax deduction at source under section 194C of the Act.' The assessee could also not adduce any evidence that the C&F agent deducted tax at source while making payment to the carrier so as to prove that the amount which was paid by the assessee to the C&F agent represents reimbursement of the freight paid by the C&F agent on behalf of the assessee to the airlines. It is not the intention of the Legislature that neither the C&F agent deducts the tax when it makes the payment to the carrier nor the assessee deducts the tax at source when it makes payment to C&F agent. If the assessee claims that the amount paid to the C&F agent by the assessee represents reimbursement, the onus is on the assessee to prove that it represents the reimbursement of the claim. Hence, provisions of section 194C are clearly applicable in the case of the assessee. [Para 6]

On second appeal:

In the instant case the assessee was following mercantile system of accounting. As per the agreement the sales made by the assessee were as distributor/ commission agent of the principal. The property remained with the principal till the goods were sold by the assessee. In the circumstances the mere fact that the assessee had accounted for the purchase and sales in its final accounts would make no difference. The mere existence of accounting entries in the books of the assessee were not decisive of the fact that the sales and purchases belonged to the assessee. It was true that the sales tax collected would be a part of trading receipt but such trading receipt would be of that of the principal and not of the assessee-distributor/commission agent. Merely because the liability to pay sales tax was on the agent, it would not convert the receipt of the sales tax collected as trading receipt of the assessee.

It was only for the purposes of collection of tax under the Sales Tax Act that the commission agent was made liable to pay sales tax jointly and severally along with the principal. In those circumstances though the assessee was jointly and severally liable under the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, the sales tax collected would not form part of the assessee’s trading receipts and consequently, not even the expenditure. In fact the assessee had not claimed the expenditure in its profit and loss account and the receipts of the sales tax collection as well as the payments made therefrom were directly shown in the balance sheet under the head ‘Sales tax collection account’.

The assessee’s claim was, therefore, allowed and directions were issued not to disallow sales tax liability under section 43B.

Commission on purchase not covered under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' :

The conjunctive 'and' between the words 'clearing' and 'forwarding' indicate and mean that where clearing operations are separate from forwarding operations, levy of tax would not be attracted i.e. there would be no charge of tax if the transaction involved only one of the two components of the conjuncted service namely 'clearing' and 'forwarding'. The expression a clearing and forwarding agent in relation to clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner' contemplates only one person operating both as the clearing and the forwarding agent; and if a person has rendered service as forwarding agent without rendering any service as 'clearing agent' he could not be considered to have rendered both services as a 'clearing and forwarding agent'. [Para 2]

'Clearing and forwarding operations' would be various activities having a bearing on clearance of goods and would normally involve documentary processes and arrangements for transfer of goods to their destination; and may also involve clearance at subsequent stages during forwarding operations. A clearing and forwarding agent normally undertakes the following activities :-

(a)

Receiving goods from the factories or premises of the principal or his agents;

(b)

Warehousing these goods;

(c)

Receiving despatch orders from the principal;

(d)

Arranging despatch of goods as per the directions of the principal by engaging transport on his own or through the authorised transporters of the principal;

(e)

Maintaining records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; and

(f)

Preparing invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 3]

Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of the enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of goods, the service would not be a taxable service as defined in section 65(105)(j) read with section 65(25) which defines a clearing and forwarding agent. [Para 4]

In this case, assessee neither receives goods from the factory premises of the principal; warehouses such goods; receives despatch orders from the principal; arranges despatch of goods as per directions of the principal by engaging a transport on its own or through authorised transporters of the principal; nor maintains records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; nor even prepares invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 5]

Hence, assessee, in no manner, engages in any of the six enumerated activities which constitute clearing and forwarding operations. It never has custody of the picture tubes; does not receive them from manufacturers of the tubes; does not warehouse the picture tubes; does not receive despatch orders from manufacturers of picture tubes which are directly forwarded to manufacturers of the TV sets; does not arrange despatch of goods as per directions either of the manufacturers of picture tubes or manufacturers of TV sets; nor engages transport on its own or through authorised transporters of manufacturers of picture tubes or manufacturers of TV sets; and does not maintain records of the receipt and despatch of picture tubes and the stock available at the warehouse; nor prepares invoices either on behalf of the principal manufacturers or manufacturers of TV sets. [Para 6]

There is neither the conjunctive service of clearing and forwarding provided by the assessee nor either of the services of clearing or forwarding. As the assessee has not provided any of the core enumerated activities of clearing and forwarding operations, it has not directly or indirectly provided any service connected with clearing and forwarding operations in any manner to any other person. That the assessee was not a consignment agent is also not in dispute. [Para 7]

Therefore, assessee is not liable to Service Tax under the taxable head 'clearing and forwarding agency'. Even otherwise, commission agents were exempt from service tax vide Notification No. 13/2003 dated 20-5-2003 from 1-7-2003 upto 9-9-2004. Revenue proceeded on the basis that the assessee had provided 'clearing and forwarding agency' service, contrary to the distinct classification w.e.f. 1-7-2003; the services provided by it constituted Business Auxiliary Service. [Para 8]

FACT: ■

The assessee was an individual and carrying business as a commission agent by selling chillies on behalf of farmers to registered dealers (GST Dealers). The assessee filed the return of income for the assessment year 2022-23 admitting a total income of Rs. 10.51 lakhs.

■

The CPC processed the return of income under section 143(1) wherein it was observed that the CPC had allowed the tax credit amounting to Rs. 10,271 as against Rs. 48,593 claimed by the assessee in the return of income.

■

The assessee also filed a petition under section 154 seeking re-processing of the return by allowing the correct TDS credit claimed by the assessee, wherein the CPC had rejected the petition filed under section 154.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The CBDT Circular No. 452, dated 17-3-1986 relied on by the assessee and the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Thota Venkateswarlu v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 290 (Viz) of 2024, dated 27-8-2024] wherein the Tribunal has relied on the decision of this Bench in the case of Yegneswari General Traders v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 39(Viz) of 2024, dated 18-3-2024] have been gone through. From the above it is clear that Kaccha Arahtias turnover includes only the gross commission and not the sales effected on behalf of their principals. In the present case, it is a fact that the assessee is only a licensed commission agent in Agricultural Market Committee Yard, Guntur. Therefore, the Circular issued by the CBDT (supra) squarely applies to the assessee and hence the assessee is acted only as an agent (kaccha arahtia) and therefore it is eligible to get credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source and there is no short fall of TDS as concluded by the revenue authorities. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to grant credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source in the case of the assessee. [Para 7]

■

Considering the identical facts and circumstances of the assessee's case with that of the appeal decided by the Tribunal in the case of Yegneswari General Traders (supra) wherein the Tribunal has relied on the decision of this Bench in the case of Thota Venkateswarlu (supra) and Subba Reddy Mareddy v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 96(VIZ) of 2024, dated 25-11-2024], following the principle of consistency, there is no hesitation to set-aside the orders of the revenue authorities and direct the Assessing Officer - CPC to grant credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source in the case of the assessee. Thus, the grounds raised by the assessee are allowed. [Para 8]

■

In the result, appeal of the assessee is allowed.[Para 9]

The assessee, a manufacturer of excisable goods, utilized services of commission agents for procuring the orders for its finished goods. The assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid by the commission agents on commission received by them. The Deputy Commissioner disallowed the said credit. The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order of the Deputy Commissioner and allowed credit to the assessee.

On appeal :

■

There is no dispute with regard to the fact that, the assessee is a licensed commission agent operating in the Agricultural Market Committee Yard in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, with a valid certificate of license, as a commission agent, under rule 49 and section 7(1)(b) of the Andhra Pradesh Agricultural Produce and Livestock Market Act, 1966. As per AMC regulations, the assessee receives 2 per cent commission from farmers on sales to purchasers/traders/exporters, and the same has been offered as income in the financial statements and paid relevant taxes. The buyers/traders/exporters deducted TDS under section 194Q in respect of sales on the total sale value and reported in the PAN number of the assessee. Similarly, the buyers/traders/exporters had deducted TDS under section 194A in respect of interest payment on delayed payments and reported in the PAN number of the assessee. [Para 7]

■

Since the assessee has considered only commission income as its income and, after relevant expenditure, offered net profit for taxation, it claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders in terms of sections 194Q and 194A. In total, the Assessing Officer allowed proportionate credit for TDS on the ground that the assessee has offered only the part of the income, whereas it claimed TDS on the entire sales value. It is found that, once the assessee is operating as a commission agent, then the income of the assessee is net commission income received from the farmers, but not the total sales value of the farmers. Since the law provides for TDS under section 194Q on total sales value, and further, the assessee has raised sales invoices in its name, the traders have deducted TDS on the entire sales value, but the fact remains that, the assessee has considered the total income accrued on the total sales value being commission received from the farmers, as its income. Therefore, the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A, has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee and thus, the provisions of section 199 read with rule 37BA(2) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 are complied with. Therefore, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) that Assessing Officer has rightly allowed proportionate credit as per section 199 read with rule 37BA(2), is incorrect, going by the facts, because, there is no finding from the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) that, the income on which TDS has been deducted under sections 194Q and 194A has not suffered tax in the hands of the assessee. Since the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194A and 194Q has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee, the assessee has righty claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders and reported in Form 26AS. The Assessing Officer, without appreciating relevant facts, allowed proportionate credit for TDS, even though the assessee is entitled for credit for the entire TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A. The Commissioner (Appeals), without appreciating relevant facts, simply sustained additions made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 8]

■

This issue is squarely covered by the decision of Tribunal, Visakhapatnam Bench, in the case of Bala Krishna Traders v. ITO [ITA No.302/Viz/2025, dated 18-7-2025] where, under identical set of facts, the Tribunal has allowed credit for TDS as claimed by the assessee, on the basis of Form No.26AS filed for the relevant assessment year. A similar view has been taken by the Coordinate Bench of the Tribunal, Visakhapatnam, in the case of Gorla Srinivasa Reddy v. ITO [ITA No.503/Viz/2024, dated 20-12-2024], where, under identical set of facts, allowed credit for TDS as claimed by the assessee. In this view of the matter, considering the facts and circumstances of the case and also by following the decisions relied upon by the assessee, the Assessing Officer is directed to allow credit for TDS, as claimed by the assessee, on the basis of Form No. 26AS filed for the assessment year under consideration. [Para 9]

■

In result, the appeal filed by the assessee is allowed.[Para 10]

That the assessee had concealed the particulars regarding the commission which was not directly accounted for in commission account and profit and loss account. The profit and loss account was the part of the return of income filed by the assessee. The accounting entries passed in books of account was with the intention to avoid direct flash on the commission payments to sister concerns particularly when services were not rendered against commission payments amount to concealment of particulars. The particular of a commission furnished by the assessee were also inaccurate in the sense that the assessee claimed the commission expenditure against which no services were rendered. The commission expenditure claim of the assessee was not accordingly true claim, not accurate, not exact or correct; it was an erroneous and it was an inaccurate statement of the commission claim. It was neither a case of interpretation of any provision of the statutes nor it was case of two views on the issue. There was no force in the submissions of the assessee, that in earlier years penalty under section 271(1)(c) were initiated on the similar disallowance but the Assessing Officer himself had dropped those penalties. It was found that in those years the Assessing Officer dropped the penalty proceeding as the assessments were quested by the Tribunal on the ground that notices under section 148 were not in accordance with law. When the assessee furnished inaccurate particulars of the income, such case was squarely covered by the provisions of section 271(1)(c) and penalty was accordingly, leviable. In the return of income, it was the claim of the assessee that the assessee had incurred commission expenses. The heavy burden was on assessee particularly when the commissions were paid to sister concerns. The assessee had failed to discharge its burden as no materials were produced to show that the commission paid against the services rendered. Thus, the assessee had failed to substantiate its claim both in quantum matters as well as in penalty proceedings. The Assessing Officer had examined the commission payment in detail by exercising his power provided in the Act by examining books of account at the time of assessment proceedings, by making survey, by taking statements and other examination of post survey proceedings. The claim of commission expenditures of the assessee was found false. There was substance in the submissions of the department that the top executive officers of the assessee had admitted that those sister concerns companies existed only on paper and accommodative bills were issued. The assessee had failed to submit any material basis on which it could be said that the claim of the assessee was a bona fide claim. The manufacturer/service provider had two options upto 31-3-2008 —

Maintain separate inventory - Maintain separate inventory and accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services. In such cases, he should not avail Cenvat credit of the inputs and input services which are used in exempted final services at all — Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules. Really, rule 6(2) had become impractical to a manufacturer w.e.f. 10-9-2004 i.e. date from which he is eligible to avail Cenvat credit of input services also. It may be possible to maintain separate records for inputs used in exempted goods but it is practically impossible to keep separate records of ‘input services’ as many of such ‘input services’ (e.g. telephone, audit, courier, construction etc.) are bound to be common.

Pay 10% ‘amount’ if separate inventory and records not maintained - If the manufacturer/service provider opts not to maintain such separate accounts, he has to pay an amount equal to 10% of the ‘price’ of such exempted goods. Such payment can be made by debit to Cenvat credit account or PLA [rule 6(3)(b)].

Education cess and SAH education cess is payable only on ‘duties of excise’. ‘Amount’ is not ‘duty’. Hence, education cess or SAH education cess is not payable on such ‘amount’.

9.11-2 Credit of service tax limited if service provider does not maintain separate accounts

Till 31-3-2008, in case of output service, if he did not maintain separate accounts, he could utilise Cenvat only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable on final product. He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services [The limit was 35% upto 10-9-2004].

For example, assume that service tax payable on output service is Rs 100. Service tax paid on input service is Rs 15. These input services are used both for taxable output services and exempt/non-taxable output services. In such case, assessee can avail and utilise credit of entire Rs 15. However, if tax paid on input services is Rs 75, and these are used both for exempted and output services, then assessee can actually utilise credit of only Rs 20. He will have to pay balance in cash, even if credit of Rs 55 is still available in his books.

He may take credit of Rs 75 in his Service Tax (Receivable) Account, but can utilise credit of Rs 20.

The balance may remain in his Service Tax Credit Account. He can utilise it in future if opportunity arises.

In Mundra Port and Special Economic Zone Ltd. v. CCE (2011) 33 STT 364 = 15 taxmann.com 33 (CESTAT), it was held that this credit could be carried forward on 1-4-2008 and utilised later.

Note that this provision does not apply w.e.f. 1-4-2008.

9.11-3 Treatment of opening balance of Cenvat credit as on 1-4-2008

Assessee always tries to utilise Cenvat credit first and then pay through PLA/GAR-7. However, despite his efforts, some opening balance is possible particularly in initial stages of production/provision of services. In case of assessees utilising Cenvat credit only to the extent of 20% service tax payable on output services, balance credit remained unutilised.

Issue is eligibility of Cenvat credit of opening balance and whether provision of ‘proportionate Cenvat credit’ will apply to opening balance.

It is well settled that Cenvat credit is indefeasible. Credit once validly taken cannot be denied in absence of specific statutory provision (Even such statutory provision cannot be confiscatory in nature).

CBE&C, vide circular No. 137/72/2008-CX.4 dated 21-11-2008 [20 STT 19 (ST)] has clarified that the accumulated credit as on 1-4-2008 will not lapse and can be utilised as there is no provision of periodic lapse of Cenvat credit. This would apply to assessees who were availing entire Cenvat credit but utilising only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable on taxable output services.

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds. It filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year declaring it's total income.

Subsequently information was received from Investigation wing that assessee-company had made bogus payment to 'R' and 'RS' which were paper companies without having any business activities. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted said additions.

HELD: Issue relating to bogus purchases

The Commissioner (Appeals) has categorically noted that assessee has submitted the evidences with respect to the Ledger accounts of the transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of the assessee showing the payment made to the parties. Assessee has also shown the mapping of corresponding purchases and sales. The argument of the department is that one-to-one mapping shown by the assessee is not correct for the reason that in the purchase bills of these parties there is no narration with respect to the quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as the colour etc. To support the same, the assessee has submitted the other beans of the other parties, which have been accepted by the Assessing Officer as genuine purchases. On perusal of those bills, also there is no mention of number of diamonds as well as the colour of the diamonds. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the purchase bills the assessee should have mentioned this details as that is not the trade practice and that is also not the reason why the Assessing Officer has rejected those purchases. In Castrol India v. CCE (2016) 53 GST 141 = 64 taxmann.com 244 (SC), uniform price was charged. If payment was made in time, cash discount was later allowed. Assessee paid excise duty on provisional basis and later claimed refund. Thus, interest was inbuilt in price. It was held that refund is admissible [However, issue of unjust enrichment can arise]. Position if quantum of discount not known at the time of removal - Sometimes, exact quantum of discount is not known at the time of removal, e.g. cash discount, year end discount etc. In such cases, assessee should go in for provisional assessment. He should pay lower duty and then pay difference later. If he pays higher duty and then claim refund on basis of discount actually given, he will have to prove that duty burden has not been passed on to customer. This might become difficult and refund may not be granted, even if eligible. Hence, it is advisable to pay lower duty on the assumption that discount will be passed on and then pay differential duty later.

Of course, the problem that may be faced by assessee is that, he may be unable to recover the differential duty from his customer. In such cases, the differential duty will have to be paid from his own pocket. The assessee should take proper precautions in this regard (like keeping interest bearing deposits from dealers).

Cash price in case of cash discount - In case of cash discount, one may fix a 'cash price' and pay duty accordingly. In addition, a 'interest on receivable' for (say) 30 days may be charged in the invoice. No duty is payable on 'interest on receivables'. If the buyer pays earlier than (say) 30 days, credit note for differential amount should be given.

Commission to Selling Agents not allowed as deduction

12.4-3 'Commission' means a percentage paid to the agent from the profits of goods sold or business obtained - Concise Oxford Dictionary. Commission is the percentage or allowance made to a factor or agent for transacting the business for other - Webster's New International Dictionary.

'Commission' is different from 'trade discount'. As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, 'discount' is a deduction from bill or amount due given, especially in consideration of prompt or advance payment or to a special class of buyers. - . - The commission payable to selling agents is for services rendered by them as agents and hence is not in the nature of 'trade discount'.

Sometimes, goods are sold directly to a buyer and overriding commission is paid to selling agents/commission agents. Sometimes (particularly in international transactions), buyer is asked to make payment of commission directly to the agent. Such commission is not deductible from 'transaction value'. If it is paid separately by buyer, it is clearly includible, as obviously, it is paid by buyer on behalf of seller.

Service charges paid to a selling agent (MP Laghu Udyog Ltd.) for procuring orders is not allowable as deduction, when goods were supplied directly to various departments of State Government. Trade discount is available only if given to a customer or trader - Siddhartha Tubes v. CCE 2006 (193) ELT 3 (SC) - confirming Siddhartha Tubes v. CCE 2005 (182) ELT 333 (CESTAT).

Commission to selling agent is not allowable as deduction - Raymond Ltd. v. CC 2005 (190) ELT 465 (CESTAT) * Raymond Ltd. v. CC 2007 (214) ELT 529 (CESTAT).

Brokerage given to agents forms part of assessable value - Deekeens Polyesters v. CCE (2009) 234 ELT 129 (CESTAT).

Discount to chief stockist not permissible when direct sale is to sub-stockist - In CCE v. Goetze India 2005 (179) ELT 186 (CESTAT), assessee was selling goods directly to sub-stockists giving them 25% discount. He was giving further 2.5% to Chief Stockist.

In Nirlon Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (190) ELT 334 (CESTAT), it was held that commission paid to indenting agent is not allowable as deduction (The order is sketchy and exact decision is not clear).

Dealer and agent cannot be same person for same consignment - A wholesale dealer can act as dealer for same or other seller. However, such duel role cannot be performed by him for same consignment - Hewlett Packard v. CCE 2004 (167) ELT 399 (CESTAT) - assessee's appeal dismissed by SC - 167 ELT A137.

Direct despatch to buyer but invoice in name of dealer - In CCE v. Mag Torq Powder Clutches (2009) 236 ELT 610 (CESTAT), goods were directly despatched to ultimate buyer but invoice was raised in name of dealer at dealer price. It was held that the buyer (from manufacturer) is a dealer and not commission agent. Hence, price charged to dealer is the assessable value and not the price charged by dealer to the ultimate buyer.

Rule 6(6) of Cenvat Credit Rules states that provisions of rule 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply in case of excisable goods removed to SEZ, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting.

Rule 6(7) as inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012 specifically provides that provisions of rule 6(1) to rule 6(4) shall not apply to (a) services provided to SEZ unit or developer for their authorised operations, without payment of service tax or (b) export of service.

On appeal:

Facts

The assessee was a manufacturer of Grinding Media and it had :

procured orders from their purchasers Associate Cement Companies (hereinafter referred to as ACC);

forwarded the said order to their subsidiary company viz., Well Cast Steel Ltd (hereinafter referred to as WSL);

goods were delivered by WSL directly to ACC and raised the invoice in name of the assessee denoting therein 4 per cent CST and a discount amount for such sale.

Department demanded service tax on allegedly received commission by assessee classifying same under 'Business Auxiliary Services'.

The assessee argued that :

the entire transaction is of trading and

they have not acted as a commission agent ; and

entire issue is hit by limitation.

Assessee's Arguments

The goods in question were consigned by the WSL directly to ACC in Jharkhand.

The assessee being manufacturer of Grinding Media was having capacity constraint hence got the order manufactured from its own subsidiary company.

As per provisions of section 6(2) of Central Sales Tax Act, second sale can be effected by transfer of documents of titles to such goods during their movement of goods from one state to another. WSL directly delivered the goods to the customers of assessee that raised commercial invoices on the assessees' name giving him discount. Transit sale is accepted form of sale for claiming exemption from payment of CST. There is no specific condition in section 6(2) of CST Act by which exemption can be disallowed in the case of transit sales on the ground that sales are made to pre-determined buyer. Rule 6(6) of Cenvat Credit Rules states that provisions of rules 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply in case of excisable goods removed to SEZ, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting.

Hence, these are not 'exempt goods'.

9.6-5 Exported service is not 'exempt service' for purpose of rule 6

Rule 6(7) as inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012 specifically provides that provisions of rule 6(1) to rule 6(4) shall not apply to (a) services provided to SEZ unit or developer for their authorised operations, without payment of service tax or (b) export of service.

This provision continues even after 1-4-2016.

Rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules as amended w.e.f. 1-7-2012 also provides that Service which is exported service as per rule 6A of Service Tax Rules, is not 'exempted service'. Same provision is continuing after 1-4-2016 also.

If the service is not 'export' as per rule 6A of Service Tax Rules and if the payment is not received within the period allowed by RBI (which is presently 9 months), the service will not be treated as 'exempted service' - Rule 6(8) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012.

Thus, provision of proportionate reversal or payment of 'amount' under rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules will be required if export is not as defined in Rule 6A of Service Tax Rules or payment in foreign exchange is not received within period allowed by RBI [It may be noted that, even then, service tax is not payable if place of provision of service is outside the taxable territory].

If at a later date (but within one year from the period as allowed by RBI) payment in foreign exchange is received, the assessee can take back the Cenvat credit which he had reversed earlier - proviso to rule 6(8)(b) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 11-7-2014.
