Thus, it is imperative that such commission agent who enters into the contract with the foreign principal, quantifies the amount payable towards maintenance and repair.

After warranty period, if the maintenance and repair work is undertaken by way of annual maintenance contract or otherwise, that will be a contract between the Indian service provider and Indian service receiver and the tax is payable on the amount so realized from the Indian customer towards the above service.

Import of service and commission agents

12. Like Indian commission agents are representing the foreign principals and canvassing the product and obtaining the orders, it is also a common commercial scenario for the Indian companies to employ commission agents abroad who can move around and obtain orders based on which the goods can be exported from India to the customer identified by the foreign commission agents. The commission so paid to the foreign agents is for the services rendered outside India. However, with the introduction of new set of Rules ‘Service Tax (Provided from Outside India and received in India) Rules, 2006, which came into effect from April 19, 2006, it is an unfortunate situation that the commission so paid by Indian principals to the foreign commission agent will be treated as a taxable service under the newly introduced section 66A read with the above-mentioned new Rules. As a result, the Indian principals will be deemed to be the service provider and, accordingly, service tax is payable on the commission amount remitted by them outside India since the same is paid for the services provided from outside India by the foreign commission agent, but received in India by the Indian principal.

If a foreign commission agent undertakes the job of erection, installation and commissioning of the goods imported by the Indian principal and charges the customer separately, question of service tax liability will not arise on Indian principal, since such services are rendered/provided and used/consumed outside India, which will not attract service tax. If, however, foreign commission agent raises separate bill on the Indian principals for such activities or for undertaking maintenance or repair work during warranty period, such service will attract service tax under the new Rules and Indian principal will be liable to pay such service tax.

Reimbursement of expenses

13. Normally, commission agents obtain reimbursement of expenses from their principals based on the terms of contract and till the introduction of new Valuation Rules, 2006, not only the commission agents, but also other service providers were not including such expenses reimbursed by the service receiver in the value of taxable service and this has resulted in a heavy loss of revenue to the Government. However, the valuation concept has undergone a sea change with effect from April 18, 2006 with the introduction of substituted section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994 and introduction of a new set of Rules titled Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, which came into effect from April 19, 2006.

Rule 5 of the above rules clearly indicates that any expenses incurred by the service provider during the course of rendering the service will form part of the value of taxable service and service tax payable on such amount. As a result of this stringent provision, the reimbursement concept has undergone a major change and only when a service provider acts as a Pure Agent, and fulfils all the eight conditions laid down under Rule 5(2) of the Valuation Rules, 2006, such amount can be excluded from the value of taxable service. Thus, there is no more free lunch to the service providers and service tax is now payable on the value of taxable service which should include, inter alia, any expenses incurred for rendering the output service. For example, if a chartered accountant in Mumbai undertakes the audit of his clients in Chennai, the air travel expenses, hotel expenses, taxi expenses, etc., cannot be excluded as a reimbursement of expenses on actuals, but are to be included in the value of taxable service since these are incurred for rendering his output service.

Billing

14. It is a common commercial practice in respect of services received from commission agent, that generally neither bill nor debit note is raised by commission agents on the principals. On the contrary, periodically, the principals either issue credit notes and account the commission payable or as and when payment is made to the Commission Agent, the same is accounted in the books of account.

5.4-1 Services of Commission agent

There were disputes about eligibility of Cenvat credit on services provided by commission agent. Hence, following explanation has been added to rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, w.e.f. 3-2-2016 after sub-clause (C) -

Explanation - For the purpose of this clause, sales promotion includes services by way of sale of dutiable goods on commission basis.

The drafting of the explanation is faulty. Firstly, it is not clear what is meant by 'this clause', since firstly, any of sub-clauses (A), (B) and (C) of definition of 'input service' has no relation with 'sales commission'. Secondly, commission agent really never sales the goods. He only 'facilitates' sales. Thirdly, the explanation only refers to sale of dutiable goods. Be as it may, at least issue of eligibility of input service of commission agent of goods has been sorted out.

The explanation has retrospective effect - The amendment dated 3-2-2016 does not specifically state that it is retrospective. However, in my view, it does have retrospective effect, for reasons stated below.

Right from beginning, department has consistently held (as per circulars/instructions discussed below) that input service of service tax paid by commission agents is eligible 'input service'. SERVICE TAX - SMALL SERVICE PROVIDER EXEMPTION - CLUBBING OF PARTNER'S RECEIPTS WITH THAT OF FIRM

1. Our partnership is registered under service tax and has been paying service tax under commercial coaching services. Now, the partners are also individually providing the same services however their receipts are less then Rs. 9 Lakhs. Please clarify whether partners are liable to pay service tax on the basis of their relation with firm and whether partners' receipts can be clubbed with that of the firm ?

As per definition of 'person' under section 65B(37), person is defined to include firm as a separate category of persons. Therefore, for purpose of service tax, firm is a separate person from its partners and same view would apply in respect of claim of small service provider's exemption.

However, creation of bogus entities or bogus separation of receipts in order to claim SSI-exemption has been held to be impermissible under Central Excise and same attracts clubbing of turnover.

In short, if resources are same (i.e., infrastructure, finance, staff, management, branding, control are same), then, clubbing would get attracted.

SERVICE TAX - COMMISSION FROM FOREIGN COMPANIES - LIABILITY TO SERVICE TAX

2. We are providing services of commission agent to Singapore based foreign company for the sale of iron ore. The commission is received in foreign exchange. Please clarify whether this would be liable to service tax ? Can there be any tax planning ?

As per rule 2(f) of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012, intermediary is defined to mean "intermediary" means a broker, an agent or any other person, by whatever name called, who arranges or facilitates a provision of a service (hereinafter called the 'main' service) or a supply of goods, between two or more persons, but does not include a person who provides the main service or supplies the goods on his account. As per rule 9(c), the Place of Provision of services of an intermediary would be location of such intermediary (w.e.f. 1-10-2014).

In view of definition under Rule 2(f), commission agents and other agents, or the like would be liable to service tax on their location basis. Accordingly, Indian commission agents of foreign companies are liable to service tax w.e.f. 1-10-2014, even if the commission is earned by them in the foreign exchange.

Hence, it appears that your services are liable to service tax. We would suggest of any tax planning in view of very wide words used.

Nevertheless, if it can be shown that the services being provided are consultancy services, not relatable to supply/sale of goods, then only, rule 9(c) read with rule 2(f) would not apply.

CENVAT CREDIT - WORKS CONTRACT SERVICES v. TRADING SERVICE

3. We are having 2 divisions : trading division and service division (works contract services). Can we take credit of input services received from sub-contractor which is used exclusively to provide works contract service ?

Since trading activity is also an exempted service under rule 2(e) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004; hence, you become provided for taxable as well as exempt service and have to comply with the provisions of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Therefore, you should either maintain separate accounts and, if not, pay 7% (6% up to 18-5-2015) of the value of exempted services of trading as per rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

The provisions of rule 6 override provisions of all other rules.

SERVICE TAX - DISTRIBUTORS v. COMMISSION AGENTS

4. We are distributors of products of Johnson & Johnson. The following is the procedure :

J&J supplies to us @ Rs. 100 (invoiced) ;

We sells to our customer @ Rs. 100 ;

Bad debts, if any, are borne by us ;

We raise a debit note of Rs. 10 towards profit margin on sales ;

On confirmation J & J raises credit note of Rs. 10 on us.

Thus, we end up paying Rs. 90 to J&J.

Whether we are liable to pay service tax ? Whether our practice needs amends ?

In our considered view, your practice is very well in order. There is no service tax liability, as you are not an agent of J&J; in fact, you buy from J&J and sell to the customers. The fact that J&J invoices you first and title apparent gets transferred would show that there is pure sale of goods to you and by you to your customers.

It appears that this practice is being adopted by J&J to control your profit margin.

Explanation 1.—For the purposes of sub-rule (2), "pure agent" means a person who—

(a)

enters into a contractual agreement with the recipient of service to act as his pure agent to incur expenditure or costs in the course of providing taxable service;

(b) neither intends to hold nor holds any title to the goods or services so procured or provided as pure agent of the recipient of service;

(c)

does not use such goods or services so procured; and

(d)

receives only the actual amount incurred to procure such goods or services.

Explanation 2.—For the removal of doubts it is clarified that the value of the taxable service is the total amount of consideration consisting of all components of the taxable service and it is immaterial that the details of individual components of the total consideration is indicated separately in the invoice.

Illustration 1.—X contracts with Y, a real estate agent to sell his house and thereupon Y gives an advertisement in television. Y billed X including charges for television advertisement and paid service tax on the total consideration billed. In such a case, consideration for the service provided is what X pays to Y. Y does not act as an agent on behalf of X when obtaining the television advertisement even if the cost of television advertisement is mentioned separately in the invoice issued by X. Advertising service is an input service for the estate agent in order to enable or facilitate him to perform his services as an estate agent.

Illustration 2.—In the course of providing a taxable service, a service provider incurs costs such as travelling expenses, postage, telephone, etc., and may indicate these items separately on the invoice issued to the recipient of service. In such a case, the service provider is not acting as an agent of the recipient of service but procures such inputs or input service on his own account for providing the taxable service. Such expenses do not become reimbursable expenditure merely because they are indicated separately in the invoice issued by the service provider to the recipient of service.

Illustration 3.—A contracts with B, an architect for building a house. During the course of providing the taxable service, B incurs expenses such as telephone charges, air travel tickets, hotel accommodation, etc., to enable him to effectively perform the provision of services to A. In such a case, in whatever form B recovers such expenditure from A, whether as a separately itemised expense or as part of an inclusive overall fee, service tax is payable on the total amount charged by B. Value of the taxable service for charging service tax is what A pays to B.

Illustration 4.—Company X provides a taxable service of rent-a-cab by providing chauffeur-driven cars for overseas visitors. The chauffeur is given a lump sum amount to cover his food and overnight accommodation and any other incidental expenses such as parking fees by the Company X during the tour. At the end of the tour, the chauffeur returns the balance of the amount with a statement of his expenses and the relevant bills. Company X charges these amounts from the recipients of service. The cost incurred by the chauffeur and billed to the recipient of service constitutes part of gross amount charged for the provision of services by the Company X.

FACT: The appellants were engaged in the manufacture of tobacco products. They entered into an agreement with RZC, appointing the latter as their agent for the purpose of marketing their product, booking orders, managing, supervising and developing of the market. In consideration of the services rendered by the said agent, the appellants were to pay commission at the rates mentioned in the schedule to the contract on the net sale proceeds of the orders received through the agent. The appellants were issued show-cause notice, alleging that as they were availing services of RZC, who were working as ‘clearing and forwarding Agent’ on commission basis, they were liable to pay service-tax. The appellants took a stand before the adjudicating authority that the service rendered by RZC did not come under the purview of clearing and forwarding agent and the same was entirely different. As such, the question of payment of service tax did not arise. During the course of personal hearing, they contended that after the amendments in the Service Tax Rules through the Finance Bill, they should have been issued a fresh show-cause notice. The Commissioner confirmed the service tax of certain amount, not paid by the appellants. In addition, he also imposed penalty on the appellants and their director.

On appeal :

HELD: In the Trade Notice No. 59 of 1999, dated 4-10-1999, issued by the Mumbai Commissionerate-I, the clearing and forwarding agent has been defined as ‘any person who is engaged in providing any service, either directly or indirectly, connected with clearing and forwarding operations in any manner to any other person and includes a consigning agent’. The details of the activities given in the said Trade Notice are only few of the activities undertaken by clearing and forwarding agent, as is apparent by the use of the expression ‘normally’. As such, it is clear that the activities given in the said Trade Notice are not exhaustive but are inclusive in nature and describes the jobs to be normally undertaken by the clearing and forwarding agent. As per the definition of clearing and forwarding agent, he is a person who is engaged in providing ‘any’ service, either directly or ‘indirectly’ connected with clearing and forwarding operations, in ‘any’ manner to any other person. The use of expression ‘any’ and ‘indirectly’ in the said definition of clearing and forwarding agent, is indicative of the fact, that the scope of the services to be provided by clearing and forwarding agent is quite wide. He is not only the person who is actually dealing with the goods who has to be termed as clearing and forwarding agent. Even if the services are indirect, but the same are connected with the clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner, of the other persons, he would be covered by the definition of clearing and forwarding agent. In the instant case, admittedly, RZC was procuring orders from the dealer and passing on the same to the appellant, from whom they were receiving the commission, in lieu of services so provided. The said services were definitely connected with the clearing and forwarding operations of the various tobacco products being manufactured by the appellant. It is further seen that the taxable service has been defined as any service provided by clearing and forwarding agent ‘in relation’ to clearing and forwarding operations in ‘any manner’. From the above, it is clear that the service has to be relatable to the clearing and forwarding operations and can be in any manner and it is not necessary that the said agent must deal with the goods directly. As such, the lower authority had rightly concluded that RZC was a clearing and forwarding agent and services provided by them were liable to tax. [Para 9]

Sr. Advocate is that the said explanation only provides that procedure for computation and since this change is procedural in nature it will have a retrospective effect. Ld. Sr. Advocate also argued that in case of traded goods, the value addition by the appellant is only the difference between the sale price and the purchase price of the goods which is not so in the case of manufactured goods. On a query by the Bench that since Ld. Sr. Advocate is arguing that only the value addition should be taken in respect of the traded goods, then why the same criteria should not be applied in the case of manufactured goods i.e. take the differential amount between the selling price and cost of various raw materials. Ld. Sr. Advocate stated that in case of manufactured goods so many things go into production process like labour, electricity and many other services and it will not be appropriate to take the value addition. In support of his contention that in case of traded goods only value addition should be taken, Ld. Sr. Advocate took us through the judgment of the Court (5th Chamber) dated 14-7-1998 in case C-172/96 which was passed on a reference under Article 177 of the EC Treaty by the High Court of Justice of England and Wales, Queen's Bench Division. We have gone through the said judgment carefully. In the said case, the issue was how to determine the turnover for purpose of value added tax in case of transactions in different currencies by the First National Bank of Chicago. The Bank used to purchase various currencies at a certain rate in other currencies. Similarly, the Bank used to sell various currencies in other currencies. The difference between the two is generally understood as spread and would be the income of the Bank. The question was what should be considered as the turnover for purpose of VAT. It is in that context, the said court has held that the spread the difference between the selling price and purchase price should be taken for the purpose of VAT. In the present case, the dispute is not relating to computation of turnover for purpose of charging a tax as there is no tax liability in case of traded goods. The question is how to apportion the credit of tax on the input service between the manufactured goods and the traded goods, whether we should take the turner of the manufactured goods and traded goods for apportioning the credit of the service tax on input services or some other criteria should be followed. We, therefore, do not find any applicability whatsoever of the said judgment in the facts and circumstances of the present case. Another judgment quoted by the Ld. Sr. Advocate is the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Meerut V. Sharvan Kumar Swarup & Sons reported in (1994) 6 SCC 623. In this case, wealth-tax was applicable on various assets. A new rule was inserted with effect from 1-4-1979 to determine the market value of properties. The question was whether the new inserted rule can be used for determining the value of properties for earlier period and hence determine the wealth-tax. It is in this context that the Hon'ble Supreme Court has taken a view that the same would be applicable to all the proceedings pending at the time of its enactment. In the present case, as mentioned earlier, it is not the computation of tax but apportionment of the credit of service tax on input services availed for manufactured goods and traded goods. As we have already held that trading was not a service and therefore cannot be considered as an exempted service before 1-4-2011, therefore, the substantive provision itself did not exist before the said date. Under the circumstances, we are of the view that the said judgment is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case."

Cenvat Credit : If an assessee has taken input service credit of common services used for both taxable and non-taxable services, his entire credit cannot be denied; department may only seek compliance with rule 6(3) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004

receipt, consumption and inventory of input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and take Cenvat Credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing output service on which service tax is payable."

Further, sub-rule (3)(c) of the above said rules reads as under : "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) and sub-rule (2), the manufacturer or the provider of output service opting not to maintain separate accounts shall follow either of the following conditions as applicable to him, namely :

The provider of output service shall utilize the credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services."

From the above-said provision, it is clear that where an output service provider is availing credit on inputs and input services and providing taxable as well as exempted services without opting to maintain separate account of inputs and input services received and used for the exempted services and refrains to avail Cenvat Credit on such inputs/input services, he has no other option but to use Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on the output services. Therefore, the intention of the law is, the assessee shall either maintain separate account of input and input services for exempted output services and not to avail Cenvat Credit thereon or to utilize Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the service tax payable on output services. Therefore, if the assessee decides to avail Cenvat Credit directly related to the taxable output services and utilizes the same fully for payment of service tax on output services and simultaneously avails Cenvat Credit on common inputs and input services without maintaining separate account and utilizing such credit only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable, it will defeat the intention of the legal provision which is explained in the example given below :

Let the input service credit availed on input services used exclusively for taxable output service is Rs. 10,000.

Common input services which are used partly for taxable and partly for exempted services, credit availed fully of Rs. 20,000.

Let service tax payable on the taxable output service be Rs. 50,000.

The correct way to utilize the Cenvat Credit for the above said situation would be 20% of Rs. 50,000, i.e., Rs. 10,000 which can be utilized out of the total credit of Rs. 30,000 (Rs. 10,000 related to the taxable output services and Rs. 20,000 credit on common input services used for taxable as well as exempted output service). Therefore, the balance amount, i.e., Rs. 50,000 minus Rs. 10,000 Cenvat Credit utilized = Rs. 40,000 has to be used as to be paid through TR-6 challan.

Had Cenvat Credit been utilized as explained in the query, the assessee can utilize the credit of Rs. 10,000 which is directly related to taxable output service plus another Rs. 10,000 i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 service tax payable on output service = Rs. 20,000 and the balance amount of Rs. 30,000 would have been paid through TR-6 challan.

However, it may be noted that the provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, do not provide for more than one set of Cenvat Credit record for input service credit i.e. one for the input service credit related to taxable output service and second common input services credit account which are partly used for taxable output service and party for exempted services nor this sort of arrangement is prohibited, but considering the practice followed under Central Excise, I am of the opinion, that under above stated example, the assessee can avail total credit on Rs. 30,000 (10,000 + 20,000), but utilization will be restricted to 10% of service tax payable i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 = Rs. 10,000 and balance amount of Cenvat Credit unutilized (Rs. 30,000 total Cenvat Credit minus Rs. 10,000 credit utilized = Rs. 20,000) will be carried forward to the next month. It is further clarified that the law does not restrict the assessee to take Cenvat Credit on common input service only to the extent of 20% of service tax paid.

In the above said example the common input service credit of entire Rs. 20,000 can be availed and it is not restricted for availment of credit upto 20% of Rs. 20,000 i.e. Rs. 4,000.

Opinion : In short, if the assessee does not opt for separate account as envisaged under Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, he can avail the credit on the common inputs services fully but he can utilize the total credit available at the end of the month not exceeding 20% of service tax payable.

In fact we are not able to agree with the Commissioner’s view that even if Cenvat credit on common input services is not taken, appellant is required to maintain separate accounts. For ready reference we re-produce rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 : "(2) Where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails of CENVAT credit in respect of any inputs or input services except inputs intended to be used as fuel, and manufactures such final products or provides such output services, then, the manufacturer or provider of output service shall maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and take CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing output service on which service tax is payable."

5. The very beginning of the rule shows that only where a provider of output service avails Cenvat credit in respect of input services and uses the same and he is engaged in providing exempted as well as taxable services then only he is required to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and utilisation of input services. There is no detailed discussion on applicability of this rule and the requirement of maintenance of separate accounts by the Commissioner in the impugned order. However, in view of this provision we agree with the learned advocate that unless the department shows that appellants have availed credit of input services which have also been used for providing any of the exempted services, the demand cannot be sustained. For this purpose there is a need for verification of the claim made by the appellants that they have not taken credit of service tax paid on all the common input services and their number is only ten. We would not like to go into all other issues at this stage since we have concluded that on this ground alone the matter is required to be sent back for verification of actual position as per the records. On revenue’s appeal : HELD: The facts were that on the basis of a letter dated 19-11-2008 from ‘R’ Ltd. to the assessee, it claimed to be an agent of the former in respect of sale made to the Indian Navy and Coast Guards. The enclosure to this letter, forwarded by the assessee to ‘R’ Ltd. in regard to services rendered by four sub-agents in the relevant year, had also been confirmed by ‘R’ Ltd. The paperbook contained evidence regarding payment of commissions to these parties and accounting for the same in their returns of income. ‘K’ had confirmed that it displayed a small version of RO system of ‘R’ Ltd. in its shop and it used to provide information to persons or concerns through the assessee. Further, ‘E’ stated to the effect that it was passing on information in regard to prospective buyers to the assessee for following up the orders and the commission was received on completion of the orders, i.e., on receipt of payments. The same statement of the proprietor of ‘B’ was recorded, who confirmed business dealings with the assessee for the years 2003 to 2005. In the case of ‘M’ Ltd. there was an agreement dated 10-4-2004 in force and said firm also confirmed the receipt of commission from the assessee. As against the aforesaid, evidence was found in the course of survey of ‘R’ Ltd. which was interpreted by its Assessing Officer to mean that payments were made to the assessee by cheques and after retaining its commission, the balance amount was returned to ‘R’ Ltd. The evidence produced by the assessee in the course of assessment led to a conclusion that the sub-agents had provided some information regarding prospective buyers, for which the commission was paid to them. The evidence seized from ‘R’ led to a conclusion that the assessee was used as a conduit for passing on the money to it after retaining commission for providing bogus bills. However, both sets of evidences did show that the assessee was paid at the rate of 5 per cent of the value of the order, out of which it paid an amount at the rate of 3.75 per cent either to the sub-agents or to ‘R’ Ltd. The whole of the evidence, including the bills raised by ‘R’ Ltd. on its clients, showed that the assessee and its sub-agents were in the same position insofar as the mentioning of the names in the bills of ‘R’ Ltd. was concerned, i.e., neither the name of the assessee nor of the sub-agent appeared on the bills. The assessee did not claim to have dealt with the Government departments directly. It had dealt with sub-agents and ‘R’ Ltd. for communication of information about prospective buyers. The revenue had also not been able to prove that the payments were against the public policy. The provision contained in the Explanation to section 37(1) uses the words ‘which is an offence or which is prohibited by law’. No evidence had been produced to show that payment of commission to the sub-agents was either an offence or it was prohibited by law. [Para 5]

INPUT SERVICES USED FOR SELF-MANUFACTURED AS WELL AS TRADED GOODS

We are manufacturers of engineering products. We also are traders of those products, i.e., we procure these goods under our brand name and sale. We have appointed selling agents for sale of our products (both self-manufactured and traded). We pay selling commission to our indenting agents. The selling agents charge service tax on the commission. We avail Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission paid by us on traded goods as well as self-manufactured goods, and utilise the same for payment of excise duty on our self-manufactured products. Department has issued a show-cause notice to us, informing that we are not eligible for service tax paid by us on commission attributable to traded goods. Please advise.

You are eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax paid both on self-manufactured goods and traded goods, for the following reasons -

(1)Definition of ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is very wide. As per inclusive part of the definition, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’, since the words used are ‘such as’ and not ‘viz.’.

(2)The inclusive part of definition clearly covers ‘sales promotion’. The inclusive part of definition does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’.

(3)Cenvat Credit Rules do not require any one to one relation between input and output.

(4)Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not require distribution of Cenvat credit in any particular ratio. Entire credit of service tax at HO or depot or branch offices can be transferred to any unit without any restriction. The rule makes no distinction between services used for manufacture and services used for other activities like trading, financing, etc.

(5)The Finance Minister in para 148 of his Budget Speech on 8-7-2004 has stated as follows, "I propose to take a major step towards integrating tax on goods and services. Accordingly, I propose to extend credit of service tax and excise duty across goods and services".

(6)Thus, the Cenvat Credit Rules have to be interpreted keeping this goal in mind and, hence, cannot be interpreted narrowly. As per doctrine of purposive interpretation, an interpretation which advances purpose of the Statute should be preferred over an interpretation which defeats the purpose.

(7)It is clear that after introduction of the Cenvat Credit Rules, the whole company is treated as one single entity for Cenvat credit. The definition of ‘input service’ and ‘input service distributor’ has abolished distinction between ‘goods’, ‘manufacture’ and ‘services’. Entire company is treated as one unit for purpose of Cenvat credit, as is the position under ‘Goods and Service Tax’ (GST) which has been set as the goal. Even concept of ‘LTU’ (Large Taxpayer Unit) is a step in that direction.

(8)Even assuming that there is some ambiguity (though really there is none), it is well-settled principle that the benefit of doubt goes to assessee.

Thus, Cenvat credit availed by you is legally correct.

However, you must keep in mind that current decisions of Tribunal are highly conservative and, hence, ultimate result is uncertain. You should be mentally prepared to pay interest @ 13%, if final decision goes against you.

Decision in the case of National Engineering Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 21 STT 188 (New Delhi - CESTAT) 4.2 The assessee was an agent of a foreign company, i.e., GMC. It procured orders/contracts from Indian Railways for GMC and received commission on which service tax had been paid under the category of ‘Business auxiliary services’. The commission, however, was not received directly from GMC, but was received through Indian Railways in Indian currency. As per understanding between GMC and Indian Railways, GMC received payment from Indian Railways after deducting the commission payable to the assessee. The assessee filed refund claim on the ground that the services provided by it to GMC on which service tax had been paid were export of services in terms of rule 3(3). The Assistant Commissioner rejected the refund claim on the ground that since the commission was received in non-convertible Indian currency, in view of the proviso to sub-rule (3) of rule 3, same could not be treated as export of services. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assistant Commissioner. The appellant pleaded that when the Business Auxiliary Service, taxable under section 65(105)(zzb ) of the Finance Act, 1994 is provided by a service provider in India to a recipient located outside India and service is used in or in relation to commerce or industry of the recipient, the same has to be treated as export of the service in terms of sub-rule (3) of rule 3 of Export of Services Rules, 2005. That the conditions (a), (b) and (c) of the proviso to sub-rule (3) are applicable only in a situation where the service recipient abroad has any commercial or industrial establishment or any office relating thereto, in India, and only in such a situation the conditions mentioned in clauses (a ), (b) and (c) of the proviso have to be satisfied. One of such condition being that the payment for such service is received by the service provider in convertible foreign exchange; that GMC, did not have any commercial establishment or office in India and therefore, the proviso to sub-rule (3) of rule 3 was not applicable; that in view of this, the business auxiliary service provided by the appellant to GMC had to be treated as service export and, therefore, no service tax was payable in respect of services and the appellant was eligible of the refund of the service tax paid by it.

The Tribunal held that just because commission was received by the appellant through Indian Railways in Indian Rupees as Indian Railways made payment to GMC in foreign currency after deducting the commission payable to GMC, it could not be said that the service provided by the appellant to GMC, USA was not export of service under rule 3(3) of the Export of Services Rules and, therefore, the appellants were held eligible for refund of the service tax paid on such service exported to GMC, USA.

The Tribunal further held that in the case of ETA Travel Agency (P.) Ltd. (supra) cited by Ld. DR, the offshore service receiver had an office in India and the commission had been received from the bank account of such local office of the offshore service receiver and in view of the facts of the case, the Tribunal held that the service had been provided and received in India and it was not a case of export of service. Therefore, as per Tribunal, this judgment of the Tribunal was not applicable to the facts of this case and, therefore, the Tribunal held that the service provided by the appellant to GMC, USA had to be treated as ‘export of service’ under rule 3(3) of the Export of Services Rules. The Tribunal also followed the decision of National Engg. Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 17 STT 398 (New Delhi - CESTAT), given in the appellant’s own case even the reasoning were different.

Trading activity - Whether a service

As regards the issue as to whether trading activity can be called a service, it is quite clear that since trading activity is nothing but purchase and sales and is covered under Sales Tax Law, it may not be appropriate to call it a service. Trading activity cannot be called a service and, therefore, it cannot be considered as an exempted service also. [Para 5]

Applicability of Cenvat Credit Rules (and Service Tax Credit Rules) on trading activity

Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 provides that where output service provider does not maintain separate account, he is to follow the procedure or avail the options available under that rule. Rule 6 is applicable only when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation in rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity was not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions. [Para 7]

Eligibility for availing input service tax credit

In cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, there arises a situation where an assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable goods. There is no provision to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that the appellant choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what will be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appeared to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles was deducted and the balance only will be availed for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition was not against the law in view of the fact the there were several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal, wherein a view had been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit. 6G.2.1-2 KACHHA AND PACCA ARHATIAS, CLARIFICATION - A pacca arhatia is not, in the proper sense of the word, an agent or even del credere agent. The relation between him and his constituent is substantially that between the two principals. On the basis of various Court pronouncements, following principals of distinction can be laid down between a kachha arhatia and a pacca arhatia: —

(1)

A kachha arhatia acts only as an agent of his constituent and never acts as a principal. A pacca arhatia, on the other hand, is entitled to substitute his own goods towards the contract made for the constituent and by the constituent's goods on his personal account and thus he acts as regards his constituent.

(2)

A kachha arhatia brings a privity contract between his constituent and the third party so that each becomes liable to the other. The pacca arhatia, on the other hand, makes himself liable upon the contract not only to the third party but also to his constituent.

(3)

Though the kachha arhatia does not communicate the name of his constituent to the third party, he does communicate the name of the third party to the constituent. In other words, he is an agent for an unnamed principal. The pacca arhatia, on the other hand, does not inform his constituent as to the third party with whom he has entered into a contract on his behalf.

(4)

The remuneration of a kachha arhatia consists solely of commission and he is not interested in the profits and losses made by his constituent as is not the case with the pacca arhatia.

(5)

The kachha arhatia, unlike the pacca arhatia, does not have any dominion over the goods.

(6)

The kachha arhatia has no personal interest of his own when he enters into a transaction and his interest is limited to the commission agent's charges and certain out of pocket expenses whereas a pacca arhatia has a personal interest of his own when he enters into a transaction.

(7)

In the event of any loss, the kachha arhatia is entitled to be indemnified by his principal as is not the case with pacca arhatia.

It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts has to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods by way of formula as provided in the rule itself; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It is the settled law that reversal of the credit taken on the inputs is as good as non-availment of the credit on the inputs.

Under the Central Excise Act, 1944, levy is on manufacture but payment is at the time of clearance. It has been decided by the Board that credit of the duty paid on common inputs is admissible when used in the manufacturer of the final product (exempted and dutiable) provided the said credit of duty paid on inputs going into the exempted category of the final product is debited in the RG 23A-Part II account before the removal of exempted final product on actual or pro rata (estimated) basis. The facility of reversing the credit taken is neither explicitly given nor necessarily implied in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002. It was held in that context that the credit taken but before utilization reversed, will amount to not taking the credit and the benefit of exemption cannot be denied.

In view of the above reasoning, the Tribunal held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are not applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. In other words, it is equivalent to reversal of credit on inputs. Therefore, according to Tribunal, the appellant had satisfied the requirement of not taking Modvat Credit on the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Once the inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted goods irrespective of whether such inputs are used in the manufacture of dutiable goods, such manufacturer can avail of credit only in terms of rule 6(3).

u A power to give benefit encompasses within itself the power to put conditions and restrictions under which credit is available. Power to give benefit also carries with it power to take it back or withdraw it. The rule if properly read starts with the words ‘Cenvat credit shall not be allowed’. Therefore, rule 6 makes it clear that insofar as inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods are concerned, no Cenvat credit is allowed. The rule making authority, however, noting that inputs may be used both for manufacturing final products which may be dutiable and other final products which are exempt, has provided that such manufacturer will be given credit insofar as inputs used for manufacturing of dutiable goods are concerned, if accounts are maintained in terms of the rules. Therefore, merely because the assessee contended that he was willing to forego credit on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final product it does not warrant a departure from the requirements of rule 6(2) and 6(3). The rules contemplate that on failure to maintain accounts in terms of rule 6(2) the consequences would be in terms of rule 6(3)(a) or (b). It is not possible to read down the rule as ‘amount not exceeding’ as was sought to be contended on behalf of the assessee.

u Rule 6(1) is clear; the Cenvat credit cannot be availed of on inputs used in the manufacturing of exempted goods. It then adds the words ‘except in the circumstances mentioned’ in sub-rule (2). A Court cannot read into the said rule something different or render otiose the words. The rule mandates specifically that an assessee seeking to avail Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, the only method by which he can avail of the credit is by following sub-rule (2).

u In our opinion, the taxing machinery has to follow the method provided more so by the Assessing Officer. He cannot disregard a rule. It is not open to an assessee to contend that because he has chosen not to maintain the records as required, revenue authorities even against the grain of the language of the rule, must estimate the inputs used in the manufacture of final dutiable products and, accordingly, pass necessary orders. It is also not possible to accept the contention that because they are familiar with the procedure of ascertaining the amount of credit, that by itself makes rule 6(3)(b) directory.

u Once the law itself has laid down the circumstances under which credit can be availed, it is that method by which the credit can alone be availed. It is not open to an assessee to contend that some other method is also available and the assessee has the choice of claiming credit or reversing the same. Such an argument is devoid of merits considering the clear language of rule 6(1).

u Pro rata credit, it is submitted, has been statutorily provided in Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from 1-4-2008 and the principles and basis enshrined in those rules can be applied for the past period. The submission is that it is only a rule of evidence and such rules of procedural law, can be applied for the period prior to 1st April, 2000 also. Learned counsel seeks to rely on the judgment of the Supreme Court in CWT v. Sharvan Kumar Swarup & Sons [1994] 210 ITR 886/76 Taxman 620 and in CWT v. Laxmipat Singhania [1978] 111 ITR 272 (All.). In our opinion, it is not possible to accept such a submission. Once there be rules in force, it is those rules which are to be applied. Rules subsequently made may be as a result of experience cannot be made retrospective unless so provided. In the instant case, the rule is prospective from the date the rules come into force and cannot be applied retrospectively.

Certain identified issues in Rule 6(3) and 6(3A):

6. Though the issues are numerous which still need clarity since the statute is still in its nascent stage, some of the identified issues are as under :

(i) Rule 6(3), Opt in - your choice, Opt out - no choice during the financial year

The sub-rule clarifies that an option would be exercisable both in the case of goods and services as manufactured or provided by the assessee. He cannot opt for Option 1 for goods and option 2 for services or vice versa. Also, exercise of such option cannot be withdrawn at any point of time during the financial year. He may change his option from the next year onwards. Thus, though the choice of opting in for the non-maintenance of separate books of account is open during the financial year, yet the option to opt out of it is unavailable to the manufacturer of service provider for that financial year.

(ii) Meaning of the term - ‘exempt’

The sub-rule does not define the term ‘exempt’ for the purpose of this sub-rule. Technically speaking, exempted goods/services are a sub-set of taxable goods/services. Exempted goods/services are specified by a notification by the Central Government and, accordingly, no duty/tax is leviable on them. However, there are other goods or services which are non-taxable and cannot be called ‘exempt’ technically. For example services of an advocate.

Having said this, the interpretation of the term ‘exempt’ is important for the calculation of duty/tax in respect of the Cenvat credit attributable towards exempted goods/services. Thus, extension of the term ‘exempt’ on non-taxable goods/services or otherwise would change the entire computation. For example when a provider of taxable services is providing exempt services and also is engaged in trading of goods (non-taxable), whether he needs to pay an amount equal to Cenvat credit attributable towards trading activity also, as he has to do in the case of exempt services. The answer is in affirmative when we equate trading to an exempt service and not otherwise.

Further, a larger question would be whether in case of an assessee engaged in the provision of taxable service and non-taxable service, would the computation under rule 6(3A) be applicable on him ? The question would be answered as ‘YES’ when non-taxable is equated as ‘exempt’ otherwise the answer is ‘NO’.

The more logical calculation would be to take out the Cenvat credit attributable towards non-taxable activities and then apply rule 6(3) on the balance Cenvat credit. Thus, the assessee should avail only the credit excluding that which is attributable towards non-taxable activities.

(iii) Choice of option - whether premises-wise or assessee-wise

Further, another point worth mentioning here is that the term used by the statute for availment of choice is manufacturer/service provider and not premises of manufacturer (factory) or service provider. Even the definition of ‘manufacturer’ under central excise uses the word ‘person’ and not ‘factory’. Accordingly, one school of thought might interpret that the availment of the options above should be same throughout all locations across India and the option cannot be availed of differently for different premises.

Expressing it with an example, Mr. X is a service provider having offices in Delhi, Mumbai and Pune, all three offices being separately registered with service tax department. Mr. X is providing taxable services under the category of ‘chartered accountant services’ and also availing the exemption provided thereunder. Thus, he is the provider of both taxable as well as exempt services. Now, the question is whether he can opt for option I for his Delhi and Mumbai offices and option II for Pune or will he have to opt for a single option for all his offices since the sub-rule uses the words ‘service provider’ when offering the choice.

FACT: The appellant initially availed Cenvat credit on the inputs. After utilising the same in manufacture of exempted goods, it reversed the credit. However, the department on finding that the appellant had not maintained separate records regarding the various inputs, used in the manufacture of exempted as well as dutiable goods, raised demand for payment of 8 per cent of value of the clearance of the exempted goods under rule 6.

On appeal :

that they provide to the airlines. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle was cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case was gone. From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l),the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided that it is made taxable. Therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. It may also be said that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air travellers. If in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-travellers. On the other hand, it may be said that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited. The tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the petitioners that because of section 67(k ), the nature of the tax itself changes was incorrect. Section 67(k), which provides the ‘measure of the tax’, is not unconnected with the main levy of the tax. The provision of section 67(k ) does not in any manner alter the nature of tax and does not shift it from the service rendered to the customer to the service rendered to the airlines. The contention, therefore, was clearly incorrect on facts.

The further argument that the notification dated 26-6-1997 restricts the tax to the commission alone and is repugnant to the scheme of the tax was obviously incorrect. The basis of the argument that the commission received from the airlines by the air travel agent is taken a measure for imposing a levy on a different service rendered to the customer by the agent, was itself incorrect. Therefore, the argument that the impugned provision of section 67(k) is repugnant to the general scheme of the Act was to be rejected.

As far as the second contention of the petitioner with regard to rule 6(7) was concerned, the language of rule 6(7) itself suggests that it is an optional matter. Therefore, the members of the petitioner-association, who had not exercised the option would had no concern with the validity of that rule while those who had opted for it, and majority of them having done so, could also not challenge the said validity.

In fact, it was not necessary for the High Court to take stock of the petitioners’ contention regarding the unconstitutionality of the rules but, even otherwise, there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found with that rule much less in the light of the submission made by the petitioners. The High Court was in complete agreement with the department that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration section 93 and section 94(2)(a ) jointly. Indeed, there is a specific power under section 93 to grant exemption in any manner. Section 94(2)(a) speaks of the rule-making power on the subject of collection and recovery of service tax under section 66 and section 68. What is suggested by rule 6(7) is nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations. It was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule-making power. It does not amount to an independent levy again. Therefore, it was to be held that there was nothing wrong with the rule in question. This rule provides for an independent measure as the basic airfare. For this reason, no merit was found in the writ which was liable to be dismissed.

Joint and several liability of certain class of dealers

6. (1) (a) Where a dealer who carries on the business of supplying goods in the course of execution of a works contract entered into by him (hereinafter referred to as a contractor) through another such dealer (hereinafter referred to as a sub-contractor) directly or otherwise, and the sub-contractor executes such works contract and each or either of them is liable to pay tax under this Act, then notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, the contractor and the sub-contractor shall be jointly and severally liable to pay tax in respect of transfer of property in goods whether as goods or in some other form involved in the execution of such works contract.

(b) If the contractor proves in the prescribed manner to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that the tax has been paid by the sub-contractor on the turnover of the goods supplied in the course of execution of the works contract, the contractor shall not be liable to pay tax again on the turnover of such goods.

(2)(a) Where a dealer who bonafidely buys or sells for an agreed consideration (hereinafter referred to as the commission agent) any goods specified in Schedule II on behalf of his principal, such commission agent and his principal shall both be jointly and severally liable to pay tax under this Act.

(b) (i) If the principal on whose behalf the commission agent has sold the goods proves in the prescribed manner to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that tax has been paid or payable by his commission agent on such goods, the principal shall not be liable to pay tax in respect of the sale of such goods.

(ii) If the commission agent who has sold goods on behalf of the principal proves in the prescribed manner to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that the tax has been paid by his principal on such goods, the commission agent shall not be liable to pay tax in respect of the sale of such goods.

(3) Where any dealer or person with a view to evade payment of tax or in order to claim any input tax rebate which he otherwise is not eligible for or was carrying on business in the name of or in association with any other person either directly or indirectly, whether as an agent, employee, manager, partner or power of attorney holder, guarantor, relative or sister concern or (in) any other capacity, such person and the dealer in whose name the registration certificate was obtained shall jointly and severally be liable for the payment of tax assessed, re-assessed, interest payable and penalty imposed under the Act and such tax, interest and penalty shall be recovered from all or any of such persons as if such person or persons are dealer under the Act.

ANNEX 9.1

[PARA 9.2-6]

CIRCULAR NO. 754/70/2003-CX, DATED 9-10-2003

AVAILMENT TO CREDIT ON INPUTS USED EXCLUSIVELY FOR THE MANUFACTURE OF EXEMPTED FINISHED GOODS

I am directed to say that Board's attention has been drawn to the availment of credit on inputs falling under Chapters 28 and 29 used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods by certain assessees manufacturing finished goods falling under Chapter 30 of Schedule to Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. It has been reported that these assessees are subsequently reversing an amount @ 8% of the price of the exempted goods under clause (b) of sub-rule (3) of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002.

2. The matter has examined in Board in the context of admissibility of such credit or otherwise. In this connection, your attention is invited to sub-rule (1) of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 which prescribes that no Cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of inputs which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The said sub-rule makes an exception of the circumstances in which such credit on inputs used for the exempted goods can be availed. Sub-rule (2) of the said rule gives an option to the manufacturer to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in for the manufacture of exempted and dutiable goods and in case, he does not opt for the separate records, clause (b) of sub-rule (3) requires a manufacturer to pay an amount equal to 8% of the total price of the exempted goods excluding sales tax and other taxes as paid. Thus, it is clear that the option to maintain the separate accounts or payment of 8% of the price of the exempted goods can be exercised only in respect of common inputs used for the manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods. Where any inputs are clearly identifiable as used only in or in relation to the manufacture of final products which are exempt from payment of duty, CENVAT credit is not admissible on such inputs which are used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted final products. The circumstances specified in sub-rule (2), sub-rule (3) do not cover, or envisage availment of credit on inputs used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted final products.

3. It is therefore, clarified that no credit can be taken on inputs which are used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted final products. It may also be seen that this position was the same in erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944 and there has been no change in this principle. The procedural facility is prescribed to take care of the practical difficulties which may be faced by the manufacturers using the same inputs in both dutiable and exempted final products. Necessary action to recover the credit wrongly availed of, if any, may be taken at your end.

It took credit of duty paid on all the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, including exclusive inputs (other than common inputs) and paid 10 per cent on the sale price of exempted goods cleared in domestic market. By the Notification No. 27/2005, dated 16-5-2005 rule 6(3) was amended by inserting Explanation III clarifying that credit shall not be allowed on inputs and input services used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted service. Pursuant to the above amendment show-cause notices were issued to the assessee demanding the Cenvat credit relatable to (i) the exclusive inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods which were cleared on payment at 10 per cent of the sale price of the exempted goods; (ii) the exclusive inputs removed as such; (iii) the exclusive inputs used in the finished goods exported; (iv) the exclusive inputs used in the finished goods removed to 100 per cent EOU; (v) the exclusive inputs lying in stock; (vi) the exclusive inputs used in the finished goods lying in the stock. The demands were confirmed by the Commissioner.

HELD (PER TECHNICAL MEMBER)

It is seen that rule 6(1) specifically prohibits Cenvat credit being allowed on such quantity of inputs as used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Therefore, there is no authority in law for availing Cenvat credit on the quantity of inputs intended or used for the manufacture of exempted goods except in terms of rule 6(2), which allows the manufacturer to avail the Cenvat credit only in respect of that particular quantity of inputs, which is intended to be used in the manufacture of dutiable goods subject to their maintaining separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of final products. But if separate accounts are not maintained, though Cenvat credit is availed, then sub-rule 3 of rule 6 provides for payment of amount equal to Cenvat credit on dutiable inputs for cases covered under sub-rule (3)(a ) and in respect of all other inputs, sub-rule (3)(b) of rule 6 provides for payment of an amount of 8 per cent or 10 per cent of total price (excluding sales tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods), of the exempted final products charged by the manufacturer for the sale of such goods at the time of their clearance from the factory. Thus, reversal of the credit taken or availed under rule 6 is not contemplated by the rules. [Para 15]

If the interpretation put by the majority order is held to be correct, it will render the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) ibid providing for payment of an amount equal to 8 per cent or 10 per cent rather otiose. This militates against an interpretation, which renders it superfluous and is of no significance. [Para 16]

It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacturer of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts had to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It cannot be given, as the amount of reversal of credit has to be worked out in a manner prescribed in the Rules. There was no such prescription prior to the amendment. This decision of the majority will make the amendment superfluous. Such interpretation has to be avoided. [Para 23]

In the light of the aforesaid discussions, it was held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. [Para 26]

Facts

The assessee was a manufacturer of Grinding Media and it had :

procured orders from their purchasers Associate Cement Companies (hereinafter referred to as ACC);

forwarded the said order to their subsidiary company viz., Well Cast Steel Ltd (hereinafter referred to as WSL);

goods were delivered by WSL directly to ACC and raised the invoice in name of the assessee denoting therein 4 per cent CST and a discount amount for such sale.

Department demanded service tax on allegedly received commission by assessee classifying same under 'Business Auxiliary Services'.

The assessee argued that :

the entire transaction is of trading and

they have not acted as a commission agent ; and

entire issue is hit by limitation.

Assessee's Arguments

The goods in question were consigned by the WSL directly to ACC in Jharkhand.

The assessee being manufacturer of Grinding Media was having capacity constraint hence got the order manufactured from its own subsidiary company.

As per provisions of section 6(2) of Central Sales Tax Act, second sale can be effected by transfer of documents of titles to such goods during their movement of goods from one state to another. WSL directly delivered the goods to the customers of assessee that raised commercial invoices on the assessees' name giving him discount. Transit sale is accepted form of sale for claiming exemption from payment of CST. There is no specific condition in section 6(2) of CST Act by which exemption can be disallowed in the case of transit sales on the ground that sales are made to pre-determined buyer. In the entire transaction, the only thing that requires determination is whether the transfer of property in goods took place while the goods were in transit or not; in the given case, it is so. Benefit of section 6(2) of the CST Act cannot be denied for subsequent sale made to pre-determined buyer is the law settled by the apex court.

The assessee and WSL procured requisite valid statutory documents, i.e., E-1 Form and C-Form for claiming benefit of payment of CST under section 6(2) of the CST Act from the sales tax authorities and the said transactions have been accepted by the sales tax authorities and completed the assessments from time to time holding that there was an interstate sale. ACC the ultimate purchaser has issued C-Forms to the assessee which has been produced before the authorities.

It is the burden on the revenue to establish that assessee had provided taxable services which fall under the category of Marketing/Promoting of Goods, which has not been discharged by the revenue in the case in hand.

Discount given cannot be considered as commission.

At the most, there may have been a breach of provisions of CST Act and may not have service tax angle and definitely not a Business Auxiliary Service.

WSL had discharged Central Excise duty on the entire sale value of the goods to ACC on a price on which assessee has sold the goods, hence the same transaction cannot be taxed under Service Tax.

Revenue's Arguments

The assessee had acted as a commission agent within the definition of 'mercantile agent' as per section 2(9) of Sale of Goods Act.

The assessee having placed an order on behalf of ACC to WSL, have represented themselves as commission agent or Del Credere Agent.

The assessee had purchased the goods for their principal and supplied it in accordance with the law. Since the manufacturer is located in Karnataka and the assessee is located in Gujarat, the goods undisputedly moved from Karnataka to the purchaser who is in Jharkhand and the goods did not come to Gujarat at all. Movements of goods indicate that it was not a trading activity but an activity as mercantile agent known as commission agent as the goods are sold to the client ACC in Jharkhand, which is very evident from the fact, on reading the invoices raised by WSL which indicates direct delivery of goods to ACC Jharkhand.

Even if for argument sake, it is taken that the transactions between the assessee and WSL is a transit sale, CST should have been paid on so called sale price of WSL to assessee which is absent in the case in hand and the procedure prescribed in section 6 of CST Act, which is not done.

There are two different prices indicated on the invoices one from WSL to assessee and another from assessee to ACC. Payment of excise duty under rule 9 of the Valuation Rules does not alter the status of the assessee as the commission agent.

The entire modus operandi was unearthed only after thorough investigation and claim of the assessee as to demand hit by limitation is incorrect.

The Service-tax liability arises when there is promotion/marketing of products; which in the case in hand is very evident.

On a plain reading of rule 6(1), it is obvious that if inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted goods, credit is not allowed except in the circumstances mentioned under sub-rule (2). A manufacturer who avails of the Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of final products which are chargeable to duty as also exempted goods, the manufacturer has to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products and the quantity of inputs used for the manufacture of exempted goods and take the Cenvat credit only on that quantity of inputs which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. A plain reading of this rule does not lead to any ambiguity, absurdity or defeat the provisions of the Act. Rule 6(2) and rule 6(3), read together mean that in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted products no Cenvat credit is allowed. It may, however, happen that the inputs are used in the manufacture of both exempted and dutiable goods, in which event if the register as required is maintained the credit can be taken for the quantity of inputs used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. If records are not maintained as required, the duty has to be paid in terms of rule 6(3). The presumptive tax payable in terms of rule 6(3) has been recognized and accepted by the Supreme Court in CCE v. Ballarpur Industries Ltd. 2007 (215) ELT 489. Rule 6(1) does not lead to the construction that if the manufacturer without maintaining the books, does not take credit for the duty paid on inputs for manufacture of exempted goods, rule 6(1) is satisfied. Rule 6(1) is satisfied only when the requirements of the rule 6(2) are satisfied, which requires register to be maintained for separate accounts of receipt, consumption and inventory of the inputs. Rule 6(3) provides that if separate accounts are not maintained then the amount has to be paid by a manufacturer. [Para 18]

The rule has to be read together to understand its object. Once a manufacturer manufactures from common inputs two final products, one dutiable and the other exempted, rule 6(2) would be attracted and on failure to maintain separate records, rule 6(3) would apply. Rule 6(1) in such an event would result in denying to the manufacturer Cenvat credit. Once the inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted goods irrespective of whether such inputs are used in the manufacture of dutiable goods, such manufacturer can avail of credit only in terms of rule 6(3). [Para 19]

A power to give benefit encompasses within itself the power to put conditions and restrictions under which credit is available. Power to give benefit also carries with it power to take it back or withdraw it. The rule if properly read starts with the words ‘Cenvat credit shall not be allowed’. Therefore, rule 6 makes it clear that insofar as inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods are concerned, no Cenvat credit is allowed. The rule making authority, however, noting that inputs may be used both for manufacturing final products which may be dutiable and other final products which are exempt, has provided that such manufacturer will be given credit insofar as inputs used for manufacturing of dutiable goods are concerned, if accounts are maintained in terms of the rules. Therefore, merely because the assessee contended that he was willing to forego credit on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final product it does not warrant a departure from the requirements of rule 6(2) and 6(3). The rules contemplate that on failure to maintain accounts in terms of rule 6(2) the consequences would be in terms of rule 6(3)(a) or (b). It is not possible to read down the rule as ‘amount not exceeding’ as was sought to be contended on behalf of the assessee. [Para 24]

Rule 6(1) is clear; the Cenvat credit cannot be availed of on inputs used in the manufacturing of exempted goods. It then adds the words except in the circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). A Court cannot read into the said rule something different or render otiose the words. The rule mandates specifically that an assessee seeking to avail Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, the only method by which he can avail of the credit is by following sub-rule (2). [Para 26]
