Mathew John, Technical Member - The appellant is in the business of executing turnkey projects in the field of rural electricity infrastructure and household electrification on turnkey basis mostly for State Electricity Boards. For execution of such contracts the appellant-company uses goods which are manufactured by it and also goods manufactured from other manufacturers.

2. The appellant entered into contracts with various Power Corporations and split the contract value with separate considerations specifically agreed upon for, -

(a)Material Supplied

(b)Civil Construction

(c)Erection and Commissioning

no service tax is paid for the value of material supplied. In respect of Civil Construction they were paying tax on 33% of the consideration received availing benefit of Notification 1/2006-S.T. They were paying tax on the consideration received for Erection and Commissioning.

3. For procuring such contracts the appellant uses the services of Commission Agents. This commission is paid on the full value of contracts that is for both material value and service value. Insurance premiums are also paid for the full value of the contracts.

4. The dispute involved in this case is whether the appellant is eligible to take credit for the full amount of tax paid on the commission paid to the Agents and for the full amount of tax paid on insurance premium paid. While the appellant claims that they should be allowed to take credit of the full amounts of such taxes paid, the Revenue contests that the commission paid should be split into that relating to procurement of goods and that relating to services by dividing the total commission and insurance premium in the ratio of value of materials supplied and value of services rendered and credit should be allowed only on service tax paid on commission and insurance relatable to value of services. Since the appellant had taken credit for full amounts of taxes the Revenue has issued a show cause notice dated 26-6-2008 demanding the excess credit taken which stands confirmed along with interest and penalties. The tax amount so demanded is Rs. 1,32,69,499/- for the period April, 2006 to Dec., 2007.

5. The Counsel for the appellant argues that valuation for the purpose of charging tax and allowing credit are two different issues and the Revenue has made a mistake by seeing the latter in the context of the former. They argue that they are eligible for exemption under Notification 12/2003-S.T., dated 20-6-2003 for the value of the project corresponding to the value of materials supplied and that should not be reason to deny credit in relation to tax paid on services relating to procurement of materials because procurement of materials is a necessary input service for erection and commissioning.

6. The Counsel for appellants also contest the demand on grounds of limitation. They contend that credit taken was declared in their ST-3 return and therefore there is no ground for invoking extended period of limitation.

7. The Revenue on the other hand submits that the appellant had two distinct contracts with their clients for supply of materials and for Erection and Commissioning. Just because commission and insurance premium are paid on the sum of the values of the two contracts it does not mean that services for executing the first contract is input service for executing the second contract.

8. We have considered arguments on both sides.

9. The matter is contentious. Under Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules credit can be taken only on tax paid on any input service received by a provider of output services. (For sake of clarity the portion of the rule dealing with inputs, excise duty thereon and final products is not being discussed since that situation is not dealt with here). Output service itself is defined under Rule 2(p) as a taxable service. When the contract for supply of material is a separate contract the service used for executing the contract cannot be considered as used in providing output service. A reading of the provisions of Rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules along with Rule 3 prima facie suggests strength in the stand of the department.

10. However the objection of the appellant that extended period of time cannot be invoked in this case prima facie is in appellant’s favour because the details of credit taken were being reported in ST-3 returns. We note that the demand which is within the period of one year is about Rs. Thirty lakhs. Having regard to this we order that the appellant should deposit an amount of Rs. 30 lakhs within eight weeks of receipt of this order for admission of the appeal. Subject to such deposit the balance dues arising out of the impugned order shall be waived and there shall be stay on collection of such amounts during the pendency of the appeal. The sales tax collections could be taken to be a trust fund in which the assessee had no interest. As a matter of fact the primary liability to pay sales tax on sales effected by the assessee was independent of the fact whether he collected sales tax from his buyers or not. The statute enabled the dealers to collect sales tax with a view to pass on their liability to their buyers. Therefore, if the sales tax collected by the assessee from his buyers during the year of account is in excess of his actual liability towards sales tax for that period, such excess would go only for his benefit. Therefore, the Tribunal was not correct in holding that the excess collections were not trading receipts of the assessee.

The decision of the Supreme Court in Chowringhee Sales Bureau (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1973] 87 ITR 542, fully supported the revenue’s stand that sales tax collections should be taken to be trading receipts and as and when the amounts are paid to discharge the sales tax liability, such amounts will have to be deducted.

So far as the separate accounts maintained by the assessee were concerned, they had been kept only on cash basis, that was, the sales tax collections made had been credited and the actual sales tax payments had been debited on the respective dates of collection and payment. Neither the sales tax collections nor the payments made by the assessee which had been recorded in the separated accounts had gone into the general accounts maintained by the assessee for his business, as the assessee had always been contending that he had been making collections as an agent of the Government and even the excess collection would have ultimately to be paid to the Government. In these separate accounts as and when the amounts had been paid to the sales tax authorities, they had been debited. An assessee may employ one method of accounting for one part of his business or one class of customers, and a different method for another part of his business or another class of customers. He may also keep accounts in respect of different parts of the same business on different basis. If such different methods are employed regularly and consistently the profits have to be computed in accordance with the respective methods, provided it results in a proper determination of the true profits. The assessee should, therefore, be taken to have adopted the cash basis so far as the sales tax collections were concerned and, therefore, the principle of the decision in Chowringhee Sales Bureau P. Ltd. v. CIT [1973] 87 ITR 542 (SC) would stand attracted. Therefore, it was held that the assessee had maintained his accounts in relation to the sales tax collections only on cash basis and, therefore, only when he pays out the amount for discharging his sales tax liability, he can claim deduction.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The assessee was registered with the Department for providing taxable services falling under the categories of Consulting Engineer, Maintenance or Repair Services and, Erection, Commissioning and Installation Services. It had entered into a contract with ‘B’ for supply and installation of BTS, Microcell and other Microwave equipments for telecommunication network. The invoice for the supply of telecommunication equipment was issued from its corporate office and the invoice for service portion was issued from its branches. The assessee was taking the Cenvat credit of tax paid on the input services used in the provision of taxable output services as well as the Cenvat credit distributed by its Corporate Office (i.e., input service distributor). It was noticed that the Cenvat credit distributed by the corporate office also pertaining to the input services used exclusively for the procurement of telecommunication equipments. The revenue took a view that the assessee was engaged in the sale of telecommunication equipments from its Corporate Office which was a trading activity and a non-taxable service outside the scope of the Act. Therefore, the trading activity fell within the meaning of exempted services as defined under rule 2(e). According to the revenue as the assessee had not maintained separate records at its Corporate Office for the input services commonly used in the taxable output services provided from the branches or in the exempted services provided from the Corporate Office, it was liable to utilize the Cenvat credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding twenty per cent of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services in terms of rule 6(3)(c). However, the assessee had utilized the entire Cenvat credit available with it towards the discharge of service tax liability on the taxable output services. Thus, the Commissioner confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had utilized excess Cenvat credit which was liable to be recovered from it. Besides that, the Commissioner also confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had wrongly availed of the Cenvat credit on insurance service, foreign consultancy service, etc., which were used exclusively in the provision of exempted services and, were utilized towards payment of service tax. The Commissioner also confirmed the demand disallowing the Cenvat credit on the services, viz., flower arrangements, garden maintenance, outdoor catering, real estate agent’s services for residential accommodation of its employees distributed by its Corporate Office on the ground that same could not be termed as input services defined under rule 2(l).

4. Rule 5 enunciates the taxability or otherwise of any expenditure incurred by a service provider in the course of providing a service, as part of taxable value. The position is briefly stated as under :

(1)All expenditure or costs incurred by the service provider in the course of providing a taxable service forms an integral part of the taxable value, irrespective of whether separately indicated in the invoice or bill issued by the service provider to his client.

(2)Expenditure or cost incurred by a service provider as a pure agent of his client (generally known as reimbursable expenditure) is not includible in the taxable value.

(3)However, if the service provider acts as an undisclosed agent, i.e., acting in his own name without disclosing that he is actually acting as an agent of his client, he cannot claim the expenditure incurred by him as reimbursable expenditure.

Role of C&F Agent :

Ordinarily, a C & F agent receives goods from the factory or premises of the manufacturer (the Principal) or his agents and stores these goods, dispatches these goods as per orders received from the Principal, arranges transport, etc. for the purpose and prepares invoices on behalf of the Principal. In respect of such service, the C&F agent receives commission on the basis of agreed terms. Therefore, an essential characteristic of any service, to fall in the category of C & F agent, is that the relationship between the service provider and receiver should be in the nature of principal (owner) and agent. The C & F Agent carries out all activities in respect of goods right from the stage of their clearances from the premises of the principal to its storage and delivery to the customers. [Para 5.4(iv)]

Premises of C&F Agent is Place of Removal under section 4(3)(c) of Central Excise Act, 1944 :

The clearing and forwarding agent is an agent of the principal. The goods stored by him after clearance from the factory would therefore, be stored on behalf of the principal, and as such the place where such goods are stored by the C&F agent would fall within the purview of sub-clause (iii) of clause (c) of section 4(3) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and as such would be the place of removal. [Para 5.4(vi)]

Services eligible for input service credit prior to 1-4-2008 :

Viewed from that light the services rendered by the C&F agent of clearing the goods from the factory premises, storing the same and delivering the same to the customer would fall within the ambit of rule 2(l) of the Rules as it stood prior to its amendment with effect from 1-4-2008, namely clearance of final products from the place of removal.

However, such services would not amount to sales promotion and would not be eligible for input service in that sense. [Para 5.4(vi)]

25.1 Trading and Hospitality Services

Distributive trade services and hospitality services fall under section 6 of Classification of Services.

Headings for distributive trade are - (a) wholesale trade (9961) (b) Retail Trade (9962).

Heading for hospitality services (Accommodation food and beverage services) is 9963. Groups in this heading are - Accommodation Service (of hotel, campsite) (99631), Accommodation service (rooms, hostels) (99632) and Food, edible preparation and beverage services (99633).

25.2 Services of commission agent

Services of commission agent in wholesale trade fall under 99611.

Services of commission agent in retail trade fall under 99621.

Note that services of Clearing and Forwarding Agent (C&F) do not fall under this head.

The GST rate is 18% (CGST 9% and SGST 9%) or IGST 18%.

Commission Agent is not required to register if his receipts of commission are less than Rs 20/10 lakhs per annum - Persons who supply goods or services or both on behalf of other taxable persons whether as an agent or otherwise require registration under GST even if his turnover is below Rs 20/10 lakhs per annum- section 24(1)(vii) of CGST Act.

There was misunderstanding that all commission agents require mandatory registration under GST irrespective of his commission income (i.e. even if income from commission is below 20/10 lakhs per annum).

Now it has been clarified that such registration is required only by C&F agents who stock and sale goods on behalf of Principal. Registration is not required by ordinarily commission agents who do not deal in goods or services themselves, if their annual turnover is less than Rs 20/10 lakhs - CBI&C Circular No. 57/31/2018-GST dated 4-9-2018.

Position in respect of del credere agent - Del credere agent is similar to commission agent. The only difference is that he guarantees payment to supplier of goods or services, if recipient does not pay. In some cases, the del credere agent himself pays to supplier and then recovers amount from recipient. In some case, the del credere agent advances short term loan to buyer and then buyer pays to the supplier.

CBI&C, vide circular No. 73/47/2018-GST dated 5-11-2018, has clarified that if del credere agent is like ordinary commission agent, there is no impact on GST liability.

However, if the del credere agent (DCA) received the goods and then supplies as per para 3 of Schedule I of CGST Act (i.e. he is C&F Agent), the value of interest will be included in the value of supply of goods by DCA to the recipient as per section 15(2)(d) of CGST Act. [Note that in this case, there are two separate transactions and tax invoices. The first transaction is when supplier raises tax invoice on DCA (who is similar to C&F Agent in this case) and second is when the DCA (who is similar to C&F Agent in this case) issues tax invoice on buyer].

We have considered the submissions of the parties and perused the material available on record. On a perusal of the assessment order, it is very much clear that in the course of assessment proceedings, the assessee has furnished every necessary details in respect of payment of Rs. 3,28,88,794 made to CFS/ICD operating under JNPT/BPT. On a perusal of the relevant details/documentary evidences, it is found that before the Assessing Officer, the assessee has not only produced the bills raised by the CFS/ICD on the assessee but also the bills raised by the assessee on the importers towards expenditure incurred on behalf of them. It is also noticed, in the final invoice drawn by the CFS/ICD submitted before the Assessing Officer all particulars of transactions were noted such as importer's address, liner code, vessels particulars of transaction, vessels' name and item code, description, rate charged, etc. These facts prove that the payment made by the assessee to the CFS/ICD were for/on behalf of importer of goods to whom the assessee rendered services as custom house agent. In fact, on a perusal of the observations made in the assessment order would reveal that the Assessing Officer has also accepted the fact that the assessee has made the payments to CFS/ICDs on behalf of its clients/importers as a custom house agent. The only reason for which the Assessing Officer has treated the payments to be subject to deduction of tax is, the assessee has directly paid them to the CFS/ICDS and it has received payments from the importer who have also not deducted tax at source on such payments made to the assessee. In our view, non-deduction of tax by the importers on the payments made to the assessee would not fasten the liability on the assessee under section 194C. When the Assessing Officer admits the fact that the assessee has made payments to CFS/ICD on behalf of importer as a custom house agent and the documentary evidence produced by the assessee also proves such fact, the Assessing Officer cannot disallow the payments under section 40(a)(ia) alleging non-deduction of tax by the assessee. When the expenditure/payment does not relate to the assessee, merely because the assessee has made payments on behalf of its client would not attract the liability of deduction of tax on the assessee. More so, when the assessee has not claimed such payments as expenditure by debiting to its Profit & Loss account. When the payments were made by the assessee on behalf of the importer and subsequently the assessee has raised bills for such payments on actual basis apart from separate bills raised for agency commission and it is evident that importers have reimbursed such expenditure to the assessee on actual basis and has also separately paid agency commission as per the bills raised, the payment to CFS/ICD logically has to be treated as expenditure of importers and not the assessee. Therefore, as a natural corollary if there was any default in deduction of tax on such payments, made to the CFS/ICDs, the liability should be on the person claiming the payment as expenditure. The assessee having never claimed these payments as expenditure, provisions of section 40(a)(ia) are not attracted. Even otherwise also, if the entire issue is looked at rationally and dispassionately it is to be noticed that during the relevant previous year, assessee has earned gross commission income of Rs. 83,47,952, which has been shown in the Profit & Loss account and the Assessing Officer has also not disputed the income shown by the assessee. Therefore, for earning such income of Rs. 83,47,952, neither the assessee can be expected to have incurred expenditure of more than Rs. 3 crore nor the disallowance can be made of that amount. In fact, the Tribunal, Mumbai Bench, in Rank Shipping Agency (P.) It cannot be said that the commission that the air travel agents get from the airlines is independent of and distinct from the services that they provide to the air-travellers and is relatable to the business that they provide to the airlines. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle was cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case was gone.

From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l), the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided that it is made taxable. Therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. It may also be said that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air travellers. If in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-travellers. On the other hand, it may be said that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited. The tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the petitioners that because of section 67(k), the nature of the tax itself changes was incorrect. Section 67(k), which provides the ‘measure of the tax’, is not unconnected with the main levy of the tax. The provision of section 67(k ) does not in any manner alter the nature of tax and does not shift it from the service rendered to the customer to the service rendered to the airlines. The contention, therefore, was clearly incorrect on facts.

The further argument that the notification dated 26-6-1997 restricts the tax to the commission alone and is repugnant to the scheme of the tax was obviously incorrect. The basis of the argument that the commission received from the airlines by the air travel agent is taken a measure for imposing a levy on a different service rendered to the customer by the agent, was itself incorrect. Therefore, the argument that the impugned provision of section 67(k) is repugnant to the general scheme of the Act was to be rejected.

As far as the second contention of the petitioner with regard to rule 6(7) was concerned, the language of rule 6(7) itself suggests that it is an optional matter. Therefore, the members of the petitioner-association, who had not exercised the option would had no concern with the validity of that rule while those who had opted for it, and majority of them having done so, could also not challenge the said validity.

In fact, it was not necessary for the High Court to take stock of the petitioners’ contention regarding the unconstitutionality of the rules but, even otherwise, there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found with that rule much less in the light of the submission made by the petitioners. The High Court was in complete agreement with the department that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration section 93 and section 94(2)(a) jointly. Indeed, there is a specific power under section 93 to grant exemption in any manner. Section 94(2)(a) speaks of the rule-making power on the subject of collection and recovery of service tax under section 66 and section 68. What is suggested by rule 6(7) is nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations. It was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule- making power. It does not amount to an independent levy again. Therefore, it was to be held that there was nothing wrong with the rule in question. This rule provides for an independent measure as the basic airfare. For this reason, no merit was found in the writ which was liable to be dismissed.

order, the assessee had entered into agreement with various companies for providing C&F agent service. The facts brought out by the Commissioner (Appeals) further clarifies that as per agreement between the assessee and companies the assessee is providing various services which include distribution of goods for which the assessee has charged commission and other income, etc. The agreement between the parties further specifies various expenses to be incurred by the assessee on behalf of the clients and reimbursement of such expenses by the clients. It is admitted fact that in line of C&F business the C&F agents will incur various expenses while rendering services to their clients and the same will be reimbursed by the clients against invoices/debit notes. In the instant case also the assessee has incurred various expenses on behalf of clients and while billing to the clients for services rendered a separate bill/debit note has been issued to recover various expenses incurred on behalf of the clients. The assessee in the books of account has accounted services charges/commission received from the clients for rendering C&F agent service as its income but reimbursement of expenses has been squared off in the parties account. On the other hand, the clients have deducted TDS on total payments made to the assessee including reimbursement of expenses. Thus obviously there will be a difference between total payments made by the clients and TDS deducted thereon as per Form no. 26AS and gross receipt booked by the assessee in its books of account. The Assessing Officer has noted difference in gross receipt as per books of account of the assessee and gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS. The assessee has explained difference between gross receipt and claimed that said difference is on account of reimbursement of expenses. The assessee had filed reconciliation explaining difference with party wise service charges received and reimbursement of amount received towards reimbursement of expenses. The Assessing Officer never disputed these facts. However, he rejected reconciliation filed by the assessee only for the reason that the assessee could not prove with sufficient documents that reimbursement of expenses was accounted in the books of clients. [Para 7]

The reason given by the Assessing Officer to make addition towards difference in gross receipt appears to be baseless and incorrect because the assessee can file whatever evidence the Assessing Officer wants to prove its financial transactions with its clients but it is incorrect on the part of the Assessing Officer to expect the assessee to produce books of account of its clients. The only reason for the Assessing Officer to make addition towards difference in gross receipt is doubt and suspicion on expenses booked by the clients in their books of account. The Assessing Officer is miserably failed to understand the concept of accounting because deduction of TDS on total payments including reimbursement of expenses itself is a sufficient proof that the clients have accounted expenses incurrred by the assessee on behalf of the clients. The clients have deducted TDS on total payments including reimbursement of expenses because of this there is difference between gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS reported by the clients while deducting TDS under sections 194J and 194C, when compared to gross receipt reported in the books of account of the assessee. The assessee is following the method of accounting as per which it was accounting service charges received from the clients towards rendering various services as its income and reimbursement of expenses is squared off in the parties account. The assessee has filed a party wise reconciliation along with ledger account explaining the difference. As per chart filed by the assessee the gross receipt towards C&F service charges and other income exactly matches with gross receipt booked by the assessee in its books of account. The assessee had also reconciled difference between reimbursement of expenses and as per bills filed by the assessee amount received from clients towards reimbursement of expenses is more than the amount of difference noticed by the Assessing Officer from Form No. 26AS. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making addition towards difference in gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS and as per books of account of the assessee.

The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts and also by considering reconciliation filed by the assessee has rightly deleted addition made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 8]

The appeal filed by the revenue deserved to be dismissed. [Para 9]

Indeed, there is a specific power under section 93 to grant exemption in any manner. Section 94(2)(a) speaks of the rule-making power on the subject of collection and recovery of service tax under section 66 and section 68. What is suggested by rule 6(7) is nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations. It was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule-making power. It does not amount to an independent levy again. Therefore, it was to be held that there was nothing wrong with the rule in question. This rule provides for an independent measure as the basic airfare. For this reason, no merit was found in the writ which was liable to be dismissed.

The assessee was awarded a contract by the State Government under the Sujalam Sufalam Spreading Canal Pipe Line Project for laying pipelines. The assessee by considering the said service as falling under the category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ paid the service tax on the same after availing the benefit of Modvat credit and filed due service tax returns with the department. Based upon the enquiries conducted and investigations made, the revenue entertained a view that the above laying down of pipelines did not amount to providing services under the category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’, and the service being non-taxable, the assessee was not entitled to avail the Cenvat credit. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee raising demand by invoking the provisions of rule 6(3)(c), which provide for restriction for utilizing of Cenvat credit to the extent of 20 per cent only, in the event of non-maintenance of separate accounts for inputs and input services used for both exempted and taxable services. On adjudication, the Commissioner held that inasmuch the services of laying down pipelines had been held to be a non-taxable service, the same could not be equated with exempted services and, as such, rule 6(3)(c) could not be invoked. He further held that as the assessee had maintained separate Cenvat credit accounts project wise, the allegation of maintenance of a common credit account was incorrect and, as such, rule 6(3)(c) had no applicability. He, accordingly, dropped the demand. Though in the instant appeal the assessee did not dispute service tax liability, yet challenged impugned order on ground of limitation.

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and trading of synthetic fabric. During the year, it paid certain amount as agency commission and overseas commission and claimed deduction of the same. It stated that (i) the agency commission had been paid to the local agents for their services provided for introducing to overseas parties, to whom it sold the goods on principal to principal basis, (ii) in the invoices from the gross amount of sales deduction upto 12.5 per cent had been given in the name of commission, and (iii) in the books after recording gross sales, the deduction was separately recorded as overseas commission.

The Assessing Officer accepted the local commission paid, but disallowed the overseas commission under section 37(1) on the grounds that (i) no services had been rendered by the overseas agents inasmuch as no details/documents of further sales by these agents had been furnished by the assessee, (ii) from the perusal of sample contract notes furnished by the assessee with overseas agents it was evident that the same was a contract for purchase and sale of goods and commission had been merely deducted from the sales invoice at a flat rate without rendering of any services by these overseas agents, and (iii) in all such contract notes name of the Indian agents who introduced the assessee to these overseas parties had been written for which commission had already been paid by the assessee to the Indian agents. Thus, for the same invoice, commission had been paid to local agents as well as overseas agents. He, therefore, added the amount of overseas commission to the income of the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the impugned addition made by the Assessing Officer.

The assessee was carrying on business as commission agent of foodgrains and entries in its books of account showed that payments to ‘P’ were made on behalf of ‘S’. Thus, the assessee derived income only by way of commission on aforesaid transactions. A press note issued by the Ministry of Finance has clarified that payment made by commission agents for goods received by them for sale on commissions or consignment basis does not attract section 40A(3) because such payments are not expenditure deductible in computing taxable income of the commissions agent.

In the instant case, the Department also had not brought any material on record to prove that the assessee had made purchases of goods in question on his own account and not on commission basis. The genuineness of the transaction and the identity of payee had not been disputed. The assessee had also explained the exceptional circumstances under which the payment had to be made in cash. Therefore, on facts, the payments made by the assessee in his capacity as commission agent did not attract section 40A(3) and even if this section was assumed to be applicable, payments in question were clearly covered by exceptional circumstances provided in rule 6DD(j). Hence, the addition was deleted.

Relevant case law 4. The validity of rule 6(7) was challenged in the case of Airlines Agents Association v. Union of India [2002] 121 Taxman 298 (Mad.). The High Court upheld the validity of rule 6(7). The High Court held (i) that there was absolutely no breach of any fundamental right by passing rule 6(7) and nothing wrong could be found in that rule, (ii) that this rule would have to be viewed taking into consideration sections 93 and 94(2)(a) jointly, (iii) that what was suggested by rule 6(7) was nothing but a probably more beneficial calculation, which would spare an air travel agent of so many other botherations, and (iv ) that it was, therefore, clear that no fault could be found with the rule at least on the ground that it was beyond the rule-making power.

In Airlines Agents Association’s case (supra), it was contended that the commission paid by the airlines is in respect of services to the airlines and not services to the customer and, therefore, the said commission should not be taxed. The High Court rejected that contention and held as under:

". . . It is not as if the air travel agents get a fixed commission or income from the airlines irrespective of the passages booked by them in favour of the customers in the nature of a ‘retainer fee’ or ‘guarantee money’, at least that is not the case pleaded before us. Therefore, unless the air travel agents book the tickets and thereby unless they provide the services to the customers, they do not become entitled to any commission. Their commission is entirely dependent on and connected with the passage they book for the customers. It cannot, therefore, be said that the commission that the air travel agents get from the airlines is independent of and distinct from the services that they provide to the air-travellers and are relatable to the business that they provide to the airlines. On the other hand, since there is no guarantee money given or no fixed commission given, which has no nexus with the bookings that an air travel agent achieves for the airlines, it has to be said that the air travel agent’s commission is integrally connected with the booking that he makes and in the process, the services that he gives to the customers. Once this hurdle is cleared, the very basis of the argument on behalf of the petitioners’ case goes away. From the specific language of the provisions, particularly of section 65(3) and section 65(48)(l), the nature of the service, which is taxed, is absolutely clear. It is only on the basis of the service that is provided which is made taxable. In our opinion, therefore, the commission that the air travel agents get is on account of this service because in the absence of this service being given to the customers, an air travel agent is not to get anything. We may also say that the customer gets the service not for any extra charges. The air travel agents are not supposed to charge anything more than the value fixed for the passages by the airlines. Therefore, the commission that is earned by the air travel agent has a direct nexus with the booking that he makes for the air-travellers. If, in the process, the airlines is benefited and offers some commission, that would not change the nature of the service provided by the air travel agent and it cannot be said that the service is provided only to the airlines and not to the air-traveller. On the other hand, we may say that it is because the air travel agent gives service to the air-traveller that the airlines is benefited, the tax is intended and in reality is imposed as against the service provided by the air travel agent to the customer in the absence of which, there would be no question of any commission. The contention of the learned counsel that because of section 67(k) the nature of the tax itself changes, is incorrect." (p. 305)

The principals, agreed to give commission of 1 per cent of the purchase price besides the reimbursement of expenses incurred for the purpose of purchasing rubber and other commodities. The assessee was buying rubber and latex from the agricultures from Keral for and on behalf of its principal as their agent. The dealings in rubber are controlled by the Rubber Board. The Rubber Board had also intimated the principals that the assessee had been recognised as their agent to purchase and despatch rubber on their behalf.

The CBDT in Circular No. 452, dated 17-3-1987 has laid down the principles of distinction between kutcha arhatiya and pucca arhatiya. On a perusal of distinctions between kutcha arhatiya and pucca arhativa as enumerated in the above circular and further illustrations given by the CBDT Circular Nos. 564&572, dated 5-7-1990 respectively wherein it has been made clear that turnover and sales are interchangeable and sole reliance cannot be placed on the definition of ‘turnover’ under section 2(o ) of the Haryana General Sales-tax Act, the contrary definition as contained in the Central Sales-tax Act cannot be ignored Since the assessee was receiving commission @1% of purchase value besides reimbursement of expenses incurred for the purposes of purchase and if the Assessing Officer’s contention was accepted that the assessee was trading in these items, there was no question of receiving fixed commission and there should, in fact, be bearing of profit or loss in each separate transaction depending on market conditions but this was not the case of the assessing authority nor it was borne out from the record. The Assessing Officer had not worked out the profit as such earned by the assessee from trading in rubber and latex. Therefore, taking into consideration the facts that the Rubber Board had registered the assessee as an authorised agent to purchase and despatch rubber on behalf of different principals no sales as such had been effected by the assessee, the goods purchased were transferred to the principals at the cost price, the goods were transferred not against ‘C Form’ but against ‘F From’ of sales tax issued by the transferee, the commission agency agreement between the principals and the assessee etc., the role of assessee was that of agent and not of trader. Secondly, according to the CBDT Circular Nos. 564&572 dated 5-7-1990. The turnover and sales are interchangeable and as the assessee had not made any sale rubber or latex, the total transaction conducted to earn commission would not be regarded as ‘sale’ or ‘turnover’ of the assessee. In view of the above facts and circumstances, for working out 80HHC deduction, it was the commission earned which was to be considered for working out the said deduction and not the aggregate transaction made to earn commission and, hence, no interference was needed with the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

The assessee was an agent of a foreign company, i.e., GMC. It procured orders/contracts from Indian Railways for GMC and received commission on which service tax had been paid under the category of ‘Business auxiliary services’. The commission, however, was not received directly from GMC but was received through Indian Railways in Indian currency. As per understanding between GMC and Indian Railways, GMC received payment from Indian Railways after deducting the commission payable to the assessee. The assessee filed refund claim on the ground that the services provided by it to GMC on which service tax had been paid were export of services in terms of rule 3(3). The Assistant Commissioner rejected the refund claim on the ground that since the commission was received in non-convertible Indian currency in view of the proviso to sub-rule (3) of rule 3 same could not be treated as export of services. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assistant Commissioner.

On appeal :

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1984-85 - Assessee-company was carrying on business of manufacture of moulded luggage - During relevant accounting year assessee paid certain commission to its agent M, who obtained orders from Canteen Stores Department, Government Department - M, which was a textile firm, stated in a letter that it appointed B, who was able to render services to assessee - In an affidavit filed on behalf of B, it was admitted that they had received certain commission in question from M by account payee cheques, deposited in its account - Assessee had already been allowed deduction in respect of commission paid to M in earlier years - Whether it could not be Said that M had not rendered any services to assessee merely on grounds that there was no correspondence between assessee and M and that B had withdrawn entire amount in cash immediately on deposit in its account and as such it was an allowable deduction - Held, yes.

FACT: The assessee-company was one of the topmost moulded luggage manufacturers. During the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1984-85, it paid certain commission to its agent M and claimed deduction. On enquiry the assessee submitted that the commission was paid by account payee cheques for obtaining orders of supply of the goods manufactured by the assessee, from Canteen Stores Department, Government of India, Ministry of Defence. However, the IAC disallowed the deduction on the grounds that M was a small partnership firm dealing in textiles, that M had never any dealing with Canteen Stores Department before and after the aforesaid deal on behalf of the assessee, that the major portion of commission was paid by M to another concern B, that there was no correspondence between B and the Canteen Stores Department, that the bank account of M and B revealed that commission was received in the year in question but the payments to B were made in subsequent years and immediately after depositing the cheques, large amounts were withdrawn in cash which were highly suspicious in nature.

On appeal, there being a difference of opinion between the members of the Tribunal, the matter was referred to the opinion of the Third Member under section 255(4).

HELD (PER ORDER OF THE THIRD MEMBER)

The assessee was an agent of a foreign company, ‘GMC’ and had provided services of sourcing of the contract from Indian railways. The assessee wrongly paid service tax under category of ‘Business auxiliary service’, on the commission it got from ‘GMC’ through Indian railways. Later it claimed refund of same as it was exempted under rule 3. The adjudicating authority rejected the refund claim on the ground that it was hit by rule 3(1)(b) as assessee had received commission in Indian rupees instead of convertible foreign exchange. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the adjudication order.

On appeal :

Rule 9(1)(c) refers to challan on the document showing payment of service tax. In terms of rule 6(2) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994, the assessee is required to deposit service tax in form, i.e., TR-6 Challan and, therefore, TR-6 Challans submitted by the assessee should have been taken to be an adequate proof/evidence of payment of service tax entitling it to claim the Cenvat credit. The impugned order of the Commissioner was, therefore, liable to be set aside on that ground alone. However, the Commissioner had not dealt with that and other aspects of the matter and, therefore, the matter should go back to him for a fresh consideration. [Para 4]

The amendment relevant for the present purpose was made under the Notification GSR 790(c), dated 3-12-2004 with effect from 1-1-2005. No Cenvat credit is available on inputs and input services which are used in providing output services which are exempt from levy of service tax [Refer to Rule 6(1) of the Credit Rules]. What are the Cenvat credit restrictions which apply to a service provider who is engaged in providing both taxable and exempt services?

As per Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, a service provider of both exempt and taxable services shall have following two options for claiming the Cenvat credit on inputs and input services:

Option A [Rule 6(2)] – Maintenance of separate records - The service provider shall maintain separate accounts for receipts, consumption/use and inventory of inputs and input services which are used in providing services other than exempted services. The Cenvat credit shall be available only on those inputs and input services which are used for provision of output services, excluding exempted services.

Option B [Rule 6(3)] – Non maintenance of separate records - Where a service provider opts for not maintaining separate records, the Cenvat credit can be paid under any of the following three methods:

pay an amount equal to 6% of the value of exempted services;

pay an amount equal to the Cenvat credit on inputs and input services attributable to exempted services, as determined under sub-rule (3A) of Rule 6; or

maintain separate accounts for the receipt, consumption, inventory of inputs and take the Cenvat credit only on inputs used for the provision of output services, excluding exempted services and pay an amount equal to the Cenvat credit on input services attributable to the exempted services as determined under sub-rule (3A) of Rule 6.

Commission on purchase not covered under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' :

The conjunctive 'and' between the words 'clearing' and 'forwarding' indicate and mean that where clearing operations are separate from forwarding operations, levy of tax would not be attracted i.e. there would be no charge of tax if the transaction involved only one of the two components of the conjuncted service namely 'clearing' and 'forwarding'. The expression a clearing and forwarding agent in relation to clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner' contemplates only one person operating both as the clearing and the forwarding agent; and if a person has rendered service as forwarding agent without rendering any service as 'clearing agent' he could not be considered to have rendered both services as a 'clearing and forwarding agent'. [Para 2]

'Clearing and forwarding operations' would be various activities having a bearing on clearance of goods and would normally involve documentary processes and arrangements for transfer of goods to their destination; and may also involve clearance at subsequent stages during forwarding operations. A clearing and forwarding agent normally undertakes the following activities :-

(a)

Receiving goods from the factories or premises of the principal or his agents;

(b)

Warehousing these goods;

(c)

Receiving despatch orders from the principal;

(d)

Arranging despatch of goods as per the directions of the principal by engaging transport on his own or through the authorised transporters of the principal;

(e)

Maintaining records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; and

(f)

Preparing invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 3]

Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of the enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of goods, the service would not be a taxable service as defined in section 65(105)(j) read with section 65(25) which defines a clearing and forwarding agent. [Para 4]

In this case, assessee neither receives goods from the factory premises of the principal; warehouses such goods; receives despatch orders from the principal; arranges despatch of goods as per directions of the principal by engaging a transport on its own or through authorised transporters of the principal; nor maintains records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; nor even prepares invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 5]

Hence, assessee, in no manner, engages in any of the six enumerated activities which constitute clearing and forwarding operations. It never has custody of the picture tubes; does not receive them from manufacturers of the tubes; does not warehouse the picture tubes; does not receive despatch orders from manufacturers of picture tubes which are directly forwarded to manufacturers of the TV sets; does not arrange despatch of goods as per directions either of the manufacturers of picture tubes or manufacturers of TV sets; nor engages transport on its own or through authorised transporters of manufacturers of picture tubes or manufacturers of TV sets; and does not maintain records of the receipt and despatch of picture tubes and the stock available at the warehouse; nor prepares invoices either on behalf of the principal manufacturers or manufacturers of TV sets. [Para 6]

There is neither the conjunctive service of clearing and forwarding provided by the assessee nor either of the services of clearing or forwarding. As the assessee has not provided any of the core enumerated activities of clearing and forwarding operations, it has not directly or indirectly provided any service connected with clearing and forwarding operations in any manner to any other person. That the assessee was not a consignment agent is also not in dispute. [Para 7]

Therefore, assessee is not liable to Service Tax under the taxable head 'clearing and forwarding agency'. Even otherwise, commission agents were exempt from service tax vide Notification No. 13/2003 dated 20-5-2003 from 1-7-2003 upto 9-9-2004. Revenue proceeded on the basis that the assessee had provided 'clearing and forwarding agency' service, contrary to the distinct classification w.e.f. 1-7-2003; the services provided by it constituted Business Auxiliary Service. [Para 8]

The payments for purchases had not been made by cheques through banking channels. Besides, the assessee had not produced any evidence, nor placed any material to show that those parties/farmers existed in the respective villages. [Para 7.2]

Two sister concerns of the assessee had purchased the agricultural produce in auction through the assessee. The purchases made by them in the presence of the officials, supported by documentary evidence were genuine. It was a fact that the amounts due from the two sister concerns had been shown outstanding and the nature of such credits was purchases of cotton and narma from the assessee and such entries appeared in their books of account. The assessee, in his books, had shown the amounts due from his sister concerns as sundry debtors and the corresponding credit entries in their books of account justified such action. Therefore, no fault could be found with the entries made in the books of account of the sister concerns, because their balance sheets depicted correct position about their assets and liabilities. But if the credits appearing in the balance sheet remained unexplained, the same would warrant addition in the instant case, because the credits appeared in the balance sheet of the assessee. If those credits were not genuine, the balance sheet would show the difference on asset side, higher than the total of liabilities. Therefore, the addition under section 68 would be called for in the instant case, and not in the cases of sister concerns. [Paras 7.3]

In the instant case, the assessee had not carried on any trading on its own. He had earned income by way of Dami on the transactions effected through him as a commission agent. Income received by way of Dami was fully supported by documentary evidence. Therefore, the question of rejection of book results did not arise in the instant case. Thus, the objection raised in that regard was untenable. [Para 7.5]

3.2 Calculation of value of common inputs in case of exempted final products - The formulae as given in rule 6(3A) are only in respect of Cenvat credit attributable to (a ) inputs used for provision of exempted services and (b) input services used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services.

There is no formula to calculate Cenvat credit attributable to value of inputs used in manufacture of exempted final product, when inputs are common. In any case, consumables, fuel, dies, toolings, etc., will be ‘common inputs’ in most of the cases.

In absence of any formula, the only option with the assessee is to calculate the same either on basis of input-output ratio, or on the basis of formula similar to the one applicable for calculation of inputs used for provision of exempted services.

3.3 Treatment of traded goods - A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods. The sale may be within India or outside. Obviously, there will be many common input services. Now, traded goods are not ‘exempt goods’. It is also not ‘service’, since one is not providing services to anyone else. Further, one cannot provide service to oneself.

Including the entire value of turnover of traded goods into dividend (above line) will be highly unfair to the assessee since the services attributable to such traded goods will certainly not be proportional to value of the traded goods, in cases where the assessee is both manufacturer as well as trader.

As the formulae stand today, turnover of traded goods can neither be included in divisor (below the line) nor the dividend (above the line). This would give higher Cenvat credit to the assessee. It would be fair to provide some percentage of turnover of traded goods (by way of rules), which should be added to dividend (above the line) to give fair results.

If no such provision is made in rules, there is a strong case to argue that it is not includible in divisor as well as dividend at all, since it is neither exempted goods nor exempted service (rather it is not ‘service’ at all).

3.4 Supplies to EOU, SEZ, etc. - Rule 6(6) states that provisions of rules 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply in case of excisable goods removed to SEZ, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting.

According to strict interpretation, this turnover shall not come either in denominator or in dividend. This would be unfair. It will give absurd results, particularly when sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., are large, as amount to be reversed will be very heavy. Sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., should appear in denominator, as per correct VAT principles.

3.5 Services specified in rule 6(5) - As per rule 6(5) in case of specified 16 services, full Cenvat credit of input service is available even if these services are partly used in manufacture of exempted final product/output services. This rule has not been amended even if rule 6(3) has been recast with effect from April 1, 2008. Cenvat credit in relation to these services should be outside the calculations made as per rule 6(3A) and entire credit will be available, without any reversal.

3.6 Treatment of opening balance - An assessee always tries to utilise Cenvat credit first and then pay through PLA/GAR-7. However, despite his efforts, some opening balance is possible, particularly in initial stages of production/provision of services.

Principally, the formula should apply to opening balances also.

3.7 Service tax paid under reverse charge method - In cases where service tax is paid under reverse charge method (particularly GTA services and sponsorship services), what would be the treatment ? As per amended rules, in case of GTA service, this amount should be paid by GAR-7 challan and not by cash with effect from March 1, 2008. However, this is not ‘output service’ as per amended rule 2(p). Hence, it appears that this amount is ‘input service’ and will be ‘service tax paid’. It will neither appear in divisor nor in dividend, but proportional reversal will have to be made.

This question relates to a situation where the C&F agent makes the payment to the airlines or other carrier of goods or passenger. In reply to this question, the Board has clearly laid down in Circular no. 715, dated 8-8-1995 that 'As regards payments made to clearing and forwarding agents for carriage of goods, the same shall be subjected to tax deduction at source under section 194C of the Act.' It is not the intention of the Legislature that neither the C&F agent deducts the tax when it makes the payment to the carrier nor the assessee deducts the tax at source when it makes payment to C&F agent. (1) There is no such provision which you have in mind. The sub-agent is liable for service tax on commission. He can raise invoice on main agent and then main agent can avail of the Cenvat credit of service tax paid by him. Thus, there is no double taxation.

FACT: ■

The assessee was an individual and carrying business as a commission agent by selling chillies on behalf of farmers to registered dealers (GST Dealers). The assessee filed the return of income for the assessment year 2022-23 admitting a total income of Rs. 10.51 lakhs.

■

The CPC processed the return of income under section 143(1) wherein it was observed that the CPC had allowed the tax credit amounting to Rs. 10,271 as against Rs. 48,593 claimed by the assessee in the return of income.

■

The assessee also filed a petition under section 154 seeking re-processing of the return by allowing the correct TDS credit claimed by the assessee, wherein the CPC had rejected the petition filed under section 154.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The CBDT Circular No. 452, dated 17-3-1986 relied on by the assessee and the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Thota Venkateswarlu v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 290 (Viz) of 2024, dated 27-8-2024] wherein the Tribunal has relied on the decision of this Bench in the case of Yegneswari General Traders v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 39(Viz) of 2024, dated 18-3-2024] have been gone through. From the above it is clear that Kaccha Arahtias turnover includes only the gross commission and not the sales effected on behalf of their principals. In the present case, it is a fact that the assessee is only a licensed commission agent in Agricultural Market Committee Yard, Guntur. Therefore, the Circular issued by the CBDT (supra) squarely applies to the assessee and hence the assessee is acted only as an agent (kaccha arahtia) and therefore it is eligible to get credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source and there is no short fall of TDS as concluded by the revenue authorities. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to grant credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source in the case of the assessee. [Para 7]

■

Considering the identical facts and circumstances of the assessee's case with that of the appeal decided by the Tribunal in the case of Yegneswari General Traders (supra) wherein the Tribunal has relied on the decision of this Bench in the case of Thota Venkateswarlu (supra) and Subba Reddy Mareddy v. ITO [IT Appeal No. 96(VIZ) of 2024, dated 25-11-2024], following the principle of consistency, there is no hesitation to set-aside the orders of the revenue authorities and direct the Assessing Officer - CPC to grant credit of the entire amount deducted as tax at source in the case of the assessee. Thus, the grounds raised by the assessee are allowed. [Para 8]

■

In the result, appeal of the assessee is allowed.[Para 9]

The assessee utilized the credit of service tax paid on input services and the credit allotted to it by its Corporate Office as ISD (Input service distributor). There was no allegation or finding that the assessee had provided taxable and exempted services. The assessee was one of the constituents of a company engaged in trading of telecommunication equipments. The Corporate Office of the company raised invoices for sale of the equipment. The Department had treated it as a provision of exempt services relying on definition of exempted services under rule 2(e ). [Para 4]

In the case of Bhel-Ge Turbine Service (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2010] 27 STT 214 (Bang. - CESTAT) it was held that exempted services mentioned in rule 2(e ) covered only services which were notified and, prima facie, could not be interpreted to include the services on which no tax was levied under section 66. Therefore, prima facie, the trading activity involved did not constitute exempted services for the assessee to come within the mischief of rule 6(3)(c). Therefore, prima facie, the demand of service tax in that regard was not sustainable. [Para 5]

Credit of service tax to the tune of Rs. 15,12,673 transferred by the Corporate Office as ISD, was found to be inadmissible, as the same pertained to supply of telecommunication equipments which constituted exempted services. Similarly, part of the credit to the extent of Rs. 1,53,30,380 received by the assessee on transfer by the ISD was held to be not admissible for the reason that the Corporate Office had failed to follow provisions of rule 6(3)(c). Credit of Rs. 87,111 was found relatable to input services, such as flower arrangement, garden maintenance, outdoor catering, real estate etc. distributed by the Corporate Office, found to be not admissible input services. [Para 6]

The basis of those demands was that the credit transferred by the Corporate Office was not admissible either as it did not qualify as an input service or as the Corporate Office had not fulfilled the conditions of rule 6(3)(c). The Corporate Office registered with the service tax department could not be held to have rendered the taxable and exempted services for the reason that it was engaged in trading activity. Therefore, these demands were, prima facie, not sustainable. [Para 6.1]

The Tribunal in the case of CST v. Godfrey Philips India (P.) Ltd. [2009] 22 STT 259 (Ahd. - CESTAT), held that the eligibility or otherwise of service tax credit has to be examined at end of ISD only . Therefore, prima facie, adjudicating authority had no jurisdiction to raise question of admissibility or otherwise of impugned credit allotted by ISD and availed of by the assessee. In the circumstances, there was to be total waiver of pre-deposit requirement of the dues adjudged against the assessee and recovery thereof was to be stayed. [Para 7]

The assessee is in the business of clearing and forwarding agent. As per fact brought out by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order, the assessee had entered into agreement with various companies for providing C&F agent service. The facts brought out by the Commissioner (Appeals) further clarifies that as per agreement between the assessee and companies the assessee is providing various services which include distribution of goods for which the assessee has charged commission and other income, etc. The agreement between the parties further specifies various expenses to be incurred by the assessee on behalf of the clients and reimbursement of such expenses by the clients.

It is admitted fact that in line of C&F business the C&F agents will incur various expenses while rendering services to their clients and the same will be reimbursed by the clients against invoices/debit notes. In the instant case also the assessee has incurred various expenses on behalf of clients and while billing to the clients for services rendered a separate bill/debit note has been issued to recover various expenses incurred on behalf of the clients. The assessee in the books of account has accounted services charges/commission received from the clients for rendering C&F agent service as its income but reimbursement of expenses has been squared off in the parties account. On the other hand, the clients have deducted TDS on total payments made to the assessee including reimbursement of expenses. Thus obviously there will be a difference between total payments made by the clients and TDS deducted thereon as per Form no. 26AS and gross receipt booked by the assessee in its books of account. The Assessing Officer has noted difference in gross receipt as per books of account of the assessee and gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS. The assessee has explained difference between gross receipt and claimed that said difference is on account of reimbursement of expenses. The assessee had filed reconciliation explaining difference with party wise service charges received and reimbursement of amount received towards reimbursement of expenses. The Assessing Officer never disputed these facts. However, he rejected reconciliation filed by the assessee only for the reason that the assessee could not prove with sufficient documents that reimbursement of expenses was accounted in the books of clients. [Para 7]

The reason given by the Assessing Officer to make addition towards difference in gross receipt appears to be baseless and incorrect because the assessee can file whatever evidence the Assessing Officer wants to prove its financial transactions with its clients but it is incorrect on the part of the Assessing Officer to expect the assessee to produce books of account of its clients. The only reason for the Assessing Officer to make addition towards difference in gross receipt is doubt and suspicion on expenses booked by the clients in their books of account. The Assessing Officer is miserably failed to understand the concept of accounting because deduction of TDS on total payments including reimbursement of expenses itself is a sufficient proof that the clients have accounted expenses incurrred by the assessee on behalf of the clients. The clients have deducted TDS on total payments including reimbursement of expenses because of this there is difference between gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS reported by the clients while deducting TDS under sections 194J and 194C, when compared to gross receipt reported in the books of account of the assessee. The assessee is following the method of accounting as per which it was accounting service charges received from the clients towards rendering various services as its income and reimbursement of expenses is squared off in the parties account. The assessee has filed a party wise reconciliation along with ledger account explaining the difference. As per chart filed by the assessee the gross receipt towards C&F service charges and other income exactly matches with gross receipt booked by the assessee in its books of account. The assessee had also reconciled difference between reimbursement of expenses and as per bills filed by the assessee amount received from clients towards reimbursement of expenses is more than the amount of difference noticed by the Assessing Officer from Form No. 26AS. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making addition towards difference in gross receipt as per Form No. 26AS and as per books of account of the assessee.

The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts and also by considering reconciliation filed by the assessee has rightly deleted addition made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 8]

The appeal filed by the revenue deserved to be dismissed. [Para 9]

Now this specific provision has been deleted w.e.f. 1-4-2008. 9.11-1 Options available to manufacturer manufacturing both dutiable and exempt goods

The manufacturer/service provider had two options upto 31-3-2008 —

Maintain separate inventory - Maintain separate inventory and accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services. In such cases, he should not avail Cenvat credit of the inputs and input services which are used in exempted final services at all — Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules. [Maintenance of separate records for ‘fuel’ was not required. This relaxation has been removed w.e.f. 16-5-2005].

Really, rule 6(2) had become impractical to a manufacturer w.e.f. 10-9-2004 i.e. date from which he is eligible to avail Cenvat credit of input services also. It may be possible to maintain separate records for inputs used in exempted goods but it is practically impossible to keep separate records of ‘input services’ as many of such ‘input services’ (e.g. telephone, audit, courier, construction etc.) are bound to be common.

Pay 10% ‘amount’ if separate inventory and records not maintained - If the manufacturer/service provider opts not to maintain such separate accounts, he has to pay an amount equal to 10% of the ‘price’ of such exempted goods. Such payment can be made by debit to Cenvat credit account or PLA [rule 6(3)(b)].

Education cess and SAH education cess is payable only on ‘duties of excise’. ‘Amount’ is not ‘duty’. Hence, education cess or SAH education cess is not payable on such ‘amount’.

9.11-2 Credit of service tax limited if service provider does not maintain separate accounts

Till 31-3-2008, in case of output service, if he did not maintain separate accounts, he could utilise Cenvat only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable on final product. He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services [The limit was 35% upto 10-9-2004].

For example, assume that service tax payable on output service is Rs 100. Service tax paid on input service is Rs 15. These input services are used both for taxable output services and exempt/non-taxable output services. In such case, assessee can avail and utilise credit of entire Rs 15. However, if tax paid on input services is Rs 75, and these are used both for exempted and output services, then assessee can actually utilise credit of only Rs 20. He will have to pay balance in cash, even if credit of Rs 55 is still available in his books.

He may take credit of Rs 75 in his Service Tax (Receivable) Account, but can utilise credit of Rs 20.

The balance may remain in his Service Tax Credit Account. He can utilise it in future if opportunity arises.

In Mundra Port and Special Economic Zone Ltd. v. CCE (2011) 33 STT 364 = 15 taxmann.com 33 (CESTAT), it was held that this credit could be carried forward on 1-4-2008 and utilised later.

Note that this provision does not apply w.e.f. 1-4-2008.

9.11-3 Treatment of opening balance of Cenvat credit as on 1-4-2008

Assessee always tries to utilise Cenvat credit first and then pay through PLA/GAR-7. However, despite his efforts, some opening balance is possible particularly in initial stages of production/provision of services. In case of assessees utilising Cenvat credit only to the extent of 20% service tax payable on output services, balance credit remained unutilised.

Issue is eligibility of Cenvat credit of opening balance and whether provision of ‘proportionate Cenvat credit’ will apply to opening balance.

It is well settled that Cenvat credit is indefeasible. Credit once validly taken cannot be denied in absence of specific statutory provision (Even such statutory provision cannot be confiscatory in nature).

CBE&C, vide circular No. 137/72/2008-CX.4 dated 21-11-2008 [20 STT 19 (ST)] has clarified that the accumulated credit as on 1-4-2008 will not lapse and can be utilised as there is no provision of periodic lapse of Cenvat credit. This would apply to assessees who were availing entire Cenvat credit but utilising only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable on taxable output services.

Similarly, persons such as call centres, who provide services to their clients by dealing with the customers of the client on the client's behalf, but actually provided these services on their own account, will not be categorized as intermediaries.

15.10-2 Service on principal to principal basis is not intermediary service

Service provided to foreign Principal on principal to principal basis is not intermediary service.

For example, service of marketing consultant is not 'intermediary service', if he gets his fees at fixed rate and not on basis of turnover achieved.

In GoDaddy India Web Services P Ltd. In re (2016) 54 GST 681 = 67 taxmann.com 324 (AAR), assessee was providing various types of services as 'bundled service' to its foreign Principal. In addition to providing marketing and promotion service, assessee was also providing services of supervision of call centre services and payment processing services. It was held that the place of supply of service is outside taxable territory and hence service tax is not applicable.

In ABS India Ltd. v. CST (2008) 17 STT 223 (CESTAT), assessee had subsidiary company in Singapore. Assessee-company booked orders in India for sale of goods manufactured by subsidiary in Singapore. Assessee received commission from its Singapore subsidiary. It was held that service was delivered to subsidiary. It cannot be said that service is delivered in India.

15.10-3 Ironical situation - Receiving foreign exchange is taxed

This provision has created an ironical situation. If Indian commission agent provides service to Principal outside India, he is required to pay IGST, though he is receiving payment in foreign exchange. On the other hand, if a foreign commission agent provides service to Indian Principal, the Indian Principal has to pay him in foreign exchange but no IGST is payable.

Thus, a transaction where actually India received foreign exchange is subjected to IGST, while transaction where there is outflow of foreign exchange from India is not subject to IGST.

15.10-4 No IGST and no reverse charge on services provided by foreign Commission Agents to Indian Principals

In case of foreign commission agents providing service to Indian Principal, the place of supply of service is outside India. Hence, no IGST is payable even under reverse charge.

15.10-5 Money transfer service provided to foreign entity by Indian supplier of service is intermediary service and subject to IGST

Foreign Money Transfer Service Operator (MTSO) (like Western Union) provide service of transferring money from outside India to Indian recipient in India. This is similar to Money Order service. The facility is used by persons outside India for remitting money from outside to India to their relatives in India.

Remitter located outside India (say A) approaches Money Transfer Service Operator (MTSO) (say B) located outside India for remitting money to a beneficiary in India (say E). A pays money to B. For this service, B receives fee/commission from A.

B appoints agents in India (say C) (who is usually a Bank or post office or some financial entity) for delivery of money to E. C is paid fee/commission from B for providing this service. C may deliver money directly to E or C may appoint sub-agent (say D) for this purpose. Usually no fee is charged from E but sometimes, some fee/charges may be recovered from E also.

CBE&C has clarified vide CBE&C circular 180/06/2014-ST dated 14-10-2014 as follows - In aforesaid case, relations between C (Indian Bank or post office) and B (foreign MTSO) are not on principal to principal basis. C (Indian Bank or Post Office or other financial entity) is an agent of MTSO. This, C is intermediary in services. Liability only of C&F Agents, not of commission agents - As per aforesaid clause (a), the agent will be liable for GST on value goods or services only if he undertakes to supply any goods or services or both on behalf of any principal (like consignment agent). Commission Agent is not required to register if his receipts of commission are less than Rs. 20/10 lakhs per annum - Persons who supply goods or services or both on behalf of other taxable persons whether as an agent or otherwise require registration under GST even if his turnover is below Rs. 20/10 lakhs per annum- section 24(1)(vii) of CGST Act.

There was misunderstanding that all commission agents require mandatory registration under GST irrespective of his commission income (i.e. even if income from commission is below 20/10 lakhs per annum).
